Guide

  1. Begin Reading

Intro

Here is a definition of “quicksand”, straight out of the dictionary[1]:

Quicksand, (noun). Sand readily yielding to pressure; especially: a deep mass of loose sand mixed with water into which heavy objects readily sink.

Depending on where you live, you’ve probably also seen signs like this at some point in your life:

You need signs like that to warn you of the danger. Quicksand looks solid when undisturbed, but walking into it causes liquefaction. And that’s when you start to sink.

I think many companies that develop software should have a sign like that somewhere in their offices. Why? Here is the second definition of “quicksand” from the same dictionary page[1]:

Quicksand, (noun). Something that entraps or frustrates.

Again and again, software development projects fail for various reasons: unclear project goals or requirements, poor business decisions, lack of planning, poor communication, bad technological choices (like choosing the wrong programming language or the wrong architecture), complexity and size of the project, poor prioritization, project management mistakes, unrealistic deadlines, office politics, and many more. Even if the project succeeds, the result is often a combination of cost overruns, late product deliveries, poor quality, lots of frustrated people, and jokes like this one:

“Developer to Team Lead”: We cannot do this project. WE CAN NOT! It implies a significant design change, and no one in our team understands this model. And, above all, no one in the company knows the programming language in which this application was written. So, even if someone wants to work on it, they can not. In my personal opinion, the company should never have gotten itself involved with this project.

“Team Lead to Project Manager”: This project will involve a design change. Currently, we do not have anyone with experience in this type of project. Additionally, we don’t know the programming language. We will have to organize a lot of training sessions if we are to take this project. In my opinion, we are not ready to engage in projects of this type.

“Project Manager to Head of Department”: This project involves a design change, and we do not have much experience in this area. Also, not many people in the company are well prepared for this. In my opinion, we could do the project, but we will need more time than usual.

“Head of Department to Upper Management”: This project involves redefining the design. We have some people who have worked in this area, and others who know the programming language. So they can train other people. In my opinion, we should accept this project but with care.

“Upper Management to CEO”: This project will show everyone our ability to remodel the design of an entire system. We have all the necessary knowledge and people to execute this project successfully. Some employees have already provided training in this field to other employees. In our opinion, we should not let this project escape us.

“CEO to client”: This is the type of project in which our company specializes. We have executed many such projects for many important clients. Trust me when I say that we are the best company in the field to do this kind of project. It is my opinion that we can execute this project successfully in the required time.

Many software projects have enough messed up things happening with them that they have the potential of generating a few jokes of their own. Another one of my favorite jokes is “Project delivered on time!”. The funniest jokes will be the ones you have lived through, because beneath the humor lies an undesirable situation you somehow got accustomed to. With time, just like with a frog being slowly boiled alive[2], we get so acclimatized to such situations that various problems just start to look normal, and we don’t do anything about them anymore. If jokes start surrounding your project, it might be people’s way of dealing with the working environment slowly slipping into a state of normalization of deviance[3], since humans use jokes as a coping strategy to make light of bad situations.

If you’re in your first software development job, you might have no idea what I’m talking about. Yet! Instead, you probably find software development challenging and lots of fun. You’ve most likely been busy and focused on things like “What books should every programmer read”, “10 programming languages to learn next year”, “What every software developer should know about such and such”, “10 ways to improve your code”, and so on, and so forth. And that was just to get your appetite going. You then discovered design patterns, modular architecture, source control, concurrency, scalability, the cloud, functional programming, IoC, unit testing, TDD, regex, refactoring, code reviews, and principles like SOLID, KISS, DRY, YAGNI, or SRP. You know… the tools of the trade, the things you need to learn, the things you need to practice, the things that earn you the big bucks, or reputation and recognition on developer communities like Stack Overflow[4]. You have a blast learning all of these things. You don’t feel entrapped or frustrated. So, where is the problem? Why do we need the warning signs?

First of all, these things are all about you. “You” need to learn. “You” need to do. “You” need to master the various topics. But unless “you” are building the next successful business out of your parents’ garage and working on becoming your own boss, it won’t be just about “you”. Most likely, you will start working in a company on a software project that isn’t going smoothly and might possibly be heading towards partial or total failure. I mentioned above some reasons why software projects fail, but those represent the “macro” issues. They are the results of smaller things that happen every day. Little things that combine in unfortunate ways to cause lots of harmful effects. And those things won’t be just about “you”. They will also be about “others”.

Secondly, most of the things I mentioned above gravitate towards the technical. You might be tempted to say, “Well, duh! Isn’t this Information Technology dummy”? It is, but it’s also about businesses. And every business is a people business. You will not just write code all day long until you retire; you will do lots of stuff that won’t be coding but interacting with others in the company (or outside of it). With time, you take on new roles and responsibilities - you might lead teams and manage projects, you might mentor novices, hire and fire people, communicate with clients and executives, and all sorts of stuff that isn’t technical in nature.

So this book isn’t about the technical stuff, the languages, the tools, or the patterns. These are important too. But there are plenty of good books on each of those topics. This book is about the situations when, despite using all of these goodies you have at your disposal, you can only scratch your head and say, “WTF happened?”. This book is about what happens in the trenches, things that aren’t technology related. It’s about some bad things common to software projects that people discover the hard way, by ending up in a situation that they didn’t recognize. You will walk into such situations just like you walk into quicksand. As time passes and you pay more attention and get more experience, you will recognize some of these things as annoying and disruptive to your daily work, causing unnecessary suffering and frustration to people working on software projects. It’s a bunch of tiny things, “micro” things that contribute to the “macro” issues.

Heads up

This book is my attempt at a “Heads up!” for the new generations to know what else to expect when pursuing a career in software development. Young developers make the same mistakes as other developers did before them. People focus on technologies and how to use them best to write great software, while everything else just happens to them. Similar to learning how to drive a car, you start by concentrating more on the car and how to handle it, and only later on how to handle yourself in traffic. But we all know that being a driver isn’t just about handling the car. It’s about doing so on the road, in various weather conditions, together with other drivers, motorcyclists, pedestrians, or animals, paying attention to one’s surroundings, and following and respecting the meaning of traffic signs. You might be a badass driver, drifting or doing donuts in parking lots, or breaking with your left foot, but if you don’t know the meaning of signs like “dangerous curve to the right, slippery road, railway level crossing, or give way”, then you will be in for some unpleasant surprises. The signs are useful to let you know what you might encounter on the road ahead. Concentrating on the car and your driving skills is good, but it’s even more important to pay attention to what’s happening on the road. Similarly, good technical skills are a must for building software, but don’t neglect what’s around you: your environment and the things you encounter, challenges with the potential to transform into unpleasant situations that entrap or frustrate.

Just because you enjoy programming, don’t think that a software development job will be just about programming in a company of like-minded people, working side by side with your developer buddies, eating pizza, sipping energy drinks, mastering the tools of the trade, and producing software that you can all be proud of. Some stuff will inevitably go into the weeds. So when the honeymoon is over, some of the things I mention in this book will be waiting for you around the bend. Be aware, be prepared, and pay attention to the warning sign.

I’m not trying to scare you. That’s not my intention. There are a lot of positive things in software development. First of all, it’s a lot of fun. Then there is always something new to learn or discover. You are not limited to working in just one domain; considering everyone needs software these days, you can combine programming with various other disciplines. You work with a lot of other smart people. You are part of a community. You can work from home. You solve problems; the more complex, difficult, or challenging the problem, the more proud you feel when you make something work, you feel a sense of accomplishment. It’s that satisfaction of creating something useful out of nothing (programming is an intellectual activity; you basically think a program into existence), something that other people use, sometimes that might even make a difference in their daily lives. You get a nice feeling when you see the result of your work. It’s even more satisfying than assembling a sliding door wardrobe from scratch, all by yourself.

And the pay is pretty good too :).

But the reality is that, inevitably, many projects become “stained” by something. Developing software is fun and challenging, but often it’s also hard and frustrating. Not just because the software itself is complex, but also because the process of making it is not without its challenges. Users never know what they want, the problems you are trying to solve might be very large and complex, you have technical, budget, business, legal, security, and time constraints, you depend on software you can’t control (like operating systems, programming languages, libraries, frameworks, or platforms), it’s almost impossible to test all potential inputs and execution paths, there is that elusive bug that keeps manifesting itself from time to time, and you just can’t figure out its cause, and the list goes on and on and on.

Nothing new

What I write in this book is common knowledge. I haven’t discovered anything new, haven’t solved any mystery, haven’t reached some higher level of understanding after scientific research, or aggregate the results of an IT survey with 50,000 respondents, from 2,500 companies, from 10 countries. I’ve just been around the block for a while. I’m trying to share some of the things I’ve learned at each stage of my career, highlight some of the things that can go wrong, and try to give some solutions I think might work to make things better. Anyone like me could have written a similar book. After a good amount of years working in this industry, in various contexts, with multiple people, you can write a book like this too. It’s about experiences and lessons learned the hard way, things I wish I had known much earlier, or done differently, if only I had better understood them at the time.

I did a lot of dumb things and learned the hard way in the past 15 years or so. I’ve moved from being a young grasshopper[5] to senior developer, to Team Lead, to coach, and various mixed positions, both technical and managerial. Each stage brought new challenges and quicksands. The views, opinions, conclusion, and recommendations I write about in this book are thus my own, based on my own experiences. This is a personal story, and yours is likely to be different from mine. This book is about the quicksands you might encounter on the job, just like I did. If you are young, like writing code, and you are passionate about technology, it makes perfect sense to make a living from what you enjoy doing. But the way you program or build an application for yourself, or for school projects, won’t be the same as when working in a company on projects with tight constraints and with lots of other people involved. There will also be frustrating aspects of being an employee programmer or developer.

I can’t offer an exhaustive list of all of the problems you will encounter, and I can’t talk about everything in great detail either. Nevertheless, I want to draw attention to some situations I have encountered more often and try to come up with some solutions based on my understanding and experience, so you too can recognize certain situations you are heading for and attempt to do something about them. Although I’ve done lots of things and had various responsibilities throughout the years, my perspective on things is, for the most part, that of a technical person. So you might view the same situations through different lenses. You might agree, disagree, and everything in between. Always use your judgment when trying to apply some of the proposed solutions. There are no guaranteed answers in this book. Some of the recommendations I offer may not apply to your situation, or things might not evolve exactly as described here. Your mileage may vary. Always look at the broader context to figure out what can actually work for you and within your environment.

There also isn’t a certain progression in which these issues occur. You might not encounter them all, but you also can’t steer clear of all of them. Many are not only specific to the software industry. Workplace issues can be found in any company. They come bundled together with having a job, and jobs sometimes may be unpleasant to some degree (that’s why they pay you money to do it). Absurdity happens in the workplace because, as Scott Adams - creator of the now-classic book “The Dilbert Principle”[6] - mentions: “everyone is an idiot”.

Another thing to be aware of is that I don’t always explicitly say throughout the book to what role I refer to when I talk about things, like for a programmer, a developer, Team Lead, manager, and so on. I can’t say, “As a developer expect this”, “As a Team Lead be aware of that” because many roles can have the same title in several companies, but not identical responsibilities. You might even be a developer with responsibilities of a Project Manager, or even vice versa. It’s for you, from the context, to infer whose responsibility it is to avoid or fix some situation. And because responsibilities increase or change as your career progresses, you may have to come back to the book and reread it. Maybe now you’re a programmer, and project management matters are not on your radar. But after a while, they may be. Perhaps you will even become a Project Manager. Who knows? Some things are valid for when you’re a junior, others for when you’re a senior, and some for when you’re a Team Lead, for example. The quicksands are different in your new environment and in accordance with your new set of responsibilities.

When I started in this industry, all I knew was how to write code. It never even crossed my mind that I would write such a book. Many things interacted for me to get where I am today. Some were good, positive things. Others… not so much. The same thing happens with software projects. Many things interact to create either a good or a harmful situation, similar to how quicksand is formed: you need the right quantity of water and sand, certain friction between sand particles, water having no way to escape from the mixture, the force of the upward water opposing the force of gravity, or the right amount of pressure applied on the surface.

There are many other useful books that mention the topics covered here. Still, I couldn’t find one that addresses a lot of them together. So I tried to cover a lot of ground. Maybe I insisted too much on some things, perhaps some of them I mentioned too briefly, maybe I repeat myself, and I’m sure I forgot some. But this is my attempt, and I hope it’s successful, and you will find it useful. You be the judge of that. If you can learn from my mistakes and avoid some quicksand with what information you extract from this book, then I declare myself happy. If you encounter situations that I didn’t mention in this book, want to send me comments, questions, or feedback, I would love to hear from you at quicksandssoftwaredevelopment@gmail.com. With this being said, let’s now put up some signs to warn about the quicksands and avoid falling in it.

Staff developers

So you got a job as a programmer! The interview was easy - way too easy. Or maybe you are a good programmer. But you already knew that :). A few weeks pass, and you start to notice strange things. The codebase is a mess, there are no requirements for new features, you know more stuff than some of the senior developers in the company, some stress themselves with lots of work while others are continually slacking off on social media or watching movies online, there are tons of incidents in production, one in every five deploys is being rolled back, there is continuously shifting priorities, general disorder, and confusion, and the list can go on. What happened?

Many things, as you will discover throughout the book. But sometimes it starts with hiring bad people and then, somehow, forgetting to fire them. I’ll talk about hiring developers here since they are the essential people on any software project, and also because I haven’t hired any managers or bosses till now; that would have been cool though :).

Neglected process

Lots of software companies don’t know how to hire good developers. And that’s because they don’t pay enough attention to the hiring process. They don’t think of it as a critical aspect of their business. Instead, they believe it’s Human Resources’ job to hire people, so they should handle the thing. That’s mostly true, but too many things are left up to them to decide. HR is expected to handle everything from start to finish as a well-determined checklist of steps. A technical person evaluating the skills and knowledge of the candidate (i.e., the most important aspect of the developer interview) is just seen as another checkbox on that list.

HR does handle recruitment, but the department has other roles too. They make sure the company and employees are complying with employment laws. They manage the employer-employee relationships, handle retention and firing of employees, and enforce company policies. They manage employee pay, compensation, and benefits. They handle training and development programs, monitor employee performance, and all sorts of other stuff. They will handle all the recruiting steps that involve writing a job description, advertising the position and looking for candidates, making phone calls, track candidates’ applications, setting up interviews, reserving meeting rooms, conducting interviews, do background checks, and manage all the paperwork in the process. But another thing they do is screen developer CVs without being given proper rules for how to do so.

HR isn’t tailored to the company’s specifics, so they are not prepared to screen developer CVs or evaluate their technical knowledge. Sadly, they often do that because they are left alone to deal with most of the process. In recruiting developers, HR might eventually learn that HTML and CSS go together with JavaScript, or that Java and C# are rival languages, and that SQL is something OracleDB and MySQL have in common, but that’s pretty much it. But since they are the HR department, it’s part of their job - the job of hiring people - to screen CVs. So they will try to make it work, often similar to the way they usually do with any other CV they receive, in a matter of seconds (as some studies[7] have shown). I perfectly understand to reject a CV because of bad grammar and spelling mistakes, or if the candidate used their police lineup identification photo for the CV picture, or if the picture is from that time when they were drunk in the toilet at the mall… but too much “box-ticking” can hurt. CVs can end up in the trash if they use the wrong font, the format is the same as everyone else’s CVs, they aren’t tailored to the job description, have too many or too few pages, don’t contain the right keywords, they are not accompanied by a cover letter, or break some rule of the top résumé trends du jour (“OMG! You still have an objective statement? And you listed ‘Reading’ in your hobbies section? OMG!”). By the way… there is no correct font.

Writing a good CV that catches the attention of someone in HR is hard on almost everyone (especially if it’s the first CV you write). Because you don’t write CVs every day, but only once every few years, you can’t get better at it with practice. For programmers, this is even worse because true programmers aren’t wired for this sort of thing. A CV isn’t coding or problem-solving, or technical stuff they are good at. A CV is mostly marketing. So good potential developers can get excluded at this screening stage, just because their CVs didn’t look fancy enough to catch someone’s attention.

Besides screening CVs, HR people might also decide on how programmer interviews should take place. “Let’s start with an IQ test. Yes, programmers are smart. Let’s use that as eliminating criteria. We should follow that with some psychological and/or personality type test to see if the candidate exhibits ‘nerd behaviors’ (i.e., well-suited for a programming career)”. Then somehow, HR decides that the best candidates to look for are introvert geniuses that hang their toilet paper like this:

Then, for preliminary interviews, they might spend some of the company’s money on standard programming questionnaires (most of which can be found online, already solved), or on completely irrelevant multiple-choice tests with questions like this in it:

The more questions like this, the more expensive the test is.

By the way, that’s actually a question I received on an online preliminary test for a job interview. I gave them bonus points because the code was properly formatted (although not by Java Code Conventions; for example, the opening curly brace for the main method should be at the end of the line, not on a new line). A lot of online tests don’t even have that since they are, in fact, online surveys built for questions like “How satisfied are you with our services? Very satisfied, Satisfied, Neutral, Unsatisfied, Very Unsatisfied”, or “How did you find out about our new toothpaste flavor? From my dentist, From friends, From family, From the tooth fairy”, or “Do you like surveys? Yes, No, Bite me”. The same test also required me to write the method signatures of ByteArrayInputStream’s constructors, which apparently I was supposed to know by heart.

If I see questions like these in tests for an interview, I start to worry about what’s happening and think seriously if I still want to work there. And who comes up with these things? And where do you draw the line? “List in order all of the conversions and flags for the String.format() method?”. Any decent developer can tell you those are bad questions to ask; however, they don’t get involved enough in the hiring process, and things like this are still considered a good way to screen out developers’ CVs by HR people who, unfortunately, don’t know any better.

And these tests are divided into several levels of difficulty, like for a junior, mid, or senior. Some questions are difficult, and some are easier. But if you ask me, they are not enough to differentiate the seniors and the juniors because knowledge and experience is not a linear progress for all developers, over all possible projects and technologies they have worked on. A junior is not someone who can answer 30 questions out of 100, while a senior answers them all. And how many questions should there be? 100? Neah… too many. Maybe 30? But now they are too few, so you need a different set of questions for juniors and seniors. Which are the questions that only a senior can answer? Are they a carefully kept secret that juniors don’t know? There is no clear line of demarcation, of course. Juniors don’t stop at one point, and from there on, you are a mid-level developer and from some other point down the line, a senior, or whatever levels you take into consideration. HR and bosses like those lines of demarcation so they can balance them against salary offers, but we’ll get to that later…

Then, there is also a standard HR interview that tries to collect as much information about the candidate’s qualifications and experience for the job, information that can later also be used to do background checks or ask for references. HR will try to determine if the candidate has a bad attitude or shows a lack of interest for the job, or try to identify any red flags like, for example, avoiding eye contact, unexplained gaps in employment, complaining about the previous or current employer, or constantly bragging. HR will also present the company, the company policies, benefits, development opportunities, asking the candidate for salary expectations, and explaining the next steps in the interview process. You know… a classical HR interview. Hopefully, HR will know how to get the information without resorting too much on cliché interview questions that only elicit rehearsed answers, like “What is your greatest weakness?” (I always wanted to answer with “chocolate”), “How do you handle stress?”, “What is your favorite book?”, or fancy ones like “Why are manhole covers round?”, “How many ping-pong balls can you stuff into an airplane?”, “If you were a tree, what kind of a tree would you be?”, “If I have three oranges and you have five oranges, how much does a can of orange-flavored carbonated drink cost at the convenience store downstairs?”

So basically, a lot of the hiring process is based on some standard programming tests and a typical HR interview. If you pass these, only then do you get to talk with some technical person. Assuming you even do talk to someone technical. As an example, I once applied for a job at a small company. An HR lady greeted me at the door, then handed me a pen and a multi-choice questionnaire with 33 fancy questions in it. “You have 30 minutes”, she says. I got 31 questions right. She then said I did very well and that she will set up an appointment in the following days for me to meet with the Managing Director. A couple of days later, I met with the Managing Director for 15-20 minutes. And that was it. They wanted me to work for them. In all honesty, I would have expected this to be the start of the recruitment process, not all of the process. A hiring mistake can end up costing a lot (in money, time, frustration, etc.), so it should be given proper attention.

A different approach

So how might you go about improving this process? The answer is: by not neglecting its importance and by having developers more involved at each step.

HR can handle the legal and organizational aspects of the interview and possibly assess if the candidate can adapt to the company’s corporate culture, but when it comes to technical aspects, it’s the developers that need to take responsibility. For example, standard programming questionnaires try to place developers into buckets that someone (i.e., whoever created the tests) thinks are appropriate. But you are hiring for a particular position, so if you do want to use programming quizzes (maybe you have way too many applicants and need a way to shorten the list in one swoop), it’s better to use your own questions, for your particular context, for your specific team and project. And this is one instance where developers need to be more involved in the recruitment process, so they can define these questions. If they are not, and developers neglect the hiring process, HR will be forced to try and make something out of it to select developers, “‘cause we can’t just pick someone off the street, can we?”

What follows is my stab at the problem, my ideas on trying to conduct better interviews. I ended up with this method after years of trial and error. I learned from HR persons, applicants, my interviews, and other interviewers. I’ll probably not stick with this approach forever, I’ll adapt it as I learn new things, but it’s what worked for me so far. And just to emphasize what I said in the introductory chapter of this book, I’ve reached many of these conclusions the hard way; this is a method created based on my personal experiences and struggles.

And this method is presented to you, the reader. I started the chapter by mentioning a few warning signs that you might discover when you get your first job in a company where people might not have paid enough attention to the hiring process. But eventually, you might reach a point in your career when you need to be sitting on the other side of the table, in the position of the interviewer, having to hire developers. A major problem is that most developers don’t have any training in conducting interviews, so they can fail just as miserably as if you would let HR handle the whole thing. So you should learn how to do it properly before you hold your first interview because when it comes to hiring people, the saying “prevention is better than a cure” applies.

You don’t have to take the next steps as something written in stone. Give it a deep thought, then create your own process. Add anything to this that you consider necessary or useful. Use each interview as a learning and improvement opportunity. For example, I often avoid having interviews over the phone, and so I’ve chosen not to talk about that. But this doesn’t mean that you have to skip them. Maybe you still want to have an extra screening process over the phone or Skype, if you find it necessary. I’ve given up on phone interviews because, every time, I had problems with the connection on one side or the other, there is often background noise, the candidate doesn’t prepare properly for the conversation since somehow they think it’s not as serious as the actual interview, if they already have a job, they schedule the call during lunchtime then try to rush the conversation so that they can also grab something to eat, or they schedule the conversation late at night, after work when they are already tired. I once even heard someone else in the room whispering answers. So that’s why I try to avoid them if possible. As such, use or adapt any of the steps that follow.

If you need to fill in a developer position in your team, and you’re the one doing the hiring (maybe you are a senior or a Team Lead), you need to get involved right from the start in the whole process. For example, work with HR to create a job description. You know best what skills and qualities you are looking for in a new hire. You know the team, you know the project, you know the technologies, you know everything you need in order to fill the vacant position. So you - the developer - draft the job description, then refine it together with HR. A job description - just like a CV - is marketing, and HR will have some ideas on how to attract the attention of possible applicants, but it’s also nice if people can recognize a developer’s input in there. So don’t simply hand them your requirements then let HR phrase the job description. Work with them. That way, you learn some new stuff, and you can also avoid cliché HR statements like “fast-paced working environment”, “ability to multi-task”, or “young and dynamic team” to sneak into your job description and possibly deter experienced developers from applying. Also, work with them on job ads, flyers, or whatever HR might want to use to reach out to candidates. Make sure the relevant information from your requirements is there in a pertinent format, more so than any HR embellishments.

Once the position is opened, you need to define the minimum passing requirements for received CVs and communicate those to HR. Be specific. Most of the time, it should be less than what you are looking for, just to make sure no possible candidates get excluded by the initial screening. This is specific to the open position but might include a Bachelor’s degree in Computer Science, a minimum of N years of employment, knowing a particular foreign language well, knowing such and such programming languages, having a license to operate heavy machinery, or whatever else you think is needed. This is the minimum requirements for a CV to make it into the next phases of the interview. I want to emphasize: it should be less than what you are looking for. You might end up reading some not-so-good CVs this way and waste some 15 minutes of your time, but you know better than HR to include or exclude a programmer CVs, so set that limit somewhere lower just to make sure HR doesn’t get overly enthusiastic when screening candidates. Don’t overdo it, though, and end up with very loose requirements. It’s already sad that the entry bar is lower lately, with so many companies looking for developers. So keep your standards high. If someone can spell “computer”, that’s not reason enough to invite them to an interview.

Then let HR do their job of looking for developers and sifting through all the CVs they receive. Make sure to tell them that if they have any doubts about any particular candidate or CV, that they should pass it on to you. Sometimes people get highly recommended by someone and might potentially be considered for the job even though they don’t match on some of the minimum requirements. So, you decide on those candidates.

Prepare

Then, if a CV passes the initial HR screening, read it carefully, and decide whether the candidate should be invited to an interview or not. At this point, you are deciding to have an interview based only on what’s written in the CV. If the decision is “Yes”, HR can set up the interview. If the candidate accepts, then you need to prepare for the interview. If you go in unprepared or without a discussion plan, you will have an unstructured interview, which sets you up for failure right from the start. Developers who don’t prepare for the interview end up asking superficial questions, often whatever goes through their minds. Or they print some interview questions from the first links in the results of an Internet search (the same links from where it’s possible the candidates have learned the answers and most likely the same questions the standard HR tests were based on, the ones that got the candidate to this point). Worse still, they might be thinking, “well… the candidate did excellent on the standard test, let’s just discuss now, get to know each other better”. And so they will let the candidate steer the discussion in any direction, or stick to some particular subject exploring it until the allocated time expires, or the candidate is a bullshit artist[8], or tricks the interviewer into doing most of the talking. When that happens, the interviewer starts to think the interview is going well; then they like the candidate, they believe they deserve a chance and think they are appropriate for the job, and then say “hire”. Some time passes, and they find out (happens more often than you think) that they didn’t get a good developer, they got a bad one or an average one at best. If they are really lucky, they will get a good developer, but luck should be the last thing to count on when hiring someone. So take some time to prepare. It’s not enough to just read the CV once; you need to “analyze” the CV and try to find out more about the candidate before the interview.

At this point, I need to make an aside, which is that inexperienced developers should not conduct job interviews (that’s why I said above, senior or Team Lead). Inexperienced developers don’t have enough… well… experience to keep a hiring discussion at the right level. They need to have mastered their skills, not just have “an idea” or “be exposed” to the topics they will be addressing at the interview. If they don’t know the full answer to a question they are asking, and the implications the answer might cause, they also don’t have the necessary skills to evaluate the response of the candidate. And they might even make a fool out of themselves (and the company). Even if you are an experienced developer, you still need to master the subjects you are discussing. For example, a senior back-end developer should probably not interview a front-end developer on their own. If you are in such a situation, take someone with you that knows what they are doing, prepare, then agree on how you are going to conduct the interview (who asks what, on what areas you should focus on, who starts and/or ends the interview, who responds to questions the candidate might have, and so on). When I say to prepare for the interview, it doesn’t mean you learn the answers to the questions you ask the candidate, before you ask them. What I mean is, you need to have enough information about the candidate to keep the discussion moving down the right path to allow you to make a correct assessment and determine if the person is suitable for the job.

To prepare, start from the CV and look carefully at the number of years of experience, roles the candidate had, companies they worked for and for how long, in which field those companies carry out their activity, projects or products they worked on, if there are any gaps in employment, languages or technologies that they used (even those I’m not familiar with but would be curious for the candidate to tell me a few things about), frameworks, libraries, etc. Try to identify anything that you think is relevant to know or discuss at the interview. Take notes and write down some questions based on what you find in the CV. I usually write those down directly on the CV. I highlight a section or scribble the question next to it.

I usually don’t care how the CV is formatted or what font is used, but I do pay attention to some of these things also because a sloppy CV might be an indicator of a careless developer (if the CV looks neglected or contains grammatical errors, I might start wondering why you were unable to write it properly; I also start thinking about how you might behave when working on the company’s multi-million dollar project).

Then I look for more information about the candidate online. A profile on social media or professional networks, looking for a personal website, blogs or articles, personal projects, or contributions to online projects, finding some code online that they have written that I can look over, etc. There are often links provided in the CV, so I don’t even need to “play detective”. Basically, I try to build an idea of the environments the candidate was exposed to, to better ground the conversation when we eventually meet face-to-face. If something catches my eye or is unclear from the CV or from the information I find online (a short time in many jobs, time overlaps in jobs, some parts of the CV with many details while others with none, sloppy code written somewhere), I note another question or two to ask about that as well.

It’s also tempting to ask around to see if someone you know has already worked with the person. During my research, I sometimes find they’ve worked in some company where I know people inside. I might ask around to see if they were a good developer and a nice person, or a bad developer and troublemaker. I don’t do this if the person is still working at that job, though. I don’t want to be the one breaking the news that they are looking for another job. But when I do ask, I take the response with a grain of salt. You cannot always precisely determine the relationship your acquaintance has with that person and how closely they interact or work together. But say you do find out something like “rumors have it that they didn’t leave the last company on their own”. What do you do with that information? Is it true? Is it just gossip? Maybe if it’s true, is the problem with the person or was their boss a moron and a total jerk and inevitably there was a conflict, and the candidate ended up loosing? Learning about the candidate from someone else can be useful information, but if you don’t know exactly what the context is (or was), it can influence you in the wrong way. Take the information, but try to find ways at the interview to touch on the issues and form your own opinion. From personal experience, I can say that the bad rumors are usually true while the good things are usually exaggerated. But that’s not a rule. Try sticking to your hiring plan with everyone, no matter who they are, or what recommendations they have, and try to form your own opinion, instead of making decisions based on the things you have heard from acquaintances. Maybe the candidate did well at that job in a certain context, but perhaps the context is different for the job you have open, and they wouldn’t do as well here. That’s why you have an interview with them: to find out if they can fill the position. Don’t make decisions based on other situations and other contexts. I strayed twice from my process because someone said the person is good and that the interview is just a formality, and so on… and in both cases, a mess came out of it that I’ve lived to regret. Don’t make the same mistake.

Try not to get yourself influenced by what you find out during your analysis of the CV and research on the candidate, either. Basically, that means not fall into the trap of judging the book by its cover. You should avoid forming opinions at this stage. Preconceived assumptions or jumping to conclusions too fast can affect the way you conduct the interview. Wait for the actual discussion to conclude what the applicant can or cannot do. For example, if the person has a degree from a very prestigious university or has worked for the best tech company in town before applying for your position, don’t assume you will be interviewing a superstar candidate. Another thing you might do would be to assume that the person might be overqualified for the job, or ask for a lot of money given their amazing CV. Try not to form opinions at this point, or you will cling to those throughout the interview and end up evaluating the candidate incorrectly. Instead of forming opinions, just note yourself some questions to ask at the interview to clarify every point.

I then prepare a list of technical topics for the interview. Note that I said topics, not questions. An interview should be a discussion, not an interrogation. At this point, it’s also worth mentioning that a lot of HR departments would prefer to have some standard scoring or rating for each interviewee so that later they can compare one candidate against another. Similar to the standard programming questions I mentioned above, this often implies that you should ask each of the candidates the same set of questions to get consistent results. The idea is that you evaluate the responses to questions, assign a score to each answer, sum all the points together and, in the end, hire the person with the highest number of points. We all know about this system. It’s used in school where students get grades on various tests; then, a GPA is created. In theory, this might seem to work, but in practice, not so much. A job interview is not like an exam in school. At school, everyone was taught the same subjects, they were provided with the same study material, and then they were given the same exam subjects during tests. People who come to an interview have different backgrounds, different knowledge, and different experience. You will not be very successful in using a small set of questions, as already mentioned above. The purpose is not to give a score to each person, but to figure out if they are a good match for the position and that they can actually do the job. In addition, since the interview is a discussion and not a test on paper, things will naturally evolve. The candidate might give you an intriguing response to some question, and you just can’t go on to the next until you ask other things to better understand the reasoning behind that response. So you inevitably end up asking different questions to each candidate, even if, in the end, you are trying to build a score only on a standard set of questions you ask everyone. For these reasons, I prefer using a list of topics and not a list of questions.

And I don’t always use the same topics either. I select them based on the requirements for the open position and what I find in the candidate’s CV. If the opening is for work on a database-centric app, I add more things on databases; if it’s a front-end position, I focus on JavaScript and Web APIs more, and so on. For example, if I’m looking for a generalist to work on a Java enterprise web application, and the candidate’s CV mentions they worked with things like Java, Javascript, SQL, Struts, Spring, React, Angular, and WebServices, a list of topics I might consider would look something like this:

Then, based on the CV and my research, I order this list of topics, from most likely down to less likely for the candidate to know. It’s worth mentioning here that I try not to hire just based on the technologies the candidate knows. It’s important in senior or architect positions for the applicant to master various technologies and know what they can and can’t do, to know how far you can push them when building an architecture or design. The more technologies you know, the better, because you have a richer tool-set to choose from when developing solutions. But the less experience you have, you are a mid, a junior, or an entry-level programmer, technology matters less while your attitude and ability to learn count for a lot more. Of course, if you need hard SQL skills for whatever open position you have and the candidate doesn’t know anything about SQL, you can’t hire them, that would be a dumb thing to do, but it’s also essential to consider how one thinks and if they can learn new things.

Another thing I need to point out here is that I’m using some of these topics to test if the candidate has a solid foundation of knowledge. I’ll talk in a later chapter why having a solid foundation is important. You might look at the topics and wonder why I bring up banalities like “abstract class vs. interface”, control structures, or things that have fallen massively in popularity like JSP, Servlets, XHR, or SOAP. The reason I do that is because I’ve often seen people that have worked with various frameworks and libraries, but they don’t understand that they function on some other underlying technology (that they have no clue about). Now everything is framework this, framework that, auto-magically this, auto-magically that, and when these fail in some way or they have to be pushed to their limit, and the abstraction gets broken, people start to look at them like they are from another planet and are clueless on what to do next. I know of cases where people worked with JQuery without knowing JavaScript. Worse, I know of Angular programmers who don’t actually want to do JavaScript. I have seen people get very excited when working with fancy Java web frameworks but have absolutely no idea how a Servlet works. I had someone at an interview who told me they know MVC. “Great! Please describe to me how this pattern works”. And they started with things like “this class”, “that other class”, how the various pieces fit together and who called who (wrong, of course), etc., to find out afterward that their only contact with MVC was an in house built framework created by some fools who had grossly misunderstood MVC, and in turn, the candidate took over and carried on with the mistakes, without being curious to study anything else about MVC. I also saw a Java architect at an interview who had major gaps in Java core knowledge. This guy was hired on a project built by someone else, and he continued it alone, and all of his knowledge was limited to the technologies used on that project. That was all that he learned. He did not study more during his spare time because he was not really interested in programming. And then, he applied for a senior position in the company I worked for because the man believed himself to be an architect. He had the title of “Architect” in the company he worked for because they preferred to give him titles instead of a higher salary, and eventually, he started looking for better-paid jobs. The man thought he was a good developer simply because he never compared himself to anyone else before. So I will test candidates for basic knowledge. I don’t want to assume that they understand all the things they should understand and find out later that, in fact, they have no clue. Sadly, I often saw cases of programmers that know a lot but don’t understand much.

Then, another thing I do is to list all the technologies, libraries, frameworks, practices, and patterns mentioned in the candidate’s CV. I usually list just those relevant for the position, but sometimes, if it’s something that I find important - like the person also knows C# although this is a Java position - I also put that on the list. You will see later what I do with this list.

Finally, there is another thing to be aware of. If you are still conducting your first few interviews, expect to be a little bit nervous. When new to recruiting, conducting interviews can be stressful for the interviewer, just like it is for the interviewee. At first, you won’t feel very comfortable interviewing someone, especially if you have to do this alone. You will worry that you might feel too nervous, say something stupid, ask a wrong question, or end up making a bad hiring decision. “What if the candidate knows more than I do? What if I can’t maintain control of the interview, and the candidate hijacks the conversation? What if the candidate becomes confrontational? How do I deal with that? What if the person is a good developer but refuses the job because they dislike me? What if I embarrass myself?” It’s normal to feel somewhat anxious in new situations, and conducting an interview is no different. But don’t worry, this will pass you after a few interviews. If it’s your first interview, you might have to practice a bit before the real thing. You might ask your HR colleagues to give you training or have a workshop or something on how to conduct interviews; you might start by asking another developer who has already conducted interviews to join them in their next interview meetings. Even if you don’t get training or practice before the interview, preparing well will reduce your stress and give you a good confidence boost.

And remember: a successful interview is like an agreement for future collaboration. It’s not a “sell-buy transaction”. The employer is not selling a job for the candidate to buy. The candidate is not selling skills and experience for the employer to buy. These kinds of interviews don’t go well. After a sale, the seller and the buyer go their separate ways; they don’t sit together in the store, eight hours a day, from Monday to Friday. So when you go in the interview, think “long term collaboration”, not “selling”. In an interview, both parties will be evaluating each other. You will try to figure out if you should hire someone or not, and the candidate will decide whether they want to work for you or not. When that conversation is balanced, there is a nice feel about the interview. When it is not balanced, one of the parties will definitely feel it. For example, if you have a candidate who is trying to sell themselves too much, you will get a bad vibe about it, as if they’re trying to distract your attention from something. You start thinking of your last encounter with a door to door salesman trying to sell you a bad product which you absolutely must buy “now” since it’s the last on stock or part of a limited offer that expires in - and they look at their watch - ten minutes[10]. You will immediately know it’s bullshit. You are being tricked to either overpay for something or buy a bad product. In the case of candidates trying to sell themselves too much, the bad product is usually their skills. If you hire them, you will be overpaying because such people will later be more interested in keeping appearances than doing a proper job. When the balance is tilted the other way, and you are trying too hard to make a sell for the company or the product you are building, saying how cool and wonderful you are, that you’re the best of the best, that everything works like a well-oiled machine in your project, that your office is at the last floor in the tallest building in town, and so on, it’s the candidate that will get the bad vibe. “What? This is the first time you have heard of us? No way… That can’t be…” These types of interviews usually end up feeling to the candidate like “We are smart, we assume you are not. Let’s take the interview as an opportunity to prove that. And when we are done, we’ll sing the company’s anthem together”. I went to several interviews where the person who conducted the discussion insisted I tell them everything I knew about their company, as if it was their mother’s company or something, and they were not just employees there. They wanted to see if I had done complete research… and that I was worthy, I guess. Very nasty interviews, and very nasty the companies in question, to be honest. It’s normal to want to hire someone who really wants to work for you, so much so that they would be willing to work for free (wouldn’t that be nice?); therefore, you want to see that they researched the company before showing up and that they didn’t come to your interview as uninterested as they probably went to other interviews, in other companies. You want someone who doesn’t just want a job; you want someone who “wants” to work for you, not “to be content” with working with you. But do not exaggerate with pretenses to such an extent that they end up being badly reflected during the interview. Even if the person really wants to work for your company, remember that at the end of the day, the fact of the matter is that people need a job to be able to pay bills and stay alive. So be careful of your attitude. Keep the discussion balanced. Just like you choose from several candidates, the candidate can choose from several jobs.

The interview

Eventually, the day of the interview arrives. HR has greeted the person, took them to the meeting room, gave them a glass of water or a coffee. It’s your time to show up. Be on time, be nice, greet the person, and thank them for coming to the interview.

I usually start things off by explaining to the applicant who I am, why the position is open, how the interview will unfold, and what to expect during the interview. This is the best time to ask the famous question of “Tell me about yourself” and get to know the person better. You can also start by making small talk (not too much though) to give the applicant some time to relax and get comfortable with the interview (most people are nervous). Be careful, though, because when you do that, it’s also very easy to step into some quicksand and touch on subjects that might be illegal, like discussing age, race, religion, marital status, or the like. HR can inform you of the topics to avoid when conducting interviews.

Once we get the conversation going, I then proceed by asking the candidate to tell me about the jobs they’ve had and the projects they worked on, which ones they liked, which ones they didn’t, and why. I will also ask what their responsibilities were and how a typical day at the office looked like at each of the jobs. You can usually figure out that info from the CV, but all CV’s are embellished. Even if copy-pasted from the web, you will often find things like “I improved X by Y percent”. Good! Now please tell me how you did that. How did you measure it? Did you have help? Were you all by yourself? Did you take the decisions or just did what was told? Any candidate should be able to explain everything that’s in their CV, with clear answers. If they can’t… red flag.

The best time to ask behavioral and problem-solving questions is when they talk about their experiences at previous jobs. I don’t just say, “Explain a situation where you had to face a difficult problem, and what you did to deal with it”. For questions like this, most of the candidates have prepared a speech and will start reciting it at the interview. They will give you an example they like (a selection from their “greatest hits”, like I heard an HR person say once). I don’t want that. As an interviewer, I prefer to find out more about what I am interested in, not to listen to a record. So I usually pick and explore something they said while talking about one of their projects. I ask how they did X, how they did Y, why they chose one way of solving the problem and not another, what difficulties they encountered, how did they overcome them, what they learned from that, if they were to solve the same problem again would they act the same or choose another approach? Why? Use something like the STAR method[11] for this part of the conversation (i.e., what was the “Situation”, what was the “Task” you needed to perform or “Target” to achieve, what “Actions” you took, and what was the “Result” or the outcome of your actions). You can also describe a hypothetical situation, such as a bug or user request, and ask them, “How would you approach something like that?” Then evaluate the answer and see if it makes sense.

While the candidate is talking about these things, look for enthusiasm or how passionate they are about the subject (actually, you should look for that throughout the entire interview, but this shows up more in this first part of the interview because of the type of questions you are asking). When you hire developers, it’s a good idea to look for passion, since passion is the fuel for most of their desire to continuously improve themselves.

Take a pen and paper with you in the interview. You will be taking notes, the candidate has something to write on, and if you don’t understand an answer, or if the candidate doesn’t understand a question, both of you can draw something to explain better.

I then do an exercise with the candidate. Remember the list I build earlier, with all the technologies, libraries, frameworks, practices, and patterns from the candidate’s CV? I ask the candidate to grade themselves on each, with a number from 1 (“I’ve read about it, maybe played with it a bit, I’m more or less clueless”) to 10 (“I’m proficient in it, I know everything there is to know about it”). Guess what happens. The good developers usually tend to grade themselves up to seven. The clueless ones give themselves tens, nines, and maybe (just maybe) an eight from time to time. This is the Dunning-Kruger effect[12] in action. People with little knowledge overestimate themselves, while intelligent people underestimate their knowledge. That is to say, clueless developers think they know everything and that they are the best. In contrast, capable developers know that even if they can use the technology to do their jobs properly, there is always more to learn about it. Even more surprising is the fact that, if during the interview, the clueless see that they don’t know the answers to many questions from the topic for which they gave themselves nines and tens, they insist that is their level and don’t want to reconsider lowering the grade.

So, with this and the list of topics in front of me, I then start asking technical questions. I focus more on the topics on which the candidate provided the highest grades (i.e., start with what the candidate thinks are their strong points). You should not rush the interview. A lot of people try to fit everything into a one-hour meeting. Don’t do that. Take as much time as needed - my interviews with a good applicant last between two and three hours. Once or twice, I even went past that. Tell HR, when they send out the invitation for the interview, to notify the candidates that that’s how long an interview might last. Three hours might seem a lot of time, but it’s not, so don’t waste it. Don’t focus one hour and a half on just one topic. Go over the entire list. If the candidate wants to pull the discussion in a certain direction, where they feel most knowledgeable and comfortable, bring them back to the topics.

All my questions are open-ended, like “What do you know about Java Lambda Expressions?” I want to see how the candidate responds. Do they start repeating some definition or text learned by heart, or are they coherent? If I interrupt during their explanation and pick on something they said and ask for further details, can the candidate expand on that? Can they give examples? Can they pick up the explanations from where I interrupted them? I do that because I want to see how they think, and I want to make sure that the concepts they are explaining to me are actually understood and not just memorized. Someone who has memorized stuff can’t jump from one subject to another very fast or continue where they left of. And understanding something is vital because it means you can apply it to different situations as opposed to memorizing things that only help you remember stuff, but not always enable you to use what you have learned. There is also a limit to how many things you can memorize, but with understanding, you can do associations and go much further, even if you don’t quite know the answer to something. Continue until you are satisfied with the answer, the candidate can’t respond or responds that they don’t know. Then move to the next question or topic. There will be things that they don’t know; there is no point insisting on that. If they are smart and genuinely understand things (which is what you want to determine), they can later acquire and understand the missing information. You can actually explain what you are doing so they don’t start feeling bad when they eventually say “I don’t know” before moving on to the next topic.

Throughout the interview, I also ask the candidate to write some code (in whatever language, pseudo-code is fine), something simple like a Fizz Buzz[13] or a recursive factorial. I then ask for explanations. For example, they might have memorized how the recursive factorial function looks like, but I ask how the final result is computed and how might the stack look like at each call. I can also ask for an iterative solution to the factorial; some candidates actually get it wrong.

At the beginning of the interview, I also tell the candidates that they can ask me questions anytime they want or pause for taking notes. Then I tempt them by saying “OK” to all the responses I get from them, then quickly move to the next question. I don’t say “Good”, “Correct”, or “Wrong”. I just say, “OK”. Whoever stops me occasionally to ask if that’s the correct response, or whoever notes stuff down to research later, gets bonus points.

After you are done with the technical questions, it’s time to explain the project they will be working on if they were to get the job. The candidate talked for most of the interview; now, it is your turn to do the talking. Talk about the job and what tasks the person will have to perform, their responsibilities, how the work environment is like, and how many people are in the team and their role. Talk about what the product does, what technologies it uses, methodologies and tools you use to build it, what challenges exist, what your plans for growth are, how many versions you will be building, and so on. You can take some architectural diagrams with you, or even deliver a small demo of the application from a laptop or tablet. You might also note some details down when preparing for the interview, just so that you don’t forget important information that an applicant might want to know (but omit confidential information, of course). Then observe the candidate’s reaction to see if they are genuinely interested or not. Bonus points if they ask questions about it.

And be honest. Don’t conceal information that you think the candidate might not like. If you hire the person, they will find out about it anyways. It’s better they don’t accept the job than to accept it then quit in the first couple of months.

A small note before going on. I’ve seen people start or recommend to begin your interview with presenting what the job will involve and what the project is all about, the reason being that maybe the candidate doesn’t like what they hear and decide they are not interested, in which case you can put an end to the interview earlier and everyone avoids wasting their time. It makes sense, but personally, I haven’t met anyone so far to get up in the middle of the interview and leave. Just as you perform some research on the candidate before having the interview, so is the candidate doing some research about your company, its field of activity, and the products it offers. If they don’t like something, they will not apply for the job in the first place or refuse HR’s invitation to come to an interview if HR is the one that found them instead of the person applying for the job. Or even if they agree to come to the interview, they won’t show up. But if there are people with some common sense, they don’t just get up and leave. So I suggest you leave this presentation for last because if you start talking about the project, the company, the team, etc., the discussion might take too long, and the time and room booking allocated for the interview might expire. And then, you quickly go through the technical questions, and you make a mess out of everything, and in the end, you cannot make an informed decision to determine if the person is suitable for the job or not. If you leave the project presentation for the end, you can talk for as long as you can, even if the time and room booking expire. You can continue in the hallway, outside in a park on a bench, in the company’s cafeteria, etc. Furthermore, this way, you also get to finish the interview on a slightly more relaxed note.

Then, as soon as the interview is over, note down the conclusions. You absolutely must do this. You might interview more candidates; you don’t want to confuse them or remember the wrong things about them. You’ll do them a disservice, and you will also do a disservice to yourself, and by the end of it all, you might be unable to weigh in a decision in choosing between two candidates who (seemed to) perform just as well. So take notes. You can write down some key ideas during the interview as long as it doesn’t slow down the pace of discussion. Note down what you liked, what you didn’t, where the candidate excelled, where they failed, where they knew just enough, and an overall impression. Don’t be stingy on the details. The interview might go mostly bad but finish on a positive note. You don’t want to remain stuck on that ending feeling. Assign your own grades to the topics on which the candidate self-evaluated themselves. Think about everything the candidate said. Have they criticized people they’ve worked with? Red flag. Have they flourished the CV to make them look better than they actually were? Red flag. Where they presumptuous during the interview? Red flag. Write down everything.

Another thing. Think about how this person will fit into the team. HR will also have an interview with them and try to determine if the person fits with the organizational culture, but make sure the person is a fit for your team also because you will be the one working with them: you and all the people from your team. So think well. Do you see them as part of the team? Will it be a good collaboration, or is there a risk that everyone will start a fight during the first task they work on together? Did they make eye contact? Was their posture open? Were they a good listener, or they just couldn’t stop yapping their mouth, making it difficult for you to ask questions? Ask yourself if this will be the case every day you work with them. Will they speak more than they will work? Did you like the person, or did they rub you the wrong way? For example, I had interviews that started with people asking me directly, “What’s in it for me? Salary, benefits, number of paid annual leave days, that kind of stuff…“. These matters are, of course, important to any employee, and they are topics that will be addressed during the interview, but to start a discussion with them, without being thoughtful about the situation, isn’t only rude but it’s also a sign that you are only interested in these things. After you take the matter of money and benefits off the table, what else matters for you? Probably nothing else. If people don’t care about their work, their teammates, the project, the clients, or anything else besides “what’s in it for them”, they will often leave shortly after being hired and go work for another company that pays them one dollar more than what they are getting from you.

If you really like the person, pay attention so that you don’t fall to the other extreme. Maybe they would fit very well in the team, perhaps they left you with a very good impression, or they remind you of yourself when you were younger, but if you like the person and you believe they would integrate well into the team, those things don’t mean that they can perform the job. They must also have the necessary knowledge and skills. That’s why it’s important to write everything down because it brings your attention to all that’s happened during the interview and focuses you on the skills you have identified in the candidate. We are emotional beings, and emotions interfere with our decision making. So make sure you consider the skills, so you don’t risk hiring someone just based on likability.

As an optional step, assuming the interview went well, you can also give the candidate a short “homework”. If, for example, you are hiring someone to work on a web application, then give the candidate a web application to build - nothing fancy, something that can be written in 4-5 hours over the weekend. Have them throw in some unit tests also. Make it clear that you are looking for style of programming, and for thought patterns, you are looking for structure, etc. Ask to have this sent to you over email once finished. When you receive it, code review it like you code review your production code. It sometimes happens that someone is good at the theoretical part but lacks on the practical one. Someone might be smart and passionate but stuck on “hack mode” or “sloppy mode”, or “whatever gets the job done mode”. I’ve had interviews where the applicant did very well during the conversation and was a very nice person, but when the homework came back, it wasn’t good: variables were named “a”, “b”, “c”, or “var”, file names were either in Camel case, Pascal case, or mixed case with underscores, with no naming consistency whatsoever, some things were not thread-safe, some caused security issues, there was a lot of code duplication, responsibilities spread all over the place… it was a complete mess. The candidate was smart but definitely picked up some bad habits along the way that became their default mode of working.

No matter the outcome of the homework, note the conclusions, and add them to the notes you took after the interview. If the assignment looks good, call the candidate back for another discussion about the homework. Discuss the issues you found at the code review. Ask why they took one approach or another. Suggest things or criticize some parts of the implementation and see how they respond. Change some of the requirements and see how they would approach making the changes. Have them refactor some code. If the homework raised some warning flags, address them. At this point, you want to make sure they are really the author of the homework and check if they get too defensive about it or starts to have a “whatever” attitude towards the improvements you are suggesting or the faults you have found. Make sure you criticize the work, not the person. And address pertinent things, not indentation with spaces versus tabs or some other nonsense like that. I’ve noticed that people who take code reviews personally and can’t handle them in a mature way (especially from strangers) are usually bad developers and are hard to work with. Again, note down the conclusions of this discussion.

HR will also have their own interview with the person. It’s their job, remember? Unless HR is rude to the candidate, make them feel uncomfortable, or they don’t prepare for the interview, this should mostly be just a formality to double-check on references, studies, and other information from the CV. Once they have their conclusions, have a chat together and get their feedback too. Think well about it, then make a decision: “hire” or “no hire”. If you have the slightest doubts about anything, then it’s better to say “no hire”. Better to risk not hiring a good candidate than to hire someone who risks struggling with the job. The cost of hiring the wrong person can far outweigh the cost of leaving the position unfilled. Unless there are some legitimate concerns for which you might not be able to hire the applicant (for example, in any domain where employees need to handle people’s money or their personal information, someone with a criminal record, or someone who is overdue on any loans they have, might be immediately disqualified for hiring), then the final decision to hire or not is yours to make, not HR’s.

Before a salary offer is made to the applicant, HR will most likely want you to fill in an interview evaluation form. Most of these documents are generic and don’t accurately summarize the information from the interview, but make an effort and fill it correctly. Remember the standard scoring or rating I was mentioning earlier when I said why I prefer topics instead of questions to discuss at the interview? It will probably be something similar to that. You will need to provide some scores or grades or specify an experience level like senior, junior, entry-level, or whatever you use in your company. Make an effort and fill in this document as demanded, even if you’ve discussed a lot more things with the candidate, and you find such a summary unsuitable. This is an official document, so make sure you use an official tone and don’t include anything that might be considered inappropriate. Attach at the end of it a summary of your notes and your recommendation: “right or not for the job”. Don’t neglect this step or underestimate it. The interview evaluation form will be used by management to understand what money they have to pay or see in what salary grid the candidate might fit within the company. Make sure you fill in all the necessary details, or someone else might decide that the salary the person asks for is too big compared with what the report says. If you are a Team Lead or a manager, you normally have access to salary information, so you can propose an amount based on the candidate’s skill level, and you can add that as your recommendation. But if you don’t have access to this information, or it’s not your job to have the “money talk” with the candidate, just make sure you give correct and complete feedback.

Be aware that if you reject a candidate, but they ask for a small salary, someone in management might find it “a chance too good to refuse”. “OK, they don’t know as much as you’d want but look what a low pay they are asking for. If we find someone else alike, we could hire two developers for the price of one”. Don’t give in to that! If your managers or bosses want to ignore your decision, then fine, so be it. But don’t change “your decision” from a “no” to a “yes” just because the situation looks like a good financial deal to others, which by the way it’s not. The person must have the right skills, the right attitude, be smart, have the desire to grow, and you have to recognize potential in them. These things don’t lose their significance just because the demanded salary is low. Nor does it, in any way, make up for the work that the employee will have to do. If the person is not knowledgeable, they continuously need hand-holding, they always need support from others, write bad code that then needs to be rewritten, or they introduce too many bugs that others have to fix, with time, the person you hired cheaply will turn out to be very expensive for the project. So stick with your conclusions after the interview and with the recommendation to not hire.

Before ending this section, I just want to mention that this part of the interview is just like in soccer: the strikers need to be effective, but it is also essential to have a good goalkeeper so that the ball does not cross the goal line. Have the wrong persons in HR or the developers conducting the technical interviews, and you may have yourself quite a problem on your hands.

Loopholes

The process I mentioned above is by no means perfect. Nothing is. No matter how well you prepare, both you and HR, a job interview is like, after the first date with someone, you decide to marry the person and move in together. In just a few hours, there is no way to get to know a person well enough to remove any doubt that they are right for you and that you will have a long-lasting relation. And the same goes for a job interview. Just from a few hours of interacting with the candidate, you can’t know for sure if the working relationship will actually turn out well. Even if you find some hiring process that seems to work really well, there can always be loopholes. I’ll talk about two of them here.

The first loophole is that for this to work and bring in good developers, everyone in the company must follow a similar hiring process and decide on comparable criteria to evaluate candidates. If you conduct thorough interviews for your team, but nobody else in the company does, sub-par employees can still be hired, just not in your team. To keep on the soccer analogy, you are defending your goal, but someone on your side scores an own goal. Then, even if you have a well-developed process for selecting employees and everyone sticks to it, it may not have always been that way, and some bad apples may have slipped by and are still employed in the company. If some of these bad apples are in a leadership or management position, they will most likely end up hiring bad developers, because a mediocre lead will hire only people that won’t challenge their position, something possible from a competent professional.
