These things can turn problematic because, as time goes on, projects evolve, new products are created, new teams will be formed, and people will move around the company. It makes sense for a company to keep its employees and assign them to different projects. It preserves the organizational knowledge, there is less or no effort or costs with recruiting and sometimes training the new employees, it increases employee interest levels, people develop new skills, it’s a way to keep a senior employee from leaving the company if they are not happy with their current position within the company, and so on. Unfortunately, sometimes, it’s even a way to avoid the inconvenience of firing someone by instead transferring them to another department, project, or team. And that team just might happen to be yours.

When another team or project has a developer to spare, do you really think that developer is the best one they have, and they are willing to give them to you? Even if they paid attention to the hiring process and give you a good senior developer, for example, who says that developer is a senior from your point of view also? Or maybe the person has done the bare minimum and managed to get by without being fired, and they might not pull their own weight. Or perhaps they have an attitude problem and be a bad match with everyone else in your team, making them hard to work with.

So if you are getting people from other teams within the company, ask yourself what you are getting. Have them pass through the same interview, technical evaluation, and homework. Don’t count on others having done a good job at hiring people. Protect your own team and project from sub-par developers (or maybe I should say “try” to protect your team and project from sub-par developers since sometimes you don’t have a word to say in the matter, e.g., if a project ends and a team is split between working on other projects, the alternative might be to let those people go or pay them to sit around and do nothing, so top management will impose them on you).

The second loophole is with internship programs. There are various reasons for which companies offer internships. Maybe the company wants to make use of some cheap labor (sometimes even for free) to fill in a shortage of staff over a certain period of time and for some tasks, maybe it’s to promote the company, a way to benefit from some tax reductions, or even genuinely giving back to the community. But most of the time, it’s an opportunity for the company to assess and test out potential employees for a job without the complications of actually hiring someone, kind of like a “test run”. There is always a shortage of qualified workers, but it’s even more problematic when demand is high, and for developers it is high, since almost everything nowadays has software inside. There are simply not enough software developers to hire, so people jump on interns and seek to “grow them in house”. There are fifty-fifty chances of success, so many companies invest in such programs. Fifty percent is better than nothing, right?

When it comes to recruiting interns, many companies have a “lighter” recruitment process than for employees. It’s somewhat expected since they are looking for students or fresh graduates who only have academic experience and lack “real work experience”; in fact, that’s most likely the reason they are applying for the internship, to get real work experience. But because these people have no experience, it doesn’t mean that you have to neglect the interview and take into consideration only their graduation major and a 200 words cover letter in which they express their motivation to work in your company and mention how the internship would help them achieve their career aspirations.

Most seasoned developers will expect the graduates to know little, so they have low expectations from them. Probably they won’t want to waste time leading an interview for an intern position. Perhaps they will send one of the junior developers from the team to conduct the interviews (and I already mentioned above why that’s a bad idea). So there is a risk of the interview process to be neglected even if developers are more involved and don’t just let HR handle it. Then the work of the intern might get neglected too, based on the same reasoning of having low expectations. The intern then sticks around for three months or so, and if they don’t step on anyone’s toes, drop some live database, or accidentally email their password to everyone inside the company, at the end of the period, they might get an offer to work there. Since they are already working in the company when they get an offer for a permanent job, they might bypass the “real” interview that everyone else went through. Sometimes things turn out well, and if you are lucky, you get yourself a smart, hard-working person. But again… don’t count on luck.

If you have an interview process, use it also for recruiting interns. You will inevitably adapt it a little bit for what a graduate might know (or not know), and focus less on the person’s skills and more on other things such as the candidate’s personality, attitude, motivation, enthusiasm, if they can fit well within the organization and team, if they have good communication skills, basically to focus more on what the candidate’s potential than on what they have done so far. But the structure of the interview should remain the same.

For example, start with crafting a job description. It’s mostly HR that initiates internship programs as a company-wide program in which all departments must participate, not on your solicitation. But that doesn’t mean you have nothing left to do. Discuss with HR the requirements you have from an intern. Think about what they might help you with on the project. Build a job description with HR, and although it’s indeed one with fewer responsibilities than for a regular job, it’s still a serious job description. Then lay down the minimum criteria for CV screening. Internship or not, applicants must submit a CV, right? What does a CV need to contain to pass beyond the first filter? To mention a major in Computer Science, for example, or maybe good English skills, or the candidate to have had a summer job in something related to your domain of activity, not just in fast food restaurants. If you have too many candidates (which might happen in a big city, with many universities), you can use some test questions as an additional selection criterion. As I already mentioned, use your own questions that are relevant to the context in which you make the selection of candidates.

Then, once you have some interviews scheduled, prepare for the discussion with candidates just like with any other job interview. Do your research, note down questions you want to ask the applicant, and try not to be influenced by what you find or if someone knows the candidate (sometimes company employees make recommendations, like a young relative, neighbor, or friend). For interns, I usually skip on making the list of languages and technologies mentioned in the CV for the purpose of having the applicants grade themselves from 1 to 10, depending on how much they think they know a subject matter. I do that because graduates don’t usually know enough to try to evaluate themselves. Best case scenario, they might have gotten a good grade at their latest exam on that technology, so they think they are a 10. I also take this into account when building my list of topics to discuss at the interview. During my research, I look at what university they graduated or are still attending and look over their curriculum to see what kind of subjects they’ve studied. I usually keep topics like control structures, inheritance, exceptions, recursion, data structures, etc., but I exclude some more advanced ones like maybe concurrency or multi-threading, which may not have been part of the subject matters they studied (but if such topics were part of their curriculum, I add them :)).

When the day of the interview arrives, during the discussion where I find out more about the candidate, I will also adjust my questions. I can’t ask about actual projects they have worked on (unless they had some previous, maybe part-time, jobs), but I can ask about school assignments and what courses they liked most, and why. Then I go through the topics and ask technical questions. I want to see if the candidate understood the topics that were taught to them. For most people in education, an exam grade is their entire purpose (“I didn’t quite understand a subject in class! Hmmm…. Is it for the exam? No? Later then…“), so it’s not as bad if they didn’t understand some things, as it would be, for example, for an employee that didn’t understand the things they worked with. So I try to focus on finding out if they are smart, passionate, and like learning. I might also ask where else - beyond required reading at various courses - they look for learning resources.

I also give them homework (tuned to their level, of course), something to keep them busy for a few hours. How they do the assignment is important, but more important is the fact that they actually do it. Many graduates will not do it unless they are truly interested in the experience they get from the internship, and not just getting a paycheck. Those who won’t do the homework will turn to other internships where there is less hassle to get in. Note that if you are offering unpaid internship positions, the homework might be a little bit over the top, so you might skip it. Instead, you might pay attention in the interview to what questions they ask and how much they are interested in the position. If they ask few or no questions, you should question their motives for applying for the internship.

And finally, before ending the interview, you must make sure that the applicant understands what the internship consists of. The purpose is to gain “real job experience”, but if the applicant never had a job, they don’t know what “real job” means. Help them figure out what will be expected during the internship. This will not be an extension of school, with individual study where they are placed in some corner of the office and given some books to read, or being asked to make coffee in the morning, and maybe, from time to time, joining the team out for lunch. The intern will have to work with other people on a product. Explain what schedule they will have, what work they will have to do, what responsibilities they will have. To realize that they have to give 100% every day, not like the school where you just make an appearance every day and then try to give 500% in the evening just before the exam. The candidate might be good, and you want to take them in your team, but you have to make sure they understand what awaits them, so they make an informed decision when accepting the internship and not realize two weeks later that it was a wrong choice that they don’t like anymore.

Match check

So now you have a new member in your team. There will probably be some sort of on-boarding. HR will present company policies, the company structure, and will give the new employee a tour through other departments. Papers have been signed, email was set up, access rights were configured. The employee received office supplies and an access badge. The workstation was prepared, and they have a desk where to work from. The new employee can now go to work.

As a continuation of the on-boarding, then there is a period when the new employee gets to know their team members better and starts working with them, you explain in detail the project and the technologies that are being used, you explain the working methodology, you prepare documentation for them to study before being assigned their first task and actually contribute to the project. You offer them all the training and support needed to be able to do the work they were hired for. Basically, you set them up to have a positive start and become productive as soon as possible. And here is where people begin to make a mistake. They get caught up in the activities needed to get the new employee up to speed, and they neglect to validate the hiring decision.

It doesn’t matter how good your hiring process was or that you took all the necessary measures to make sure you hire a good employee. Shit can still happen. The new person might always be late for work, always present excuses for personal failures, get into conflicts with other people in the team, heck they might even discover that they actually hate the project, but stay just because they have bills to pay. Even an intern that is a temporary hire and isn’t expected to produce much can end up impacting your team’s morale and productivity. So what do you do? You have to validate that the person is actually a match for the job you matched them with. It’s like the difference between theory and practice. With the interview, you made sure the candidate is a match, in theory. Now that the person actually works with you, you verify that match in practice. The point is not to believe that your job is over once you hired the person. You can still mess it up.

If you get the wrong people, in the long run, they might cause frustration and turnover among other team members who do good work. So you want to avoid that. So once the person is on board, keep an eye on them. In most countries, employees may not be terminated “at-will” unless they are in a probationary period. For example, in my country, once someone signs the labor contract, a probationary period may be established to check the employee’s skills. It’s a maximum of 90 calendar days for most employees, except for managerial positions where it can reach a maximum of 120 calendar days. During this period, the employee can be terminated without prior notice and without the need to provide motivation. This may vary from country to country, but what’s usually common is that once this period passes, it becomes more difficult to fire someone.

People tend to make bad use of this probationary period. When faced with what looks like a sub-par employee, they might think “they are just a little slow to start”, but still look promising. Or they’re otherwise a nice person, and at least they are trying. Some might think they didn’t give them enough attention while being busy dealing with other things, so they blame themselves for the new employee’s poor start. Or the project might be too complex for someone to become proficient in a short period of time, so “give it some more time”. Or maybe this person was hired as part of building a new team on a new project and might not even have had a chance of writing any code, just read specifications, taking part in training, and all sorts of kick-off activities. So you don’t even know what they can actually do. By the time you get to actually see what work this person can take on, you might notice that it ain’t that much.

From the start, you need to make sure the new employee knows what is expected of them. Set upfront goals and standards of work with the employee to make sure they are understood and met. Your expectations should not come as a surprise to the new employee when you have a meeting with them at the end of the probationary period. If something happens during this period, address it immediately, don’t wait 90 days or whatever time the legal probationary period is. Constantly assess the situation and make sure the new hire gets all the support, training, and guidance needed to help them achieve the expected outcomes. You need to have continuous discussions with the new employee throughout the entire probationary period to evaluate their progress. Also, note that the probationary period is not for the new employee to prove “they are worthy”. It is for you to figure out if they are a good match for the position. You have your part to play in this matter to make it happen, like providing the necessary support, training, etc. But at the same time, you need to monitor the progress and see how they behave, how they solve situations they encounter, and how the person is actually performing in the new role.

Note that with interns, it’s even easier to screw things up and not pay enough attention to them, since they are not real employees and don’t usually have deadlines on the project as everyone else does. They do real work and contribute what they can, but their priority is to learn things and discover how it is to work in a company on a real project. As many internships have a short duration, you have to be careful. Talk to the intern and explain to them what expectations exist and how their work will unfold, so they don’t think that they can surf the Internet all day long, occasionally doing some simple tasks here and there, and in the end, receive a paper for school where it’s written that they attended an internship program in the company from date X to date Y. They need guidance and time from other team members to explain how things work. They need training and support, just like any other new employee, even though most of the time, it’s in their interest to learn by themselves. And this is what you have to monitor throughout the internship. Give them some real work to do, like for example to build tools to support the development team or the deployment, maybe some tasks on manual testing to familiarize themselves with the application and learn how to interact with the rest of the team, and gradually delve into the code of the application… the real application. Pair them with someone, or assign someone to oversee the intern, and have them work on useful things that move the product forward. Don’t give them unimportant work that you then throw in the bin, just so they have something to do. There is nothing more exciting for an intern than to know they have contributed to a piece of the application, that something they have tested, or a bug they fixed, or a feature they developed, is deployed in production and is used by real users.

Don’t make the mistake of thinking that once the internship is over, you get rid of the interns, and they are gone forever. Take serious care of them because, in the end, besides providing something like an internship assessment form they may need at the university, you will probably also have to determine whether in the future, after completing their studies, the intern is worthy of being offered a full-time job in the company. So strive to build a correct assessment, in case the company makes decisions in this regard. Who wouldn’t want a smart, young developer that’s also, most likely, “inexpensive”? If the intern got along well with everyone, and you gave them a good assessment for the simple fact that they made good coffee or knew how to photocopy documents double-sided, you may not be able to resist accepting them in your team when the company’s higher-ups decide to hire them. So don’t let your interns to their own devices and evaluate them on appropriate criteria, just like you do with a new employee. See if they are open to learning from others, if they can apply the notions that are explained to them, if they adapted well to the company and work environment, how well they understood the business, if they are an organized person, if they are idle if nobody is paying attention to them or if they are proactive. See if they are a responsible person that requires minimal supervision or if you have to micromanage them, if they are punctual, show good attention to detail, and accept criticism and feedback. Are they genuinely interested in software development, or are they complaining that the industry is nothing like they imagined? Pay attention so you can determine if they are a good developer or someone with potential. Just like you decide for employees, at the end of their probationary period, whether you want to continue with them or not, so with an intern, at the end of the internship, you must be able to make an informed decision about offering them (or not) a full-time job afterward.

And even if you do use the probationary period well, you can still end up in a bad situation. Terminating someone’s contract after the probationary period ends is more complicated, and people know this. During the probationary period, some will actually be nice and helpful and show good progress (people change their behavior when they know they are observed), but once the period expires, they show their true colors and start taking it easy, do sloppy work, or start behaving poorly. I’ve seen this happen a few times. And an employee who can’t or won’t pull their own weight will eventually affect the whole team. If you don’t do something about it, at any given time, things can go south, and you start having problems with everyone, not just with this person in isolation. People can also change over time. They can start as hard-working people and, along the way, get complacent for various reasons. That’s why, at regular intervals, you have to evaluate the situation (keep your finger on the pulse, so to speak) and take action when you see something is wrong. And now, we reach the thing we all know under the names of performance reviews or performance appraisals.

Performance reviews

After you’ve hired a developer, you then have to see how they behave over time, how they work with others, what the quality of their work is, how they have evolved since you hired them, etc. Performance reviews and appraisals are a good way of doing this. If you are in a position to hire developers, like a Team Lead, for example, then you are also in the position of having to conduct performance reviews.

Just like with hiring developers, lots of companies don’t pay enough attention to doing performance reviews, and again, things turn out bad. This is another thing that’s considered as something that the Human Resources department should do. And rightly so, this activity is part of the functions of the HR department. But just like with hiring developers, the implementation of the process can leave much to be desired. When HR is left in charge of the entire process of evaluating developers, you can end up with another generic process, with a new batch of questions like those for the job interviews, but questions that are now not just for developers but for everyone: business analysts, secretaries, salespersons, and anything in between, using a system that only pits people against their colleagues and creates competition between team members. As an aside, I once had HR and management trying to impose programming quizzes at the yearly appraisals (talk about trying to optimize for the wrong thing). The entire matter was useless, and a lot of time was lost. While Team Leads were trying to convince HR that it’s a bad idea, many developers were already brushing up their knowledge and started practicing quizzes on office hours, with very few people still working on the products. Others took the test and emailed everyone else the answers. It was a complete mess. We eventually settled for the standard questionnaire we got in previous years, with grades ranging from 1 to 5 where everyone got a 3 (i.e., meets expectations) with some occasional 4s (exceeds expectations). This is one of the things that is often wrong with performance reviews: that clueless people conduct them.

To know if an employee is doing a good job, you must be able to do their job and know how to do it correctly, then compare the employee’s work with the expectations resulting from this knowledge. However, many times, a manager doesn’t know how to do the subordinate’s work, especially in IT. So obviously, a manager without technical expertise has no way to evaluate a developer. A manager can evaluate soft skills at most, but not technical skills. So they have no way of knowing if a developer’s work is good or if changes need to be made to it, they cannot set technical goals, and so on. But very often, a person in management is the one doing performance evaluations for a developer. Sometimes it’s even worse; you can have a manager that, besides noticing you come in daily for work, has no clue what you are doing. It may sound ridiculous, but again, it happens. In addition to that, when a manager performs the evaluation, the discussion is often unidirectional (because of the different levels in the organizational chart) and is perceived as if it were a sit-down with your parents when you were younger, and you did something wrong. So everyone ends up hating performance reviews. With time, people have become accustomed for performance reviews to be that patronizing and uncomfortable, but mandatory process, to which HR subjects all the company employees once a year, an activity that everyone does in a hurry, as something to be set aside so that everyone can then return to their work.

Then there are many who say that performance reviews are not fair to the employees, that they are not objective (if you quarreled with your boss and they lose, be sure they will keep that in mind when discussing your salary increases), that they only focus on the negatives (doing your job well is nothing exceptional, it’s just what is expected of you, but any mistake must be analyzed, discussed in great detail, and punished), that they are a practice rooted in the past, that they set useless one-year goals that immediately get invalidated by changing conditions, etc., and it’s suggested to give up on performance reviews altogether. However, if you have a company with employees who do a job, it’s normal to want to periodically evaluate them to make sure there are no problems with them, and they are still doing their job properly. If you go to a restaurant and order something, and your waiter is never around when you need them, you try to get their attention, but they pretend they don’t see you, they get your order wrong, they are rude, they slam your food on the table, or they are clumsy, and they drop your food, what will you do in the end? Will you leave a tip or not? If all the waiters at that restaurant behave like this, will you go back a second time? It’s the same with performance evaluations in a company. If the restaurant owner finds out that’s the waiters’ behavior, that they are mistreating the customers, or that they are unskilled, do you think they will praise them or fire them? If the other waiters are professionals in their work, do you think they will like what they see? Or will they believe it reflects poorly on their work and the restaurant? It’s the same in a company. Why wouldn’t companies evaluate the employees that work for them? It’s normal for companies to verify that the money they spend on salaries doesn’t go to waste but goes to people who do their job properly. It’s normal for companies to receive good service from your part and have a way to evaluate whether or not they want you to continue working for them. So, the problem that many have with appraisals is not necessarily related to the idea of the appraisal itself, but to its faulty implementations, as I already mentioned.

Another problem then is that classic HR appraisals are inefficient also because you cannot measure everyone according to a single set of standards, especially developers. But many appraisals, that’s exactly what they do. They are pursuing standardization and uniformity because otherwise, you can’t compare people’s performances (with each other or the same employee over multiple evaluations). That’s why you get standardized questions at the interview, standardized questions on cognitive tests, standardized questions at the performance review, so that you have a basis of comparison, because the process has this belief embedded in it, that “if you can’t measure it, you can’t manage it”, just like in school when based on one’s grades you can figure out if the student is doing well or not and what the educators can then do about it. Oddly enough, sometimes the educators don’t do anything about it. A student moves on with their other colleagues to the next topics in the curriculum, no matter if they are an A student or a C student. And many times, the same thing happens with performance appraisals in a company. An employee gets a score of 4.95, another one 4.34, another one maybe 3.26; then, everyone goes about their business as usual once the entire evaluation process is over.

But you can’t really put a number on that, especially for developers. A developer is a knowledge worker[14], and knowledge workers are hard to evaluate objectively. You can’t put a finite measure on their productivity. A lot of managers or HR people would cringe if they read this, but it’s true. You can’t measure a developer’s productivity. Developers have different skills; they might not work on the same modules of the application, they don’t do the same activities, some work better alone, others work better as a team, but all of them contribute to the success or failure of the project. You can’t exactly quantify each developer’s contribution unless they all produce widgets in isolation, according to precise specifications, and then compare how many widgets were done, how well the requirements were meet, and what the bug rate is for each developer. Or you might look at how many lines of code each developer writes per hour; the more lines per hour written, the more productive the developer is, “right”? (note: in case you did not catch it, this is sarcasm)

Because grades are a simple system that we all know how it works, it’s tempting to grade employees just like students are graded. An A student is better than a B student, isn’t it? But what if the grade would also be a way to measure the quality of the education that is provided to the student? Is it possible the teacher didn’t do a good job of explaining a topic, and that’s why the B student got a B? So is the grade for the teachers too? Does it reflect what a good job they did? Then is an A at one school equivalent to an A at any other school, or even between two different teachers at the same school? For that matter, should grades be assigned as letters like in the United States or the 1-10 range like we have in my country? Or maybe as a percentage? Should the municipality invest more money into schools where students have lower grades or higher grades, to improve the education or reward it, respectively? If one student got an A and then a B, is that a sign that they are no longer paying attention? What if they got a B than an A? Is that a sign they are paying more attention or put in more effort? So for whom are grades anyways? Are they feedback to the student about their progress or show the areas they should improve upon? Are they for parents to know how their son is doing in school (or how he’s being educated, if you believe that to be the same thing), be proud of them, or make decisions based on the grades? “No new smartphone for you, young man, until you improve your grades”. Are the grades used to motivate the student in some way (to make a greater effort and work for a higher grade)? Are the grades for top universities to know to enroll only good students? What do they prove?

What I’m saying with all of this is that, although assigning grades then trying to draw some conclusions or make some decisions based on them is a simple system and we all understand it and are used to it (we’ve all been to school and been graded using the same approach), it’s too simple to reflect the underlying situation. You don’t have all the information or all the details needed to do a proper evaluation of how students are doing solely based on their grades. Especially if you try to do that determination from a distance. That’s similar in the case of appraisals. It’s easy to get them wrong because they happen from a certain distance. And flawed methods of evaluation or comparison performed from a distance don’t help you in any way to find out if something is going well or not. From the inside, you do know. Viewed from outside, maybe the students’ grades all present the same image, but seen from inside, the situation is different. Your student colleagues know you are not good at math or that you’re clumsy in gym class. Your teachers also know things like this. They know from the daily interaction with you, they don’t need grades (like two per semester, as I received in school, for example) to know if you are doing well or not, or whether you are smart or not.

School grades are a controversial subject, just like appraisals are. Grades cannot summarize your performance on several levels by assigning it a single dimension. It’s the same with appraisals. People know from your daily work, whether you are a good employee or not, not from “a grade” you receive once per year. And even if they only look at that, they know there is so much more than that. If Jane and Jessica got an A in math, the teacher knows that Jane has just studied while Jessica is gifted and will become a great mathematician in the future. But from the outside, you can not make this difference. The teacher can’t give Jessica a special grade to actually show everyone that she’s gifted. This is why an appraisal conducted by a manager or someone who doesn’t do your job isn’t going to work. Only other developers you work with know how to see beyond appearances, see in-depth what’s behind what others see from a distance.

There is only one real way of evaluating a developer: it takes a good developer to recognize another good developer. Only a knowledge worker can evaluate another knowledge worker. You can’t really measure developer performance. There isn’t a well-defined process or something universally valid through which we can do an objective evaluation. But other developers know. And not only regarding technical skills (like writing quality code, writing efficient or bug-free code, or choosing the proper design) but also for other things (if their work actually brings value, if they keep their skills up to date, if they are a team player). People working in a team see stuff. They don’t work in a vacuum, or with horse blinders on their eyes, or with their heads stuck between monitors. They also observe what is going on around them. Consider soccer again for one second, or the majority of team sports. It is the team that wins the match. Sure, the strikers score the majority of the goals, but the defenders are just as important. The goalkeeper is even more important. If a team member has poor performance or is indifferent about the game, other players on the field notice this. The coach on the bench sees too. Even the spectators notice.

It’s the same with a software development team.

People involved in a team effort see when someone lacks focus or skills, doesn’t contribute with equal efforts to the work, is disengaged, doesn’t want to grow, or people just don’t trust them. They don’t need to have HR forms with handpicked questions with a 1 to 5 ranking, or a percentage up to 100, to know who does a good job and who doesn’t. They just know. People notice when someone’s code has a lot of issues during testing or code review, or if the implementation is so bad that someone else has to rewrite everything from scratch. Someone creates bugs faster than they can type? Everything is on version control, so people can see that Michael didn’t commit anything in the past two months, and during the Daily Stand-Up, he says the same thing since he’s been hired. If a senior doesn’t deliver as much as they should, what are they doing? If someone doesn’t attend meetings they should, or they don’t read important emails and don’t respect company policies, do you think that goes unnoticed? Or what if they come to work at different times each day, they don’t respect people’s time, and when the team needs them, they are never there? If someone never lets anybody know the status of their work, and always respond with “I’m almost done” when asked about it, what are they doing? A person is extremely stubborn and always causes conflicts for the most trivial reasons imaginable? Someone in the team has to be micromanaged all of the time in order for them to do something vaguely productive? Some do their fair share of the work while others find a nice and comfy spot and just watch from a distance? People see and understand these things.

There are certainly exceptions, but most of the time, software gets written by teams; developers, testers, designers, and so on. Success and failure is the team’s result. So the team must function well. People need to get along well and have the necessary skills to do the required work, to be satisfied with their daily operations, to enjoy coming to work and have the satisfaction at the end of the day that they did a good job. The quality of the code depends on how the team works. Weighing different situations, comparing solutions, and being able to make good decisions, also depend on how the team works. Everyone has to pull in the same direction, and everyone needs to add value in their own way. When something’s not right, things come to light. And as a Team Lead, for example, you have to be there when that happens, so you can identify and prevent problems. You can’t wait for a standard performance review that happens once a year that often focuses on the wrong things, to try to draw some conclusions on how the people in the team are performing. Another better alternative must be found. And this option consists of observing things carefully and having open discussions with each of your team members on a regular basis.

Frequent discussions

Here I must admit I’m preaching what I don’t practice. I’ve been guilty of skipping on proper appraisals myself, then had to sit down alone in a meeting room, trying to remember what all the people in my team did in the last 12 months. This is obviously a bad thing to do. You can’t wait one year to tell people that they are doing a good job, that they have things to improve, or that they are struggling and failing miserably. Feedback needs to be provided on a continuous basis. Nothing sophisticated or very official, just developer talking to developer. And I mean an honest, open discussion, with all the cards on the table. A developer should not feel like visiting the doctor and being told that “you eat junk food, you’re not doing any exercise, you’re overweight, the cholesterol is through the roof, the blood test results are outside the normal ranges, and here is what you need to do: take these pills and see you next year for another checkup”.

The discussions should be relaxed, nothing formal or very structured. However, they shouldn’t be completely improvised, or you will end up discussing topics off the top of your head, or by exhausting one subject while ignoring others, similar to how it can happen during job interviews. So prepare ahead of time so that during the discussion you stay focused on what you want to talk to the employee. As with the interview, if you ask questions, ask open-ended questions. You want a discussion to find out and figure out things, not just to tick some check-boxes. If people get the impression you are filling a questionnaire, everything will seem forced or mechanically done.

People need to know what is expected of them (by you or by the company). If something needs improving or fixing, discuss what that is and how you will proceed next to resolve it. Maybe it’s something the employee does wrongly, and they should stop, maybe there is some knowledge that the employee should get to know or some skills to develop, maybe they need help from another member of the team, maybe they need help from you as the Team Lead, maybe they are doing well but just need some encouragement from time to time, maybe they are afraid to get out of their comfort zone and need a push. Or maybe, for example, you have a developer who is working hard on one application, they know it inside out, they dream it at night, you really have nothing to disapprove of, but the application is limiting their way of thinking. You can identify these things and help the person grow, maybe for a promotion, or maybe for a future project, or to widen their horizons, perhaps even assigning them some people to supervise and mentor (even if they don’t like it, it’s not a tragedy, but they might find out that they enjoy the new responsibilities), and so on. Maybe the person is a bit careless lately. If there isn’t enough pressure, some might wonder off in Internet land then do sloppy work. These people need a little bit of focus and a reminder from time to time to stay the course.

Remember, it’s a conversation. Don’t fall into the trap of doing “one-way evaluations”, as I mentioned above, or the discussions will lose their worth and become formalities, and people will participate only because the Team Lead wants to have their way and be more classy than HR, which at least limit this torment to only once per year. Also, these discussions, if performed responsibly, work out better if people don’t think about salary increases, being disciplined, or getting fired afterward. Most people appreciate a good discussion in a more relaxed setting. If you do these “I just want to check in with you to see how everything is going” meetings often enough (once a month or so, or every couple of sprints if you are doing iterative development), people will get comfortable with them and won’t perceive them the same as a one-off, stress loaded, performance appraisal meeting.

Every now and then, during these discussions, you can also ask the employee to do a self-evaluation. All of that “tell me about yourself” thing you ask during the interview seems to vanish once you start working with the person. I’ve been asked during interviews what my main duties and responsibilities were, what are my greatest strengths and weaknesses, what I liked and disliked about working with previous organizations/projects/teams/people, what was most and least satisfying about my job, or what elements of my job I found most difficult, what I could have done better/smarter in such or such situation, or what areas I would like to focus on in the future (like technologies, career, or skills related), but once I was hired, very few people cared to know about these things from me. Sometimes maybe a question like this would slip in the HR questionnaire, but otherwise, nobody really bothered. You are working with the person for fuck’s sake. Ask them how they feel, if they are well, or if they need help with something or from someone. Ask what motivates them or would motivate them further, if there is something they don’t like or if they have ideas to improve things, and how would they do it, etc. You surely won’t see things the same way. You see them from different perspectives, whether related to the project, the company, or the employee’s performance. Maybe you think they are doing a good job, but the employee is dissatisfied with themselves; or vice-versa, you are unhappy, but the employee feels they are doing what is expected of them. During the evaluation, you express your expectations from them, but these expectations must also match their expectations about themselves; you don’t know if the two align unless you also ask what they think.

Self-evaluation is useful for the employee to think of themselves in regard to their role in the company, to better understand the contribution they are making and the impact they have in the workplace. It makes them move away from work automatism and think more carefully about the activities they are doing, it helps them think about their strengths and weaknesses, what their achievements are, what new skills or knowledge they acquired or still need, what goals to set themselves going forward, or what other responsibilities they would like to have in the future, all of this before you tell them about it. A self-evaluation also engages the employee in the discussion, rather than simply participate in it and expecting you to do most of the talking.

As I mentioned, people see stuff, and they often see them differently. If the discussions you are having are sincere and you are a fair Team Lead, you communicate honestly, and with calm, people will open up to you and be honest. Developers will not open up to HR or at the annual performance review where everything is still under HR’s umbrella, and any wrong saying can negatively be reflected on salary increases. You have better chances to find out more if people are relaxed and, most importantly, they feel safe. However, be aware that if people feel that you don’t really care about these discussions, but you do them because someone from HR made you do it, or you read somewhere that supervisors should have frequent interactions with subordinates, then you’d better not waste your time with one-on-one meetings… save yourself for the annual review.

These will not be comfortable discussions at all. Some things are hard to say or hear, people are not always receptive to negative feedback, for example, but things must be said by their name. In trying to protect the participants’ emotions, be careful not to send messages that are too vague or end up losing their importance. If there are concerns with an employee, those must be put on the table, discussed, and understood.

Whatever the things you identified as necessary to be improved or changed by the employee, you then need to define in what improvement will consist of, agree on a plan to do it, and state clearly that it must be sustainable over time. Set goals together, time limits until those goals should be met, and establish how you will evaluate whether or not they have been achieved. Even if it is something on an ongoing basis, you must be both aware of the implications so that nobody can later say that they didn’t know or didn’t understand. It’s important to note here one error some people make, and that’s to set goals that have little to do with the work the developer does or with the project’s objectives. They use SMART goals[15] (i.e., specific, measurable, assignable, realistic, and time-bound) but neglect to consider that the objectives you agree upon should concern the employee’s productivity, not be just criteria that can be evaluated in the next yearly appraisal. The “R” in SMART should also stand for “Relevant”. If the goals are not relevant for the work, it’s better not to assign them, because if the goals count for their next evaluation, the employee will focus on those and neglect the work. So don’t have objectives like taking some certifications in who knows what technology or language, or participate in hackathons, or watch video tutorials or read some book who’s content they won’t use on the job. Every time some manager set up irrelevant objectives for me, I always thought that “Update your resume” would be a nice objective for next year also. So assign objectives that help them become better at the work they are doing, not something that makes them look for work someplace else because the goals are silly or unfair. For example, if they are a front-end developer, ask them to discover what happens in the back-end, instead of depending on an API and everything else to be just a black box. Or maybe do code reviews with other developers, participate in architecture meetings, or be more involved in planning, learn the business better, mentor the junior team members, or gain some leadership experience. It might also mean improving their English or communication skills, for example.

Then, the employee has to work on those goals. But be careful, you must help them where they can’t handle things by themselves. Do more training or mentoring, involve them more, challenge them more, give them more responsibilities (or maybe less if they have too much on their plate), give them more freedom and autonomy. Perhaps the person is not in the right position to exercise their full talents, so change what work they do if you can. Pair them with some of the veterans of the project or have them mentor others. Give them better tools, push them beyond their comfort zone, give them more recognition for their work if that’s what’s needed. Do whatever is needed from you and dedicate your time to help equip them with everything they need to succeed and reach those goals, or set up an environment where they can do it on their own.

These discussions allow you to give people feedback often and continuously. But you still need to monitor their progress. If you have frequent talks, you may focus on each conversation individually and end up ignoring the bigger picture. And you don’t want to have one discussion stuck in your head and somehow have it weight more than other discussions you had with the employee either. For example, if the employee screws up something, you pull them aside, discuss things and agree on how to solve the problem, but you don’t want to risk getting stuck on that particular problem. People tend to remember negative things better than they remember positive things. Maybe the employee just had a bad day. Don’t let that define them. So write stuff down at every meeting. When you agreed on things, what things you agreed upon, what needs to be done, and so on. Then, once every three months or so, you should have a formal meeting to build a summary of your discussions and shape a larger perspective on each person’s progress to see if the person’s performance is on an upward or downward trend over a slightly longer period of time. And when I say to have a formal meeting, what I mean is that whatever you agree during the meeting to be signed by the employee as a commitment that they will make an effort to deal with anything that needs to be dealt with. Then, when that time of the year for performance appraisals arrives, you already know the situation of everyone, you don’t spend time remembering stuff, you don’t risk focusing on a recent event that’s still fresh in memory, and for the employee, there will be no surprises during the evaluation.

It doesn’t seem nice to write about every single thing on everyone, and that it’s formal - I already said earlier that developers don’t like these formalities, and you as an evaluator will hate it also - but this is the reality of working in a company. As a Team Lead, it’s your job to make sure everyone receives the support, training, and guidance needed to help them achieve the desired outcomes, but each employee must also want to make the necessary efforts and grow. If they don’t want to, you can’t help them by force. So progress needs to be objectively documented in writing, discussed with, and signed by the employee, otherwise, if the employee’s performance is progressing from bad to worse, you won’t be able to get rid of them without the proper documentation, or you’ll risk being sued (well… you can always be sued, but the documentation gives the company a better fighting chance). If you only tell people that more is expected from them and they need to improve, it doesn’t mean they will do it. Having a formal document signed by the employee (which signifies that they will commit to doing it) means you are serious about them getting their act together and about the consequences if they don’t.

Bad apples

The problem with only one evaluation per year is that it doesn’t properly reflect the evolution of the employee during that year, with all their ups and downs. Many things can happen during an entire year, and your “single event” evaluations may be “meets expectations” year after year, and all of a sudden, a really bad one and you no longer want to have the person in your team. If you didn’t do proper evaluations and didn’t document progress and how things evolved, then good luck in trying to get rid of that person. Things can get ugly, with disputes, lawyers, etc. Because things can get complicated, many don’t bother with trying to get rid of the bad performers. And then you are basically left with two options. You either start micromanaging, essentially trying to force them to work by continually observing and controlling the tasks they perform, hoping that all this extra “attention” they get will make them quit on their own (but it’s not very realistic because how many people can you micromanage? 1? 2? 3? How many? And still do your own job in the meantime), or try to ignore them, or give them work on less important tasks to keep them away from the possibility of doing more damage. Either way, the bad employee will still be with the company, they will receive a salary for not doing a proper job, and can negatively influence others with their behavior. For example, think of teenagers who are influenced by what they see on TV, from actors, or from music artists. They don’t know them personally, they will probably never meet them, and yet, they are influenced by them. Think only at what would happen if they spent five days a week, eight hours per day together. Won’t they be affected? People in a team influence one another, and you want this influence to be a positive one, not negative. One rotten apple does spoil the whole barrel.

If you keep “bad apples” around, what will happen is that other team members will have to work harder or work overtime to compensate for the person who isn’t doing a good job. Or at least for a short while, they will. That’s because, in time, this will cause the competent and formerly-motivated employees to shift down a gear also. Why would they work hard when slackers or jerks are being tolerated, seem to be pampered, and get paid a salary just like all the other employees that are doing their job to the best of their abilities? Team morale will be affected too. Focus will move from the work they are doing (which isn’t important it seems, otherwise it won’t be acceptable for some to receive money but contribute nothing) to the salary they are getting, which should be increased considering that they are actually working. When such behaviors are accepted, and everyone gets paid the same, people begin to think like “if you can’t beat them, join them” (and studies have found that a single negative employee can cause a 30-40 percent drop in a team’s overall performance[16]). For example, in places where individual bonuses were tied to the overall team performance, I’ve seen good achievers slow down their pace, giving up their bonuses just because they couldn’t stand for their lazy colleagues to receive the same bonus if, overall, the team would have done well without their participation. If bad performers actually receive salary increases, then it’s even crazier. If you work hard and receive a 5% salary increase while someone who sits around doing nothing receives 2% (even if it’s because of a company policy that every year everyone should receive at least something to cover inflation), would you find it fair? Bad employees should not get any kind of raises; they should get the boot.

You need people in your team that have the right attitude and the right skills. If you find someone under-performing, assuming you did everything in your power to help them get back on the right track and you notice that they don’t improve and nothing else seems to work to recover the employee, then you have no choice, you have to fire them. You cannot endlessly invest time and effort in someone. People that don’t pull their own weight create situations inside the team that feel like driving your car with the handbrake on. Everyone gets frustrated, and it’s usually the good employees that have enough and decide to leave. And then what? You have to hire other people, the cost of the project increases, things get delayed. Not fun. So don’t keep an inadequate employee on the bench, hoping the rest of the team doesn’t notice them idling around. The only way others don’t see what they are doing is if they no longer work in the company.

Even if they have toxic people in the team, and it seems very logical to fire them, people usually hesitate to do it. In this way, they let a bad situation perpetuate indefinitely, a situation that is not at all fair to those who actually do good work and produce results. Firing people is the thing people dread doing the most while at work. They don’t even use the word “firing”. It sounds bad. They use “let go” or say that they give the person “an opportunity to work somewhere else”. Most of the time, it’s an unpleasant activity that often results in strong emotions and offenses. Sometimes people fear possible litigation, as I said before. So they run from this responsibility or delay it, hoping it won’t be something they need to do. Sometimes they feel responsible or sorry for the person (a job termination sometimes affects not only the individual but also other members of their family). At other times they are adamant in trying to salvage a bad employee, or lie to themselves that things will be better, that they haven’t yet found the key solution to bring the person on the right path, but they will eventually find it (which is often a refusal to acknowledge a possible fault of their own for hiring the person). Or maybe they think it’s their fault for not offering the person more support, or maybe blaming themselves for not recognizing the signs or something. Sometimes the firing happens to some good people that are unfortunately not made for being developers; they have what it takes only up to a certain level, and from there on, no matter how much they try or how hard they work, they just can’t seem to grow anymore. Effort alone isn’t enough; they also need to produce results. The effort gives them more chances before people start thinking about firing them, but at some point, that effort must materialize in some positive outcomes. If not, the other team members will carry them for a while, but not forever. So you have to fire them too, even though they are nice people that do try their best.

Firing someone is never an easy decision, so you should think very carefully about it… but sometimes, it is the only solution. And it is another unavoidable reality of business, especially if you are in a leadership or managerial position. So get past your fear of firing people and get rid of the bad apples. It may seem like you are doing a disservice to an employee, but on the other hand, you are doing more good for the others who remain. When you manage a team, it’s like being a gardener: you plant the seeds, you grow the flowers, and you pluck the weeds out of the soil.

If you end up having to fire people, HR can help you a little better than with interviews or appraisals. The dismissal process is usually well put together because it must comply with legal regulations and also because the company doesn’t want the risk of being sued by the employee. The dismissal discussion is intimidating for all parties (it takes place with a witness, notes are taken and various documents signed, the employee’s access card is taken away, etc.), but assuming you did your part correctly, you had frequent, honest, and open conversations with the employee, problems were identified and addressed, the employee had all the support needed to come around but they didn’t, that the person’s progress and how everything unfolded is properly documented, then the meeting won’t come as a surprise or shock for anyone. You will feel bad before and during the firing of the person, but many times, after everything’s over and done with, you will see that it was a good idea, and the only regret you have is that you didn’t do this earlier.

You should also notify the rest of the team about this decision. Tell them the reasons why the person is being fired as honestly as possible. You don’t want everyone to start coming up with different scenarios for which someone got fired, or even imagine that they might be next. But if you ended up in this situation and everyone paid attention to what was going on around them, it won’t be a surprise for them either.

Firing is a hard thing to do. It’s not just unfortunate that you got to a point where you had to do that, and that the experience itself is unpleasant, but afterward, you have to divide the work of the former employee to others, you have to open a new position, start a recruitment process and so on. However, you can do these things, and they will be under your control. But there will be matters over which you will not have control or have the necessary authority to solve them or influence them. I’m talking about the working environment, most popularly known as “how we do things around here”. You might call it organizational culture, but I’ll stick with “the working environment”. To me, organizational culture is about the values, the goals, and the mission of the company, something deliberately positive; the working environment can be a different kettle of fish, and often is.

The working environment

Another problem with classic HR appraisals is that the performance assessment happens mostly only for those who do the actual work (from the bottom half of the corporate hierarchy) and less for those who run the company or make important decisions (with equally important consequences, if not worse). Processes, procedures, standards, and all kinds of other activities and systems within the company are also neglected. The whole context in which the employees work gets completely ignored. If you have bad processes within the company or the bosses are a bunch of idiots, not even the mother of all appraisals (of employees) will reflect the correct performance situation of the people working in the company. The wrong decision from the part of the CEO or an imposed, counterproductive way of working can demotivate all employees and decrease their productivity.

You look at the people and the team as a whole so you can make a good assessment, but you also need to look beyond that, on everything that happens on the project and throughout the company. The working environment plays an essential role in an employee’s performance. It’s not fair to evaluate someone and ignore these aspects that don’t depend on the individual. Ideally, any problems related to the working environment should be fixed, but if you can’t, because you have no authority over them, at least be aware of how they affect people’s work so that you don’t rest something on the employee’s shoulders that doesn’t depend on them. What you expect to obtain from an appraisal will not improve an employee’s performance unless there are things they can have control over. Obviously, you can’t have a discussion with your work environment, with processes or systems, but you can with people. So ask each person you talk to face-to-face about the problems they see in the team, on the project, and in the company. And don’t be afraid to ask difficult questions. If no one is complaining, it doesn’t mean that everyone is happy and content. Ask them what they think. Depending on your context, you could ask, for example, what would you improve to make the workplace better or people’s jobs easier? What gets in the way of people doing their work? What’s your opinion about company policies like X, Y, or Z? What problems and good parts do you think this project has? What could be done differently to improve it? What goes well or wrong during your day to day work? What could be done differently to improve the wrong parts? How do you get along with your colleagues/coworkers? How well does communication occur between you and the others? Can communication be improved? What are your colleagues’ strongest/weakest points? What could your immediate supervisor do to improve their management style? Many will not want to answer certain questions, especially those related to their colleagues or hierarchical supervisors, but even avoiding the answer may be an indication that something is not right.

Some problems that will come to light after these discussions will not be about the employee. Maybe they’ll be about you. Perhaps they’ll be about the company, higher executives, colleagues, or the work environment. Some issues will be about them, and it’s their job to fix them, but other frustrations concerning you or the processes, procedures, system, etc., are external to them. Remember that the point of these discussions is to help the employee do their job better. This can sometimes mean making adjustments to the working environment instead of trying to improve people’s individual performance.

Following the discussions about the working environment, you will find some things you would normally expect, like people not liking meetings, or that there is too much noise in the office and people have to wear headphones, but you can also find out things you weren’t aware of. You may be surprised to find out that people don’t know what others are doing, for example, or that no one has properly defined their role within the team. You may also find out that some don’t want to learn the business because it takes time out of their programming work, or that the Team Lead should probably not spend so much time in meetings but do more mentoring and coordination within the team. Maybe you find out about yourself as a Team Lead that you don’t delegate properly, or you’re perceived as a control freak. You must be able to receive criticism without getting angry or defensive. Some will think that you, as a Team Lead, must solve all of their problems, but you choose not to do so. And they also can find out that maybe it’s not in your power to fix all the problems, and they can understand and accept the situation, instead of secretly accusing you that you don’t care, ‘cause if you did, you would have done something about it. If you can’t change something, people need to be aware. But if it is in your power to change something, then do it. For example, at times, I had “friendly” discussions with bosses, Team Leads and managers, who, after listening to all my sorrows and pains, to all the things that I see wrong in the environment and that affect my work, things that I would like to change or improve and my solutions for doing so, they patted me on the shoulder, smiled, and told me “nice chatting with you”. Then nothing. No actions. No follow-ups. Nothing. The supervisors seemed well-intentioned and willing to help everyone, and they wanted the working environment to be better, but they were “all talk and no walk”. Some things were not in their power to solve, but those they could fix, they chose to ignore. What started like good one-on-one meetings slowly transformed into something useless and a complete waste of time.

Sometimes, people have no major problems with the working environment; they have only small frustrations from time to time. It helps them to have someone to talk to, vent the frustrations, or ask for advice, then happily get back to work. But if what they tell you are indeed real problems, something that’s not just letting off some steam, then you need to address them. The appraisal is to find out where you can help the employee, why they need help and how best to offer it, or what stands in their way and how you can remove that obstacle for them to improve on their own. Problems won’t get fixed just by talking about them; you have to actually do something. Improve the external issues and get rid of bad apples so that you get a healthy environment where people can grow and work to the best of their abilities. If you do not have the necessary authority to repair problems, escalate it above and then follow the evolution of things. Send reminders, insist on your bosses and superiors to do something.

Then even if you do everything well, you have honest, transparent conversations, you help everyone, you get rid of bad apples, work on external issues, etc., there is one other thing to be aware that can disrupt things: salaries. Developers constantly compare their skills with others, so if they find out that their colleague who does the same work as they do, makes more money, they will find it unfair. This then leads to envy, hard feelings, and all sorts of awkward situations.

Lots of times, you end up in such situations because companies keep salaries confidential (in that employees are not allowed to discuss with their peers how much money they make). It would be nice if all companies had objective and transparent pay scales, and no one would mind if everyone’s salaries were taped to the kitchen fridge one day[17], but in most companies, salaries are supposed to be a secret. Everyone wants to work you as hard as possible and pay you as little as possible. That’s just how things are. Then, salary also depends on each individual’s bargaining power (which differs from person to person), and it’s used as a way for companies to save money. If the fair market value for your experience and skills is, say $80,000, but you ask for $70,000, do you think the company will say “no, no, no, that’s not fair. You should get $80,000. We will give you $80,000”. Most of them won’t; they can use the $10,000 difference for something else. And sometimes it’s just market conditions that drive wages up and down. If the company absolutely needs to hire someone, they will have to pay “the price of the day”, and so when new people come, they come on higher wages than last year or a few years ago, even if you consider all the yearly raises or adjustments for inflation.

Aligning salaries with skills isn’t simple to do, since you don’t offer the salaries from your own pocket, but it’s again something to be aware of and something that you must try to do. If two people know and do mostly the same things, they should have largely the same salary. You can try using the appraisals to align wages with skills for everyone, so that when people learn how much others are making (which often happens), they can continue to focus on their work and not think about money all of the time (which negatively affects the work and effort of the employee), think they are in an unfair situation, or start thinking about “what other companies might pay for the same job?”

Exit interview

And finally, expect good people to leave. Even if the working environment isn’t dysfunctional in some way, and you and the company have done everything in your power to create a healthy environment, even so, people will leave. It’s normal. Employees are not married to the job or the company. They can go to work on their own project or startup, they might leave on a journey around the world, join a monastery, or take time off to write a book. It’s a dynamic industry with a lot of opportunities, so maybe they receive an offer they can’t refuse from another company. Some will leave after six months, others after ten years, depending on their situation or needs. The average is about 3-4 years for a job; then, most developers want to make a change to vary the monotony of their work or avoid getting stuck into a rut. If they can’t work on another project within the same company, they will go someplace else. Sometimes internal salary increases can’t keep up with market demands, so one might also be forced to go somewhere else after 3-4 years just so they can get a higher salary.

Before an employee leaves, there is one last thing you need to do: have an exit interview.

Just like any other stage in the employee’s life-cycle, an exit interview is something HR is in charge of. And just like the appraisals, again, they will have some standard process to do it. A form with some useful questions like “What made you start looking for another job?”, “Why are you leaving?”, “Would you consider working again for this organization in the future? Why/Why not?”, “How was your relationship with your manager?”, followed by a face-to-face discussion with someone from HR who doesn’t really care you are leaving, just wants to collect some data from you before you go. Questions like these might also be asked: “What would you have changed about your job?”, “Were you happy with your pay and benefits?”, “Did you receive enough training to do your job well?”. You’ll recognize these as similar to the ones above about the working environment. Isn’t it more meaningful to ask such questions to the people who still work in the company and want to improve things, not to those who are leaving the company and no longer care?

Logically speaking, the purpose of an exit interview is to identify areas where the company is doing well and where it needs to improve, identify the causes of turnover and figure out what can be done to prevent people from leaving in the future or at least stay longer with the company. However, an exit interview is too late to ask for these things. Those who leave have their minds elsewhere already (on their next job, future plans, etc.) and no longer care about any possible improvements you might bring to the working environment because they will no longer be affected by any changes since they are already on their way out. And everything turns into a formal discussion, which must be held because it’s part of the company rules. And just like the appraisals, they are poorly implemented, with the difference that if at the appraisals the company spoke to the employee, during the exit interview, the employee speaks to the company. An exit interview often seems like a kind of reversed appraisal. But unlike appraisals, where something usually happens (an increase in salary, someone getting fired, some changes done, some goals established, etc.) with an exit interview, often nothing happens. Unless the employee had enough and goes supernova in a very emotional way at the exit interview (which HR might dismiss as “venting”), most probably they will play the “it’s not you, it’s me” card when leaving, just to make sure they don’t burn any bridges by being honest or trying to avoid being labeled as a complainer if they do voice out any opportunities to improve the company or the working environment. So whoever reads the summaries of exit interviews thinks all is good and nothing needs to be improved, so nothing happens. Sometimes, the exit interview summaries are not even read by anyone other than the HR person who holds the interview, and that more from a sense of duty or proper HR practices than from the sincere desire to change something throughout the company. And so, a lot of things remain unchanged.

So let HR do their exit interview, fill in their questioners, or whatever, but have your own exit interview with the employee also, preferably before the one with HR. It’s more likely they will be honest and share more with you (a fellow developer) than they will do with HR. It is usually recommended to have such a discussion in the middle of the notice period when the person has overcome the emotional aspects of their resignation, but they have not yet mentally decoupled from the work or the company, but I prefer to talk as soon as possible. The sooner you talk with the employee, the greater chances for them to be more forthcoming and more sincere.

If you had regular and honest discussions with each of your team members for the appraisals, then what you will discuss at the exit interview will not be a surprise. But you can still discover things that people may not have wanted to tell you when they were working there. This discussion doesn’t need to be official; you don’t need to take any notes, just a face-to-face meeting in which you seek to collect some feedback - the last feedback. So listen rather than talk. During the appraisals, you discussed everyday work issues, during the exit interview is your chance to find out what that person wants to do with their career, in which direction they want to go, and why they could not do so in their current position.

And do something with the feedback you receive. Try to become better, do something for the team, identify problems that could have been prevented if you only had done something different when interacting with the person in their daily work, find the causes for which people are leaving and address them so that you prevent other people from quitting, communicate the problems above if any of the identified issues are not in your power to solve. If the person was a difficult one, had a bad attitude, or lacked the skills, and if you are the one who hired them, think about the interview you had, revisit your notes from the interview, and see if there were any signs back then that now are clearly visible. Was your interview technique flawed? Did you get influenced by someone? People were delighted with the low salary the person asked for, and they closed an eye on the lack of experience? Could matters have been prevented?

It’s really important

Before ending this chapter, I want to stress out again the importance of hiring and retaining good developers, people with the necessary skills but also with the right attitude, who are a good fit for your team and keep things moving smoothly. Don’t hire wrong people that can cause you problems. They will cause you problems! Hire good developers. Once hired, look out for them and make it so that they are productive. For this, you need a mechanism to identify the shortcomings or difficulties your employees face, help them grow and equip them with the necessary tools to do their job better, and remove the obstacles identified within the organization. Performance appraisals created by HR are not enough. You need decent appraisals on a regular basis, not just an awkward discussion once a year, which everyone then wants to forget until the same time next year when everything starts all over again with the pledge that things will be better.

Hiring and retaining good developers is similar to looking for, and owning, a pair of shoes. You must select a pair of shoes that fit properly from heel to toe. Then, you also need to take care of the shoes. You don’t use them in the wrong terrain, you keep them clean and dry, you polish them, etc. You normally don’t buy a pair of shoes two sizes smaller, that don’t fit well, give you blisters when you walk, hurt your feet when standing, and then forget about them in the back of a closet when you realize they are unsuitable, right?

Continuous learning

If you want to stay a good developer for a long time, then you need to be constantly learning stuff. It’s what gives you a competitive advantage. It’s also what keeps you in the game. Not learning new things for 2-3 years may potentially make you obsolete.

Most technologies tend to be replaced by better ones, or even by improved versions of the same technology. That’s because new needs always arise. If some problem is difficult to solve using current technology, or usage of the present technology is inadequate or lacking in some way, then people will start looking for better, more effective solutions, given that they have “an itch to scratch”, so to speak. And then people having the same “itch” start using the new technology, and it goes mainstream until it eventually turns into demand and supply, demand and supply for programmers that know the technology. If you’re not familiar with the currently sought out technologies, you might no longer be part of the supply. Just like people slowly give up on the services of a doctor who did not keep up with the progress in medicine or to a handyman who doesn’t use new materials, tools, or techniques, in the same way, companies give up on hiring software developers who are no longer up to date with current technologies. So you have to be aware of what is happening, to try to expand your mind, your career options, and try to remain “relevant”.

If you don’t like learning (or better said, “love learning”), you’re not passionate about what you do, you don’t want to put in the effort, or have better things to do with your time, then maybe software development isn’t for you.

English
