Let’s start with something very obvious and important to learn, but often neglected by many developers: learning a decent amount of English.

If English is your native language, good for you. There’s one less thing you need to worry about. But if it’s not, then you need to be able to read, write, speak, and - most importantly - understand English. You also need to make yourself understood to others. I have seen many developers using automatic translation tools, thinking it will do the trick. But it won’t necessarily work if what you want to express is complex. These tools are getting better and better, but you still risk getting back just a mot-à-mot translation, which may not reflect the same meaning of what you meant to say. And this applies in both directions, from your language into English, and from English into your native language. For example, did you ever read a poorly translated restaurant menu[18]? Were you absolutely sure you were ordering what you thought you were ordering?

English is not just for translating restaurant menus correctly. We live in a global economy, and opportunities can now come from almost anywhere on the planet. Care to guess which is the dominant business language in the world? A lot of the content on the Internet is in English. A lot of programming books are in English. What you are reading now is written in English. I could have written this in my native language (not English), but I wanted to reach more people with my content, thus… English.

Then there are conversations. In today’s business environment, a lot of accents are placed on face-to-face communication. According to Harvard Business Review[21], “Face-to-face communication contact is the broadest bandwidth communication you can have in professional life”, and when people cannot meet face-to-face, many use voice or video conferencing. That means talking, listening, and understanding things in real-time. In any company, there is a lot of written communication, but written communication isn’t carried out in real-time. You have time to rephrase sentences, you have time to look up words in the dictionary, there is spell checking, you can ask a colleague for help. When you are having a live conversation with someone, it’s different. Everything takes place in the here and now. You can’t ask someone to endlessly repeat what they said because you didn’t understand them. You cannot search the dictionary for words or terms in the middle of the discussion. If you did not understand or did not speak properly, what’s done is done. And so, problems in communication and in understanding occur.

To make things even more complicated, from what I’ve noticed, those who happen to be native English speakers don’t usually make an effort to simplify their wording when communicating something to non-English speakers, to reduce the risk of their audience misunderstanding things. It’s not something they do on purpose; that’s just how they talk in day to day life with other native speakers. For example, they might use familiar phrases and mistakenly assume that everyone understands them. If you apply automatic translation on idioms, you might do more harm than good. An automatic translation tool, for example, might not know what things like “beating a dead horse, a piece of cake, just what the doctor ordered, kicking the can down the road”, or “cutting corners”, might mean and translate them in a way that makes absolutely no sense to someone from another language. Just to give you an example of how fragile automatic translation is, if I type “a piece of cake” in my translation tool of choice, and translate it to Romanian, which is my native language, I get back “fleac”, which is the English meaning of “very easy”, “insignificant”, “trivial”. So the meaning of the idiom was translated correctly. But if I type just “piece of cake”, I get back “bucată de tort”, which literally means a piece of a cake you can eat. Just one letter added or removed, and I got back something completely different. So don’t count on translation tools. They are good, but not very good. You risk losing the true meaning of the phrase.

To give you another example, one of my neighbors has the following sign on his front gate:

He’s assuming all burglars know English. Luckily, the dog picture helps with getting the message across.

So if you are not a native English speaker, then put in the effort and try to be fluent in the language so that you actually understand expressions someone else takes for granted. And if English is your native language, keep an eye on the person you are talking to, to spot signs of confusion; it’s also your responsibility to make sure that what you say gets correctly understood.

Then, another problem I encountered is not that people don’t know English, but that they can’t pronounce it properly. For example, there are many English accents. French people speak a certain way, German people a certain way, Indian people a certain way, Australian people speak a certain way, and so on. Even across England, there are multiple accents. Inevitably, people speak with an accent that is specific to the area in which they live. The English words are the same, but the way the sounds comes out of people’s mouth is different. For someone who doesn’t understand someone else’s accent, the other person’s English seems broken. So you have to try to speak English clearly. My suggestion is to strive for Standard American English pronunciation, not necessarily because I think it’s the best, but because of a particular exposure factor: Hollywood movies. So if you don’t speak English well, practice. Watch movies and see if you understand everything without reading the subtitles. Compare the way you speak with how the actors speak. Heck, you can even talk with your phone. Change your language settings to American English and talk to any AI personal assistant you happen to have installed on your device, and see if it understands you.

Communication is not something that needs to be deciphered or feel like solving riddles. It must be conducted as fluently as possible. It doesn’t necessarily need to be perfect (for example, many English natives reading this book may have probably noticed some clumsy or awkward wording), have complete mastery over the language, getting the grammar precisely right, or know all the words in the dictionary, but you have to reach a level where you can communicate without lose of information or giving rise to misunderstandings - otherwise, things become frustrating.

One final word before I move on to the next subject. In the previous chapter, in my list of topics for the interview, you may have noticed that I also have an “English” item. I also check language skills during the interview by having a part of the conversation with the applicant in English. Maybe you’re a good developer, but if English is the official language for all communications done inside the company, and the job opening involves interactions with many people, but you are incredibly awkward or unskilled when you speak English during the interview, then you will most likely be turned down for the position. Unless you spend all your time writing code inside the server room having no interactions with other living souls, then a bad mastery of the English language can often be an eliminating criterion when applying for jobs.

Solid foundations

After English skills, what you need to have is a solid programming foundation. Concepts like operators and control-flow structures, data types and data structures, flowcharts, understanding binary and hex, common algorithms (like sorting and searching, traversing trees and graphs), Big-O notation, recursion, pointers, objects and classes, compiled vs. interpreted languages, testing, debugging, asynchronous vs. synchronous code, multi-threading, and concurrency, how to organize your code, how to read a stack-trace or an error message, sane programming principles (like the proper way to name stuff, avoiding code duplication, removing magic constants, high cohesion and loose coupling), various programming paradigms (imperative, declarative, OOP, functional, event-driven), refactoring, logging, security, design patterns, design principles like SOLID, how your computer or the network works, what spaghetti code is, or realizing that reading and understanding code is more difficult than writing it. And the list can go on. Basically, I’m referring to the tools that you can use, no matter in what programming language you write code into. If you are a graduate with a computer science degree, some of these things may have been taught to you in school. But don’t count on what school teaches you. School can’t prepare you adequately. It simply can’t because it can’t keep up with the fast-evolving software industry. So the foundation you (may have) received with your formal education may not be a very solid one. School can’t give you all the proper skills for a job in a professional setting. If you don’t know such concepts or school has done a poor job teaching some of them, then you have to learn and fill in any gaps on your own.

These concepts can be applied to a wide range of problems. Many new ideas are sometimes just old ideas repackaged in a different way or with a shinier wrapping. If you are already familiar with the old ideas, it will be easier for you to understand the new ones. So, in the long run, it is better to invest first in this foundation and then in technologies. Technologies come and go. A solid foundation remains and will help you pick up any new concept or technology or adapt to new languages and platforms easier because you can recognize these concepts in most programming languages, but perhaps expressed in different ways or sometimes with variations in how they work. They are also a means of communication. Someone might explain a more complex concept with analogies or more straightforward or basic concepts such as these, that may capture the gist of the problem. If you don’t know these notions, you won’t be able to understand the explanation. Sometimes it’s assumed that you know a few things. Take, for example, books for learning a new programming language. Most of them don’t teach you about data types, or control structures, or operators, or functions, or scope, or classes, or inheritance, or whatever. They teach you how these are expressed in that particular language, and it’s assumed you already know how they work.

So far, I’ve used the word “learning”, and I will continue using it. But don’t think it means just “knowing stuff about something”. By “learning”, I mean educating yourself on things, practicing those things, and growing a skill that you can apply on the job. The point of learning is to build skills, i.e., the ability to use the learned knowledge on specific problems. Besides university education that teaches you the theory, consider certifications as an example. If you have a certification, then it means you took some time to learn the subject matter, prepared for and passed an exam. But at the end of the day, what do certifications prove? They prove precisely that; that you can learn some material, then pass a test. That’s it. They don’t confirm you actually understand the material or that you can apply it to something useful. Knowing the material doesn’t necessarily translate to skills at work. It’s like the difference between knowing about skiing and knowing how to ski. You might pass a written test on skiing very easily but find it hard to keep your balance or avoid all those trees moving in your direction when you actually try it. As a developer, at most, you should expect tests at the hiring interview; after that, people expect you to do real work. And you need skills for that. That’s also why people with jobs get “training” while people in school get an “education”.

In school, your practical skills are mostly used for homework, not real-world problems. You are given clear instructions and requirements, you then spend a lot of time trying to find the best solution for your assignment, you maybe look for that algorithm or obscure mathematical formula that makes your program run in O(1) no matter what, maybe write beautiful documentation to get some extra points, then you turn in your homework, you take your grade, and “au revoir”. It’s not like that at work. You still look for the best solution to your problem, but the result is now usable software, not a grade. Now you turn in “your homework” and take care of it throughout the lifetime of the project or while working in the company. The solution you find must be maintainable and (if necessary) extensible. And unlike school, once you get your grades and your diploma, no one then makes you to retake your exams because the technology changed, to change your diploma because a new model came out this year, or that the papers you received no longer comply with current laws and must be replaced with other documents within the next six months. When school is over, it’s over. You get your degree and walk away. In software development, it’s different. The result matters, but it’s not permanent. Did you get to a result? Good. That result is valid and good now. Within a year, it may no longer be enough and must be changed, must be improved, or must be scaled. Long story short… you must take some more exams :). Note also that the approach is also different, or in other words, the end cannot justify the means. It doesn’t matter how you got a grade (if you don’t get caught, you might even cheat), it matters, on the other hand, how you built software, so it doesn’t haunt you at night or cause you trouble later on. For all these things, you need a solid foundation, so you know what you are doing… because many have no clue what they’re doing; but I’ll get to that later.

So if you’ve just finished your education and you’re applying for your first job, be aware that in the professional world, it’s all about applying the knowledge to build something people will use. It’s not about taking an exam where you regurgitate something you might have learned by heart. So you will need a different mindset. Besides, now you get paid a salary, so everyone expects you to produce useful things, not grades.

Another thing that happened in school was that you were told what to learn and in what order. What was in the curriculum, basically, a curriculum where others laid out a map for you of what needed to be learned. Don’t expect that to happen any longer. From now on, you need to be self-taught. You have to decide what to learn, from where to learn it, and in what order. And speaking of order, you will most likely not learn things in a specific order anymore. For example, in the first year of college, you learned some topics, then in the second year, other topics having those of the first year as prerequisites, and so on. At work, you learn seven different things at once, in a bizarre order. For instance, I’ve encountered several situations where front-end developers first learned JQuery and only then JavaScript. An unfortunate situation, but one that happens more often than you can imagine. If at school it was about finding out how things work, at work, it’s about delivering products first, and possibly figure out how it works later… if at all. Sadly, sometimes you acquire skills first and knowledge second. You might do something and only later discover what you have actually done (or maybe your colleagues will find out after you no longer work in the company). You will be thrown headfirst on many occasions. You have to expose yourself to things; you have to apply yourself, focus, or jump through hoops. You have to figure out things pretty much on your own. Nobody has the time to hold your hand and explain to you stuff, unless that is actually their job (like a Team Lead, or a coach). At work, the team deadlines don’t change because you are a freshly hired junior. Everyone has their own work to do. It’s not like in school where teachers and assistants are there to explain things to you. On the job, people are there to work. You are there to work. You have to get things done. Things that get sold, not graded. And in the beginning, you do them somehow, regardless of how, just so they work and you get to respect your deadlines. You think that “I’ll fix it later”. Then “later” never comes, because after you finish something, there is something else to do. You do not have an inter-semester vacation. This means you will pick up bad habits, and as you know, bad habits are hard to shake. And things like this happen daily. It is as if you were given an exam not only from the topics you did not learn but also from topics that were not even taught to you. At school, it would not be fair, but at work, it’s totally acceptable.

Then, when you need to solve a problem, you won’t even get exact requirements like when you received problems at an exam. Some requirements may contradict one another, you might need to gather and analyze requirements on your own, you might not know what tools to use, you might catch and ignore exceptions, you might reinvent the wheel because that’s what you did in school while not knowing there was already something implemented that you could reuse. You might have considered just the “happy path”, and QA then points out the shortcomings in your design, which you will patch by adding another “if” to an already very complex set of conditions. You might commit too late (because again, in school, this wasn’t important). Your PC crashed? Ups… Start all over again while everyone is giving you the stink eye. String concatenation of parameter values in an SQL query? That’s fun. And so is debugging for two days only to realize you misplaced a semicolon or that you accidentally declared a variable global. And you will do these things on an existing codebase that you don’t fully understand yet. So you will make many mistakes. If you have a solid foundation of notions and skills, it will allow you to minimize these mistakes or make better use of them to learn.

Mistakes

A developer’s job is not like the residency of doctors in the hospital or the lawyers’ apprenticeship in a law firm, where at first you do something under supervision before you can work entirely on your own. As a developer, you learn as you go, on the job, directly on the company’s product, in production, with live data, often without anyone to oversee what you are doing. It’s impossible not to make mistakes. If you work on an existing project that’s been around for some time, you will also surely discover many examples of mistakes others have made. Bad code isn’t written just by bad developers but also by inexperienced developers. Good or bad, everyone is inexperienced at first. Even those who are now experts made a lot of mistakes. Actually, that’s exactly what makes an expert, someone who’s done all the mistakes one can make; here is a joke about it:

The son of a prosperous businessman asks his father:
– Dad, what’s the secret of your success?
– Two words.
– What are they?
– “Correct decisions”.
– Hmm… And how do you know what the right decisions are?
– One word.
– What’s that?
– “Experience”.
– Hmm… And how do you get experience?
– Two words.
– What are they?
– “Wrong decisions”.

A typical progression for many developers in the job market is sometimes this: they learn things, they apply what they’ve learned, they make mistakes, learn from those mistakes, become good at their job, they repeat these steps until they become proficient, reach a plateau of knowledge in their current company, go to another company where they learn new things, make fewer mistakes (or make entirely new mistakes), become proficient in doing the work in that company, reach another plateau, move to another company, and so on. What also happens in such cases is that other developers have to deal with the consequences of the mistakes made by others before them. To a certain degree, you will follow a similar course and deal with similar issues. Sometimes, you can stay in the company long enough to clean up your mess and improve your code, but if you no longer work on the application or the company, the code remains untouched. To give an example, I once worked with a very skilled senior developer. At one point, I had to make some changes to an application he built many years before, and I found some things that didn’t make sense with the implementation. Knowing the man and knowing he was a good developer, I thought that maybe there was nothing wrong with the code, but something that I’m missing. I went to him with the code in question and said that “I’ve found some issues with this code of yours. I don’t understand why it is like it is. Am I missing something? Can you have a look?”. After a short conversation where I explained my concerns, he looked at the code, smiled, and responded, “That’s all I was capable of doing at that time. The code is wrong. You should fix it”.

So expect to make mistakes, and expect to find lots of mistakes in someone else’s code. It’s important that you learn from all of them.

A smart man learns from his mistakes. A wise one learns from the mistakes of others - Unknown

When I say mistakes, I don’t mean “stupid mistakes”. I mean “honest mistakes”. Dropping the production database because you didn’t pay enough attention to which server you were connected to or what you were doing is a stupid mistake. An honest mistake is something you did for a good reason, with the knowledge you had at that time, expecting a good outcome but getting back an unexpected or wrong result. Honest mistakes help you grow and add to your experience. Stupid mistakes, on the other hand, don’t build experience; at most, they make you more careful in the future. You will be making both honest and stupid mistakes, that’s what being human means, but you should try to eliminate the silly mistakes and learn a lot of things to try to minimize the honest ones. For both kinds, it is essential not to persist in your mistakes. That would be a sign that you are not learning, and in the developer profession, if you do not learn continuously, you do not last long. So learn from your mistakes. They help you grow.

Let me be clear. I’m not saying to go to work tomorrow and fuck everything up on purpose, to see what you can learn from the experience. What I’m saying is that you can make some mistakes in a “controlled” setting. For example, if you have a personal project at home, one that you don’t publish to users but only use to learn new things, you can make mistakes there. You apply more of your knowledge, find out how stuff works, experiment to see what works and what doesn’t, etc. Some companies recognize this as a way to learn things, especially when you are building something that has never been done before. So part of their policies might include building proof of concepts or prototypes for the developers to make mistakes, learn from those types of projects, then with the lessons learned, in hindsight, start working on the real application. Because software is often built as a novelty (otherwise, you would have used existing software), mistakes will inevitably be made. So, by creating something fast, you rapidly make mistakes that you learn from and avoid when it’s time to build the real thing. It’s what a long time ago when Waterfall[22] was still the typical way of developing software, was known as “Plan to throw one away”[23]. The idea was to make mistakes on a “test subject” and not directly on the project you would deliver to the client (where you would discover the mistakes too late, on an already released product).

Then another way to recognize mistakes is to read about bad practices, anti-patterns or code smells. You will not always make mistakes in unique ways, others have already made the mistakes you are making now, and many may already be documented. Look at this book, for example; it’s about mistakes that you should try to avoid, mistakes that I and others before me have made and continue making.

And finally, another excellent way to learn is to participate in code reviews. If someone reviews your code - someone more experienced, or at least someone with a different perspective on things - they can catch and point out your mistakes, or suggest better ways to implement something. Code reviews are an excellent way to learn from your mistakes since if you make any blunders, after the code review, you will have to fix them yourself.

Mentors

If you are lucky, you will find a mentor to take you under their wing, to share with you from their experience, without you having to make all sorts of possible mistakes. Having a mentor can take your development to the next level faster than you could do on your own. Instead of struggling through the swamp of information and piecing together all sorts of bits to gain knowledge, a mentor can tell you where to look for more details or where the quicksands are hidden.

But a mentor doesn’t mean that you’ll be all set for becoming the best developer, and everything that follows will be a breeze. A mentor won’t solve all of your career challenges. It’s not similar to unlocking the next level in a video game. You have to make an effort and learn on your own. What a mentor can do is to encourage you and build your confidence, making themselves available to answer questions, share their knowledge and experience, identify lacks in knowledge or misunderstandings and recommend relevant study material to fix it. They can condense information into small digestible nuggets, letting you make certain mistakes to figure it out for yourself, or offering new perspectives when they see you heading too much in the wrong direction or when you get stuck or struggle. A mentor can and help you achieve your goals in the best way possible. But ultimately, it’s your effort. They won’t drive the process and tell you exactly what to do. A mentor is there to provide guidance, not download information in your head or feed you with a spoon.

What you can learn most from a mentor is related to experience. If you’ve just started out in the field, a mentor is a person that has already reached the place you want to be, and they can point out different landmarks in the direction you want to go.

If you do find a mentor, then good. Excellent even. But be careful, though. Often juniors meet some senior with awesome technical skills, turn them into a role model and then stick to them like chewing gum to the sole of a shoe, thinking that some of the skills will rub off if they mimic the behaviors or the beliefs. “OOP must be shit if they say so. Test-Driven Development must be the solution to everything if they say so. IDEs are for pussies; all you will ever need is Vim”. Staying up until 03:00 A.M. coding is the most important skill to have since that’s what shows up most often in the war stories you hear from your mentor; that and the “I’m the best, fuck the rest” attitude. So be very careful. It’s often easier to follow someone else’s opinions rather than having your own, especially if it comes from someone you look up to. And then you can easily end up thinking that “what worked for them will surely work for me”.

There is good and bad in everyone, and we all make mistakes (in case it wasn’t already clear from the previous sections). Don’t think a mentor is the same as a Jedi Master or a Shaolin Monk that spreads wisdom around. You can get good and bad advice from anyone. So think critically about what you’re told and about the advice you’re given. And this is most important if your mentor is “assigned” to you. I mentioned in the previous chapter that some companies try to grow their developers in house. Newly hired interns and graduates are sometimes paired by HR or management with a senior developer who is supposed to handle them. And HR will call these seniors “mentors” as if seniority is the only pre-requirement for mentorship.

Most of the developers I’ve met don’t have it in them to be mentors, or they think they wouldn’t be good at it, and for this reason, they don’t even try. Others have big egos and make the mentoring all about themselves, of how great and smart they are, so they become control freaks and demand the mentee to do all their biddings. I have a “mentoring” item in my list of interview topics, and I always bring this subject into the discussion with applicants, but it’s hard to find someone with mentoring skills since developers rarely receive any training in this area. And assigning unskilled mentors never works. Many lose patience; they neglect their mentees or yell orders instead of providing advice or hints for people to reach their own conclusions. Some are bored because they already have a few other juniors under their supervision, and they keep repeating the same things over and over again. Some forget who they are talking to, so they explain topics at their level of understanding, forgetting how it was like to be a novice. Some might not even be real seniors; their ten years of (so-called) experience is just one year repeated ten times (mostly on that crappy application nobody else in the company wants to touch). And often, seasoned developers view things from their own perspective, recalling their own successes and failures, then try to create from the mentee a duplicated image of themselves; “I did this, you must do this. I avoided that, so you must avoid that. My career path will become your career path”.

Pure blooded programmers often suck at this mentoring thing (or most other soft skills for that matter), while those with leadership skills have too much to handle trying to keep in balance too many things to also have the time to be a true mentor; a part-time mentor, at most. It’s a Team Lead’s job, for example, to help those in their team grow, but don’t expect hand-holding all day long. So my suggestion would be to make an active effort to learn from everyone (juniors, seniors, developers, testers, managers, strangers on the Internet…) and don’t obsess too much about having a mentor.

Technologies

Going back to what you have to learn, a foundation is very good; it’s a stepping stone for other things. But it’s insufficient. Companies hire on technology too; if they have an ASP.NET project, they will not look for a PHP developer, for example. You might get an entry job with fundamentals only, but beyond your first job, most companies won’t hire you if you are unfamiliar with the technologies they are using. So it’s important, besides building some solid foundations, to ask yourself what technologies you should learn. Something you use at work for starters. But what then? Learn something well, but then it disappears in a few years… whoops!. Was it lucrative as a Flash developer so far? Sure! But there is no future on this path anymore. Did you specialize in something that is now only used on legacy applications? Whoops again. So maybe you’ll try some technologies that look good on your CV? Perhaps something that might be big in the near future, like artificial intelligence, the Internet of things, augmented and/or virtual reality, or blockchain technology? You never know what will happen with technology in the future. Something can look very beneficial now and feel like you are digging in a gold mine while in the future, turn up completely wasteful, and actually feel like having dug your own grave. Just like trying to predict the stock market or the winning lottery numbers, trying to predict what will happen to technology in the future is impossible.

So how do you decide on your next thing to learn so that you reach a happy outcome?

Most people get into new technology because of hype (especially if you are a front-end developer; I have nothing against front-end developers, but seriously now… get off the “hype horse”). Something new, fresh, or exciting gets your attention. People around you are talking about the thing. You see a lot of interest in the developer community about it. You check it out to see what it’s all about. You are curious. You like it, and you start learning it. Or maybe you hate it, in which case you no longer pay much attention to it. Is it the right decision to learn it? A wrong decision not to learn it? Or maybe it’s the other way around all together? You don’t know. The community could gather around some new technology, it could be the hottest topic at every conference, you can feel people’s enthusiasm as they contribute documentation and projects on GitHub, with libraries, frameworks, and tooling appearing. It will look like the new best thing since sliced bread, only to then see those trends reverse, fall, and forever remain into a phase that in the Gartner’s Hype Cycle[24] is suitably named “the trough of disillusionment”:

You can’t just think if you only like something or not. You also have to consider if the technology looks like something with potential, something that you think will help you going forward. It’s that “predicting the future” thing all over again. Chances are, however, that you might find yourself working with one of the major languages like C#, Java, JavaScript, Python, or PHP. So go from there… I suppose.

Just remember that it won’t be easy. And you never know ahead of time if you are making the right decision. For example, although I’ve always thought of myself as a full-stack developer, I’ve tended to gravitate towards back-end technologies. I know JavaScript, and I’ve built some very heavy front-end clients with various frameworks, but I have done few things with CSS. I never learned CSS beyond elementary usage because fiddling with pixels on the screen just isn’t my thing. I simply don’t like it. I find it wasteful to spend a few hours trying to make some text properly fit inside a div on ten versions of three different browsers. I’m generally a patient person, but arranging stuff on the screen drives me completely insane. I understood the need to learn CSS, but I eventually decided to invest less effort in that direction.

Another thing is that I don’t know PHP because it never attracted me. Writing HTML, PHP, JavaScript, and MySQL within the same file (that was the style back then) didn’t quite sound right to me. So instead, I moved to C, C++, and later Java and C#. Did I make the right decision? Who knows. It’s worked out pretty well for me… I guess. Was another path more successful? I will never know. It’s too late for me to start again. Now, in all likelihood, if I were to start over again, it makes less sense to learn C or C++ because they are not so much in demand anymore. There are few C++ jobs and almost none for C in my region. And this gets me to the next point. Think about money and employment too.

Yes, yes, something is cool, and you like it, you are following your heart and your passion, you create beautiful designs in that language, your code simply flows. But you also have to eat. You might be a big Haskell fan, but you might end up a hungry fan if there are zero Haskell jobs in your area. So look at something that’s also in demand, so you can get a good-paying job. You can combine it with what you like to do and whatever attracts you, but don’t forget you have bills to pay, maybe car payments, or even a mortgage. Try to think long term. My advice is to not jump directly onto something very new. Give it some time. It’s just like going shopping. You see something you want, you think you need it, and you want to buy it. Wait a few more days and see if you still want it as much, and if you truly need it. Only then buy it. Do the same with technology. When you find out about something new, study a bit, find out a few things about it, then let it sit for a while before deciding if you want to go deep or not. Of some help in deciding is the number of jobs you find in the respective technology. If there aren’t any, you can afford to wait a little longer. You can revisit the decision when jobs start showing up.

However, try not to fall into the other extreme and get into some technology only for the money. This usually involves old, niche, exotic, or sometimes even proprietary languages that few people know. COBOL[25], for example, might be very well paid in your country (especially since all the specialists are now retiring), but can very easily be outsourced to other countries and be performed by armies of young graduates who get paid less. If you are in said outsourcing country, then maybe that works for you, but be careful not to risk getting stuck in that technology. Another (extreme) example I encountered was a programming language built in house and known only by four people (one was already dead, one was retiring, and a fifth person was in training to learn it). If you’ve invested a lot in such technologies and find yourself out of work, it will be difficult for you to find another job if you don’t know other technologies or if your mindset is stuck in that technological paradigm. You don’t want to become a “one-trick pony” or end up by “putting all of your eggs in the same basket”.

Specialist vs. Generalist

Speaking of a one-trick pony, another aspect to think about is the following: what kind of a developer do you want to be? Some companies are looking for generalists, others for specialists. This is another thing that’s hard to decide upon. You get to an interview, and people look over your CV, and what do they see? “Hmmm… I see you did a year of C#. Then you moved to Java for five years, then C# three years, now you want Java again. Hmmm… you seem undecided. You still don’t know what you want to do when you grow up or what? Usually, a developer chooses a language and specializes in the technology stack of that language. You just go back and forth”. Then you go to your next interview. “Hmmm… I see some C#, Java, JavaScript, Python, web services… Hmmm… Sorry but not enough. I mean, no mobile development, no Swift or at least Objective-C or something. Hmmm… I see you have an interest in Haskell. Why didn’t you learn Scala instead? And I don’t see you contributing to any open source projects! What the heck have you been doing all this time? You call yourself a developer?”

There are advantages and disadvantages to whether you choose to become a specialist or a generalist.

Specialists are the answer to the increasingly complex applications we have today. Now more than ever, there is a need for specialization. Having someone doing all of the work on a large application, end-to-end, is becoming less common. We have front-end developers who don’t do any work on the back-end, back-end developers who don’t do any front-end, we have database administrators or SQL developers, we have deployment engineers, someone else takes care of configuring the network, and so on. When companies hire someone, they are usually looking for a specialist in one of these areas. So, as a specialist, you are more “attractive” to employers. You (usually) also make more money. But if you want to be really good at something, then you need to invest the time. The time that you invest in mastering a subject is time that you take away from learning other things. If then the technology you specialize in dies out or is replaced by something better, or if it disappears, so does your investment in it. Another disadvantage is that if you look for another job, you will be able to apply only to those positions that match your specialization. With time “professional deformation” can also appear, which is a tendency to not be able (or willing) to look beyond that specialization, which then means you can lose the broader picture when solving problems since you try to fit and solve everything using your expert knowledge alone.

I suppose it is tempting, if the only tool you have is a hammer, to treat everything as if it were a nail - Abraham H. Maslow[26]

As a generalist, you can solve a broader range of problems since you don’t have the narrow focus created by your specialization. Having an understanding of a broader collection of subjects can be an advantage as it gives you more options or solving techniques when approaching a problem, allow you to see the bigger picture better or easier, or how different things interact with each other. You are also less restricted with your career options as you can apply for a broader set of jobs. But this doesn’t mean that a generalist is better than a specialist. You are now a “Jack of all trades”, which comes with its own disadvantages. You can easily overlook some details since your knowledge of a specific topic might not go deep enough; you can end up building a solution that works, but be unable to recognize how poor it is. It is also just as time-consuming (if not more) than specializing in something since you need to focus your attention on multiple things instead of one. And you are not as valuable to a company for the simple fact that you are… well… not a specialist.

You don’t know who is looking for what: for a specialist or a generalist. Again, you have to think carefully to see what would be best for you in the long term and what kind of developer you want to be. When it comes to your broad knowledge and your areas of expertise, you will meet the following types of developers[27][28]: I-shaped, T-shaped, PI-shaped, and Comb-shaped. These are just fancy ways of referring to combinations of depth of knowledge and breadth of knowledge, saying that you can be a specialist, a generalizing specialist (i.e., generalist with one specialty), someone with expert knowledge in two areas, or in three or more, respectively.

You will most likely end up being at least a T-shaped developer. Except for academia, where you can research a topic in complete isolation (the I-shaped type), in the real world, applications are heterogeneous beasts. You can’t have something build exclusively with one technology (well, maybe you can, but it’s not always practical). There might be some Java or C# on the back-end, some SQL, some Python scripts, HTML, JavaScript, CSS. You might have an API exposed with REST or whatever. You can’t really be isolated from everything. For example, let’s say you want to do just CSS (you won’t be much of a developer, but for the sake of argument, let’s assume it). You still need to learn HTML. CSS without HTML is useless. Then, you discover that some things are impossible to do with CSS only, so you might need to use some JavaScript or some jQuery to add some extra effects. Then maybe after the project grows in size, you might discover that SASS would bring a lot of benefits compared to writing everything in plain vanilla CSS. Or maybe you wrote some jQuery, a lot of it actually, and you realize some JavaScript framework might be useful to clear up the code and make everything more manageable and more readable. Then you want to have your thing, whatever it is, available on mobiles and tablets, so you need to learn responsive and mobile design. UX skills will also be important. Maybe there is no point in doing all of this from scratch; WordPress might do just fine, for example. But maybe the self-hosted WordPress version doesn’t cut it for what you want to do, or maybe you want full control over it, or maybe you want to create your special themes. What do you do? For starters, you might learn some PHP. Maybe your application then becomes very successful, but during the holidays, traffic increases so much that your server can’t handle it anymore. Hence, you figure you need more processing power during that period. You might move your solution into the cloud because it might be cheaper than buying a server that stays mostly unused for the rest of the year. As software becomes increasingly complex, there are more and more pieces that you need to use or put together to build a working result: various programming languages, frameworks, different types of databases, message brokers, IDEs, build tools, version control, virtualization, multiple operating systems, multiple browsers, and device compatibility, garbage collection, performance optimizations, memory management, configuration management, multi-threading, the cloud, security considerations, and so on and so on. There will be something you will need and use the most, so you will probably specialize in that, while everything else will fall in the general category of “I know just enough to get stuff done”, but you also need to learn these well enough to build something useful. There are tools that help you and make your job easier, but you have to learn those too and understand how to use them.

And depending on what you work on, or on your reasons for doing a certain work, your specialization may change over time. You might replace the vertical bar of the T-shape with something else, while the horizontal bar becomes wider. You might become a PI-shaped developer when you acquire your new expertise, but in time you will forget the old one or fall behind on what’s needed to keep it up to date. I’ve rarely seen PI-shaped or Comb-shaped developers. I’ve also rarely seen someone who started as an I-shaped developer and then moved to a T-shaped. Most new developers don’t belong to any category. They are dot-shaped developers (for lack of a better name): they haven’t specialized in anything, they are still building the foundation, and they need to invest lots of time and lots of effort to develop their skills in both the horizontal and vertical direction.

Too much information

You need to keep learning as the industry evolves and the technology environment changes. But there’s a catch. You can’t absorb the information at the same pace the industry advances. You simply can’t. That means you will never know everything you would want to know about something. If you try to know everything about everything, you will only end up disappointed and overwhelmed. Just being “aware” of things, and not fully knowing them, is a reality of the industry. The sooner you realize and accept this, the better for you. To give you an example, when I was younger, I had this impression that I could learn everything there is to know about a language, like Java. I wanted to know as much as possible so that I can be well prepared to handle any situation that would present itself, be it some solution to code or some problem to fix. So I was reading the Sun Certified Programmer for Java Study Guide (back then it was still Sun), then I started reading The Java Language Specification only to realize that I need to also read The Java Virtual Machine Specification, then see what’s interesting over at the Java Community Process website, and so on, and so on. I tried to do the same with other things as well, like data structures. There are so many of them[29] that by the time I would read about the last one, I had already forgotten about the first. And here comes another catch: it’s all about repetition.

Learning is an active process. We learn by doing. Only knowledge that is used sticks in your mind - Dale Carnegie[30]

If you don’t revisit your knowledge, you will surely forget things. When you continuously learn new stuff, less and less time will go into rehearsing the stuff you already know. When it comes to applying the information, you can be really good at a skill only if you practice it often; otherwise, you will forget that too, or at least get rusty. If you don’t use your knowledge often or refresh your memory on older topics, slowly, they will fade away as you invest most of your time in the new things you are learning or using. So you need to apply what you learn so that the information is consolidated in your mind. In addition to that, when you learn something but don’t apply what you learned, you don’t even know if you understood the information correctly or not, if it’s enough or not, if it’s good or bad. Nothing! There is no materialization of your knowledge, to look at it and evaluate it. Learning is useless if you don’t do anything with the information. It’s “input” only. You need “output” too. I come back to the example of the certification. Have you taken a certification exam and passed the test? Congratulations! However, the real test is to use that information to make an application that the people can use; otherwise, the diploma you received does not help you with much, unless you really wanted to frame it and hang it on your wall.

When talking about mistakes, I mentioned personal projects that you could use to apply what you learn (if you can’t apply them at work, for example). That’s one way of “doing”. Doing can also mean to take part in a community like Stack Overflow. You learn a lot when you try to explain notions to others. Explaining a concept helps you grasp it better. You often need to simplify it without losing its essence, and you can do that only when you know the subject well, and you can structure the material in such a way as to be easily understood by others. You might also need to explain things in different ways for different people. This not only improves your communication skills but will often reveal gaps in your knowledge. So answer other people’s questions. Find questions that are slightly beyond what you currently know, or about things that you thought you knew, but the question someone else asked makes you doubt that or puts things in a different perspective. Find the fix or the solution, then formulate a response to explain it to others. People might have follow-up questions or will ask “why?” or “how?” multiple times, making you delve deeper into the subject until you find you need to learn more things in order to respond again, thus increasing your understanding of the subject even more. If you make mistakes or misunderstand something, you can be sure you’ll get immediate, honest feedback from other users. You can also read the answers others have posted to the same question, answers that may contain further details, and so on.

And the sheer volume of information you need to learn is staggering. And that applies even when you have the information nicely available in some book or something. Try searching a topic on Google, and you get more than a million results.

Getting information off the Internet is like taking a drink from a fire hydrant - Mitchell Kapor[31]

There is too much information that’s not always readily available, and you need to spend time looking for it. Then, whatever you find, you don’t know if it’s any good or if it’s garbage until you go through it. You don’t know if there are essential things that you are missing or if it’s something you need to learn right now, or you can get back to it later. You think everything takes too much time to learn, you find out you can’t explain something you thought you understood, and you eventually get frustrated and angry, or start to feel guilty that you are ignoring some information or that the pile of unread books on your desk grows larger and larger and that you have so many bookmarked sites to read later that the bookmark manager of your browser crashes when you try to open it. And when you finally learn something very well and are pleased with your achievement, a new version of it becomes available, and you feel compelled to learn it too. Everything starts feeling like you’re on a hamster wheel, and no matter how fast you run, you never seem to be getting where you want to be. There are simply too many of the things you think you need to know or you want to learn, and you can easily feel overwhelmed. This causes what’s called “information anxiety”[35].

I think the more you know, the more you realize just how much you don’t know. So paradoxically, the deeper down the rabbit hole you go, the more you might tend to fixate on the growing collection of unlearned peripheral concepts that you become conscious of along the way - Dave Ward[36]

The old days when the official language documentation was enough, or you had some good technical journals you could consult are long gone (assuming you’ve lived those times). I remember looking for stuff in the Turbo Pascal[37] help files and in the only three printed books that existed about the language in my country. It seems silly now. Today, there are books on every programming language. Many, many books. And many blogs, feeds, podcasts, online tutorials, and a high amount of other sources. If you run into some issues, you’ll have to do research and look for information mostly online, where any clown can have an opinion, and any fool (like me, for example) can write and publish a book, without you knowing if the content is valuable or not. A lot of things now, unfortunately, are similar to looking for a needle in a haystack.

But there is also a good part, which ironically is that there is indeed this ton of information available. You can learn a lot without costing you a fortune, with many of the resources being freely available. We live in this wonderful age in which almost all information is at your fingertips if you have an Internet connection. The problem, unfortunately, is that we now have great quantity but not necessarily great quality, and it’s your job to put the pieces together from what you read on the first (hopefully) two pages of your Google results. You will spend a lot of time searching online, and you will eventually look for some answers you can’t find. You start wondering if you are the first to need some information or if you are completely lousy at writing good search queries. And to add insult to injury, some of those searches will occur late at night or during some urgent situation when there is a problem with the production environment, and you’re trying to find out something about that weird error message you’re getting and which you’ve never seen before, and the clock is ticking, and the sysadmin insists on rebooting the server, and your boss is on the phone asking you why it is taking so long, with you constantly trying to multitask (which by the way… you can’t).

So what do you do? As I said earlier, you need to accept the fact that you can’t learn everything. Then you keep learning even if you know there is no end. You need to step on that hamster wheel and keep a constant pace of running. Be curious and learn stuff. When you encounter a problem that you don’t know how to solve with what you already know (and this will happen often, rest assured), you’ll just deal with it when it happens. You will then learn enough to find a solution (you should also make sure you understand the solution, not just copy-paste code from Stack Overflow :)). If you want to specialize in something, you will put a lot of intentional effort in that direction, but for many other things, you’ll go more in-depth when something comes up. It’s not ideal, since you basically stumble in darkness and from time to time you turn on a light, and maybe you don’t even like where you’ve ended up, and you have to go back, but that’s how it is, there is not much that can be done about it.

Also, try to focus on one thing at a time and, most importantly, don’t try to rush learning. Sometimes, developers have a tendency to try to learn a lot of things at once. That’s because you either look at others that know more things than you, things that you still haven’t learned, so you think you’re not learning fast enough, or you might discover other things you weren’t aware of initially and in order to move on, you have to learn them and understand them too (and there are increasingly more things, while the available time to learn them remains the same). Then, if you get stuck in something, you might also be tempted to move on to other things (because you can’t use all your time on one subject, can you?). But similar to trying to eat a burger in one mouthful and probably choke on it, trying to stuff too many things in your head too fast will result in “cognitive overload”[38]. You won’t be able to process the information, understand it properly, or retain it; you will be merely reading it. In simpler terms, it means that the one who chases more rabbits catches none. So, focus! Prioritize things. Decide what is a must to know and what is nice to know. What you need now is top priority, what is just cool can wait a while, and sometimes you can even completely ignore. Don’t worry if you think you’ll miss something significant; if it’s important, it will find its own way back to you. Focus on what you have on your plate right now. It’s very easy to go too quickly through the material and not really learn much, just bits and pieces from many topics, which then create even more confusion for which you must then invest even more time to clarify them. So don’t spread yourself too thin.

It won’t be easy. Won’t be easy at all. Especially since sometimes you will throw yourself after too many things because of peer pressure. Being part of a community can help you learn, you can get advice, feedback, people can share their experience. But a community can also influence you in a not so good way. You see, developers that are smart and passionate about stuff will often express their feelings… strongly. It’s a nice way of saying that they might put people down or mock others that are not doing what “they” are doing. “F# is cool, let me show you. Were you learning JavaScript? Put that aside, and let me show you how awesome F# is. What?… You don’t know TDD? What are you thinking? You should never write any code without a test first. You don’t know ReactJS? What frameworks do you use? That’s so last year…”

People all have their own preferences, and many will try to win you (or lure you) over to their side. What will you do? Do you also learn that stuff - whatever it is - or not? Do you want to be cool like them or…? Will you make your own decision on what to learn, or will you be peer pressured into one? It doesn’t even need to be your team members or that friend of yours who insists you give their favorite language a try; online communities can also have an impact on your decision. Is the community right about the appropriate things to learn, or do you think you know better? Peer pressure can be good for you. It keeps you productive and focused on your learning. If you see other motivated and knowing stuff you don’t know yet, you start to pick up the pace; you don’t want to be left behind, you want to be part of the group or the community. But peer pressure can also be bad for you, making you feel like you’re in high-school with others encouraging you to smoke, to be like everyone else that does. The difference is that in high-school, you knew for sure that smoking is bad for you, but about learning X, Y or Z, you have no idea. Is it bad or not?

Sometimes you can’t even ask yourself this question. You have to learn something simply because you need it at work. Many new programmers think their experience on the job will be more of the greenfield type[39], working with the coolest people, on the coolest things, with the coolest technologies. But the reality is most projects you will be working on will be brownfield development[40]. Companies don’t rewrite their applications any time a new technology shows up. You will have something in place that will constrain you and require you to get a detailed knowledge of the system. That means that you will have to learn things like old frameworks, old languages, or old practices. To give you an example, a long time ago, I was a web developer working on a front-end application for a mainframe back-end that was running COBOL. I wasn’t a COBOL developer. There were specialized teams of people that did just that all day long. But I still had to learn it to understand the integration between the front-end and the back-end, to be able to trace messages back and forth, debug errors, build my code more efficiently knowing what happens behind the scenes, and so on. COBOL is a very old technology, but sometimes you might also need to work with modern technology that you have no intention of learning or even exploring, but you will have no other choice. Another personal example is SharePoint[41]. For a while, I also did SharePoint development. It just happened that was what the company was using at that time. So I rolled up my sleeves and started building what needed to be built, even though I had no interest in becoming a SharePoint developer.

Problem-solving skills

Next on your list of things you need to learn is problem-solving skills.

First, solve the problem. Then, write the code - John Johnson[42]

Software exists to solve problems. And code is just how you choose to implement the solution for that problem. You often get in a situation where the software does not solve the problem or solves an entirely different problem. And that’s because people didn’t spend enough time to really understand the problem. Developers because they jump too quickly to writing code (developers tend to solve anything by writing code; similar to the “professional deformation” I refereed at earlier), bosses because they want to see something working as soon as possible, the client because they just want to get rid of the problem as soon as possible. Often you get halfway through the implementation when you realize something can’t be done, that you misunderstood or did something wrong, or that a better way was available or that the solution would have been possible in another way. Then, what do you do? Well, you go ahead with the solution you originally started with. You try to patch it out somehow, trying to get your code to work, changing this here, adding that over there, pile more code on top of what you already wrote, you’re almost there, just a little bit longer. And in the end, you finish with a convoluted implementation simply because you found it OK to go ahead with that solution than to throw it all away and start from scratch.

It is essential to analyze the problem from the start. That allows you to avoid acting on your first impulse and implement the first solution that goes through your head. If you invest a little time beforehand to analyze the problem, you can end up with a far better solution and far better results. So start by solving the problem first.

There is no special technique to do that. It’s just common sense. You do it in your daily life with all the problems you encounter. When some situation occurs, and you have to solve it, you start by analyzing the problem, by defining it correctly, to know what it’s all about and figuring out what you have to do. Is this really the problem you have to solve, or is it a symptom of the problem? Is it really a problem? For example, sometimes users may have a problem, and they ask you to solve it. They tell you they need such and such then ask how much time it will take and how much money will it cost. But if you question them for a while to see what problem they are trying to solve, you find that there are other alternatives. Sometimes you don’t even have to solve that problem because the problem is actually somewhere else. This is a familiar situation for help-desk workers or for those who participate in Q&A sites. It’s called the “XY problem”[43]. Someone has problem X, but instead of asking for help with problem X, they ask for help with another issue Y that they think will take care of problem X. If you don’t know what’s happening, you can end up spending a lot of time and effort solving something else than the actual issue. So poke at the problem, ask questions, ask for details, look at the problem from multiple sides, see what you are dealing with, understanding what problem you need to solve, and making sure you actually solve the right problem and not someone else’s attempt at a solution for the problem.

If the problem is too big, break it into smaller pieces. If you try to solve a big problem in one bite, you may not get anywhere, the problem may look too intimidating or seem impossible to solve. But it’s easier if you approach different pieces of it and solve those; afterward, the smaller solutions then fit together to solve the large, initial problem. It isn’t so hard to do. You already do this all the time when you write code. Every line of code solves something, those lines of code form functions or methods that solve something, the functions or methods form a class or module that solves something, and so on until you have a fully working application.

After gathering information about the problem, analyzing it, and building an image as complete as possible about what the situation involves, what needs to be done and what obstacles, limitations, or constraints there may exist, it’s time to think about some solutions. Are there more ways to solve the problem? What looks like the best course of action? Choose the solution that seems the best, make a plan about how to do it, what might happen and how you would act in each situation, then take that course of action and start implementing the solution. Then monitor your progress. Did you discover new things as you are implementing the solution? Do these new facts change something? Do you go ahead with the solution? Do you take a step back and reevaluate things? If new problems show up, adjust your plan accordingly, and solve the problems that occur using the same approach. Then, at the end, after you have implemented the solution, you should evaluate the outcome and take time to reflect on the problem. Often, it’s only at the end that you have a complete picture of the problem and its solution. What if you did this? What if you didn’t do that? What assumptions did you make? Which of them proved right or wrong? What did you initially miss and found out later during the implementation? What if you were to start all over again? Would you do something different? Think about the result you achieved. Does it work properly? Is it consistent with what you wanted? Evaluate your actions and the result and try to learn from it all.

Give the other steps for solving the problem the same importance that you give to the step of implementing the solution. When you implement the solution, your attention becomes narrow. You’re focusing your efforts on making the chosen solution work, and you will tend to go ahead with it even when signs show you that maybe the solution you are working on isn’t the best approach. That’s why it’s important to think carefully from the start, to build confidence for a solution with a decent chance of success. Of course, you must also avoid to fall in the other extreme and end up with analysis paralysis[44]. Do an analysis and look for good solutions until you have a reasonable level of confidence in one of them since you can never be 100% sure. Each time you solve a new problem, you actually test a theory or assumption. You find out in the end if your theory was good or not. This is how you gather experience: by learning from the result, similar to learning from mistakes, as I mentioned earlier. You learn to make fewer mistakes by first making a lot of mistakes. Similarly, you learn to solve problems better by solving many problems or trying to solve a problem in different ways.

The more problems you look at, the more angles you look at them, the more solutions you try to find, make plans, implement them, observe the results and adapt your solutions to what feedback you collect, the more your problem-solving tool-set, so to speak, increases. Please note that it’s not just about solving many problems of the same kind, but many problems of different types. Companies want to hire people with years of experience because they know they have encountered many situations, they’ve made mistakes, and solved many types of problems; thus, they have discovered and learned about a wider range of solutions that they can apply. If you always solve the same type of problems, you are either a specialist in your field or, in fact, you might not have years of experience, but a single year of experience repeated several times. You need to always learn new things so that you can solve different problems. A plumber who has a one size wrench will only be able to tighten screws of that size. One that has an adjustable wrench can tighten screws of all sizes. But still, both of them are limited to tightening just screws. A plumber with a complete toolkit can do or fix all sorts of things, not just tighten screws.

Just like you can learn from other people’s mistakes, you can also learn from how others have solved problems. And there are several ways. Algorithms you might have learned in school are, for example, solutions to problems, problems that were already solved, in many different ways (for instance, look at how many ways there are to sort a list). Have you also thought about that solution? Would you have solved it differently? Which solution do you think is the best? What are some pros and cons of each? Then, you could participate in code reviews. Code reviews are great for learning from others or receive advice on how to solve a problem. If you find something interesting, like an open-source project, a framework, or a library, and ask yourself, “how does this work?”, you can look inside the source code and see. You might also try to solve some challenges on sites like Project Euler[45]. The problems there are mathematical in nature, and they probably won’t compare to the real problems you have to solve at work, but they help you look at things from several directions, understand the problem first and think how best to solve it before writing the first line of code. In addition to that, others have already solved the problems, and you can find different ways to solve them online. Sometimes how tools are implemented is also interesting. Take Git[51], for example, which is more of a data structure than a classical version control system. It’s very interesting to see how its data model was implemented. Sometimes the solution turns out to be ingenious and not even the most obvious. An example of this is reCAPTCHA[52] used in the digitization of books. Instead of working on OCR software, the reCAPTCHA creators let people identify the words that were too illegible to be scanned by computers. People were already solving challenges with random words, so why not make something helpful out of that? A great example of first solving the problem.

Practice will help improve your problem-solving skills. However, be aware that this doesn’t mean it will make any problem easy to solve. Software is complex and made up of lots of pieces that interact with each other. You will find problems that are not subject to such a logical analysis in which you are looking for solutions, you choose the best one, and then you happily start coding it. Consider bugs, for example. Say you have an error in production, you don’t know what’s causing it, it doesn’t reproduce on the testing environment. What do you do? Start digging; that’s what. You can’t identify such a problem as easily as something isolated, like a label that has a typo inside it and you know how to go straight on target to fix it. Some bugs are caused by interactions between multiple things, maybe things that occur far away from where the problem manifests itself, sometimes having nothing to do with your code. I found, for example, bugs in the JDK and in web servers. I found bugs in databases, in the network adapter of servers, and even inside the operating system. You will chase these bugs until you go completely insane. The normal problem-solving steps that you are used to will not work. You get frustrated, nothing makes sense, you don’t know what else to try. So, sometimes, problem-solving skills mean to do trial and error or going with a process of elimination. “Well… at least I’m not getting that error anymore” means progress, even though you don’t quite know why you are no longer getting that error. You thus need the right amount of perseverance. Too little, and you will give up on the problem too soon. Too much, and you might actually go too deep on a wrong path until recognizing that what you are doing will never work. Sometimes it helps to take a step back, take a walk, or if you are at the end of the working program, to go home. Your brain will solve the problem during your commute, while taking a shower, while you sleep, or whatever. You must recognize when to push forward and when to give up and move the fight to another day.

You also have to learn that many things don’t get solved necessarily by writing some code. Maybe the solution is to update a driver or a library or get your manager involved in some matter. Sometimes you may have to say “no” to the client. In certain cases, you might need to work on preventing problems from appearing instead of solving them like, for example, to commit code on source control regularly to catch errors sooner. This way, in the event you break something, chances are high that it’s because of the last changes you made. If instead, your entire team commits code once a month or before a major release, finding the cause of an error will be like looking for the needle in the haystack.

Business domain

And to solve the right problem, and solve it well, you must know the domain in which you’re working. Banking, health care, education, gaming, telecommunications, flower shops, whatever, you need to understand the nature of the business, how it operates, what makes it tick, what the priorities are, and what problems you’re trying to solve. Nobody can feed you with a spoon and offer everything you need for you to write the code and cover all eventualities, so you have to be capable of filling in the gaps, see opportunities, or recognize things that might not align with the business. You will need to interact with a lot of people, and you must be able to understand them and then translate the domain rules into executable code. You have to feel comfortable with the domain. I wouldn’t go as far as saying that you have to like it, but it doesn’t have to be frustrating either. If you don’t like the financial sector, for example, writing code or focusing strictly on technical challenges and problem solving will not help you overcome the discomfort.

Every company does business in its own way. In some, you might work in their IT department, but their core business is something else than building software; they just need the software to support their internal processes. Others make software to sell on a DVD or offer it as a SaaS solution. Others offer B2B solutions; they are service providers building software for others, or whatever. It doesn’t matter. You need to know what they are doing and how they are doing it. When you move from one company to another, you have to learn their business. If you take a very good programmer from one domain and have them work in another domain that they don’t understand, they will build wrong software, but of good quality :). Not knowing the domain or the business you are supporting will feel like being in the subway of an unfamiliar city in a foreign country. You keep looking at direction indicators, the writing is in another language, you wonder if it’s OK to go to the left or maybe to the right, you ask people for help to avoid getting lost. It’s not like on the subway at home where you don’t even have to think about where you’re going; you know the routes by heart. It’s the same if you don’t know the business domain. You eventually end up where you need to be, but you might not get there by taking the fastest or the shortest route. Then, gaining experience in a certain domain, like for example, the financial system, can also be an asset when looking for a new job because companies will also be interested in your domain expertise and not just in your technical skills. So keep that in mind. When you move from one company to another, you might be the greatest programmer in the world or whatever, but you also have to learn the business. Each company does something else or maybe something similar but in a different way. Being a programmer isn’t just about technologies or programming languages; it’s also about the domain.

Your investment

And guess what? Learning is something that a lot of people expect you to do on your own time and on your own money. As a company employee, you were hired to do a job, and after a short period of accommodation and training, it is assumed that you can perform that job. Otherwise, you wouldn’t have been hired, right? If you can then actually do that job or not, it depends primarily on you. It’s like this: when you get into a taxi, for example, you expect the driver to be able to drive a car and know where he is going, right? Would you accept for him to stop every few hundred meters to practice parallel parking or something? Would you accept for him to stop every few hundred meters and look up stuff on a map, or stop the car and ask people on the street for directions? You wouldn’t. That would mean he is a bad taxi driver who can’t do his job properly. It’s a little bit of a stretched example, but it’s similar for someone who needs an application built, but they can’t build it on their own, or for that matter, understand how it’s built. You have to build it for them, so people expect you to know your stuff. If you need training or need to learn new stuff, some might assume you don’t know what you are doing. They don’t understand that software applications are unique and that sometimes you do not have everything you need, or know everything you need, in order to build it. But you have to build it. You are the developer, not them. So they expect you to do your job. How you do that is up to you.

I mentioned in the previous chapter that appraisals are often inadequate because companies only have demands from their employees and ask them to do more each year, but too little effort is expended to give employees all the necessary tools and support to be successful. Training is part of this category of tools and support, and it often gets neglected. If the appraisals are badly implemented, there are high chances that you will also not receive training in that company, because they don’t exactly understand the work of developers and why they need to constantly learn new things (which does not stop them from reprehending developers during performance evaluations for not being on top of the latest technology trends… just saying). Even if they do understand, there is another reason why they don’t want to pay for training: so that you can’t use your newly acquired knowledge someplace else other than within their company.

You might have heard this saying before:

What if we train them and they leave? What if we don’t and they stay? - Unknown

Some have not heard it or have heard it, but they choose to ignore it (at least the second part). They don’t invest in employee training because they fear that others will be the beneficiaries of the result. Why invest money in you if you can use the newly acquired knowledge or skills to go get a better job somewhere else? Or maybe it’s the client that would have to pay for your training. And why would they want you to learn and experiment on their time and money, to find out things, make mistakes, and practice on their project, to then use the expertise on other companies’ projects, maybe even working for the competition since they need a similar application and similarly skilled people? Besides, you’re supposed to know what you’re doing, right? Better to give up on something good that they can benefit from than to risk another company benefiting from it. Or maybe they approve the training but force you to stay with the company for a certain period of time or pay it off if you leave, something like 100% if you leave after 12 months, 75% if you leave after 18 months, and so on.
