Which often doesn’t work as a training proposal because what do you think developers will do in such situations? They refuse the training because you never know what the future has in hold. You might like working for the company, having no intention of leaving, and be determined to stay long enough to cause the eventual payment of the training from your own pocket to be a non-issue, but what if something happens and you have to leave? Maybe a crisis situation in the family, or a once in a lifetime opportunity? If it’s a large sum of money, you’ll think twice before accepting the training. And if you refuse it, you most likely won’t receive another one, ‘cause why did you refuse? You don’t want to work in the company anymore? “Are you thinking of leaving?”

Another reason for not being offered training would be that higher-ups consider training as an expense rather than an investment - an expense not only in terms of money but also in terms of time. Training is seen as an interruption from work. If they are attending a course or a conference, the developers aren’t working, right? “We can’t take people out from development work while the course is taking place. We are under a tight schedule, and we are already running late. Training now will cost us a lot. We’ll have to postpone it for later”. This happens quite often, and if you really have important or urgent things to do all the time, then, in the end, you’ll never do any kind of training at all.

Another thing I’ve seen happening is that the company does provide courses, training, etc., but then, management expects some spectacular results because of that training. Something very visible is expected to happen: people’s productivity to increase, the team to deliver more, or the project to be completed earlier. The problem is that lots of times, with many courses in this industry, you can’t exactly measure how much you put in versus how much you take out. You can’t always measure the return on investment for the training. If the entire team takes part in a three day Scrum course, for example, how do you know then whether or not the way they use Scrum is due to that course? Could they not have gotten the same results by reading a book at home? Did that course give them that essential information to use Scrum properly, so the company reaps the maximum benefits? Or was it just a waste of time and money? You can’t really tell; there is no objective indicator to look at, especially since the results can appear over time, long after people stopped thinking about the training and no longer make any association between the improvement now and the course back then. But the expectations still stand. “We’ve spent a lot of money to send all of you to that course, and you can’t even do 100% delivery per sprint?” If it was actually the developers who insisted on having to go to that course, you could expect some trouble from management, followed by the cancellation of later training programs.

Sometimes, bosses’ expectations are even higher when, as I mentioned previously, in-house training is done, where the company tries to grow its personnel by having other experienced employees perform the training and mentoring. Management expects in-house training to be of better quality than any other course or training offered by an external provider. It’s done by the company’s employees, after all, who know in detail what’s needed on the job, so they can apply training with surgical precision. Once the training is over, any doubts or misunderstandings can be further explained because the trainers or mentors are still in the company. People can immediately apply what they learn because they have access to the application and all of the company’s resources; they are not in a hotel’s conference room somewhere on the other side of town. And the list could go on. This is the best training there is, right? Well… not really. I’ve seen this situation unfold several times. The idea for organizing such a training program usually comes from above, from upper management or HR. The implementation is done in the lower layers of the company. The idea is not necessarily bad, but the implementation often is because people have work to do, but someone must take care of the trainees as well. Middle managers won’t really pull out their best developers from working on the project or handling production issues just so they can babysit some apprentices. They still have tight schedules they need to meet. So the trainees are left on their own. They are not even given good resources to study and deepen their knowledge on their own because those resources must be sought out and sorted by the developers who should be their trainers. But even that takes time, time in which they could instead work to reach the tight deadlines. And now the “very good” training program turns into the “very bad” training program. And of course, upper management is in the dark about all of this happening; they still believe that they have their best people in charge of the training. And after a few such training program attempts that don’t provide the spectacular results upper management expected, bosses end up giving up the idea altogether and consider that training doesn’t work, not even in the ideal conditions of having the employees that know better what’s needed do the actual training.

If you work inside the IT department of a company whose core business is something else than building software, you can pretty much kiss training goodbye. In such a company, IT is a “support” department. IT helps the business. IT is not the business. Any training budget gets now split all throughout the company. Only a small part of the budget goes to the IT department. Most invest in their core business, in the departments that are essential and without which they cannot function (IT can always be outsourced, so they require less training, right?). You might get some money for books or a cheap monthly subscription for an online video learning platform, but that’s pretty much all you will get.

Training or no training from the company you work for, you will also have to learn on company time. But be warned, it’s not things outside of the scope of work; it’s only for things that you need to do your job better. Are you stuck on something or don’t know how to accomplish something? You can do some research and learn what you need to know. Did a new version of a framework you need or an enhancement for the language you are using came out? You can look it up. Has the company acquired an application in a technology you are not familiar with? You can read documentation, books, watch online courses, anything necessary to bring you up to speed. There is absolutely no problem. But I’ve met many developers who think it’s their right to learn whatever they want, and that the company must provide them with training, send them to conferences, buy them whatever books they want and give them time for leisure reading, or allow them “20 percent time”[53] to work on whatever their heart desires. Oh… and they also demand free drinks and bean bags too. But if the company doesn’t provide these things, don’t think you are entitled to take time from the working hours to learn cool new things or whatever else goes through your mind. Smart companies will invest in their employees, but if they do, they will do it for what you need to be more productive at work or what they think helps you so that in the future, you can help them. For example, they won’t send you to artificial intelligence courses if your company deals with issuing electronic invoices. Any training you receive will be work-related because at work you have to work, you weren’t hired to “be educated” in all the latest fads. You can negotiate with the employer, or as a team you can hold activities for knowledge sharing and increasing know-how that helps in your day-to-day work or make your job easier, but the bottom line is that if you can’t use it for work, it will probably not be offered by your company or even allowed for that matter. It might even get you fired. Many people think it’s their employer’s responsibility to create career development plans, invest in training, and create new learning opportunities for their employees. But that’s false. And even if they do, “you” own your own career, and “you” need to invest in developing it. So it’s your job to learn, a lot of it on your own time and money, which is what you will do anyway if you didn’t end up as a programmer by chance.

Unlearning

Learning and unlearning go hand in hand.

The illiterate of the 21st century will not be those who cannot read and write, but those who cannot learn, unlearn, and relearn - Alvin Toffler[54]

In this industry, what you know can quickly become obsolete. Things that you learned and thought will not change for a while, just did. You constantly need to update your knowledge. This is not the same as learning new stuff; it’s revisiting things you already know but may no longer be current, have become inefficient, are done differently, or are now entirely useless. You have to unlearn something and relearn something else. Now… you can’t really unlearn stuff; that would be like inducing yourself selective amnesia. But what you can do is try to make yourself “forget about it”. Whenever you want to use the old knowledge, remember the new information and use that instead. With time the new knowledge becomes the habit while the old one slowly fades away. Unlearning just means to think differently; the old information is still there, you can consciously access it for a while, but it’s no longer the first thing you think of. Relearning means setting aside your assumptions or beliefs about what you thought was the right thing to do or the best practice to apply and start fresh with something else. Sounds easier said than done? Absolutely. You’ve invested a lot of time, effort, and practice to acquire some particular knowledge, and now it’s all scrap. You don’t feel very well about it; you have this sort of attachment to the information like it’s “yours” or something, and you don’t want to let go of it after you’ve worked so long for it, you’ve built all sorts of theories and beliefs around it, maybe even a framework or two :). People are more sensitive to loss than they are to gain, so you bark an emotional response at anyone who says, “there is a new/better way of doing it”, and you defend the knowledge it took you so long to acquire.

If you are a specialist, it is even harder for you to give up on your expertise, because you give up on everything, not just a piece of it. It’s even more painful if you become a specialist by chance and not because of your personal choice. Sometimes you do a project and gain some mastery, which in turn leads to more similar projects, and more similar projects until you become a specialist in that sphere of knowledge. Without realizing it, you become trapped in the domain or technology that you have been with for many years. So if you are a specialist (on purpose or by chance), be very careful that things change. If you become a specialist in something, that doesn’t mean you can stop learning. That thing you specialized in can very easily change or disappear. Try not to hang on for dear life on that specialization, or you will be walloped when the industry pulls the rug under your feet.

Change is the only constant in software development; on multiple levels, not just having to change old written code. Methods, classes, APIs get deprecated, and so does knowledge, in general. Let go of the knowledge, the attachment to it, and the fear of having wasted the time and energy you’ve invested, and start over. It won’t be easy. Knowledge that you have used, and skills you have practiced repeatedly have left an imprint on your brain, like a riverbed for a river, to use an analogy. Now you have to create another riverbed for the water to flow in. The more you know, the harder it will be for you to do so because you’ve spent a lot of time and effort to develop a certain mindset and a particular way of thinking and doing things. Functional programming is all the rage these days, for example, but if you have been doing OOP for the last 15 years, it will be harder for you to change your mindset and think functionally. A young graduate who has not yet formed habits or biases in this way, and thus carries less baggage, has nothing to unlearn and no habits to shake of before grasping the functional paradigm, so they will have a much easier time learning the concepts than an OOP veteran.

There will also be things that you will abandon altogether. No revisiting the subject. No relearning. Just full stop. Why? Because you realize that the technology, language, whatever it is, doesn’t get you anywhere, not many people use it, or there are fewer to none jobs available for it. When it comes to too much of a niche technology, when the industry moves away from it, you just can’t stand the pain of working with it, or your employer forced that technology on you, then the decision to give it up is simple. But if you like the technology and you put in a lot of effort to master it, the choice won’t be easy, and thinking about it in the long term won’t be so simple. But you have to ask yourself, is it worth continuing to learn it? Will you still need it in the future for anything else than pet projects? Do you have the time to keep investing in it? Can you use that time for something more productive instead? You have a goal in mind, and the technology (or whatever it is) is a part of the foundation you need to build to reach that goal? If not, then you most likely need to say goodbye. Again, it will seem you are wasting invested time and energy, and you may be tempted to hold on to it and attempt to keep the information up to date and thus not lose that investment, but you have to be pragmatic and think if it can be lucrative in the future or if it’s not too hard for you to keep up to date with it. To give an example, throughout my career, I have programmed in both Java and C#. I wanted to master both, and there were plenty of jobs for the two languages. But it was too much of an effort for me. I just didn’t have enough time to invest in staying proficient in both languages and their communities. So one had to go! I gave up on C# in favor of Java. Although I personally think C# is a much more powerful language compared to Java, I like the Java ecosystem better since you can build any kind of application with open source libraries that are not always available or have an equivalent on the dot.NET platform also. Here is another example, which is not only specific to me but to everyone: did you keep up with all the topics you learned in school? Maybe with some, yes, but not with many. Are you sorry about all the things you learned in school that you forgot? Probably not, since the main purpose was to get a diploma and then get a job. So think well about the purpose for which you are learning now. Is it for pleasure? Making a living? Both? Something else? I said above to think well about what you want to learn and in what you want to invest your time; to think about the future. Well, you also have to think just as carefully about what you want to neglect or give up entirely.

Programmer vs developer

Software development is not just about technology or writing code all the time. Problem-solving, for example, doesn’t necessarily mean you will translate the solution into an algorithm or code. Sometimes to solve the problem might mean choosing the appropriate abstraction, making the right plan, having a discussion with the right person, reassessing the situation, changing a vendor, clarify ambiguously presented requirements, communicate better, and so on. You don’t always write code.

So far, I’ve used the words programmer and developer throughout the book. People sometimes use these two words interchangeably, I included. But they don’t actually mean the same thing. A programmer mostly codes, while a software developer designs systems and is involved in all stages of software development. There is no clear demarcation line between the two. They are very loaded terms for each person or company, meaning different things in different contexts, so I’ll add my own definition:

A programmer is more concerned with the (software) “trees”. A developer is more concerned with the (software) “forest”

It’s about wider activities and responsibilities, about delivering software versus just writing code.

Even if you want to remain a programmer forever, you might be unable to do so. It’s well known in the industry that, in many tech companies, the median employee age is below 40. That’s the reality. Companies prefer young programmers. The recruitment sweet-spot is someone young with 3-5 years of experience. The main reason is, of course, the salary. With this number of years of experience, you know just enough, so you don’t suck, but you still do not have enough skills to ask for a high salary to match the experience. And they can hire more, less experienced programmers at the price of only one more experienced developer. Then there are other reasons. For example, it so happens that there are more young programmers in search of a job than older programmers; every year, new waves of graduates start looking for a job. Or the government might offer financial support or tax exemptions to employers that hire people right out of school. Or if you start a new company in your garage, for example, you might not afford to pay experienced workers, but instead, prefer to train unskilled youngsters that want to learn more than they are interested in the pay (at least in the beginning).

Young people are usually more energetic and have fewer family commitments, thus fewer reasons to be somewhere else after work. Why not take advantage of that, right? Often, upper management thinks that working more hours means that more is achieved. And since working extra hours is often not a problem for young people, management makes use of that, and they impose overtime (often unpaid, which is even more work at the same salary).

There are also disadvantages to employing young people! Of course, there are! One is the lack of experience. How well do you think an inexperienced programmer can work on a large scale application, for example, if they don’t even have experience in smaller applications or medium ones? Then, many programmers are attracted by the newest technologies or extra perks, so just as quickly as they have decided to work for you, they can change their minds and go work for someone else. Even if they stay, they get frustrated easily, they might behave irresponsibly or act like rebels, think they are invincible and their logic is infallible (they also lack the experience to understand your arguments when you contradict them or try to ground them in reality), their sense of entitlement might get in the way of accepting feedback, and the list could go on. It’s not all just milk and honey. But if you’re an IT company and you have an army of programmers, every dollar counts when paying salaries.

Salary is a logical selection criterion for hiring young and less experienced people instead of older, more experienced ones. But there are also other criteria, or should I say “assumptions” about hiring more senior programmers. As programmers get older, people start to make certain assumptions about them, and because of these assumptions, it may be harder for you to get a job as a programmer when you go beyond that sweet spot of 3-5 years of experience. For example, many think that young people are more technologically savvy and have a better grasp of the latest technologies. They believe that innovation comes from using these latest technologies and so, young people are the ones who can bring fresh new ideas to the company and be more creative. Older programmers… not so much. It’s because people assume that older developers have out of date skills, don’t know the latest technologies, or can’t keep up with all the changes in technology. Combined with the belief that innovation happens if you use the latest fads, it results in the assumption that older programmers don’t have much to contribute because they are already outdated, set in their ways already, less open to new ideas, slower, and unwilling to work longer hours.

With age (although not always related) also comes maturity. Mature people have a more balanced lifestyle, are less likely to accept imposed unpaid overtime, are less impulsive, and they better understand the need to put money aside and to think about their future and that of their family. Therefore it is difficult to attract them with refrigerators full of carbonated juices, all snacks you can eat, bean bags, pool tables, board games, or other fancy perks, which are usually cheap for the company in terms of money and implementation. More adult people care about flexible working hours or availability to work from home, retirement savings plans, healthcare programs, and leadership training programs, which are more expensive and harder for a company to get right (many corporations are not even willing to put in the effort).

Even if you dispel the employers’ assumptions, and you keep yourself up to date with the latest technologies, you have a lot of experience, and you are creative, etc., it will become harder and harder to get a job as a programmer as you get older. As time goes by, people expect you to become more than a programmer. If you stick to being just a programmer, everyone will start thinking that you don’t want to grow as a professional. Not to mention that it doesn’t make economic sense anymore to pay someone with 20 years of experience as just a programmer. So you hit the main problem related to salary, and for companies, it’s hard to beat this argument. So you must be able to do something more than what (many) others can do. If a company is to pay a high salary, it must be worthwhile. So they are not looking for someone with only a hammer and a screwdriver (i.e., programmer); they are looking for someone with experience and a toolbox full of tools (i.e., developer).

Furthermore, putting aside these aspects that aren’t about you as a programmer, think also at the possibility that over time your passion for coding might turn into a chore. Programming gets old for a lot of people, so they want new challenges. As your experience and your exposure to different situations increase, maybe you will have to take on a leadership position, like being a Team Lead or a technical lead. Some might become architects, CTOs, trainers, consultants, or they might discover that they like project management, and then they choose to join “the dark side”. Some might even build their own companies, and if successful, they will do other things than write code.

So you need to be good at a lot of other things - things like communication skills, leadership skills, planning, problem-solving, creativity, and innovation - to name just a few - need to be part of your toolbox. You will not be taught these things in school, and you will not find them in any programming book because they are not specific to software development. They are not technical knowledge or skills. They are “soft skills”, things related to your attitude and your ability to deal with people. These are skills that you must have regardless of what area of work you’re in or what kind of a job you have. Neglecting to invest some time into these will be what gets you stuck in most of the quicksands. So you need to be aware of their importance in the workplace and invest some time into these types of skills just like you invest time in learning new programming languages or technologies.

Communication skills are one of the most important competencies to have. Initially, I had a separate chapter on communication to emphasize this point, but gradually, I was forced to put the ideas from that chapter all over the book. That’s because communication affects many aspects of the work that you do. Communication is essential. It’s a cross-cutting concern if you want a software analogy. What I see in many programmers, though, is that they don’t communicate properly. In fact, they often refuse to communicate; they try to stay in a permanent Vulcan mind-meld[55] with the code they are writing. But you can’t do that when you’re in an office, at work. You need to be aware of what is around you and interact on several levels on all the activities that are happening in your working environment. Developers play the most important role in a software project, I’ve said this before, and I’ll say it again. But that doesn’t mean other roles are completely expendable. You have system administrators, Project Managers, testers, salespeople, clients. As a developer, you don’t communicate with them the same way you do with other fellow developers; you have to package the message differently for everyone. Even if you refuse to acknowledge that there are other perspectives of all the people involved in a project, not just that of developers, and you refuse to interact with someone who is not a programmer (I’ve seen this happen… sadly), you won’t really have a choice. When working as part of a team of people with diverse skills, you must learn to communicate well.

And since I mentioned teams, how about doing more than just being part of a team? How about leading the team?

Team Lead

As you move forward in your career, you may have to lead a team at some point. Seniority comes with having to coach or mentor the younger developers you work with. From this to having to lead the entire team is just an extra step. Management wants someone who can ensure that everyone on the team does their job, that they can deliver and produce results without having to deal with the entire team for themselves. They want someone who represents the team and speaks for the entire team. A senior member of the team is chosen to fill this position and assigned as a Team Lead. It might be your decision to take on the role, or just find yourself having to lead a team, but at some point, you might have to do this also.

And I use the term “lead”, not “leader”, because you most likely will occupy a position similar to that of a captain of a football team who takes on some leadership responsibilities on top of their normal participation in the sport, but that doesn’t mean that they can change the “rules of the game”, which would fall into the actual definition of “leadership” that I have in mind. “Leadership” is a loaded term; it means many things to many people, but to me, it means having a calling, it means innovation, challenging the status quo, initiating change, and breaking conventions. It means envisioning a different future, taking risks, inspiring, and influencing others to turn that vision into reality and achieve something great. Leadership also means that people emerge as leaders from within their group or team; they rise to the top. You can do this as a lead also, but most of the time, you are appointed a lead by someone external to the group, and you have an explicit job description.

If your actions inspire others to dream more, learn more, do more, and become more, you are a leader - John Quincy Adams[56]

Your job as a “lead” is for people to work, not dream. That’s why I said team “lead” instead of team “leader”. As a “lead”, you are not a game-changer. You don’t get to set the vision. Others make the important decisions; others set the direction. What your boss expects from you as a Team Lead is to be in charge of the people inside the team, similarly to how a Project Manager might be in charge of a project.

So what exactly will you do as a Team Lead?

You will mostly be working and interacting with people. And this is the part where most developers (I was no exception) start to feel like slowly sinking into quicksand.

Why do people become programmers? Because they are curious and like to learn, because they like to create things or because programming is fun and challenging and gives them a sense of accomplishment when they tackle a complex problem. But it’s also because, sometimes, they like interacting with a computer more than they like interacting with other (non-programmers) human beings. We are geeks to one degree or another. And that doesn’t mean just obsessing about a narrow field like programming (in our case), but it also means being a socially inept person. So if you are a good developer, it doesn’t necessarily mean that you will be a good Team Lead.

Programming is hard, but at least your footing is on solid ground. A computer doesn’t have emotions; it’s a deterministic machine. Dealing with people is an entirely different story. And this gets me to the first issue I’ve seen in many bad Team Leads: they don’t consider dealing with people their strong suit, so while still in a lead position, they hold on to development and doing technical stuff.

Team Lead first

Technical skills don’t help you deal with people. You need skills in the “soft” category for that. When you first become a Team Lead, you are unskilled in a lot of things that pertain to your new role. That’s normal. You will learn with time. But don’t think that “this learning” is something that happens to you. Being a Team Lead doesn’t mean that you are a developer, and on the side, you do some people managing. It doesn’t mean that you can still continue to invest your time only in learning “developer stuff” and let your new role “happen” to you. It’s quite the opposite. As a Team Lead, you manage people, and on the side, you do some developing. Sometimes you will have time to write some code, but sometimes you won’t. You are a Team Lead first and a developer second. Your Team Lead duties will take time away from learning new things as a developer. So now, you have to invest time in learning what you need for your new role, just like you invested time in learning programming languages, frameworks, or acquiring technical skills.

So make up your mind from the start on what you want to do, Team Lead or developer. Embrace your new role and responsibilities or step down because I guarantee you that if you don’t know what you intend to do, you won’t be able to handle the two roles well, and you will only succeed in failing at both of them. There is a saying in my country that perfectly conveys the indecision of choosing between two things and insisting on doing both; it translates literally as “to sit with your ass in two boats”.

You might still read specifications and write code. You might still design on a whiteboard, write unit tests, perform code reviews, or work shoulder to shoulder with the other developers in the team on technical challenges. You will still be a developer, but these activities will no longer be your primary duties. As a Team Lead, you are probably the most experienced, and you can do the work of any other developer from your team, but that doesn’t mean you will, or that you should, or that is a good idea to do so. You might be on top of everything that’s technical and know the domain and the application inside out, but your job now is to assign others work, follow their tasks, and help them when and where they have problems. Your responsibilities change now to answer not just for your person and your results, but also for the team and its results.

Bosses know your name, but maybe they don’t know the names of the other members of your team. You are an abstraction of the team in the eyes of bosses who don’t want to deal with details. You are called to speak on behalf of the team. You answer for how the team behaves. This means that any failure of the team is your failure. You get all of the blame by default. It’s completely irrelevant if it’s actually your fault or not; the responsibility is yours, and so is the fault. Just like a Project Manager gets blamed for a failed project, so does a Team Lead get blamed for the failures of their team. And speaking of Project Managers, as a Team Lead, you also need to have project management skills. I’ll talk more about these in the next chapter. For now, it’s enough to say that just like a Project Manager, a lot of what you do as a Team Lead is based on communication.

Since you represent the team in management’s eyes, anything important and related to the team will pass by you or will be communicated by you. I mentioned above that you will communicate with all kinds of people, no matter who they are: customers, bosses, managers, testers, developers, suppliers, people from other departments or business units, whatever. What I said in the previous chapter about hiring, performance evaluations, salary negotiations, and firings also pertains to communication skills. As a small aside, I need to mention that, unfortunately, a large part of these interactions - more than other developers on the team are exposed to - will be with managers and bosses. You always have to keep everyone informed about status, about tasks progress, or the team’s activities versus schedule. And I say “unfortunately” because a lot of discussions will consist of you explaining to some clueless boss why something is taking so long, why it costs as much as it costs, why it should be done one way and not another, or explain to them why you need more resources and what can happen if you don’t get them. Then, there are meetings in which you escalate issues and problems that the team members can’t resolve by themselves, and since bosses don’t like bad news, you’ll have a lot of “fun” with them yelling and screaming and be more concerned with placing blame than trying to help the team. Equally “fun” are the talks you will have with your boss, to explain that your Team Lead activities take a lot of time, and no matter how you inform them of your administrative tasks and why they are necessary, your boss simply doesn’t get why you no longer program features; I mean… “You’re the best developer in the team, that’s why we made you the Team Lead”, right? And not only will you have to communicate these things up the chain, but you will probably waste a lot of time with all sorts of bureaucratic processes because this communication must be done through official channels, using a specific document template and font, and duplicating the message in a few other business dashboards also, but not before you spend some time in a meeting with your Project Manager to “massage” the news a little bit, to make sure it looks good and won’t trigger “the wrath of the gods” who might not like what’s written in there. And that’s how communication with upper management will often be unpleasant. There is, of course, also the difference in perceptions; your boss cares about different things than you do, most likely you have different communication styles, but mostly because unlike conversations with other people, your boss is not your peer. They can bark orders at you, or they can say whatever they want, but you always have to present arguments, explanations, or justifications.

And while you’re taking a beating in various meetings with your boss or waste time with ridiculous procedures, your team has to get by without you. This is your main job as a Team Lead. You have to make sure everyone knows what they have to do, that everyone has the skills and tools needed to do their job, and that they can work without you. If a Team Lead insists on remaining a developer, they will take on development tasks, maybe the most difficult ones, or the ones the team doesn’t really want to do (like writing documentation… yuck!), and when that happens, the team starts to depend on their Team Lead for certain things. The best Team Leads I’ve met or worked with were those who did everything for their team. No matter what it was, they rolled up their sleeves and dived in. Writing documentation? No problem. Stuff to configure? No problem. A rarely reproducible bug that everyone got tired of chasing around? No problem. The air conditioner doesn’t blast enough air in that corner of the office? No problem. But most importantly, what they could do besides all of these things, was to discern when they should be the ones to do them and when they had to let others do it; otherwise, the team became lazy, and people learned that the Team Lead could pick up after them, so they would begin to rely too much on their Team Lead for various things. You might be the smartest or most experienced person in the team, and think nobody else can do what you do, no one can write the code as well as you, but if you think like that and start to take the reins, you will fail. Things will take forever as the team waits for you to handle things. So you have to let them do the work, you just help them, even when your boss is breathing down your neck and complaining about things not being finished; in this situation, it would be easier to push people aside and do the work yourself, but that’s how you teach the team members to depend on you.

So beware, as a Team Lead, you coordinate people, you make sure they do their job properly, you hold things together, but the team doesn’t need to depend on you very much; otherwise, you can easily become a bottleneck. People will come to you with all kinds of problems (technical or otherwise) that they can’t solve by themselves, and they’ll expect you to be able to solve them. You’ll learn many new things as your exposure to challenging situations increases (from your work and now from that of everyone else), and it’s tempting for you to solve those situations, but as a Team Lead, you have to help your team solve them, not to solve them yourself. You are the last line of defense for doing or fixing stuff, but it’s a line that should be reached as rarely as possible; otherwise, what will happen, besides becoming a bottleneck and people waiting on you to do stuff, is that you’ll turn into a firefighter. As a Team Lead, you now have the problems of all the team members on your mind. Do you really think that you can solve everyone’s problems and challenges all of the time? You can’t! Do you think you’ll ever going to be able to take a vacation if many people depend on you? Imagine then if all of these things happen on top of you trying to stick to development work… So for starters, you need to learn how to delegate your technical tasks.

Delegate

As a Team Lead, one of your responsibilities might be to allocate work to others. Delegating work is similar to allocating work, but for a different reason. Instead of doing the work yourself, you have to instruct some other team member from your team to do it, since you now have more important responsibilities. When you become a Team Lead, you lose - and you also give away - control over some of your development work. You will have to learn to delegate this work; otherwise, you will suck at allocating work too. When you are new to the Team Lead role, you’ll still have a tendency to meddle with the work people are doing. If you’ve been a good developer for a long time, and see something you don’t like, you will be tempted to roll up your sleeves and take control. It’s like when doing pair programming with someone less experienced than you and, when you see them writing something weird or implementing something improperly, you tend to take over the keyboard and write the code yourself. “If you want a job done right, you have to do it yourself”, right? Ultimately, you can do that too, but only if you have no choice. Taking over people’s work is not a good idea. Instead, make sure to explain what needs to be done, why the work is required, why it needs to be done a certain way or another, what the expected output or result should be, and also inform people about the deadlines or priorities (this is especially important if you delegate more tasks to someone; from experience, I can tell you people will work on the easiest or smallest thing first if they don’t understand that other tasks are more important or urgent).

Once the work is delegated, you don’t just forget about it. You need to keep an eye on the progress, to have a clear status, verify the work if needed, and make yourself available to answer questions or help. Don’t confuse this with micromanaging. Delegating does not mean you pull the strings, like a puppeteer in a marionette theater; it’s like managing a small project where you play the client’s role.

Afterward, review and assess the result. If you don’t like the result, avoid the tendency to fix it yourself and, instead, instruct the team member on how to fix it. You indirectly influence the result by “guiding” the work of the people on your team.

And you have to delegate not only the work but also the decision making regarding that work; otherwise, people on the team will again become dependent on you and their decision-making organ atrophies since they are always waiting for you to make all the decisions. Something else worth mentioning is this: do not keep the cool tasks for yourself and delegate only the work you dislike doing. That’s not really delegating. You have to delegate any work that you cannot do while you are busy with things that are even more important you do. Don’t become a bottleneck again, or the team starts to have downtime while waiting for you to make one decision or another. With time, as your role expands, you might find yourself delegating a few of your Team Lead tasks as well. If something seems to be sitting in your TODO list forever, ask yourself if it might not be a better idea to let someone else do it.

Be careful, though. You delegate work or decisions, but you cannot delegate the final responsibility for the work. When you delegate (and with work allocation is the same), the responsibility and authority to do the tasks rests with the person to whom you have delegated it. But in the end, the responsibility for the result is yours as well, as the Team Lead. If they screw up, you screw up. You can verify the results, perform code reviews, or test the work, but sometimes you can’t do that because of lack of time. If you can’t thoroughly verify all their work, sometimes you just have to trust them that they did a good job. And I come back now to the importance of the things I mentioned in the previous chapter. To delegate and trust the result, you must have someone to delegate to; that is, to have a good, prepared team, composed of hardworking people who don’t wait to be told what to do, people you can trust to do the right things and make the right decisions. Do you think you could delegate work and decisions to incompetent people, or to people who don’t care? There is nothing more time consuming and exhausting than having to assign someone work and then be forced to micromanage them all the time, just to make sure the work is done properly and on time. And there’s nothing more frustrating than being held responsible and being reprimanded by your boss for the work other people do, when those people are unskilled and don’t give a rat’s ass about doing their work properly. You have to hire good people, eliminate obstacles from their path, empower and develop them, train them, coach them, and equip them with everything they need to do their job. Successful software depends on successful teams. It’s your job as a Team Lead to make sure the people in your team are doing a proper job and are working well together. It’s also your job to make sure everyone understands the project objectives, know the goals, and stay focused on being able to achieve them. You point at the target, provide guidance, keep the team focused, and they will make it happen. But of course, it isn’t that simple. Should I repeat it? “Working with people is hard”.

Motivation

People don’t behave the way you want them to behave, exactly when you want them to. You have to understand this. If you don’t, it will frustrate the heck out of you. I’ve seen Team Leads that ignore how their people are and instead expect them to be and behave differently. You as a Team Lead may be proactive, you don’t give up easily, you know a lot of stuff, you understand a lot of things, you see the meaning behind all sorts of situations, and so on, and you expect others to be like you. Not gonna happen! People are different. Some are more daring, others less, an older individual might not wait to take the initiative on things, a younger person might need a push from behind, some are scared and just need a bit of encouragement, and you can’t make others do something scary or take the initiative even if you force the issue on them. People have high expectations from you, and in turn, you also have high expectations from your people. But if someone from your team doesn’t see certain things because they lack experience, no matter how much you want that person to change and see things differently, it won’t happen. You can help them - that’s your job - but it will take time. Do you have patience? Yes? No? Well… if you don’t, then you will try to narrow the field, and you start telling people what to do. “See that you don’t forget this, don’t do that, take this into account, pay close attention to that other thing”, etc. You teach them to become lazy again, to no longer think on their own, and expect you to give them directions and draw their attention to things that pertain to their daily work. And then you start being likened to a boss like any other who likes giving orders or is a micromanagement fan. Or even worse, people begin to think that you somehow believe that they are broken in some way, and you need to fix them, in which case, whatever respect they had for you goes out the window.

People are what they are; they are not what you want them to be. If you don’t understand this, you’re going to have a lot of problems. Especially when you try to motivate them. This is related to the performance appraisals I mentioned in the previous chapter. To do good work, people need to be motivated. And as a Team Lead, it is often expected of you to motivate your people. And this will probably be one of the most frustrating things about your new role because it’s something difficult to do. I’ll mention a few things about motivation from personal experience. Let’s first start with the definition of the verb[57]:

Motivate, (verb). To make someone feel determined to do something or enthusiastic about doing it; to make someone behave in a particular way.

So how might you do that? Needless to say, you have to put some time, effort, and thought into this. First of all, don’t assume that what motivates you will be the same thing that motivates others. You can’t resume to motivating them with the same approach you would like to be motivated with. You have to consider what would motivate each and every one of them. Secondly, avoid using practices that make your developers feel like they are back at kindergarten. On some occasions, I’ve seen childish motivation techniques like offering feedback in the form of color-coded behavior charts with large red, blue, and green dots, or maybe using emoticons like a smiley face, neutral face, sad face, etc., and display everything on whiteboards that everyone in the office could see. Or the use of activities that try to make work seem more fun, stuff like collecting points, levels, badges, medals, thank you cards, or various awards. Somehow, by themselves, these were supposed to increase employee motivation. But they only showed that nobody thought about the situation enough. “We don’t want to put in the effort or time to figure out what really motivates you, but here is a golden badge. Now get back to work if you want to ever get your hand on the platinum one”. If you don’t want to spend the time trying to understand what motivates people, you might just as well resort to the classic “carrots and sticks”[58] method where you reward good behavior (usually with money) and punish the bad behavior (generally with no money or threats of being fired).

From what I’ve noticed, such “motivation” techniques work to some extent with young and inexperienced developers, or better said, young employees in general (although if you have a team just of young and inexperienced developers, the issue of motivating is the least of your problems), and doesn’t work that well with older employees who don’t feel engaged by gamification[59] concepts and actually can end up demotivated by such practices, since they feel like it’s devaluing or belittling their work. In addition to that, introducing game elements into the work encourages competition, which is something you don’t want to have between the members of a team (you want collaboration instead). Gamification might work to a certain degree when used for training or learning activities to make them more fun, but with work, it will most likely have a negative effect as some people can become more focused on collecting badges or medals than on the quality of their work.

In his book “Drive: The Surprising Truth About What Motivates Us”[60], author Daniel H. Pink mentions three important factors that lead to better performance: autonomy, mastery, and purpose. People do better work when they are in control of what they are doing, making their own decisions on how to do the work and when to schedule it, being measured by results and not by the time one spends sitting at their desk, and not having their boss constantly micromanaging or ordering them around. These things also make the job more enjoyable, so people feel more motivated coming to work. When you give people autonomy, they start feeling more empowered and less limited by what their supervisor tells them to do (or how to do it). It’s also proof that they are trusted they will do a good job, that their skills are valued, that they can make real contributions, or at least their input is being considered. It also means that people start thinking more about the “why” of their work, they start thinking about the bigger picture, and start caring more about their work and the result of their work and start to view problems as challenges that need to be overcome. Who do you think will be better at their work and produce better results? Developers that work nine-to-five and behave like black boxes that get specs on one side and produce working code on the other, without actually caring what they build? Or developers for which the work actually matters and strive to get better at what they do so they do an even better job going forward? For most developers, mastery is a purpose in itself; they have the desire to learn, to grow, and develop, they want to become craftspersons[67], they want to build well-written software to be proud of. This makes them engaged and committed to the work they are doing; they want to take pride in doing excellent work, they won’t take shortcuts and won’t give up easily, they will keep pushing on until it’s done. These people do the work not just for the money but because it’s meaningful to them. You want these types of people. And when I say “you want”, what I really mean is that “you can’t actually make them”.

The best people and teams I’ve worked with were characterized by the presence of these factors to large degrees. But that was not the entire picture. You can work on these factors, you can grant your people autonomy instead of giving them instructions to execute, you can help them grow and acquire new knowledge, you can draw them into pursuing a certain purpose… but it won’t work for everyone. For these factors to work, you need the right kind of people, people with internal drive and a high dose of common sense, professionals with a good work ethic. In plain English, people that actually “give a shit”. And not just the people in your team, but people throughout the company that affect your work. For example, autonomy is something that must be given. It’s a loss of control from managers and bosses. It’s also a matter of empowerment and trust. If your superiors don’t trust you or want to control every aspect of your work (which sometimes it also relates to trust), then you won’t have the proper level of autonomy. The desire for mastery is present in any good developer; we all want to learn a lot of stuff, we want to grow, we want to be the best at this and that, and we want to do a good job. If the project is exciting and challenging, then most developers will be engaged in their work. But if your boss yells at you to “ship it” when it’s in an incomplete stage or just a prototype, you basically ship crap. It’s hard to take pride in doing crappy work, so that affects the motivation of developers to do a good job. Why get better and try to do a good job when nobody but you seems to be interested in that? Similarly, if the project is monotonous and developers only do repetitive tasks that could easily be automated, it’s pointless to expect people to be motivated and want to be better at it. Better for what reason? As for purpose, it’s sometimes hard to find it in the workplace. “Make more money for the company or stakeholders. Do more with less, faster. Make your boss rich so they can buy the latest models of luxury sports utility vehicles and drive them to the golf course each weekend”. Do these qualify as a good purpose to have?

What drives people is something internal, something they have grown with or have invested in building on their own, for their own reasons. You might think that people that are part of the same team, department, or company, have the same boss, have the same skills, perform the same job and have the same salary should be equally motivated, right? Yet, they are not. So you can’t really show up and try to motivate them because they either are internally motivated, or they’re not. You can work on external factors to try to influence that or bring it to the surface, but whatever you do, it’s not going to place it inside people if they don’t have it, to begin with. Maybe it hasn’t surfaced yet, you can work on that, but if it’s not there, the chances are that you, as a Team Lead, won’t be able to place it in them. It is as if you were watering and caring for a flowerpot that contains no seeds. You will be wasting your time. So it depends a lot on what kind of people they are. For example, autonomy is good most of the time, but if you hire superstar developers and then give them autonomy (i.e., letting them loose), you might be in for a very nasty surprise (you will find out later why). There must be rules, there has to be someone who makes the final decisions when there is a stalemate, someone needs to have some control. Don’t think that it’s enough to bring up the three factors, and then things will take shape on their own. When people are driven, they are driven by intrinsic motivation.

Let me give you an example. There is this old parable of “The three stone cutters”. There are a few variations of the story, but the gist of it goes something like this:

A traveler came upon three workers that were cutting stone. He curiously approached them and asked what they were doing.
The first stonecutter said he’s just doing his job.
The second worker replied that he’s cutting stones to earn money to support his family.
Finally, the third proudly said that he’s building a cathedral.

All three of them were doing the same job, at the same site, but for different reasons: one to feed himself, one to take care of his family, and one for some greater purpose. All three workers were already motivated by something to do the job. Something different for each of them. Something internal. That’s why extrinsic motivators don’t work well, for example, because for each person that “something” internal is different, while many are trying to motivate or engage people from the outside, sometimes using the same techniques on everyone. But that’s not a good approach. One size doesn’t fit all. You have to take each person individually, see what makes that person tick, and only after you understand it, to think about how you could increase the level of motivation that the person already has and how to bring that to the surface, so it manifests itself in the work that the person is doing. At this point, it’s worth saying that, just like the title of the book I mentioned above, “drive” is actually a better word choice when thinking about “motivation”. Although “drive” and “motivation” can be seen as synonyms, using the word “drive” is better because “motivation” feels like a trigger to action, but then it wears off as time passes; it’s short-lived. That’s how a money incentive might work for a couple of weeks and make someone really work harder for a while, but then, they return to their typical way of operating. “Drive”, on the other hand, makes you think of action, of motion, of something that is ongoing. What drives people means what makes them do the things they do on a daily basis, not as a one-time event.

Another thing I’ve seen in some managers is that they confuse enthusiasm with motivation. Some people are more serious or grumpy, but they are dependable and perform well at their job. Others are gleeful, happier; they get excited faster or easier. They do their job just as well. However, some managers consider that the first category is unmotivated while the second has a lot of motivation; if you’re not “all teeth”, all day long, there might be something wrong with you. You have to understand that not all people are the same. If someone doesn’t have a bubbly personality, it doesn’t mean that you should jump on them and immediately subject them to motivational practices. Just pay attention to their work. Each person reaches success in their own personal way. Look at what drives each individual and see where you might step in to improve results. For example, someone could tackle more challenging work, but they lack self-confidence; you have to encourage them or expose them to situations slightly outside of their comfort zone. Someone’s job involves interaction with bosses, but they feel intimidated; you need to think about whether it’s worth exposing them to more interactions, so they overcome their fear, or if it’s better to go in the other direction and change their tasks to limit contact with bosses. Someone is a good developer but gets bored quickly, and their work suffers; maybe give them more challenging tasks or more responsibilities. Some are very analytical and won’t start to work until they figure out a complex plan; you sometimes have to push them headfirst, so they learn that things can turn well even without the perfect plan. Some are just the opposite and jump hastily in unknown situations; you have to convince them to take some time to prepare first. Some lose focus quickly; you need to check from time to time how they are progressing. Others do very well on their own; you can increase their level of autonomy. One is 20 years old and thinks they know everything; have lots of patience… and good luck to you :).

If you pay attention to the things I just mentioned, you will see that they are not ways to motivate people. People have their own different motivators and also demotivators. So what you should do is to find out what motivates each one, then intervene when you see that there is something that makes them lose that motivation. You can help them or expose them to various things, so they grow as individuals, and this, in turn, to get reflected in their results, but that doesn’t mean you motivated them. When they are in their element, they have drive; when they are a fish out of the water, that drive diminishes. Pay attention to that. I have seen many managers who put good people in a position that matches their skills, but in terms of drive, it’s very far from their comfort zone. And when things go sideways, and people start to feel miserable, the manager concludes that they are not motivated enough, since the skills are available to them.

And how do you find out what motivates each individual? A large part of it is observing people. Pay attention to what they are interested in, pay attention to what they talk about with passion, pay attention to how they behave. Then, you can talk to them and simply ask. I mentioned in the previous chapter about having periodical, honest discussions with your people. Ask them what motivates them and help them with that. Ask them what demotivates them and work on fixing that. Agree on things, then make a plan together and implement it. Monitor progress and see if the employee is actually working on those things, so you can see if they are motivated or not to achieve their goals, especially if they have chosen those goals themselves.

And understand that, if someone doesn’t perform adequately and you want a change for the better (better results, more involvement, better productivity, more progress, whatever it is), for that change to happen, you first need people to want to change. It’s like in this joke you may have heard:

Q: How many clinical psychologists does it take to change a light bulb?
A: Only one. But the light bulb has to WANT to change.

It’s funny ‘cause it’s true.

You try to motivate people because you want a change. If the situation was exactly as you would like it to be, you wouldn’t try to change anything. But just like in the joke above, people don’t change unless they want to. If they don’t want to, you won’t make them change, no matter how much persuasive work you try to do, and no matter how many motivational techniques you know. Seriously now, how many times have you had a logical conversation with yourself and decided to do something, to change something about you? I bet you felt energized; you already thought about all the benefits you’ll get, to become a different person, etc. And then how long did that last you? Did you even start doing something to make that change happen? Or, another example, how many people stop going to the gym after the month of January, even though they’ve set themselves a New Year’s resolution to exercise more every day? The desire to change fades in time, and so does the internal drive to keep working on the change if it’s not fueled by something. And that something is usually “needs”. There are many motivational theories, but what they seem to have in common is the fact that motivation is related to human needs. It’s not the basic needs for food, water, or shelter, but the more evolved ones like the need for competence, autonomy, purpose, achievement, or recognition. If someone doesn’t want to achieve anything at work, is more or less on “idle mode” unless someone is breathing down their neck and micromanages them to make sure they work, do you really think you can motivate them? You can’t. Because these people want only a paycheck at the end of the month, the satisfaction the work itself brings is not among their needs. Consequently, they are not motivated to do the work. And you can’t put these needs in people. I can’t make you “need” something, you either need it or you don’t. This is exactly the external motivation some are trying to apply, who often doesn’t match with the needs of the employees. If you give people something they need, it’s called motivating them, so motivation works. If you give them something they don’t need, motivation doesn’t work. Even if you manage to help or convince someone to change, it’s more because they wanted or needed to change but didn’t know how, and not because of your persuasion skills. Of course, you have to do something to bring this change to light; it’s not like it’s happening by itself. But you didn’t cause the actual change. You can’t directly motivate them; you can only help them and work with them to fuel their drive and bring out the best in themselves.

Before ending this section about motivation, just a few words of caution. I’ve met Team Leads and managers that think motivation is something that can be attached to, or infused into people. More even, they think that they can motivate anyone, no matter who it is, even people who they haven’t even met yet. Some still called people in for interviews and later hired them, even though they knew for a fact that they were lazy people with issues. They believed that “they weren’t properly motivated” and that under their leadership, they will turn into some role model of professionalism or something. Please don’t do that! It’s one thing to have confidence in your abilities to turn a bad situation into a good one, and it’s another to be delusional. If a candidate has the skills to do the job is one thing. If they actually want to do the job is another. If people have the skills but lack the drive, you can’t place it in them because you are not the world’s greatest life coach. That’s why you need to hire for motivational fit. In the previous chapter, when I talked about conducting interviews, I said that once we get the conversation going, I ask the candidate to tell me about the jobs they’ve had and the projects they worked on, which ones they like, which ones not so much, and why. Pay close attention to the responses you get. This is how you find out from the start what motivates the candidate. Then later, on performance reviews, when I said that the person should evaluate themselves, I mentioned talking with the employee about what motivates and demotivates them. Don’t assume these things; try to discover them or ask about them.

The working environment

So, you can’t really motivate people; you can only try to bring their internal drive to fruition. However, something that you can very easily do is to demotivate them. And this can happen not only because you do something wrong that ends up demotivating them, but it can also be caused by the work environment. Do you remember when I said you can’t ignore the working environment when evaluating an employee’s performance? Similarly, you can’t ignore the working environment when you consider people’s motivation and drive. When it comes to employees’ motivation and demotivation, many focus just on the persons and ignore the environment. But from my own experience, when it comes to people losing motivation, what I saw is that the environment is mostly to blame. People lose their drive because they work in an environment where they cannot manifest themselves to their true potential. It’s like wanting to drive a sports car at top speed on a road full of potholes. It won’t happen! The car is just fine; it’s the road that’s broken. You can’t expect people to be motivated in a broken environment. So part of your responsibilities as a Team Lead is to find out what demotivates people, or what’s missing, and fix it if you can. If not, escalate to your superiors then follow up on things until they are solved. Fix the environment first and only then make a fuss about people not being motivated enough.

But let’s face it; as a Team Lead, you’ll not be able to fix all the problems that exist within the company. Things like harmful processes or procedures imposed from above, lack of direction from management, employees being punished for bringing bad news, for honest mistakes, or disagreeing with the boss, or lots of other issues caused by bad office politics, you, as a Team Lead, can’t really fix or make go away. And even if you try, you will probably only be trying to fix the symptoms, not the root causes of the problems. But in your team, you still have to create a healthy working environment. You can’t get the most out of your people if they work in an unhealthy environment and don’t feel safe. You can find out what drives their behavior and what motivates them internally, but if there are obstacles in the manifestation of that internal drive, they will exhibit that drive only to some extent. Obstacles like that might be, for example, a lack of opportunity for growth and improvement, the presence of toxic colleagues who are tolerated instead of being removed from the team, lack of interpersonal trust or respect, which then leads to all sorts of situations where people don’t feel comfortable being themselves and instead, become worried that they might be judged or criticized if they speak their mind, have a different opinion, own up to mistakes, or ask for what might seem like a naive or dumb question. I will talk more about “trust” in a later chapter, but it suffices to say that having the team members trust and respect each other is very important because, without trust and respect, freedom of expression gets self-regulated, the fear of making mistakes sets in, which then leads to diminished courage to take risks, which in turn leads to no longer doing the right thing but the least risky thing, to analyze something indefinitely to get it right and not being blamed or criticized in case of failure, people keep good ideas for themselves for fear of being stolen by others, they start withholding information instead of sharing it with others, and these are just a few examples. If people abstain from truly interacting with others, thinking about where everyone stands and how they might react, that inevitably leads to a reduction in productivity. Have you seen police action movies, for example? When the police enter a house where they think there is a suspect or a fugitive? Do they go in casually, like walking into their own home or in a shop at the mall? No! They enter very slowly, looking in all directions. With caution. So that nobody shoots at them or attacks them. They advance slowly because the environment is not safe. The same goes for a company when something unfamiliar must be done, so people look around them to see what happens, they walk carefully, or may completely refrain from participating in the new activity. “What if I say something stupid? What if others don’t agree with my idea? What if this, or that, or the other?” It’s not at all efficient. On the contrary, when you have a safe environment, even if people say something stupid, they trust that they will not be judged, rejected, or reprimanded and that everyone will focus on the idea or the message being presented. If it’s good, it’s good. If it’s bad, the suggestion is not used, and people focus their attention on other ideas. People feel that they can share anything with the team.

Google did research as part of one of their projects, to answer the question of “What makes an effective team at Google?”[68] What they discovered was that the number one contributing factor to an effective team was “psychological safety”[69]. This notion refers to people feeling safe around their team members when offering their ideas, asking questions, taking risks or admitting their mistakes, while trusting that nobody will punish them, reject them, make them feel bad, or see them as ignorant, incompetent, disruptive or negative when they express their opinions. It’s basically people’s willingness to be vulnerable and be themselves without fear of negative personal consequences. Without mutual respect and trust, there will be fear of being judged, and people will hold back. People don’t learn, don’t innovate, and the team isn’t as effective as it could be.

So how do you build psychological safety? As a Team Lead, besides frequent discussions you have with everyone, you must also encourage discussions among team members and make sure those discussions remain constructive. Then, you have to be the first to open yourself up to the others. Share your opinions, admit your mistakes, ask for help, say “I don’t know” when you don’t know, give and ask for feedback, ask questions, include everyone in making important decisions, consider everyone’s input, be supportive and encourage people to speak. Openly acknowledge good ideas, encourage learning, while with problems, focus on solutions instead of pointing fingers at whoever caused the issues. Communicate transparently to the team whatever you discussed with your superiors, share information, and be a “shit umbrella”[70] for whatever gets thrown at the team. And if your boss punches you in the face (figuratively speaking), it doesn’t mean you can return to the team office and spread those punches around to everyone.

While psychological safety and building a healthy environment sounds good and is something really necessary, it won’t be that easy to pull off. It’s not like you can follow some practices or behave a certain way, then things just fall into place. Nope. Why? Because of people.

Many hide behind the name “resource” to fool themselves in thinking that they can manage and control human aspects, just like they can manage cost, equipment, or inventories, to avoid getting involved and stepping in some quicksand that they definitely know it’s out there. But the reality is, you don’t work with resources, you work with people. When a computer program doesn’t work the way you want, you make a change, you re-compile, you deploy, and you are done. When you don’t like the configuration of a server, you upgrade it, change the processor, add more memory, replace something, and it then works at completely different parameters. With people, it doesn’t work that way. When you don’t like the “configuration” of somebody… well, tough luck. A computer is mostly a deterministic machine. Algorithms, for the most part, are deterministic too. With people, though, there is a “Math.random()” in everyone. When software takes a decision, it just executes an “if” statement. When people make decisions, there are all sorts of unknown factors that weigh into the decision. A computer won’t behave irrationally, have mood swings, procrastinate, be judgmental, or complain that the work is boring. People will. People can have a whole range of feelings and emotions, some positive like joy, happiness, hope, confidence, enthusiasm, pride, satisfaction, or gratitude, and some negative, like sadness, anxiousness, fear, anger, resentment, frustration, depression, or hate. Different people have egos of different sizes; they have different personalities, experiences, aspirations, and dreams. Work can be a way for them to reach those aspirations and dreams, or work can be just the thing they have to do to have clothes to wear, a roof over their head, and food to put on the table. Some might work hard for that, some might be lazy. They might work hard or be lazy all the time, or just some of the time. Some might even be meteo-sensitive. You just have to learn to deal with that.

The next thing many are trying to fool themselves with, after considering people as resources to abstract away the human characteristics, is with thinking that there is a “work-life balance”. They expect people to leave their personal issues at the door when they walk into the office. Not gonna happen! The thing we refer to as “work-life balance” doesn’t really exist. People will arrive at work with their personal problems and leave home with their work problems. It’s not like people can put all aspects of their private life aside, just like they hang their coat on a hanger in the office. With petty issues, it works, with more important ones, not so much. If someone is going through an ugly divorce, that doesn’t go away when they are at work. If someone is sick while at home, they will be sick at work also. “You” being at work can’t ignore the “you” who stayed up late last night and didn’t get any sleep because of a toothache. If your cat ate your canary (and your goldfish too), you would still be upset while at work. When you are dealing with people, you are dealing with the person in front of you, but actually, there are also a lot of other things in the background that you might not be aware of, things that have nothing to do with the actual work, but can still affect it. When dealing with people, there is some sort of context involved. And this context is different from person to person and to the same person at different moments in time. This is to say that what works with one person does not work with another or vice-versa, and depending on the context, what worked with one person once, may not work with the same person a second time.

You also need to pay attention to people’s interactions with others, not only to each person separately. Someone can behave in one way when working alone, and in another way when working with others, or in one way with someone and in another way with someone else. Psychological safety turned out to be the most important factor from the Google study because people don’t always work well with each other. They might have different values, their personality might clash, their emotions might get in the way, some might have their own personal agenda and might try to use or convince the team to fulfill it, some might be very competitive and end up creating rivalry in the team instead of cooperation, some might be more dynamic and adaptable and become resentful of those who try to resist change. A computer doesn’t judge another computer. People do. A computer doesn’t quarrel with another computer and then doesn’t speak to it for the next few days. People do. Servers from a rack don’t all want to sit by the window overlooking the park. People do. You need to pay attention to the dynamics of the relationships within the team. And you will play an important role in the team because people will take you as an example, and when things become “emotional”, they will look at you for guidance or consider you an all problem solver.

So you also have to be careful about how you - as a Team Lead - interact with others. It’s easier if you’re hired as a Team Lead into a new team, but if you get promoted a Team Lead from within the team, you’ll notice that people behave differently with you, and in turn, you’ll have to treat them differently. Remember that now, as a Team Lead, you have other responsibilities. You no longer answer just for your actions and results, but for the actions and results of the team. The working relationship with your teammates changes. You continue to work side by side with them, they still do their work as they did when you were their peer, but now you can delegate or assign them work. As a Team Lead, you can also overwrite whatever they do or decide. You have the last word. The decision, in the end, is yours. You are their hierarchical superior. Add to this the fact that you can now subject them to performance evaluations (something they probably can’t reciprocate), and you’ll notice that the nature of the interactions will change, especially with friendships. Think about how you’ll interact with someone who is your “best buddy”. If your buddy suggests to add a cool technology to the project, but you disagree because the moment is not right, it’s risky, and the ROI is probably not justified, what do you do? Then they start insisting. What do you do? Or what do you do when your best buddy becomes lazy and stops contributing? Do you look away? Do you do something about it? Are you willing to fire someone if that someone is your best friend? If they get into a conflict with someone and you have to mediate the discussion, will you take the side of the presented arguments or the side of your friend? Where do you draw the line between being their friend and being their Team Lead? Do you draw that line in the same place with everyone? Do you think people won’t notice if you favor someone (even unconsciously)? They will.

You can still be friends; I’m not saying now that you have to distance yourself from everyone else and break up friendships with the others in the team, but it must be clear to everyone that you are the Team Lead and at work, this must take precedence. Just like you must be a Team Lead first and a developer second, you have to be Team Lead first and their friend second. You all have o job to perform, and your friendship should not interfere with that.
