So how should you behave? Should you be authoritative? Controlling? Should you order people around because you are in a higher position within the team? Is that the way to gain respect? No, that won’t get you very far. You will just be seen as an asshole. What then? Should you be nice? I’ve seen Team Leads believing their main job is to keep their people happy no matter what, so that nobody’s upset, so that everyone feels good at work, everything to be pleasant, relaxing music playing in the background, aromatic herbs burning in an office corner, this kind of stuff. This doesn’t work either. Nice Team Leads fail to do what’s needed when it’s needed if by any chance that makes someone upset, things like giving people honest but negative feedback, or pushing them beyond their comfort zone, or removing bad apples from the barrel. If you are nice, you might also be perceived as weak, especially by your bosses. You can’t last long as a nice Team Lead (you will probably last longer being an asshole Team Lead). So, again, how should you behave with everyone?

In my opinion, you have to be fair to everyone. That means things like the following, which are all synonyms of “fair”: just, equitable, unbiased, trustworthy, honest, honorable, impartial, objective, non-partisan. In other words, you focus on what’s right and what’s important, you make sure the same rules apply for everyone in the team, you treat everyone with respect, you don’t favor some and disadvantage others. You have a certain power as a Team Lead. It means to use that power wisely.

Fairness goes hand in hand with psychological safety. People in your team won’t feel safe if they don’t trust you, and, from my experience, people respect you more if you try to be fair. They might not like you or want to become best buddies with you, but you will have their respect. Your team members will also understand better from where your actions and decisions come from. Since people are all different, you can’t deal with everyone in the same way. What works for some will not work for others. So, inevitably you have to behave differently with each person. And people see this. If you are not fair, people will think you are acting in someone’s favor while treating unfavorably someone else, instead of understanding that you are using methods that are better suited to each individual. Then, inevitably there will be difficult decisions that you have to make that will indeed disadvantage someone. You have no way of avoiding this. The working environment is too complex to make decisions in ideal circumstances while simultaneously having all the facts. Even if you think carefully and make an objective decision, that decision could still upset some people. If you are not fair, instead of understanding that you are doing what you think is right for the project, application, team, or business, and understand that you took the best decision for most individuals given the circumstances, and to understand why the decision tilted to one direction or another, people will just become resentful and take things personally.

Trying to be fair is also important in solving conflicts. And just to be clear, by solving conflicts, I mean between people, not between Git branches. There will always be conflicts at work. Just like you can count on software to have bugs, you can also count on people that work together to have conflicts with each other. These can start for various reasons, sometimes without any connection to the actual work, but maybe because someone tampered with the air conditioner, or because it was someone’s turn to clean the refrigerator in the office and they didn’t. Earlier, when I mentioned problem-solving skills, I was mostly talking about business problems, things that you could equate with “business challenges”. But as a Team Lead, you will have to solve all sorts of problems that are, in fact, problems as we all know them, i.e., bad stuff happening. Some conflicts are in this category. You will have no choice but to deal with and solve unpleasant situations. Nobody likes problems, people don’t even want to talk about them, but problems must be exposed, they must be put on the table, and people need to get together to discuss them and solve them. And when people gather around a problem to solve it, there can inevitably be… even more conflict. People start to pick fights because human elements intervene, like emotions and feelings, differences in personalities, personal preferences for an approach or another, or a solution or another, different values, different ways of seeing things, poor communication, etc. Sometimes, a major incident in production, when everyone is running around in circles, agitated, stressed, and angry, is the ideal stage to snap at your colleagues or say something inappropriate. A conflict occurs, and then, instead of focusing on the problem and solving it, people start to place blame, saying that the problem is “in your section of code Jake, because Friday evening you left home in a hurry without properly testing. We should have realized this was your doing, ‘cause you neglected to clean the refrigerator as well”.

So be aware that you can’t escape conflict.

Anyone can hold the helm when the sea is calm - Publilius Syrus[71]

And when a conflict lands on your lap, what you need to do is to have a “resolution” for it. Fix what needs to be fixed, compromise, forgive, give in, whatever, but don’t ignore it. It will not go away. If Jane and Steve have a fight, after you give them some time to calm down, it may seem like a good idea to then arrange things so that the two interact less on the same tasks, or attending the same meetings, and so on, but, on the long run, you will lose if Jane and Steve really do need to work together. Trying to prevent a conflict from occurring is OK; if you can do that, absolutely do it. But be mindful of your solution, and actually resolve the conflict. Maybe the previous example is OK now, you have some peace of mind, but in time it will take a lot of energy to keep track of all the combinations of things or people that are “safe to interact”. Things can get out of hand and, over time, can degenerate into worse issues. And it will be harder to solve them then than it is now. “Strike the iron while it’s hot” is a saying. Otherwise, you’re just keeping a pressure pot on the fire, and at some point, it will explode, and you then have to clean stuff off all the walls. Problems rarely go away on their own if you ignore them. The next day you come to work, they are still there, and they have brought some new friends along; i.e., more problems. Any conflict must be resolved; otherwise, it pushes people apart, and you will end up not having a team, but people that all work by themselves in the same office.

So how do you deal with a conflict at work?

Just like with any other conflict in the real world: with patience and trying to remain calm, trying to see things from someone else’s perspective, focusing on the problem, event, or behavior instead of placing blame on the other, by avoiding jumping to conclusions, being an active listener, and so on. The only difference is that, as a Team Lead, you will most likely be mediating conflicts instead of being in conflict with someone.

I’ve seen complex processes to resolve conflicts. You have to listen to both sides separately, to independently verify the versions of the two parties, research possible solutions, work on each party individually before bringing both sides together; sometimes, HR must also be notified. But in my opinion, this is not a way to solve conflicts. Cold procedures like this look more like a “trial” in a court of law like somebody did something wrong, and now you are looking for evidence to blame and maybe punish someone for it. This is a classic managerial approach, where the manager thinks it’s their job to solve the conflict. But it doesn’t work like that. With an approach like this, you might “put an end” to the conflict, but you will not “resolve” the dispute because people continue to be angry and resentful. Both parties should resolve the conflict on their own. You are just there to help and make sure that the discussion remains respectful, that both sides listen to one another before speaking, and make an effort to understand each other. You help everyone understand the importance, gravity, or the consequences of the situation and why it’s necessary to resolve the conflict, then keep them focused on working on solutions. You then intervene any time one person attacks the other, people give more importance to one’s opinions than to facts, or they try to place blame, the discussion stalls or starts to diverge from the root cause of the conflict or doesn’t lead to a solution. As a Team Lead, you don’t resolve the conflict for them, you don’t make decisions for them. Mediate the discussion, guide them, make suggestions, help them figure it out - as a marriage counselor does with a married couple that got themselves into some issues in their relationship. Talking honestly helps, and over time the conflict gets consumed, and people reconcile.

Needless to say, if a conflict lasts too long or there is no solution in sight or any chance of being solved, “you”, as the Team Lead, have to make a decision and impose a solution. You are at work, remember? Results are important. The business sometimes can’t wait for conflicts to be resolved naturally. So “you” resolve it. Some might be disadvantaged by your decision, but that’s life. At work, people don’t necessarily need to be friends with each other; they just have to get along enough so that their interaction doesn’t affect their work. If you treat everyone fairly, people will see where your decision and solution came from and will understand. If instead, you treat them unfairly, you will just end up generating even more conflict, conflict in which you may end up as one of the two parties, not as the mediator. So be a fair Team Lead.

Trade-offs

Before ending this section about being a Team Lead, there is one last thing to add to it. I mentioned that, as a Team Lead, you can no longer be a full-time developer and that tasks pertaining to your new role will take up the majority of your time. There are decisions to make and things to do as a Team Lead that are your responsibility, so you will have to delegate part of your developer work to others from your team. I also said that you need to help the people in your team grow, to help them develop, so they don’t depend on you in their daily work. All fine and dandy, but there is a problem. You’ll probably have so much on your plate that you will be unable to do all of these things as well as you would like to do them. You will have to be satisfied with certain things done not entirely to your liking, or the results might be different than what you would hope for, even when you always try to do the right thing. You need to be aware that you’ll encounter many situations in which you will feel trapped between a rock and a hard place, and when that happens, you will have to resort to trade-offs[72]:

Trade-off, (noun). A balancing of two opposing situations or qualities, both of which are desired.

Let me give you some examples, so you understand what I’m talking about. First of all, you make trade-offs all the time as a developer. You might not see them as trade-offs but as choices, but they are trade-offs. You might write simple synchronized code that’s slow versus more sophisticated code with fewer locks that’s faster; you actually want simple, thread-safe code with fast performance. Another example might be going for a garbage collector or managing memory explicitly, assuming you have the option in your programming language; what you actually want is control over memory but without too much hassle. The list could go on; inheritance versus composition, exceptions versus error codes, polymorphism vs. switch statements, compiled to native code versus running on a VM, buying a server versus renting it from the cloud… and so on. You would like all of the benefits, but you can’t have them all. You have to balance things against each other and decide what is most important.

When you become a Team Lead, the size of things you put in balance increases beyond affecting a few lines of code, the architecture, the deployment, or parts of the application; it can affect every single person on your team, the team itself, the project, the business unit, the department, or even the company.

Another example is regarding your interaction with your boss and the people on your team. Developers from the team want something, and management wants something else. Maybe the client wants something too… something completely different. For instance, perhaps the application code isn’t as good as it should be, so the team wants to take some time to refactor, but then, you can no longer meet the deadline. Your boss doesn’t even want to hear it. You have to meet the deadline, so it looks like you will have to do the refactoring later. But in this job, “later” almost never comes. So what do you do? You go after the deadline and leave the application in a mess while the developers in your team start cursing you because it becomes increasingly difficult to make changes to the app? Or do you refactor and get yelled at by your bosses or customers because the company ends up paying delay fees or that other schedules get impacted? You will probably need to find a solution that will reconcile both situations. And then, why did the code end up in a mess that needs to be refactored in the first place? Did you and your team neglect best practices and common sense, and you created some issues? Or did you make those decisions consciously? I’m talking about technical debt[73] here. As a Team Lead, you will often need to make decisions when it comes to focusing on quality code or delivery, so, many times, you will be the one to decide when to take on technical debt and in what amount. When you do, you have to remember to repay at some point in time (not just “later”); otherwise, you will keep accumulating interest just like with financial debt. Your decision to take on the technical debt will be triggered by the business (I’ve never met a developer wanting to take on technical debt on their own… that is, without being pressured), but since it’s a “technical” thing, it will be your responsibility to repay it. The business will forget all about it if you don’t remind them. And when you do remind them and decide to repay it, you need to know how to defend your opinion in front of everyone.

Then you have to find the right balance between you writing code and letting others on the team do it. You can’t keep holding on to development tasks once you become a Team Lead, but there will still be situations when “you” have to handle things. Maybe something is on fire, and you know best the technology or the subject, or for security reasons only you have access, but it must be resolved immediately, and you don’t have time to teach others how to do it or give them security access. I already mentioned above what happens when you are the Team Lead, and there are certain things that only you can do: it creates a dependency on you, or worse, blockers when you are busy with other things, but people wait for you. Know-how can also be lost if only you know how to do certain things. And this is where trade-offs show up. If you do the work, you can do it right away. It doesn’t take much, but you keep others depending on you, and nobody else learns how to do it. If you teach others how to do it, you have the advantage that they no longer depend on you, but it will take much longer. When will you teach them, and when do you roll up your sleeves and do it yourself? When do you delegate tasks, and when do you keep them for yourself? Will you delegate the same types of tasks to the same people, or will you try to increase the team’s know-how so that anyone can do anybody’s work? How much time will you take from everyone’s schedule to teach them stuff, or have them share knowledge between themselves so that deliveries don’t get affected? Will you build and train a SWAT team, or are you the SWAT team? How well do you want to know the project? As a Team Lead, you need to know how each part of the application works and what role it plays in the whole architecture, but having other responsibilities too, will force you to limit yourself to a higher view of things. How deep in detail will you go (i.e., from what altitude do you want to see things, a thousand feet, ten thousand feet?), and how much do you rely on others to do the right thing? Do you check their work afterward? If you assign work to 10 people, do you think you have time to check what everyone did? You may not even have time to write down things for appraisals, or have periodic face-to-face discussions with everyone, ‘cause you don’t want to do just one silly annual appraisal, do you? Or maybe you want to? Another trade-off.

A lot of the work you will do as a Team Lead will involve trade-offs. It’s not all ones or zeros, and black or white, it will be a whole range of nuances of gray. Any choice, any option, will come bundled with something. Call it price, call it interest, call it consequences, but it will be there. And you will have to deal with it eventually. So you have to prioritize and always put in balance the advantages and disadvantages for all the options you have at your disposal (even for choosing between multiple trade-offs) and try to make the best of all worlds while at the same time remain in good relationships with everyone, even when you have to make hard decisions.

Health

When it comes to making trade-offs, another thing to be aware of is that sometimes - mostly unconsciously - you’ll place your health on one side or the other of the balance. I must admit I’m not the one to talk about this kind of subject in detail. I often don’t exercise or eat healthy, I spend all day on a computer and all night on a mobile screen, I keep a bad body posture, I sleep too much or not enough, and I don’t do regular medical checkups, unless once every ten years counts… But that aside, I just want to point out one thing: working as a software developer is not always a healthy endeavor. Programming is a mentally demanding activity that also involves sitting for the most part of the day, so naturally, this comes hand in hand with stuff like headaches, stress, tiredness, depression, lack of concentration, back pains, computer vision syndrome, carpal tunnel syndrome, gaining weight, shallow breathing, just to mention a few. Heck, there is even a book written about it: “The Healthy Programmer: Get Fit, Feel Better, and Keep Coding”[74] that explores these topics (and more) in detail, far better than I can. You might want to get yourself a copy of the book so that you become aware of a few things that you might not have thought of (consult with your doctor first, if you want to follow advice or recommendations from any book). But even if we know of these things, it seems we rarely do something about them. We keep eating unhealthy, we don’t drink enough water, we don’t exercise, we skip on periodic medical examinations, we ignore stress, we don’t get enough sleep, etc.

But even that book omits one thing that you might encounter if you aren’t mindful of how you are handling yourself. And that thing is “burnout”. Burnout might not be recognized as a disorder in many countries (it sure isn’t in mine; “just walk it off” is the suggested approach to fix it), but I can assure you it is very real. And it sucks. Huge time. You’re always tired and lacking energy, you get depressed or become irritable, you start to forget things, you lose your enthusiasm for things, programming stops being fun (lots of things stop being fun actually), even writing ten lines of code becomes frustrating and painful, and you get the feeling that no matter what effort you put in or whatever you do, it seems like you are not accomplishing anything useful at work or making progress with your learning.

We, programmers, tend to bite off more than we can chew. It’s not enough that we work long hours in the office, in a stressful environment, with lots of pressure from bosses and deadlines, but after all of that, we get home and work on our personal project, or we spend time learning new things late into the night. Things are always changing; new things are always coming up. We have to learn. We have no choice! But then we push ourselves too far. We need time to learn new things, but the day is only 24 hours long. From where can we gain some more time? We don’t cook anymore at home; we order fast-food. We don’t practice any sports because we don’t have time (and by sports, I don’t mean playing sports simulation video games). We start taking showers once every two days, shaving once a week, or just grow a beard. And of course, we cut off from our sleep time. We can sleep 4 hours a night instead of 8, right? Replace rest time with coffee and gain some extra hours a day, right?

Without knowing, you subject yourself to a lot of stress and fatigue, and you end up in a state where you feel like you’re drunk all of the time. You don’t realize what you’re doing and function a lot on autopilot, a dangerous thing to do, even for crossing an ordinary street. I still remember that night when I was returning home from the office at 10:00 PM, and I crossed the street without looking left or right or noticing that the pedestrian traffic light was red. Heck, I didn’t even realize the traffic light’s existence, although I was crossing that street at least twice every day for the last couple of years. Luckily, because of the late hour, there was less traffic, and no cars happened to pass through the intersection at that very moment; if there would have been some cars, I’m sure I would have become a hood ornament on someone’s car.

So if you push yourself too hard at work or at home, trying to improve your knowledge and skills, don’t overdo it. Know your limits and pay attention to signals your body is sending you. Learn to take care of yourself. It’s a marathon, not a sprint. Your brain will step out long before you do. And speaking of the brain, knowing how it works might help you to learn things in a smarter instead of a harder way. John Medina’s book, “Brain rules”[75], is a nice introduction to the topic if you want to find out more.

Sustained effort

Many of the things I mentioned will not be taught to you in school. There is no certification to study for, then take an exam. Whether you like it or not, you will have to practice things that are not technical in nature or that don’t involve programming, things I talk about in this book. From many of the quicksands that I give as an example, you can’t escape if you are the best programmer. Knowing ten programming languages to perfection won’t help you in such situations. You need a different set of skills. What helps is to educate yourself, to learn about other things, not just programming. For example, find out more about teamwork, leadership, what drives people, human nature, or even psychology (technology changes fast, but human nature not so much). Try to broaden your horizons. Your work as a developer isn’t about typing code all day long. I’ve met people who only wanted to read programming books, and that’s what they did. I can attest to the fact that they were very good at what they did, if you locked them in a room to work by themselves, alone, without interacting with others. Unfortunately, they were part of a team, and everyone had to endure working with them.

So you might start as a programmer, but chances are you will not retire as a programmer. And whatever you end up doing in this industry, to be good at it means you can never stop learning. It helps if you like to learn, and if you are curious, and not because you need to do it. If you learn because you have to, then it won’t be enjoyable or sustainable for a long time but will, in fact, become more and more painful as you go along. Constantly keeping up with what’s new and ditching what’s old is a full-time job on its own. So a lot will depend on your ability to filter out noise, carefully calculate the rewards and costs of different topics, and then choose the things to learn and the things to unlearn. And as I mentioned before, there is a lot of luck involved in this; sometimes good luck, sometimes bad luck. You will have to keep on doing it no matter what. To be able to keep up, you have to actually enjoy learning new things, otherwise everything will seem in vain; you will think about giving up and find a new line of work in organic farming or something.

Software projects

When companies decide to build software, there are three important things that they consider. The first one is “usefulness”. Everything starts with a problem the company needs to solve. Automate some inefficient manual activity or optimize the business processes, gain some competitive advantage by building a new product, provide clients with better service, reduce risk, increase employee collaboration and productivity, reduce costs or increase profits, whatever it is, they need a reason; they don’t build software just for the fun of it. The second one is “time”. How much time will it take for the software to be built? If it takes 20 years to build it, then you have a problem. A lot of things can change in 20 years, from markets to clients, to law regulations, the problem itself might change. So the software needs to be available for use in some reasonable amount of time. The third thing is “money”. How much is this going to cost? This is similar to “time”. The software might be useful, but it must be built within a reasonable budget. A company doesn’t have unlimited amounts of money. If money goes into building an expensive application, then it can’t be used for something else, which might bring benefits to the company just like the new software can.

You will usually find these three things under the so-called “project management triangle”[76].

This model is sometimes also referred to as “Faster, cheaper, better. Pick two”. On most projects, clients want a high-quality product, with lots and lots of features (they also want fries with that), they want it cheap, and they want it right now or else. And of course, that’s impossible to do. Picking just two out of three is a way of saying you can’t have it all. Of course, it’s not about picking just two. You can have all three of them, only in different quantities. The reason for which the constraints are represented as a triangle is to show that they are related. If time to market is essential, you might have to add more resources to the project to launch sooner, but you need to accept a higher cost. If you want to reduce costs, you might use a smaller team, but then a larger time scale needs to be accepted. In both cases, you can give up on some of the application’s features to reduce both cost and schedule (i.e., accepting to solve 80% of the problem is probably better than not solving it at all if it takes too long or it’s too expensive to fully build). So changes in one constraint require changes in the others to compensate. Manage these three components poorly, and the quality of the product will probably end up suffering the most.

So companies need to consider these three things when deciding to take on new projects. Projects start with some requirements or a list of needed features, and then you need to answer the questions of “How much will it take?” and “How much will it cost?”. How can you answer these questions? By providing an estimation, of course.

Estimations

And now follows what I personally think is the worst thing when it comes to software development: making estimations. I’ve always hated making estimations. I never seem to get it right, no matter how much I try. When it comes to quicksand, this is one heck of a soupy mixture.

There are so many issues that start from estimates that I don’t even know where to begin. Maybe with a definition. Wikipedia has this to say about an estimation:

Estimation (or estimating) is the process of finding an estimate, or approximation, which is a value that is usable for some purpose even if input data may be incomplete, uncertain, or unstable[77].

There are a few things in this definition that should already catch your eye, like “approximation”, “incomplete”, “uncertain”, “unstable”. This is how most software projects start: by having sort of an idea of what needs building, some idea of how you will build it, some kind of an idea about what team is needed to build it, and so on. To put it bluntly, you don’t know much. You just have a general idea of things. But people need that estimate to decide if they do the project or not. To be honest, if you get to this part, people have mostly decided that the project must be done, and now they want to find out what is involved in doing it.

And of course, at the beginning of the project, you know the least about the project and what it will involve. It’s not just that the client doesn’t usually know what they want or that requirements are incomplete, but it’s also the fact that you are building something that has never been built before. Most software projects are unique; if they weren’t, you could buy them off-the-shelf. You have a rough idea of how to do it since you have built software before. You know how to use or build the pieces that are part of an application, such as programming languages, databases, frameworks, UIs, tools, etc. But you don’t know precisely how long “this” application will take to build, because when you start, you don’t have complete details about it. Estimates created at the beginning of the project are subject to a high degree of error. So basically, your estimate is more like a “guesstimate” because someone must predict the future based on what they know today, and we all know that this cannot be done.

But you can’t really start a new application in any other way. People want to know how much it will cost and how much time it will take. So you need to give an estimation.

There are various methods and techniques for performing estimates. I won’t talk about that since there are many books available about the subject, like, for example, Steve McConnell’s “Software Estimation - Demystifying the black art”[81]. And besides, I really suck at estimating. It’s quicksand I’ve never been able to completely avoid, so I’m not in a position to talk “technique”. However, there are some things that go beyond technique to be aware of when doing estimates.

The first issue with estimating software is that developers make optimistic estimates. It’s not because developers are optimists or believe in “the glass is half full” world view mambo jumbo. Even pessimists give optimistic estimations. That’s because our brains are naturally designed for positive outcomes. We consistently underestimate the likelihood of adverse events happening and instead unconsciously fall in the wishful thinking trap and believe that things will go well. When it comes to estimating software, we thus tend to estimate for the ideal scenarios or the best outcomes. You tend to think in the lines of “how can we make this work?” instead of “what are the ways this could fail?” We pay less attention to the things that could go wrong or worst-case scenarios. Even when you perform something like a three-point estimation, for example, where you also need to think about the worst-case estimate, you are often optimistic about that too and underestimate the efforts to build the software. Developer ego also plays a part because we think we are in control of what we will do and how we will do it. And nothing bad can happen when we are in control, right?

Requirements

Then there is the fact that you often don’t have all of the requirements for what needs to be built. You will try to gather as much information as you can before doing the estimate, but you will encounter some obstacles. Again, there are books on how to gather requirements, and maybe you will get some business analysts to have all the fun with that, but one thing to remember is that users never know what they want. “The application should do this. It should do that. I want it to be like the old application, but better. Not quite sure how to explain it, but you know what I mean, right?” Even if customers do make an effort, you can’t think of everything from the start, especially for complex applications. You always forget stuff. Something that, when you remember that is needed, it will be necessary to be built. Sometimes you get a subject-matter expert who can’t even put in lay terms the things that are required, but only by using complex concepts which are based on other concepts that they assume you already know. Or they try to offer you a solution that you need to implement, but the problem you need to solve wasn’t even defined, to begin with. Sometimes you are not even talking to the right individuals. They give you managers of departments, who should know what they are talking about, but they really don’t. While those that report to the managers and do the work know what the software should do, but they have no interest in giving you the requirements because, in all likelihood, they will be replaced by that software… So good luck in trying to gather requirements from them. You have to get information with pliers from their mouths, like pulling teeth.

It’s very important to collect requirements from the right persons and look at things from several perspectives. A project has one or more stakeholders, the people that have an interest in your project. You have to be aware of them when you start the project. It happened to me more than once for a project to be commissioned by the head of a department or business unit, to solve a problem with their division and find out later that the project was of interest or affected (positively or negatively) other departments also. There are always communication gaps in organizations, and some executives might not always know what other executives are doing in other departments, so think hard to involve everyone from the beginning. If stakeholders show up at the end and say they want X, Y, and Z, your launch date will probably not change, but now you have to cram all sorts of extra features for your newly discovered stakeholders. Make sure you know who these are from the start; otherwise, you will estimate and try to build something from which a big piece is missing without you even being aware that it does. You need to know who’s impacted by the project. People often consider only key stakeholders, which are the ones asking for the software solution or financing the project, but there might be more. Never neglect, for example, the people who will use the software in their daily work. You need them to fine-tune things. A key stakeholder can only give you an overview reflected by their position in the organizational chart. I’ve built software before that meets the requirements presented by the stakeholders, but the ones doing the work had a hard time using the software. Pay close attention not to fall in this type of quicksand. Becoming the most cursed person in the company - because you were the one that built the software - is quite unpleasant, believe me.

Another thing to be aware of when dealing with stakeholders is that they will give you conflicting requirements and priorities. When that happens, don’t try to sort it out on your own, or actually try to build from contradicting requirements, which will be far worse. Add the stakeholders to the same meeting or email thread to try to make them figure it out and agree together on what they want before you start writing any code. Often, what stakeholders do is come directly to you to discuss requirements if they fail to work out an arrangement with each other first. Basically, they were unable to bamboozle the other stakeholders, so now they come to convince you to give them what they want. Make sure this doesn’t happen. Keep the other parties informed. Sent them back to the meeting room or add them back to the email thread so that everyone understands everyone else’s needs and priorities. Otherwise, you will receive requirements from all directions, all with a high priority, possibly everyone sending you the same Word document modified in several places without track changes active, and leaving you in the situation of dealing with all the mess.

And because you don’t know what you’re going to get, and because new things will show up along the way, to have the highest chances of succeeding with the project, the requirements you receive must be prioritized. You have to start working on the most important things first to discover as soon as possible any insufficiency or misunderstandings in the existing requirements. Building most software products is, inevitably, an iterative process. You can’t really build full requirements for software that you haven’t seen before. Because of the complexity of most of the software applications required today, you can’t know from the beginning what to include in it or what is fully needed. Doing this is like trying to write a book from top to bottom in just one sitting, without adding, deleting, editing, or reviewing anything. In reality, you need to work hard to get the first draft, and then you refine it again and again until you are satisfied with the result. The same applies to requirements. What you get initially is a draft, a draft that will most likely be refined later. To make sure you don’t waste time building or refining something unimportant, but instead build software that brings the most value to the client, you need to prioritize things, so you attack the problem from the right end.

Often, features get priority numbers like 1, 2, 3,… 100, but these sometimes just represent the order in which things will be built. The problem with just ordering is that the features basically all have the same “value weight”, or all are “in the same bucket”, so to speak. A better prioritization will first make use of something like the MoSCoW method[82], which means splitting the features in “must have, should have, could have, and won’t have” to give weight to each feature and place them into multiple buckets. Once an actual value is properly considered, you can then refine the priorities by applying the 1, 2, 3, etc. numbers within each classification (when necessary; for “won’t haves” is pointless to do so) to get the order in which to work on things. If you’ve done Agile development before and worked from a product backlog, you already know MoSCoW. Although not explicitly identified or used as such, what’s at the top of the backlog is the “must haves” then items slowly decrease in value until the bottom of the backlog where you will find the things that will eventually never be built and end their life as “won’t haves”. Use MoSCoW to make everyone aware, from the outset, of what will be worked on and what will not be, not just in what order. “You don’t want documentation at the conclusion of the project? Fine, no problem. But don’t complain at the end that there is no documentation when it was obvious that there must be, or you assumed it would be supplied”. Ideally, it would be nice if you knew the “won’t haves” ahead of time so that you don’t waste time estimating these items too, but sometimes items move from one category to another precisely based on the estimate. “Hmmm… X will take less than Y, so we could have X while Y we probably won’t have because of time constraints. Hmmm… But wait. Z takes as much as X and Y combined. Maybe we don’t do Z and do Y instead? That way, we have more features”. This is yet another thing to be aware of: instead of thinking which of the features are truly valuable, many clients think that “more is better”. So they ask for many features. If you don’t pay enough attention from the start, you can end up building bloated software along the way. Then look also at how many features of each type you have. When all the identified features are in the “must have” category, you either have a client who knows exactly what they want and nothing more, or you’re already in deep trouble.

You can also use MoSCoW within the features themselves. For example, you can build a feature in many ways, from basic functionality to a sophisticated one. For example, you might have a requirement for users to be able to take notes inside your application. You might build this from a simple text field to a WYSIWYG editor to something which resembles an online version of Word. Often, the client says they just want to be able to add notes, but when they see the first result, they ask for more. So try to decide for the “must have” and the “won’t have” so that you identify when things are going overboard.

Sometimes you can’t even do this prioritization based on the requirements because you don’t have requirements. What bothers me the most is when the software requirements come in the shape of “build what they have”, “they” being the competition. “We can’t try to identify problems or opportunities and analyze possible solutions, nooooo… just do copy-paste” - the best way of how not to think about requirements. “We want you to do the same thing as them… but better”. And to add insult to injury, “them” is a big company with 100 developers, and you work in a small company with 2.75 developers. And then another problem. Some other player comes on the market, and now you have to copy them as well.

So, you won’t have complete requirements; the ones you have will probably be changed or invalidated sometime after the project starts, but don’t worry, you will be optimistically filling in the gaps with what you, as a developer, assume it’s needed. And then you go on estimating based on “what you think” is needed.

So if people are bad at estimating and you can’t count on having complete or correct requirements, then why bother estimating at all?

Because there aren’t many other ways to evaluate the project’s potential for success. The company needs to decide whether the project should go ahead as estimated, if the scope should be reduced and if so, which are the features you can give up on, what resources are needed to hit one target or another, or if the project should be abandoned and no software built at all. You need something to do a cost-benefit analysis. You can’t dive headfirst into the unknown and see whatever comes out of it; otherwise, it would be like going to a car dealer wanting to buy a car, but you don’t know when the car will be delivered, what key features it will have, and neither how much it will cost you. They say they will call you when it arrives. Would you still want to buy the car under these circumstances? Probably not. Same with software. You must at least have an idea if you have enough money to complete the project and if it will be ready in time, even if things along the way may not happen exactly as you estimate. What other choice do you have beyond actually building the darn thing or throwing resources at it until the money runs out?

Negotiations

But as I said above, sometimes a decision regarding the project was already taken, and the estimation no longer matters for deciding what to do with the project. You may not even estimate at all; instead, you are provided with the estimate. Developers are the ones that should do estimations. They have the working experience, they have the skills to do the job and will actually perform the work, so they have the highest chances of getting it right, but sometimes, someone else already provided an estimate. “We can’t afford to lose this client”, says the CEO. “If we can prove we are the right company for this project, then other projects are guaranteed to follow. We can make a lot of money off of this client. I told them six months. We can do it in 6 months, right?” (this translates to “Congratulations, I just signed you all up for a ‘death march’[83]. Make sure you dress for the weather”). And then you go away to do your own estimate, and it’s not six months, not by any stretch of the imagination. You then present “your” estimate to the CEO, and this happens:

This is another fun part of estimates: when most estimates made by developers get communicated, bosses receive them like a raging volcano.

The thing is this: every time you are asked to build an estimate, to see how much a project will take, at the same time, your boss also “imagines” how much the project will take. Basically, their desires, or better said, delusions. If they imagined it will take 12 months, and you come up with a 9 to 12 months estimate, then the boss is happy. You just confirmed what they assumed. Good developer! Good! But if instead, you say 12 to 15 months or more… well. Bad developer! Bad! You have to explain yourself. Immediately. They can’t possibly tell the client that it can take up to 15 months. That just can’t be. “This project takes twelve months tops. Why fifteen? Are you insane? How did you do the estimate?” The boss doesn’t have to justify why they thought it would take 12 months; developers instead need to show and prove that each estimate makes sense on every little piece of the software. But it’s in vain to go through all the items and explain logically how you made the estimate and why the numbers came out like that because they will still be looking at you in amazement. There is a chapter in Steve McConnell’s book I mentioned earlier on how to communicate an estimate so that everyone understands that there are some unknowns involved, some risks, some assumptions, that depending on how things unfold, the project can last a minimum of time or a maximum of time and with some degree of confidence, a most likely duration, but the bosses still refuse to understand because they usually have no clue how software gets built.

Then, when they are given an estimate, bosses don’t really want to know the effort required to build the application. They don’t care. All they want to know is, “when can you deliver?” You provide an estimate consisting of a probable time frame in which the project can be completed, but they don’t want a range (“Why are you giving me a range? You are the developer. Don’t you know?”). What they actually want is a fixed date: Thursday, February 17, 2022, at 3:45 P.M. That way, they can insist on some milestones along the way, also at fixed dates, like for that important visit of the client at the head office next month, for the company’s New Year’s Eve Party, or just before the boss goes in a vacation to the Bahamas, so they have an extra good reason to drink margaritas on the beach. “Can’t you work the estimates to be more ‘realistic’? There has to be some leverage in there. You surely added some padding to the estimates, didn’t you?”

If you added or not padding for worst-case scenarios, your boss will assume you did. So now, a negotiation starts. Your boss likes negotiating things. From business deals to salary offers, to price of potatoes at the local market… to estimates. Unlike a developer, a boss has a different perspective on risk-taking. The developer is usually optimistic but risk-averse; the boss, on the other hand, likes risk. “Nothing ventured, nothing gained”, right? A risky expression in itself that implies that one thing (gains, success) results from the other (undertaking a risk). Which is false; you can take risks and fail, not just succeed. And then, it’s not just a simple negotiation because it involves pressure from the boss. The boss will start to put pressure on you and attack whatever you say, to get you to lower the estimate until you declare a value that they like to hear, and you answer “I’ll try” (try to make the lower estimate happen, that is). I don’t know why, but these words coming out of a subordinate’s mouth makes the boss feel better. Maybe they think you’ll go into a phone booth, you spin around for a few times, saying, “I’ll try”, and then you get out a superhero that suddenly can do more. Or maybe they think it’s words that, once spoken, take the time you would like to spend with your family or on personal activities and transfers it to the project as unpaid overtime.

Sometimes, from fear or compliance, or to get out of the uncomfortable situation in which the negotiation places them, some will say what they think the bosses want to hear. Be aware of that and don’t do it. If you know that something can’t be done in the amount of time everyone insists upon, don’t agree to those demands. If you agree, you will set unrealistic expectations, of which you, the developer, will then be responsible for. You want to escape the pressure placed on you in a negotiating meeting of a couple of hours and replace it with the non-stop pressure that you will feel during the project execution while you will be trying to make that reduced estimate happen? If that’s how your estimation came out, what’s the point in doing the estimation at all if afterward you just chop off some random value out of it that makes the boss happy? And if you say, “I’ll try”, what else does that mean? Weren’t you trying before? Do employees have more styles of working, ranging from “Don’t care”, “Whatever”, “I’ll try”, “I’ll definitely do it”, “You’ll be surprised by the results”, or what?

There are a few other reasons why people try to cut the estimate. For example, the CEO might want to make lots of money (by working you more and paying you less), or they want to attract a client by claiming the project will be done quickly. Salespeople want their commission for signing a new customer that they would otherwise lose if the project is not done. Project Managers might chase some short-term recognition knowing they won’t be in the same role when the project is delivered. Often, there are various interests at play. For example, were you ever unwell or sick and went to the drug store and had a pharmacist recommend something for your symptoms? Did you later found out that there were other meds with the same active ingredient but much cheaper while you ended up buying the most expensive thing that was recommended to you? The pharmacist may have a sales commission from the manufacturer or trying to get rid of pills that have been sitting in the store for a long time. They don’t necessarily have your best interest in mind. What they recommend helps you with your illness, the medicine is effective, they are not selling you just anything, but something cheaper did the same thing. Or, did you go to a DIY store to buy some tools after doing some research and choosing what you thought was a good option, but once there, a store employee recommended something else that you thought was inferior quality? They may have an incentive to get rid of old stocks. But you don’t even need a reason. In many situations, the following saying may also apply “Never attribute to malice that which is adequately explained by stupidity”[84]. Stupidity might be a harsh word, but ignorance is definitely a cause, especially with non-technical people involved in software development. They don’t understand all the activities needed to get the job done. So they just don’t know any better. Other times management does know things will take longer. From experience. After several projects that did not come out as estimated, they figured out that things will be delayed, so sometimes, they want to make sure that the project doesn’t go beyond even the worst-case scenario. You told them 8-10 months, so they expect the worst of 10 months, but they put pressure for you to finish in 8 months and prevent the 10 months from turning into 12 or even more.

So when you provide an estimate, you better be prepared to defend it. The problem is that estimates almost always go over bosses’ heads. And that’s because, in most cases, an estimate is useless to your boss. They deal with commitments, not estimates. So they will treat estimates as commitments (I’ll give them the benefit of the doubt and add “consciously or not”). So you might think you are negotiating an estimate, but your boss is looking for a commitment. So when you are debating over the estimate, and you say “OK”, “Yes”, “I agree”, or “I will try”, what you are actually doing is committing yourself to make the estimate happen. You are transforming an estimate into a target that needs to be hit spot on, by you, of course. Be aware of that and point it out when things turn into commitments during a conversation about estimates. An estimate is not a commitment. An estimate is not a promise that things will turn out the way you… well… estimated. An estimate is a guess. You might use different proven techniques and formulas or feed the data into a supercomputer, which then makes loud sounds and flashes bright lights, and then the estimation comes out at the end on a small piece of paper, but it’s still a guess. You might get back o more accurate estimation, but it won’t be a target that you can promise to hit. You can discuss, decide and agree upon targets you need to hit based on the estimate, and the boss and client can note those dates in their calendars, but don’t do that with the estimates themselves. For example, you might make a commitment to your boss that you will arrive at work each day before 09:00 A.M., but you can’t commit to making 20 minutes 37 seconds on your commute every time; you can only estimate around 20 minutes (plus/minus some minutes depending on traffic, the weather, etc.).

Nothing is certain with an estimate. Heck, the developer might not even have a clue of how to do an estimation. Nobody taught me how to make estimates. I didn’t learn at school. I wasn’t trained at work. I was simply put in front of the accomplished fact. Often, I wasn’t even given enough time to make a proper estimate. “Why do you need a week to estimate this project? It’s a four-month project. Tops!” I got burned a few times before researching how I could do it better, what techniques there are, and so on. And even so, I still got it wrong. Take this book, for example. Before I started writing it, I estimated half a year to write the first draft. It took me 18 months. I’ve never written a book before, so this was a completely new activity for me, one that I didn’t quite know how to estimate. So I got it wrong. Horribly wrong. Likewise, if you’ve never built the same software before, with the same people, with the same technology, and the same constraints, then how can you possibly know how long it will take exactly? Every project is new. There is always stuff you don’t know, and you don’t even know you don’t know. Most surprises will come from the business domain; if you are not already familiar with it, there is a great chance you might misunderstand stuff and estimate based on your wrong understanding of things. You might be an experienced developer and estimating since you were in kindergarten, but if you don’t know the domain or haven’t worked in it already, then you will have a lot of blind spots.

In my opinion, everyone should use the word “guesstimate”. But it’s not professional to do so, is it? Somehow though, it’s professional to take an approximation and treat it as being something certain, then hold everyone accountable for it. So make sure everyone around you understands what an estimate is, that there is a certain degree of uncertainty involved, that things are not 100% accurate but fall within a range whose endpoints have a certain probability of happening. And make sure you don’t forget it either next time you estimate something, and it comes back to 1840.53 hours long. Once you give an estimation, you are married to it.

Forgotten bits

And try not to forget or neglect stuff when doing your estimation. When making estimates, it’s good practice to break features into smaller pieces, estimate those, then put them all together to get a more accurate estimate. But focusing on smaller chunks can make you lose sight of more general aspects that apply across every feature, like project management overhead, for example. You estimate the actual development, but there are also other aspects to consider, things needed to run the project: having discussions with the client, clarifying requirements, planning things, measuring and reporting stuff, meetings, demonstrating the software, coordinating with other projects, establishing effective communication channels, etc. From personal experience, this management overhead is, on average, somewhere around 20% of the total development time. It depends on the details of the project, though; for some, it takes more, for some, less. You can use a value based on your past experiences with similar projects, but don’t forget to have an item that accounts for this overhead also.

Other examples might include code reviews. You also include this in your estimates, right? How about unit tests? Integration tests? Manual testing (someone has to actually use the thing)? How will you do deployments? Manually or automatic? How much time does a manual deploy take, and how many you think will be necessary? How much time will it take you to automate all the deployments and build a continuous integration pipeline? Where will the application run? Will it be self-hosted or in the cloud somewhere? Will you figure that later on? How much time will that setup take? Have you thought of having a way to configure the code once written, or are you going to use hard-coded stuff? If the project is underway and you notice the ship starting to sink, can you throw some stuff overboard? For example, can you reduce the schedule if you no longer do unit tests? Or maybe drop the code reviews? This means you need to know the team you will be working with. How many people? What kind of people? Will you have them available full-time? You are now doing estimations, planning resources will come later, but having important people be part-time or unavailable can really mess up a project. Even if you get the estimate spot on, if you have part-time people, their work will be affected by context switching and availability, which will add time to tasks in a way you can’t estimate beforehand. Then are they experienced seniors or juniors? If you have experienced seniors, this means fewer code reviews, refactoring, and a smaller number of bugs. If you have juniors, it can mean more code reviews and bugs, maybe even the need for mentoring and pair programming sessions. Perhaps now these don’t seem essential for the project, but they will consume your time when you will build the thing. And time spent on these activities is time not spent on building features. You can give up on some of them, but others are more important (for example, you might ditch code reviews if the team is doing well, and you have very few defects, but you can’t give up on configuring the server on which the application will run).

And since I mentioned defects… no software is “bug-free”. Why do you estimate as if you will not have any bugs? You’ll have. Nobody considers any room for error when it comes to that. You will inevitably end up chasing some obscure bug or weird application behavior that can only be reproduced on the production environment. You have to consider some time for fixing bugs, and that again depends on what kind of team you have. An experienced team will produce fewer bugs and find them faster when they occur than a less experienced team of people. Add padding directly proportional to the risk of this occurring for each item. If the feature is easy, you can use no padding, but if it’s very complex, then don’t expect everything to go smoothly; there will be some issues. However, see to it that you do not add so much padding as to estimate yourself out of a client, a project, or even a job. Use realistic values based on past experiences. And include padding where necessary, not just “because”. Don’t include time people spend on social media or smoking cigarettes on company time just because you’ve seen people do this in the past. You also don’t include padding because your boss always tries to cut down on your estimates because they assume you always add padding. Learn to hold your ground when you are pressured to reduce your estimate, don’t just play their game by adding padding, so you have some room to decrease the estimate later; otherwise, they never learn what an estimate is and that there are assumptions and risks involved.

Risks and assumptions

Believe me, you will make assumptions, and there will be risks. Building software requires simplifications, generalizations, and assumptions with which you build abstractions on various levels. You can think about most of these when estimating the project, but many details you will discover when you actually write the code. That means you will assume certain things work a certain way, which sometimes proves not to be the case. For example, have you split your application between a back-end API and a rich front-end, but you are yet to hire the front-end developer? You will assume that you have enough time to hire front-end developers while working on the back-end API. But maybe you won’t find any developers. Or you do, but when the front-end developer joins the team, they discover that it’s difficult to integrate with the back-end API because you worked on that blindly, with no true client integration to validate or invalidate your design decisions. Or you might think that new people won’t need induction time and that no one from the team will take time away from their work to train them and offer support. This is more about forgetting or neglecting the extra activity, but it’s actually the assumption that you have forgotten nothing and that you have thought of everything. Or you will trust that the technology you have chosen for the project does what is written on the package, that the integration will go smoothly and will not require additional training. Or that George, who is essential for the project to be a success, will not leave the company in the next six months. That when your tech lead says they know how to properly use a tool when necessary, they really know their business, not that they just read some blogs or watched online video conferences about how it’s supposed to work (something like this actually happened to me once, and I don’t even want to tell you what a pain it was to clean up the mess afterward), or that it’s OK to build your application on framework X because it’s stable and well maintained and will remain so in the future, that some module a vendor needs to supply you with will be ready in time and that the vendor won’t go bankrupt by then, and so on. Oh… and let’s not forget, we build optimistic estimates because we assume things will turn out well.

Assumption is the mother of all fuckups - Unknown

All these assumptions are necessary for the project to be executed (in theory) according to the estimation. But they carry risks, the risks of costing you more money or more time to solve any problems caused by your assumption being proven wrong. And these problems can manifest themselves even after you think you’ve successfully finished the project. Maybe you’re too young to know about this, but do you remember the Y2K problem? Everyone assumed two digits would be enough to represent the year in software. Then, when the year 2000 was approaching, people started to worry about the issues this might cause, believing airplanes will fall out of the sky, that nuclear power plants will meltdown, or that the financial system will crash. Huge amounts of money were spent to fix computer systems all around the world just because people made an assumption while trying to save some memory space. So you must also consider the risks when presenting an estimate. Will you try to avoid them? Mitigate them? Live with them? Will you spend time monitoring them to see how they manifest? How much time and money will be needed to fix them if one of the risks happens? If you think they are not going to happen to you, think again. During the estimation phase, you also need to identify the risks and decide what to do about them. The ones with a high probability of occurring you might need to estimate in detail just so that everyone is aware of what potential for derailment there is if they occur. Managing risk is like managing fire safety. You might have to put something in place to prevent fires or give you a better chance of fighting the fire and extinguish the flames sooner if a fire does occur. You don’t want to reach the fire location and have no fire extinguishers, no hoses, and no water, and be left with watching the whole thing burn.

Be very careful with the risks when presenting estimates. Just as you, as a developer, tend to think of the ideal path of execution when estimating, likewise will bosses and business people tend to think about risk, and they will underestimate the likelihood of the risk manifesting itself, and will subconsciously believe things will work out for the best. And that’s an even bigger problem with bosses and business people because they have a much higher tolerance for risk. Businesses often chose to respond to problems instead of anticipating and removing them. This is because they learned that you simply can’t prevent all the problems that may arise, that sometimes it’s cheaper to take risks, and in the situation that there might be a problem to cross that bridge when they get there. That goes together with what I mentioned above. “Nothing ventured, nothing gained”, right? So when you present the worst-case scenarios, the associated risks, or the assumptions on which your estimate is based, they will be tempted to dismiss them with a wave of hand and focus on the most favorable scenario. So, make sure you point out the risks you’ve identified, or on what assumptions you’ve based your estimate. Also, mention what impact or how much time or effort will be needed to deal with the situation if the risks happen or the assumptions prove wrong. The idea is for people to acknowledge the risks and assumptions, not simply ignore them.

The plan

The next thing your boss or the client wants to see is that the project is in the capable hands of a responsible person. And a responsible person always has a plan. So they demand to see the plan. You do have a plan, right?

Actually… they demand to see the schedule, the plan is just the story that explains the schedule. They are more interested in when you are done, not necessarily how you will be building it. And now the bickering starts again, because, of course, bosses or clients have a problem with the project duration. They again “imagine” when the project will be delivered. They want to mark the date when the software will be ready in their calendar, remember? If what they imagined does not match with your plan, there is a new negotiation to shorten the schedule. Most of the discussions will be about juggling with the human resources, what unimportant things you can give up on (usually, not features), or how you can arrange the work to finish sooner, like trying to tightly pack lots of books of many different shapes and sizes into a box without there being any free space remaining whatsoever. You just have to find the right combination of mixing them vertically and horizontally to make it happen, right?

“So who will work on this application, and how will they split the work? Can you have those two features built in parallel to save some time? Why not? Do we really need so many code reviews? How about unit tests? Who cares about unit tests if the application works, right? Developers should write application code, not test code. Use testers for that. They are cheaper than developers and easier to find. With how many resources have you planned this? Two seniors and three juniors? Hmmm… seniors are expensive. Sorry. What if you had one senior and four juniors? Too many juniors will take longer, you say? Why? We had an awesome internship program this year and offered jobs to some really smart youngsters. What if you had an entire army or interns? How about then? It will increase management overhead and introduce communication issues, you say? Come on; it’s not that difficult of an application. This project can basically run itself. Oh… Wait… I know. Take Francis. He’s allocated 50/50 on two projects, but one of the projects will end soon, and there will just be some maintenance left to do. You can have him with a 25 percent allocation for starters until we can find someone else to do the maintenance in his place”. I’ve seen things like this so many times it’s not even funny. And do you even know Francis? Have you worked with him before? Do you know how good of a developer he is?

People deliver projects. So it matters what kind of people you have on your team. I’ve talked in a previous chapter why it’s essential to hire good developers and what mistakes companies make doing that, but I believe that one of the biggest mistakes software development companies make is to generalize developers to the point of “resource”, to fool themselves that they can manage people with feelings like they manage cost or equipment, and deceiving themselves in thinking that they are interchangeable, like spare parts in a machine. That might work for the kind of “resources” flipping burgers at your local fast-food restaurant, but in software development, Project X with Jake, Amy, and Susan isn’t the same thing as Project X with Jake, Amy, and Robert. Susan might be a senior with twenty years of experience, while Robert might be a junior with only two. In less than a day, Robert might become as skillful as Susan at flipping burgers, and then their work is indistinguishable from each other’s, but with software development projects, it doesn’t work that way.

Ideally, you should estimate and plan the project with your team, the people who will do the actual job. It’s better this way than to make estimates and a plan on your own (if a team isn’t assembled yet), then hand them over to your team. More heads are better and produce superior results with both activities. It also makes your team assume responsibility and gives them visibility into the work to be performed. Then, if something happens, they will bypass the plan, make another plan, figure things out without waiting for you to tell them what to do, or waiting for you to update the plan. But even if the plan comes out better this way, there will still be things that won’t always go according to the plan.

Let’s face it; you can’t plan for everything. Just like estimates, plans are an approximation. They are an approximation of how you would want to do things. You will plan the work to be done, when to do it, who will do it, you’ll set up processes for quality assurance, change control, defect tracking, and communicating with stakeholders, you’ll also decide on the best way to do branching on source control or versioning for the application, you will plan meetings and software releases, you’ll plan a lot of things. But then reality happens. And when reality meets plans, reality always wins.

No battle plan ever survives contact with the enemy - Helmuth von Moltke the Elder[85]

So knowing this, what do you do with the information? Do you try to invest more time upfront and do more thorough planning, trying to cover any potential situation so that you will be prepared and know what to do when something does eventually occur? Or on the contrary, since anyways there’s a chance that things might go south, you invest less time and settle more for a general direction than a plan? To answer these questions, you need to think well about what the plan means to you.

If you think the plan is important, then when something happens, you will tend to focus on the plan. It starts to become more about the plan than about the product you are building; the product just becomes the result of your plan. A very detailed plan will give you a false sense of control and confidence that you are doing the right thing. Consider this: you made a plan for the best way you think you will build the project, so why would you do it any other way? For that reason, changes to the plan will have to be minimized because any digression from the plan is bad. There is a process, a workflow, in which everyone has to do their job exactly at the right time for the result to come out… well… according to plan. “You have a change request? Hmmm… not so fast. Let’s prepare mountains of paperwork to detail that. Then let’s have a change control meeting with a few people to decide if we approve the change or not. Is that change really so important so that we deviate from the plan? What? Mr. Taylor, who is in the change control board, isn’t in the country? When will he return? Because we need to discuss the changes to the plan…”

Remember, a plan is an approximation of how you want things to take place. And sometimes, they are really bad approximations because, instead of focusing on how to build the software, they focus more on schedule. Meaning that, people tend to organize themselves to meet the schedule instead of how to build the software. It becomes all about time. For example, everything gets planned in 8-hour tasks, as if someone can work 8 hours straight. Don’t people need to go to the toilet? Don’t people need to communicate with each other or spend time coordinating their efforts? Do they also have operational tasks to perform? Maybe some technical support for earlier releases? Don’t they attend all kinds of meetings imposed by the bosses? Nobody gets tired? Can that person who’s a developer 40% of their time, tester 33%, database administrator 15%, and analyst 13%, move between roles with no context switching cost? Did you force some things on paper so the schedule is like the boss wanted it? Did you build a large Gantt chart with lots of 4-hour tasks that span two hours one day in the evening and two hours the next day in the morning, expecting your developers to continue work just like a printer prints one page after another at the same pace, with no loss of efficiency? Did you simply count your resources instead of considering their skills? Remember… you are not flipping burgers. Susan and Robert won’t have the same output after 4 hours of work.

Then, even considering the focus on just the schedule, various time-consuming things also get forgotten. Don’t assume, for example, that if people are working on a project, somehow there is a force field surrounding them that shields them from what’s happening in their daily lives. People sometimes get married, they might get sick, some water pipe can burst in their house, and they have to take a day off, or they might resign smack in the middle of the project. Another example might be the team needing to maintain other applications, do operational work, or fix incidents in production. You will have context switching because of that, and you’ll waste time you can’t even correctly quantify. So don’t think that you can build some plans, then follow them to the letter to get a guaranteed result and meeting your schedule spot on. It doesn’t work that way. Problems can occur at any moment.

So, when reality starts contradicting your plan, don’t stubbornly hold on to it. Seriously now, by the time you change course because you feel reluctant to make changes to the plan, you might have gone a long way in the wrong direction.

Having less of a plan, or no plan at all is just as bad as stubbornly trying to stick to the plan. If you think having a plan is not important, you will most likely end up improvising in most of the situations you encounter. You might also end up doing lots of fire fighting on something that could have been prevented if you had just spent some time preparing. It’s also inefficient. Have you ever gone to the hypermarket without a shopping list? You spend time wandering through the store to figure out what stuff to buy. You might end up buying too much food, which then sits in your fridge until it goes bad and you have to throw it away. Have you ever purchased a product, got home with it, only to find out that it’s already passed its expiration date? If only you’d been more careful reading the label. Did you buy that box of doughnuts because you went shopping on an empty stomach? Going to the hypermarket without a shopping list is similar to building software without a plan. The analogy is a little bit stretched, but the idea is the same. Things take more time, you might spend more money than necessary, and you can cause waste, all because you didn’t pay enough attention or went in unprepared.

So you need to plan. What a plan does is it forces you to think about what you are building before you are building it. It’s easy to miss things if you don’t spend some time to study the problem you are trying to solve. Heck, you might even solve the wrong problem. A plan is useful to delay immediate action. It helps you avoid missing good solutions for the task at hand. Too many developers jump in straight into coding. “Man, I’m tired of all this planning, too many discussions, and meetings. Let’s write some code. We’ll figure it out eventually”.

Weeks of programming can save you hours of planning - Unknown

So, like many things in software development, you should try to keep a balance between too much planning and not enough. Plans are often obsolete the second you save them to disk, and sometimes you do have to respond to certain situations immediately, being unable to plan your actions, but that doesn’t mean you do not need to plan. So think things through before undertaking any development. What do you need to do, who does what and when, who else can help, etc. You can plan upfront then re-plan as you go. You adapt the plan you have to the new conditions in your environment. And you also avoid forgetting to look at the big picture while you focus on the tasks at hand.

Change

And speaking of the big picture: you estimate, you prioritize, you plan things out, but execution is also important. In fact, it is the most important, because, at this stage of the project, you find out whether or not you were right when you estimated things, you find out if things are going as you thought they would. And guess what? Problems always occur because all kinds of changes that you didn’t expect will come up. There will always be change. And change can occur for various reasons.

There is always the fact that requirements were unclear or that clients don’t know what they want to start with, or you have multiple stakeholders, everyone with their firm opinion about what the application should do (possibly conflicting ideas), but there is also the fact that the client changes their mind all of the time. Many times I’ve worked on the same thing more than once, write, rewrite, write again, rewrite another time, just because the client didn’t spend time thinking what they needed or couldn’t make up their mind. This causes lots of waste: a waste of time and a waste of money. You’re working at full capacity but without any meaningful results. Everyone gets frustrated, and quality suffers because when you’ve done the same thing again and again and again, in multiple ways, and it’s never done, you get sick of it, and you do whatever it takes to get it over with it. It’s like eating the same food every day. You get tired at some point, or just thinking about it makes you nauseous.

Then there are unnecessary changes that start their life with “wouldn’t it be nice if you could …?”. If I had a penny for every time I heard this asked, I would be rich right now.
