So, you built the feature, it works, it solves the problem that had to be solved, but still… the client wants something different, something extra. Maybe the background isn’t green enough. “Or that drop-down… hmmm… could you maybe replace it with some radio buttons? Can we display the user’s name on the top right of the screen, with bold font and underlined” (in case the user forgot what their name is, I suppose)? “It’s a tiny change, right?” Changes like these are simply not necessary and go beyond the actual purpose of what the feature was supposed to do, and they end up causing scope creep[86]. That’s when the scope of what you are building increases, while the budget and schedule remain the same. This is uncontrolled increase of scope, and it is sometimes visible only to the people doing the work. You get this, especially when the final client has direct access to the development team and asks them to make changes that have not been discussed or agreed upon apriori. If there isn’t good communication between the team members, it’s easy for a seemingly harmless change to turn into a full-blown standalone project. And the time you use to polish something that was already delivered is time you cannot use for anything else.

Sometimes, changes can even be necessary. As you progress through the project, and more development is done, you learn more information, and you gain a better understanding of what needs to be built and how to build it. The same thing happens to clients. They, too, discover more about what the application should do to better solve the problem they have. As you move forward with the project, you discover important or significant things that really need to be considered. Markets change, regulations change, someone comes up with a great idea, someone spots a huge problem that needs correcting. Sometimes, how people use the application forces you to make changes that were not considered in the original requirements. So, all sorts of stuff will show up that add to the amount of work you have to do, things you didn’t know you will have to implement at the beginning when you built your plan. But you will have to make those changes.

The scope of a project will inevitably increase. It’s to be expected and, frankly, quite normal. But the scope increase shouldn’t “creep up” on people. And that only happens because people say too easily “yes” to everything the client asks for and end up making changes to the application for any reason, not just for what’s actually important. So they start missing deadlines for no apparent reason, and then the boss yells at them. They get burned by this, so of course, now, they start saying “no” to everything, which isn’t any good either because you risk putting important changes in the same bucket with all the silly things that are requested to be changed.

Not every change is good for the product, and not every change is bad. Not every change is essential, and not every change is worthless. So you have to pick. I’ve mentioned prioritization above. You can handle changes in a similar way. When a change is requested, you need to analyze the change and decide what to do with it. You will probably need to build an estimation to get an idea of what effort might be involved, so you don’t jump on things without at least a clue of how much it will take. Then you decide if you do it now, or you just add it to your list of priorities. Is it “a must”, “a should”, or “a could”? Given enough time for reflection, can the change become a “won’t”? You need transparency, communication, and re-prioritization. Communication is key here. If you agree to make a change, everyone must be aware of the implications of that change (i.e., you might need to postpone something else, it might be rework, it might affect other parts of the application, have an impact on project objectives, plans may need to be changed, etc.), not to say afterward that they didn’t know about the consequences, that things take too long, or that they cost too much. For scope creep to occur, it needs the presence of the impulse to do things “now”. If you can delay that, by explaining to the client what’s involved in the change instead of just making the change, you’ll see that a lot of changes just go forgotten, a sign that they weren’t necessary in the first place, just passing fads.

If you, however, do “now” all of the silly changes of replacing the colors, the font, or rearranging components in the page so that the interface looks different, slowly, you will start shifting planned work. You can always find new things to do now, but you can’t find more time to do them. So you decide to do “later” something that you should be working on right now. And because most of the time, the meaningless changes you do “now” are things that the user can see and interact with, what gets pushed for a later time are the important things that cannot be seen. What are some of the things you need to do but always seem to be postponing? Making sure the application can be deployed in a clustered environment? Doing deploys with no downtime for the user? How about that section of code that requires stricter security rules? For 30% of users, you receive an error concerning an external API integration, but you are still postponing to investigate? How about internationalization? Platform independence? How will you manage the application from the back-office? You did build the back-office application, didn’t you? Do you want to risk that at the end of the project, constrained by time, to try to staple these on top of the application, or stick them together with duct tape? The second car in the image above might look cool with those spoilers and painted flames on the side, but if the windshield wipers don’t function and you have to work them with ropes pulled through the sunroof because that’s all you had a chance to put together, you might end up in the ditch on the first rain and discover that it was another terrible idea to keep postponing to fit the car with airbags.

Again. You have to prioritize. Prioritization forces you to work on what brings most value first, and it also helps you look at the entire picture and see what you still need to do. So to avoid all sorts of situations to creep up on you, you need to keep your eyes on the ball at all times.

Measure

As a project advances, estimations and assumptions get proven wrong, plans go astray, things change, and new work shows up with a significant impact on the desired outcomes. That’s just how it is. Although undesirable, it’s unavoidable. Let’s take an example. When you drive a car in an unknown region, trying to get to someplace, you might get lost. You eventually figure out that you’re lost. You can turn around to a location that you know is correct, or you can figure out where you are now, then see how you can get back towards your destination from there. Or you might be on the correct route, but at some point, you hit a roadblock, like construction work or maybe an accident, and you get redirected on another road. You figure out where that road leads you and look for a way to get to your destination. Well, the same happens with ongoing projects also. You make a plan of how you will reach your goals, you work towards that goal, but at some point, something might happen. You might hit a roadblock or get lost on the way.

Now, in my example, when you get diverted in case of the roadblock or the accident, you know right away that you are getting sidetracked. You can pull the car on the side of the road, look where you are, look at a map, then come up with a new plan on how you are still going to reach your destination in the best possible way. But when you get lost, you don’t immediately know that you wandered off your path. Maybe you took a wrong turn five minutes ago, or half an hour ago. You don’t know how much you drove in the wrong direction. You might not even know where you are. You again pull the car on the side of the road, figure out where you are, look at a map, then make a new plan on how to reach your destination.

I mentioned already that you need to adapt the plan for the new conditions in your environment. I want to emphasize this fact again by saying not that you simply “need”, but that you are “forced” to do so. Planning is a continuous effort. Planning is not something you can just do at the beginning. And that’s not only because you can’t plan everything from the beginning, but also because the environment changes. Some situations are a clear indication that you’ve shifted away from what you wanted, like the roadblock or the accident. Some others, like getting lost, are not so easy to notice. You might be thinking that things are going well, but your project might slowly start to drift without you noticing (i.e., you don’t know where you took that wrong turn). You eventually figure out you are on the wrong path, but it’s kind of unpleasant to figure it out when you are many miles away from where you wanted to be. To avoid that, you have to always keep track of where you are and how things are going. You need feedback on how the project is going so that you can regroup or take corrective actions, adapt the plan, or make a new one, as soon as something happens.

In project management parlance, this is called “monitoring and controlling”. You gather information related to all aspects of the project, including scope, schedule, priorities, progress, team performance, quality, cost, resources, external dependencies, risks and blockages, and communication with all parties involved. All this information helps you create a feedback loop to guide your next decisions, plan your next steps, refine and improve your work, and achieve your goals. Basically, you gather information to answer the question, “Are we doing something that gets us closer to our goals, or are we doing something that moves us away from our goals?” If everyone comes to work every day and writes code at the keyboard, it looks like you are making progress. But are you really? And if so, is it in the right direction? Without measuring, you don’t know.

And you need to have a complete image of the project, all of the time. You need to know what your progress is towards what you have estimated. If you got your estimations wrong, why is that, and how does it affect you? Are you waiting on some dependencies, and you have to chase people throughout the company to get a response on when they can be delivered? How are the people in your team doing? Maybe things go well, and everything seems on track, but the team doesn’t work as fast as you know they can. Is something slowing them down? Do they know what the goal is? Do they know if something affected the plan? Do they know what the new plan is? Can you improve things? Are there mistakes to eliminate? The risks you identified, are they manifesting themselves or show obvious signs of doing so and becoming issues? Are you at half of the planned schedule, with half of the budget consumed but only a third of the work done? Is the project in good health or in bad health?

If your boss comes to you and asks for a status update, do you know how you stand? Or do you check up on how things are going only at the end of each month when you need to prepare a status report for upper management? I’ve seen projects monitored from the perspective of upper management. Bosses or stakeholders might follow the project execution from a distance and may be forced to use more coarse-grained indicators to do so. Then, they also practice what’s called “managing by exception”. You do your job without intervention from their part, and they step in only if something happens, if you escalate some problems, or if their decision is needed (i.e., the things that deviate from the original plan, the “exceptions”). Monthly status updates on schedule, cost, or other large aspects of the project might be OK for them. But not for you. You must constantly have complete and up-to-date information about the project, which you must communicate correctly and transparently when needed, so that everyone knows what’s going on and be able to make the right decisions quickly. If your schedule is slipping or you are going over budget, your boss or stakeholders need to know. Now. Not in a month. You can’t show up in your boss’s office at the end of the month and tell them you are one month behind schedule. You get late one day at a time. The sooner you figure out something undesirable has happened, the better. If you notify your bosses too late about any problems that appeared and you were unable to solve on your own, or problems that you have not escalated in time, it may be too late to take a sensible decision. Bosses could react in the moment, on impulse, and make a poor decision in anger, panic, lack of time, or maybe even lack of options; to try desperately to do damage control. Only if you have correct and timely information about the project, only then can you correctly assess the gravity of any situation.

Define success

And in order to make good decisions that will contribute to the success of the project, you must first be clear on what “success” means. There are many ways to define project and product success, so you need to pay attention to it, to then see if you actually achieved your goals or just reached the end of the project. Try to see how everyone defines success. Identify the important things and try to put them all in balance with each other. Most importantly, though, it’s essential to solve the client’s problem. Let’s look at an example.

For a long time, there was no way to check online for the departure and arrival times of trains in the main train station of the city I live in. Most importantly, though, there wasn’t a way to see train delays. If you had to pick someone up from the train station, you had to go to the station when you knew the train should arrive, then hope it didn’t have too much of a delay. If you knew there was a delay, you could leave later from home or maybe do something useful with the extra time that otherwise you would have wasted by waiting on the train platform. So an online solution was eventually deployed. It’s a webcam placed in front of the physical arrivals and departures board from the train station. At one minute intervals, a screenshot of the physical board gets displayed. You can see the board just as if you were sitting in front of the actual board in the train station. So problem solved, right?

But was this a success or a failure? Well, let’s see. Is this high-tech? Does it use the latest technologies? Provides a friendly user experience? No. Actually, the first version of this solution was even worse. You needed Flash enabled in your browser, so it didn’t work at all on mobiles. But since the Flash program only trimmed and displayed the actual webcam capture, you could go through some hoops, and by looking at the source code, you could find the raw image URL and open that on your mobile instead of the whole page. A little bit of a pain to then manually refresh the image every minute or so, and voilà, you could see the board on your mobile too. So, as a developer, I might think this is the work of amateurs (although I don’t know the constraints of the project; I guess the main problem was that the board was analogical when the webcam was installed, not digital). As a manager, I might think this is brilliant. It’s cheap, and it gets the job done. As a tester, I can find no defects with it; there are not many places where it can go wrong, assuming the entire site doesn’t go down. But as someone who has used this page more than a few times throughout the years, hence as the final user, I don’t care about any of that. I couldn’t see the train delays, now I can. And now I can do something more useful with those 55 minutes of delay the train has in lousy winter weather instead of freezing my butt off inside the train station. So, if I’m the only one to judge, then yes, I’d say it was a success. I even take my hat off to whoever came up with the idea of using a webcam to get the job done :).

In this example, I can only evaluate the result and ask if the project or product was a success or not. But when you are the one working on the project, you can’t just wait until the end, look at what you built, compare it with the goal, then give it a “Like” or a “Dislike”. You need to define what “success” means from the beginning, figure out from the start what you want to achieve, then work towards hitting that target.

So how do you define success?

A user is probably expecting a friendly graphical interface with everything they need and is also easy to use, or an application that responds very quickly to commands and does not crash. A tester wants to look at the application and see that it works correctly, that all acceptance criteria are met, and there are no defects, or there are very few minor bugs. A programmer probably expects quality, the source code to be clean, to comply with the code review rules or best practices, that the code is well structured, and that the application is maintainable and extensible. Or maybe have the correct architecture implemented so that the application performs the same with ten thousand users as well as with one million. Or maybe the application solves a tough technical challenge efficiently and elegantly. A Project Manager might attribute success to launching the product on time, within budget, and with all the required features, or by targeting the efficiency of project execution, be that keeping stakeholders happy or having a productive and amicable communication with the customer. It might also be to capture the requirements from the beginning and minimize change requests during the project, or that the development team works at a constant, non pressured pace, as opposed to that other project where they were overworked and did lots of unpaid overtime, which caused half of the team to quit. Higher executives or salespersons might see success as the revenue growth or cost savings the software must bring, how the services of the company or the customer satisfaction will be improved, or by how many new clients they will reach with the new application. I could probably go on with the examples, but by now, you figured out already that success means different things to different people. Sometimes, conflicting things. It would have been nice for “success” to be something dichotomous, you either attain it or you don’t, but projects can actually have a certain degree of success, or you can have certain degrees of success for each category that I mentioned above. Then, if you remember the previous chapter where I talked about trade-offs, you also probably figured out that you can’t always please everyone, and respect all of these definitions. Actually, the only certainty you have is that if you try to please everyone, you are guaranteed not to please anyone.

So it’s essential to start with the end in mind and be clear from the beginning on the things that matter, the things that actually bring value. I can’t say what criteria to use to define success since that depends a lot on the project, on the business domain, and the actual software, but whatever it is, it must be something that brings value. When a new project gets started, many people get to ask for all kinds of stuff. The application should do this, do that, do this other thing, and so on. And the problem that genuinely needs solving gets diluted amidst this pile of features, of which not all bring value, and over time the project ends up focusing only on delivering features. But what brings the most value is not the features themselves, but how they help solve the problem. Delivering value is what contributes to success, no matter how you defined success. Solving the problem, that’s what success is. Can you solve the problem? If no, how much of the problem can you solve? Focus on defining the problem and shaping the solution to solve that problem. The mentioned MoSCoW method keeps people focused on why the software is needed in the first place because you work on what’s important first, the “must” items. You need to get these right before you start the project, and then, because market conditions or business needs might change while the project is underway, to make sure you continuously pay attention to what is a “must”.

So pay close attention to defining what success means from the beginning, a definition to be accepted or agreed upon by all stakeholders; otherwise, you risk that throughout the project for people to pull in different directions, each being convinced that they are pulling in the right direction.

The deadline

Before ending this chapter, I also want to mention another thing that will happen during the execution phase of your project: if you fall behind on what you estimated or planned to do, everybody expects you to make up for the lost time. Yes, your estimate was an approximation. Yes, bosses might have cut some of your estimates in half and still treated them as commitments. Yes, a lot of changes were then requested on top of the original scope. Yes, they messed with your planning because they didn’t like how your schedules came out. And yes, you still need to deliver as none of these things happened.

Three tomatoes are walking down the street: papa tomato, mama tomato, and baby tomato.
Baby tomato starts lagging behind.
Papa tomato gets really angry, goes back, squishes him, and says: “Ketchup”

And of course, it’s not enough that you have to recover the lost time, but you also have to explain yourself. Why are you behind schedule? You said it would take such and such amount of time or money, so you’d better make it happen. Now you are late. Why isn’t it ready? Why does it take so long? What do you intend to do to get back on track and hit your deadline?

Interesting word this: “deadline”. Do you know its origin? This was an actual line in prison camps, situated around the inner face of the walls at a distance of a few meters, beyond which the prisoners were not allowed to pass (and thus approach the walls with the assumed intention of trying to escape). Anyone doing so would be shot on the spot. In business terms, it means the time limit to complete the project. If you go beyond that limit, well… you get shot. They won’t literally shoot you, like with a bullet from a gun, but you are held accountable by your boss for everything that happens to the project, with all the consequences that result from that. Deep down inside, everyone knows the whole thing was a forecast, and shit can happen, but you said you would deliver some stuff by certain dates, so they expect you do so.

A product must bring value to the customer, but people become obsessed with the deadline, even at the risk of producing an inadequate product. A date in the calendar becomes more important than the thing you are building. Everyone gets sucked into this game of “hit the date” no matter what. And it starts to define what success means. Sometimes yes, the deadline is critical (I’ve worked in the financial sector, and you had to change software to meet new government regulations by date X or else), but most of the times, it’s just a way for upper management to impose control over the project (it happened to me more than once to be pressured to deliver software by a certain date, we managed to hit the date, and then… nothing; nobody used it, nobody said anything, nobody even cared). Bosses don’t do most of the work in a software project; that’s for technical people. But a boss can’t let technical people be in control of the project. The bosses need to be in control. So estimates are a form by which they believe they have control over the work being performed. That’s why they start bearing their teeth when developers’ work lags behind the initial estimates, because they feel like the project is going to spin out of control. When this happens, bosses become obsessed with mainly two things. The first is that they want to see constant progress. If they see no progress, it means there is a problem, or developers are slacking off, or something happened that jeopardizes the deadline. It’s not that they want to be kept informed on progress (which they should be if you’re doing your job properly), but they want to be informed of constant progress. And when progress is not as they expect (i.e., to match exactly with the estimates), the second obsession comes up, that of recovering delays. So, start recovering time so that bosses feel that the project gets back on track. It doesn’t even matter if the application brings value anymore; what’s important is that the work comes out as estimated. And they put pressure on developers, so they keep their foot on the accelerator pedal and move fast towards the deadline. And now this raises the question of “how do you recover time?” Time has to come from somewhere, right?

The first idea would be to add more people to the project. Under certain conditions, this makes sense and can work. Most of the time, though, it makes things worse, especially if the project is in its later stages. This is more than a 40 years old observation we all know under the name of “Brooks’ law”:

Adding human resources to a late software project makes it later - Fred Brooks[87]

Not only is it likely to add even more delays, but it also becomes more expensive because the number of communication channels will increase, slowing down the work even more. And in addition to that, the new resources are an extra cost that had not been initially budgeted. Because of the increased cost, bosses don’t particularly like this solution. So somehow, you have to do more in less time. But since you are already late, you already know that’s not possible, since your estimate just told you so: you estimated something to take some time, it turns out it takes more. So how the heck could you do the work in less time now? You can’t. Your only option is to try to gain more time from somewhere else, like cutting features, for example. But the client won’t be very happy if you cut features. Besides, if you did a good job prioritizing and only worked on features that are “must have”, you can’t possibly give up on anything. So you start sacrificing stuff. So on what are you going to give up? What will you sacrifice to make the project move faster, respect the initial estimate, and also get your boss off your back?

Sacrificing quality

Will you sacrifice quality? A lot of companies don’t eat their own food (so to speak) when it comes to building software. That means they are not the client and thus not the one to use the software or suffer for its deficiencies if the software turns out bad. So quality is not something very important to them. Remember the “project management triangle” I mentioned above? If you pull from one corner of the triangle, the other components get affected. An ongoing project is an exercise in trying to keep everything in balance, something that’s not easy to do. In most projects, the quality comes out as a result of pulling from the corners of the triangle. For a framework or an open-source library, quality might be one of the initial constraints and goals, but for many projects, it is not. More importance is given to the corners of the triangle, so what’s inside the triangle suffers. And not just for that reason. When it comes to quality, there are two major problems.

The first one is that, just like success, quality means different things to different people. It might be customer satisfaction, usability, or user-friendliness. It might be high performance, zero defects, conformance to requirements, reliability, security, and lots and lots of features. Maintainability and ease of adding new features, elegant design, or clean and readable code might also be considered quality by some. Most of the time, quality is judged by the final user of the application, based on their own evaluation criteria, and also based on the value the application provides them with. It’s something subjective. And it also means that quality will probably not be all of those things together, which in turn means that the application might not be of good quality but only be perceived as such. Let’s look at an analogy. When you buy a new car, what do you look for to determine if you are getting your money’s worth? You might look at the car body and the interior, at standard options, the size of the trunk, maybe gas consumption, or how the car handles. If you have a friend that’s a mechanic, they will also look at the engine and its characteristics. And this gets us to the second problem with quality. Most car buyers don’t look under the hood because a lot of people don’t know mechanics. They assume that everything must be there and function properly and that the engine’s quality matches with everything else on the car. But what if you have a modern car, with a nice, sexy body shape, a leather interior, and handcrafted noble wood dashboard, a good surround sound system, more standard options than you can possibly need, etc., but under the hood you have 100 hamsters on a wheel? Would you still buy the car? You won’t. You might also become outraged. Similarly, to evaluate the quality of software, many do not look under the hood. Quality is evaluated from the outside, and everyone assumes that under the hood, everything matches the rest, just like with a proper car engine.

But a large amount of what software quality means is hidden from almost everyone, under the hood. It’s the code, the architecture, the design. Only developers truly know how good the software is below the surface (assuming the developers are not lacking the necessary knowledge and skills to built a proper application in the first place and are also not completely ignorant of what technical quality means). When you open the hood of a car, even if you don’t know how an engine actually works or what all those parts do, you still can tell the difference between an engine and 100 hamsters. But if you are not a developer and you look under the hood, you have no idea if the code you see is a proper engine or just some hamsters on a wheel. And what’s under the hood plays a huge role in the long run. When you buy a car, you also look at the warranty and how expensive the maintenance is. If the car is built with quality materials but breaks down all the time, the engine stops working, and your car spends more time with your mechanic than with you, then that quality is worth much less, and the car as a whole is no longer seen as being of good quality.

If the application has all the required features and brings value, but runs very slowly, crashes often, it’s full of bugs, or the interface is so loaded that you need two months of training to learn how to use it, it’s easy to conclude that it’s not of good quality. But what if it has all the required features, brings value, works very well, never crashes, no one has found any bugs so far, and the interface is intuitive, but the application is full of unpaid technical debt and adding a small feature involves changing a dozen apparent unrelated modules over the course of 6 months, can you still conclude that it’s of good quality? If the application looks secure and different users can only access the information allowed for their role and nothing more, but this is performed from CSS with “display: none” on various HTML elements, do you think the application is of good quality? Or how about if the application works well with 100 logged in users, but when user number 101 tries to log in, it no longer works, or if the code is completely unreadable and it takes you a week to fix even the most trivial bug, or if the code is tightly coupled to an expensive database and you can’t migrate to another database provider with minimal effort? Do you still think the application is of good quality? Of course, in all these cases, the answer is no. But since these things are not visible, many start treating quality the same way a bad housekeeper would treat dirt: by hiding it under the carpet.

“But if the application works well and does what it’s supposed to do, who cares it’s shit? It’s well-tested shit”. So no problem, right? Wrong!

Sure, if you just need to build a proof of concept to test out an idea as fast as possible, or if you write an application that, once installed, will never ever be changed, then hamsters on a wheel instead of an engine might just do the trick. But, as I said in the previous chapter, change is the only constant in software development. And when there is no quality under the hood, on the long run, you lose, because every change will take increasingly more time to figure out the impact of the change, to figure out how to fit it in the existing code, how to test it, and how to make sure you didn’t break anything in the process. It will always take longer to make changes to the application if it’s of low quality. Developers know that, but unfortunately, upper management does not. Because they don’t understand software and don’t see what’s under the hood, they don’t think it’s justified to work on something internal to improve something that can’t be seen externally. Refactoring? Repaying technical debt? Take time to build the proper abstractions? Why? It costs more, and they see no immediate benefit. You might try to explain the long term benefits, but before they see that, they see a schedule to be met. While you do your refactoring or redesign, you ain’t working on hitting your deadline. They want to ship it. Nooooooow… Quality requires additional costs; they know that. They know it from everyday life, like buying a more expensive car versus a cheaper one. But unlike a car where most people can recognize between expensive and cheap car manufacturers and know the difference in quality if that’s hidden from sight, why invest more? Don’t get me wrong; bosses are not determined to do something of poor quality. I haven’t met anyone so far to want to build bad software on purpose. But because bosses don’t understand how software is built, and why certain things are important to do even if they don’t seem to be needed right now, because they don’t understand various consequences, the software can end up in a bad way. But you, as a developer, must understand the consequences, and when discussing quality, to make sure that there is a good engine under the hood. You don’t necessarily have to make it perfect or spend a lot of time and money to bring it as close to perfection as possible, but it has to be good enough, not crap.

Other sacrifices

Or maybe, in the name of the deadline, you might postpone doing important things that can’t be seen from the outside? Just as the quality of the application design cannot be seen from the outside, so are other things that are not externally visible but must be done, such as security and access rights. You might be tempted to give all users full access (on the idea that it’s just for the moment) only to make some progress on other features. Or maybe you need a mechanism to periodically back up the application databases. But again, you might postpone building such a mechanism and come to work each day, hoping no hard drives crash. Or people might start thinking like “Let’s focus on the UI for all the features, to make progress visible. On the back-end, we can have a ‘light’ solution in place of the real one for the time being. We will improve it later”. Then later never comes. And even if it (rarely) does, you will be working on things you worked on already, to do them “better”, because you initially decided to take a shortcut. But remember, your boss wants to see progress. So if you are patching up old features, you don’t get to work as much on new features, and it looks like you are not making much progress. You risk having upper management start putting pressure on everyone, which won’t give you any more time to do the job properly. I mean… from their point of view, things seemed to be working, so why do you need to mess with it again?

Will you maybe sacrifice the team for the deadline? Will you force everyone to work overtime? Unpaid overtime, of course (if it involves money, most likely bosses will give up on the idea - they don’t impose overtime unless it looks free), excessively long hours, working weekends, no compensation time… the whole package. Or do you start messing with their work, telling them to give up on code review, on good practices, or copy-paste stuff everywhere? Will you give up on writing unit tests and put more load on the manual test team instead? Will you have your automation testers write production code to add more developer power? Programming is programming, right? If they can write scripts for automated testing, they can work on the main application also, isn’t it? Are you forcing the team to take on large amounts of technical debt then holding them accountable for the consequences while you constantly complain that they can’t keep the same speed of development from feature to feature? Do you complain that on Monday, people have started rewriting the code they wrote Friday night (assuming you don’t work them Saturdays and Sundays too)? Do you try to convince your people that noooo… you are not all participating in a death march; the schedule is… realistic. Do you really want to discover how much pressure you can put on your team before they reach their limits and start burning out? Are you willing to accept or even contribute to a negative working climate within the team because you are to busy chasing the deadlines to properly do your job as a Team Lead or Project Manager?

Or do you maybe give up on analyzing in-depth the problems and situations that occur? When pressure is on, and the deadline is important, sometimes you forget to pause and reflect on things. Instead of considering things carefully, then act, you start to react to them. For example, if things don’t turn out as estimated, we rarely analyze what has happened and how the remaining work might be impacted. Did you, for example, underestimate just one piece of the application, or the whole project? What exactly? Now that we know more about the project and how things diverted from the plan, can we re-estimate the remaining part and see if we get a similar result? An estimation is still an estimation, but if the new estimate differs largely from the initial one, then that’s a warning sign. Will the parts that still need to be done be delayed also? What’s most likely to happen? But when people see that half of the estimate just flew out the window, they continue to believe that the estimate was correct and the remaining one also is, and start thinking about how to recover the lost ground. But in reality, it’s safer to assume that you probably screwed up the remaining estimate also. You need to pause, see where you are, and what you need to do next, to still reach your goals. But that means putting things on hold until you regroup. And upper management has a problem with that. They want progress, progress, progress. So you have to solve the problem on the fly; you can’t pause. You are already late, remember? And so you start “to react” to everything. You do fire fighting. You throw solutions at problems until something sticks. That’s somehow better than to seem like you’re not doing anything. It’s like some family doctors I’ve seen. They don’t know exactly what is wrong with you, but instead of sending you to a specialist or consulting other doctors for a diagnostic, they give you some medicine… for something. “Let’s try this and see how it goes. Come back in 2 months (if you’re still alive, I might add), and we’ll check the progress. It didn’t work? Let’s try a different treatment. And another”. It seems like you and your doctor are doing things to solve the problem, isn’t it? It just seems so! To truly solve a problem, you need some time to analyze it and understand it completely. You don’t throw solutions at it, hoping for something to work. You need to be mindful of every problem that occurs on the project, even when you are late. You can’t just put out fires quickly then forget about them just because you are behind schedule. You need to solve them properly; otherwise, they will come back and bite you. You think you are saving time by not applying the proper solution, but in the long run, you will lose time by having to solve the same problems once more.

When the project doesn’t come out as estimated or planned, instead of thinking “look where we are, look where we thought we would be, and if this trend continues, we will miss our target by that much”, then communicate, decide and forecast a new course of action, everyone will instead demand you to recover the time difference. People expect an application to be put in production, just like the launch of a new highway or something. They want to cut the red ribbon. They want to have journalists to take pictures. And waiters who serve small appetizers and champagne. And after the party is over, everyone goes back and starts the whole thing over again with another project.

Lessons learned

This is another issue: that we don’t learn the lessons from all of this, and we make the same mistakes, again and again, project after project. Normally, at the end of the project, you should be sitting with the team and with stakeholders and do a retrospective of everything that happened. I, however, have never participated in any project retrospective so far, or “lessons learned meeting” as it’s called in project management. So I’m also guilty of not doing this. We are too busy placing blame on someone or on bad luck if things didn’t go well, or celebrate if it was a success or even if everyone managed to dodge a bullet; some finger-pointing or a slice of cake, and we’re off to our next project, where we hope things will turn out differently, or we promise ourselves that we’ll do better in the future. We wash our hands of the previous project, and we rush to, inevitably, make the same mistakes on the next one. But you should have a project retrospective, even if it’s only you sitting by yourself and reflecting on things.

Here are some ideas about what you should think about. For example, how did the team work together? What were the weaknesses and strengths of the team? How effective was each member of the team? Did everyone understand their roles and responsibilities? Did they have all the necessary skills from the beginning? Was there certain know-how missing when you started the project? Was there extra training needed? How was the communication on the project? How was the communication with clients, bosses, or other departments? How many issues did you have to escalate? Why? How many changes were requested, or how many times did people change their minds and wanted something else? Why? Could you have prevented it? What assumptions did you make? How many came true, and how many did not? What were the risks? How many did you anticipate? Which risk manifested, and which didn’t? Do you know how the application is used? That feature that was insisted upon so much and caused the project to last longer and cost more was it really worth it? Has someone even bothered to ask the final user of the application how they fancy the new software? Where the objectives and goals met? Can you consider it a successful project? How did your estimates compare with actual project time? How much overtime was it necessary? Did you at least track this overtime, or did everyone work 10 hours a day but clocked in only 8? So what’s the real deviation from your original estimate? Should you have estimated differently?

These things should ideally be tracked as the project unfolds, similar to how you should follow an employee’s work for the performance appraisals, so you don’t end up at the end of the project trying to think about what has happened throughout it, possibly forget about some issues or situations, or remain focused on what has happened more recently and is still fresh in the memory. The purpose of a project retrospective is to inspect and learn. Now that you are at the end of the project, it’s no longer about estimates, assumptions, and unknowns. It’s done. You know everything about the project and the software. Kowing what you know now - if you were to do it again - what would you do differently? What went well, what didn’t? What would you keep the same, add, modify, or remove? What would you avoid? Why? What have you learned from it all?

You might not get a chance to improve “this” project anymore, but you could reuse lessons learned from it to help you better manage future projects and improve processes, procedures, activities, communications, teams, and so on.

You will probably never reach the far end of the graph on any project, but you should at least do something to limit the size of the oscillations.

It takes longer

Remember that there are many moving parts when you run a software project. And I can’t possibly mention here lots of details on how you should manage a project. Hundreds of books have been written on this topic. I just tried to show some of the quicksands that you shouldn’t ignore. You work on several things at once, you juggle a lot of balls, and you will inevitably drop some of them on the floor. As developers, we can try to reduce everything to ones and zeros, but things are not black or white when it comes to estimating, planning, executing, and monitoring a project. It’s not perfect quality, or we give the customer a pile of crap; it’s not cost-schedule-scope, and you choose only two, etc. As you get older, you notice that it’s a spectrum, a spectrum of options and trade-offs. When I was young and inexperienced, I was trying to see things in black or white. In the meantime, I’ve learned that the ends of any interval are hard to reach and that you must find a balance point somewhere in the middle.

And it always takes longer than what you thought. When building a software project, Hofstadter’s law usually applies:

It always takes longer than you expect, even when you take into account Hofstadter’s Law - Douglas Hofstadter[88]

The Business-IT divide

From the previous chapter, you might have felt that there are certain tensions between developers and others inside the organization. If you’ve felt that, then I can tell you it’s not just a feeling; it’s a fact. There is indeed a certain disconnect.

When you look at a company from outside, you see a business as a whole. If it’s a hypermarket, a car dealership, a bank, a manufacturing company, a service provider, an IT company, or whatever, it doesn’t matter; it’s a business. But when you look at it from inside, you will see not just the business, but how the business is organized. You have different departments, each with their own role. Some contribute directly to making the business happen; others offer support functions. For example, in most companies, the cleaning staff members can’t really be considered part of the business. They don’t contribute to the actual business. It’s a support function. Logistics or the accounting department might be in a similar role depending on the business the company provides. And inevitably, inside the company, things start separating into two camps: “the business”, that is, the departments in charge of making the business happen, that are important or essential for providing the business, or they bring in the money, and the other departments that are necessary for the company’s operation, but which are not first-hand contributors to the business activity that the company carries out.

Let me expand on that idea by using an example. Have you ever wanted to go on vacation onboard a cruise ship? Seen from outside, the business here is the whole “come sail away on an incredible adventure” to the Caribbean Islands, Bahamas, or some other exotic destination. The business is about offering clients an authentic experience in an all-inclusive trip with onboard entertainment. On the ship, you have everything from restaurants to shopping stores, bars, SPA and fitness facilities, theaters, and other activity rooms. If sitting by the pool with a Margarita in your hand after collecting your casino winnings without paying taxes is your thing, then you can do that too. The “business” is about the entertainment, the fine cuisine, the comfort of the ship’s amenities, and maybe the occasional trips on land.

But for this business to work properly, a lot of things are needed in the lowest levels of the ship. The ship’s propulsion needs to function; otherwise, you’ll be sitting in port. You need running water and electricity. The ship’s waste management facility needs to work. The cleaning personnel needs to do their job. The kitchen needs to be stacked with more foods than just potatoes. All of these things hidden from sight need to work in order for you to enjoy your trip. Even before you step foot on the ship, other things - like the ticket booking system - also needs to work correctly. All of these support functions are the things everyone takes for granted. At least until something fails. You might be going to a beautiful destination and have a luxury suite with a balcony to travel the sea in style, but if the air conditioning doesn’t work, the toilet doesn’t flush, or the ship’s autopilot malfunctions and you run aground on Snake Island[94], then your trip will suck.

Lots of companies are similar to this cruise ship example. For the business to work, a lot of support functions need to be in place. And an essential support function in a company is that of the IT department. Most businesses would not be able to function without their IT department. You have a network in place, email, access to the Internet, and lots of servers running the essential software for the employees or for client-facing applications. Just like you have to have running water in the bathroom, or for the air conditioning to work, in the same way, in a company, the hardware and software infrastructure must be present and functional so that the business can function like it’s supposed to. Only when something fails in the support functions do people become aware of their existence, and then everyone gets nervous and complains to have the situation fixed or improved… because it’s affecting “the business”.

But any company has computer networks. The same goes for email and Internet access. However, the software that runs inside the business can be the differentiator for what keeps you in the game or at the top of the game. The software can be an essential part of the business. To keep with the cruise ship analogy, the software might be the ship itself, i.e., you have the biggest and most luxurious ship, serving the best food, offering more activities, etc. If all the cruise lines had the same ships, offered the same services, and went to the same destinations, why would anyone choose one company over the other?

When working in a company whose software is essential for the business, or is the business itself, IT can no longer be considered just a support department; it must be part of “the business”. But this is, unfortunately, a matter of perspective. There are departments that are “the business” and departments that are “not the business”. It’s just a matter of how people see things and how they reason about them. Since this is a book for developers, I’ll talk about development versus non-development departments. Besides, technology plays a massive role in these different perspectives.

Us versus them

People in IT will refer to anyone in the company that isn’t working in IT as “the business”. It’s everyone who isn’t a geek programmer, developer, sysadmin, DBA, or CTO, everyone who doesn’t understand or have any appreciation for the work that happens in the IT department. It’s those people who you talk to trying to explain how something technical works or what are the technical limitations of something and, as more time passes, their confusion increases while your patience decreases. It’s those people who don’t know the difference between a programmer and a help desk officer. You know… the technically challenged. They are “the business”. Unfortunately, “the business” also sees developers differently. They see them as the geeks who don’t know or care about anything else except technology - the ones that deal with PCs, emails, and the Internet connection. Ahh… and also the ones that produce poor quality software solutions that business people are then required to use in their daily work.

That is why things split into two camps, and the two sides end up not considering themselves partners. Everything becomes an “us versus them” situation that’s known as “the Business-IT divide”. Business people do their thing; IT people do theirs. People don’t look in each other’s backyards, and everyone just goes about their own job. Some set the direction in which the project or company should move; others must provide the technical support needed to make it happen. Business people don’t care to explain their problems, and IT people don’t care to understand them. Some look at revenues, costs, and client retention; others look at code quality, the number of production incidents, or performance. Some want to make money; others want to build something they are proud of. Some throw business jargon around, IT people throw technical words around. And the list could go on. But what happens is that IT is only seen as a support department, somehow separate from the rest of the organization, not part of “the business”. And outsourcing is often a good example when it comes to this. Companies externalize email, help desk activities, or software development, but how many companies have you seen externalizing their business? You can only outsource things that you find nonessential. IT is not “the business”, IT must not be essential, so we can outsource it, right? But more about that in a later chapter.

When IT isn’t viewed as a business partner, an “I say, you do” relationship starts to develop. The business is viewed as the mind of the operation, while IT is seen in the execution role. Bosses and clients decide together what to do, they form their own opinions about how things should be and how they should unfold, decisions are made, and many important discussions take place without any input from the development team. Then they go to IT and say, “Guys, this is what we need. Make it happen”. And when things make it to IT, developers say “no”. And they say “no” not because they are jerks, but because, often, what the business wants is not possible, or because it’s not actually clear what’s needed. The things I mentioned in the previous chapter will start to unfold, and everyone joins their own side in the “tug of war”.

If the development team is seen as a support function, another thing that happens is that business people don’t get involved in software projects once these are underway. The development team keeps them engaged because they need input from the business, but left to their own devices, they do not participate. For them, the software solution is something you send somewhere to be built and then comes back as requested, similar to ordering something online, and then your package gets delivered on your doorstep. Well… that’s not how it works. When business people don’t get involved and don’t continuously collaborate with the development team, there is the risk that the software may become unusable or not incompletely solve the problem it was supposed to solve. You can’t start a project, then step out of the picture and come back at the end. It’s as if a cruise line company would like to increase its fleet by having a new ship built, but then no one from the business gets involved in the project. They get the ship designed, blueprints are created, then everything is sent away to be built from those blueprints. With building a ship, this might work, but with software, it doesn’t work that way because, for software, blueprints mean specifications made from requirements, and you already know by now what problems exist when it comes to software requirements.

Then, when IT is not considered a business partner, the only important thing becomes the software, and not also the interaction with developers. When a ship is being built, business people don’t collaborate with welders, plumbers, electricians, or painters, so why should business people collaborate with developers who build software, right? But here is where the analogy between building a ship and building software stops. When people create all the blocks that will be put together to form the complete ship, they don’t get new insight into how to build the ship. They don’t find out more about what needs to be created. They already know. They have the blueprints, they’ve built many other ships before, so they just build a ship. That’s their job. But things are different with software development. As you build the application, you find out more about what is needed. Developers are smart people, and they will make the software. That’s their job. But it’s one thing for developers to chase people throughout the company to get answers, get details, or figure out what’s needed as new information or insight becomes available, and another thing to have continuous collaboration with the business people for whom they are building that software. When custom software is built to improve how the company does business, make more money, or be more competitive in whatever line of business it operates in, you can’t leave everything in the developers’ hands and expect everything to go smoothly from start to finish. As a business person, you have to get involved. You can’t blame IT because the application came out badly just as you can blame them when email isn’t working, or you have problems connecting to the Internet. You can’t expect developers to build the application and complain at the end if things turn out bad, because, if there is a problem with the app, it sure as heck that didn’t happen at the end. Things went south at some point during development. Where were you when that happened, business person?

Cost

Because they are not considered partners, for many companies, people in IT are a cost. And what do business people try to do with cost? Reduce it, of course. Besides moving the company to a building on the city outskirts where the rent is cheaper, renegotiating contracts with service providers, buying refurbished equipment, automating things, give to charity to benefit from tax reductions, cut down on travel expenses, refill printer cartridges, or buying cheaper office supplies or a cheaper brand of toilet paper for all the bathrooms in the office, another way to reduce costs is to hire people with lower salaries. In most industries, though, not just in software development, a lower salary often means skills to match. But you can’t achieve much with poorly trained people, and sooner or later, everyone becomes aware of that. You need people with experience. But which, of course, costs more money. So if you want to keep costs low, what is there to be done given the situation? You hire experienced people, but fewer of them, right?

Most of the teams I worked with were short-staffed. Quite often, I received the explanation that “we can’t find developers”, that the demand is too high and the supply too low (what they really wanted to say was that no developers are willing to work for the money they are willing to offer, and sometimes they are eager to outsource to hire cheaper, regardless of the problems that come bundled with outsourcing). Fewer people doing more work makes sense financially, but when the software team is inadequately staffed, the workload becomes larger than what the team can handle, so everyone is put under a lot of pressure to deliver. When you have too few people in IT and too many projects, things start to be delayed, and people end up waiting a lot for technical solutions. If you have an IT department and multiple business units, each with mixed workloads, with their own needs and emergencies for software solutions, things will move slowly no matter how good the developers are. When all projects reach IT, all have a high priority, which is similar to saying that no project has any importance since, anyways, there aren’t enough developers to do them all.

You end up working on low priority requests without knowing it, then something urgent is shoved down your throat and must be delivered immediately, something that was on hold for three months because you didn’t realize it was essential to work on. And everything ends up a mess, and it’s, of course, IT’s fault. Many start to believe that it’s just bad will on the developers’ part, that they don’t want to do certain things… who knows what they do in their office all day long instead of working; playing network video games, maybe. And they get on your case and pressure you or insist for you to build them their software because they think that if they breathe down your neck, you’ll just give them what they want to make them go away. But you have too much on your plate already, and you can’t waste time engaging in this kind of behavior, so you send them away and put up all sorts of processes in place to protect yourself from business people who directly come to you and ask for stuff. “Did you create a ticket in our issue tracking system? If you don’t have a ticket, you don’t exist”. And even if they do create a ticket, it’s then put on hold. Progress on projects is slow, the approval process for new tickets is even slower; various business departments then say that it’s difficult to work with the technical department and that they can no longer wait on IT to build them their projects.

Shadow IT

And because their projects are not getting done, business people bite the bullet and build their own applications, causing what is called “Shadow IT”[95]. People start doing things in Excel, or Steven from accounting knows some programming, so he builds an application that the entire department uses. At least until someday, when Steven goes on holiday, and the application stops working, and there is no one around to fix it. Suddenly, all hell breaks loose, and nobody in the department can do any work because they depend on that application. And so they call IT, ‘cause they don’t know any technical stuff themselves. Who else are they going to call considering Steven is not answering his phone since he left on his vacation? IT then finds out about this application, and it’s now their turn to freak out. “You have a website that you uploaded to the cloud? Where did you get all this confidential data? How about security? Holy crap, the data is indexed by search engines. If you type in the right keywords, it shows up on the first page of results. Are you insane? Who authorized this? Is this a company Internet domain? Steven owns it? WTF?!”

So when IT finds out about the new application (which might pose security risks, expose confidential information, or who’s existence might even break some law or compliance regulations depending on the field the company operates in), what they want to do is shut the thing down because they know they will have to clean up the mess if something bad happens. And this is an ugly situation to be in because the business people think it’s IT’s fault in the first place for them having to build their own applications. And not only did you not build them an application as you were supposed to do, but now that they have built for themselves something they needed and that now helps them a lot, it’s still IT that is inconvenienced and shuts down their application without giving them an alternative in return. The existence of “Shadow IT” doesn’t just contribute to the Business-IT disconnect, but it can also cause animosity between the two parties.

And it’s understandable. You can’t shut down their application and leave it like that for three months or whatever, while you finish what you are currently working on so that at least you have a chance to even look over the application and see how you could help. And you try to help them, to be their partner, but you don’t have enough people, and you just added another application to the list of those you should be working on. And you are back to square one. People are again waiting for IT to work on an application for them, just like in the beginning, when they were eventually forced to take matters into their own hands and build their own software. For many companies, “Shadow IT” is a big problem, but from personal experience, I can say that “Shadow IT” is not, in fact, “the problem”; it’s a response to the actual problem, which is that the business needs important applications and IT doesn’t have the capacity to deliver them because the same business decided that IT is a cost to be reduced. People need applications to be productive. They are just trying to do their job better, and can’t wait forever for IT to provide the necessary software. It’s a blocker for them, so they go around it. “Who needs IT. We’ll do it ourselves”. If things are allowed to continue, eventually the divide becomes very large, and people start thinking they don’t need IT at all, that there is something wrong with them, and maybe they should outsource their jobs. It might even be cheaper to do that, right?

When such a situation develops, it isn’t easy to solve because both parties need to be well informed. And often they are not. It’s a communication problem that originated above all the departments involved. Each department has its own projects and priorities, and these are often not communicated with other departments. If the company doesn’t have a way - like a Project Management Office department, for example - to help with communication and coordination across projects, so that everyone understands what’s going on, and realize that the IT employees are not jerks when you go to their office to ask for help with something and they tell you to take a walk, then you are basically fucked (and also, the IT jobs will probably be outsourced).

Before moving on, there is one last thing I want to mention when it comes to “Shadow IT”, and it’s this: don’t think that all this mess always happens to poor innocent developers struggling to do what’s best for the business and getting no recognition for it. Sometimes the IT guys are indeed just a bunch of jerks. They are the ones deepening the divide because frequently they don’t want to see the big picture. Plain and simple. They’re obsessed with the cloud, big data, or what front-end framework is cooler this week or the next than of what value they can bring to the company. Sometimes they are so obsessed with technologies or playing with cool toys that they put their own interests before those of the company. “I always wanted to play with such and such technology, but the license was expensive. Hey… the company can afford it, so let’s buy a license for it, and we’ll figure out a way to stick it in some application”. Or maybe something like the following. “Hey guys, wouldn’t it be cool if we could build this application entirely functional?” It might be cool, but is it necessary? Then the apex of being a jerk (often because developers think they are so smart compared to those that “don’t get” software) is to ignore business people when they come up with ideas or requests, dismiss everything they say, and simply conclude they are all just a bunch of idiots.

Can you then blame the business people when they complain that IT doesn’t understand their needs or see all the money poured into technology, but they don’t see matching results? I’ll talk more about bad developers and what damage they can inflict on a company in a later chapter, but for now, let’s focus on how we might bridge the gap.

The real cost

The consequences of the Business-IT divide are: wasted time and missed opportunities, communication break downs, expensive software solutions that don’t do the right thing, make things more complicated instead of more efficient, and sometimes even complete failures. It also creates a context where everyone washes their hands of responsibilities, and everyone places blame on “the other side” instead of collaborating for success. Nowadays, when almost everything relies on software to work, this divide needs to be bridged.

Information technology and business are becoming inextricably interwoven. I don’t think anybody can talk meaningfully about one without talking about the other - Bill Gates[96]

The quote is from 1999, so it seems people still haven’t figured this one out. And the people that need to figure this out first and foremost are those in upper management. You need business-technology convergence for everyone to build strategies that move the company towards the same goal; otherwise, things can turn out like in the “The Swan, the Pike, and the Crab” poem[97] by Ivan Krylov[98], when everyone makes a big effort, works hard and do their jobs as best they can, but they eventually all pull in different directions, without agreeing, and just ending up canceling each other’s actions.

More even, when it comes to software companies, IT is the actual business and should be regarded as such. You can’t see the IT department as apart from the rest of the business, and just as a support function, or as a cost. You can’t have a disconnect between the business plan and the technology plan; the two must go together. As a business person, you can’t look at development like a black box or take it for granted. You need to appreciate the complexity and variety of the technology that’s running your business in the workplace all the time, not just when it goes wrong, or when the technology doesn’t do everything “the business” wants when it says it wants it.

Tech people need a “seat at the table” so they can influence and participate in management decisions, so they can offer suggestions and provide input on the actual capabilities of the technologies or the tech department. Otherwise, instead of making an informed decision from the start, you risk making a wrong one, then patch it again and again and again when the software starts being developed and you notice that the business expectations aren’t possible or are beyond what IT can actually deliver.

Working with IT on a project (or with any other department for that matter) is like having some contractor working inside your house to make changes or repairs to your property. You can tell them what you want, give them the keys to your home, let them do their job, then come back when the work is finished. But anything can happen when they are there. Each property is unique in its own way, so it might come with its unique challenges and problems. When a situation arises, the contractor can either discuss it with you, if you are present, to make the best decision together, or they will just use their experience to decide, a decision with which you might not agree. For example, let’s say you want to add some cabinets to your kitchen. The builder will need to drill holes in the wall to add the dowels and the screws to hang the cabinets. But he notices the wall is made of a glassy concrete. It’s also not thick enough. The holes will go in about two-thirds of the way, and with that kind of concrete, there is the risk that the wall will shatter on the other side, and some pieces will fall apart. What does he do? Well, he needs to install the cabinets. That’s his job. He can’t do anything about the material the wall is made of. From experience, he also knows that there is no way of avoiding some pieces of the wall falling apart on the other side. So he goes ahead and drills the holes. Some pieces from the wall fall on the other side. You come home, and you find the holes on the other side of the wall. You, of course, freak out. Besides hanging the cabinets now, you also need to fix the wall. But now imagine a different scenario. You are present while the contractor does his work, and you can go together over everything that needs to be done before the contractor actually starts to work. The contractor examines the wall and makes the same discovery as earlier. He explains to you what might happen when the holes are drilled. You didn’t expect this situation, but you need those cabinets there. And you figure that you can always fill in the holes. So you give the go-ahead, and the same thing happens: some pieces of the wall fall on the other side. But now it’s a result of your decision, not the contractor’s. So you no longer freak out. The result is the same in both scenarios, but in the first case, it’s the builder’s fault, isn’t it? The same happens when developing software also: the developer will make decisions with which you, a business person, might not agree. If you tell them what you need, leave, and come back in the end, the damage might already be done. If you plan it together from the beginning and stick around, you can decide on other options. For this example, you might choose to install smaller cabinets that need smaller holes in the wall, or maybe you find an alternative way of hanging them. But at least, there won’t be any surprises if you end up with concrete pieces all over the place.

This would be the ideal case: for management to understand the situation, to make IT a partner, and consult with them when making decisions. But it’s up to them to decide whether or not to do so. They must be the ones to acknowledge the problems the Business-IT divide causes and do something about it. IT can’t fix a situation like this entirely on their own, because the Business-IT divide is not a problem of the IT department; it’s a problem of the company. As I said, it’s a matter of perspective. The problems caused by different perspectives can also happen between other departments that don’t collaborate the way they should. Each department tries to be efficient on their own, to do the part for which they are accountable, to do the right things from their perspective, but the company overall can have a lot to lose.

When it comes to the Business-IT divide, the two groups are pretty much ignorant of how they each do what they do. Business people are not tech-savvy, and tech people are not always interested in the business, and each party has its own way of looking at things, often reaching opposite ends on a spectrum. So, obviously, to fix all this mess, you need to start by working on how business and tech persons see things - to change perspectives. But it’s not easy to change people’s perspectives. And if management doesn’t recognize the problems and doesn’t make a call to turn IT into a partner, somehow IT must be the one to make the first step towards becoming the partner. It’s a prolonged approach, which may or may not work, but it’s good to do it anyways. Namely, to interact more with the business.

Bridging the gap

As someone working in development or IT, you need to understand the business. Not just to be able to do your job properly, but also to be able to interact at the appropriate level with business people. In this interaction, the effort will probably be mostly unidirectional because business people are unlikely to ever understand the difficulties of making software unless they become developers themselves. They don’t understand the commands you may be typing in a terminal, for example. Often, they also have difficulties understanding what a terminal is. For many, the work that takes place inside the IT department is some sort of black magic. So you can’t have high expectations from them to understand the work of a developer. The other way around - for developers to learn the business well - is simpler, and with greater chances of success. Business is often easier to learn than programming, and things in most fields don’t change as often as in tech. Besides, as a developer, you need to learn the business to make sure you build an application that solves the correct problem. You need to spend more time with businesspeople and try to understand them. You might hang around with some colleagues from the marketing department, or sales, or from the call center, to see what they do, to understand their work, see how each fills their piece from the company’s operations or goals, and figure out how the software you build can help them more. And this must be done periodically, not just at the beginning of a project. Engage with them often, do workshops or something, attend their status meetings or some other more important quarterly meetings, read their newsletters. You have to keep the interaction high; otherwise, everyone goes about their own job, and silos get created inside the company. If you actually engage with them, you will see them work; you will see what problems or challenges they face, or how clients scream at them for their own problems with the company. It’s one thing to see their job description on a piece of paper, and it’s another to be in the trenches next to them. Sometimes what you find out is that the application you built isn’t helping them. At all. Worse still, it’s getting in their way. It happened to me more than once to see some head of a department, or manager, request software to work a certain way, only to discover later that that’s how the manager thought things are working. In reality, things worked another way, but no one had the courage to tell the boss they’re wrong. One second I was happy that I finished the application, and now, all enthusiastic, I was showing people how to use it, then the next second, I got a sinking feeling when I realized that I’d built the wrong thing. “If only I could have known about this sooner”.

Well, find out about it sooner. Involve business people during the entire development of the application and ask them for feedback. Show them that you care about their opinions, that you are mindful of their needs, and you are genuinely interested in helping them. Explain why some things are complicated and take longer, why some are simpler and take less, what are the priorities, what problems turn up. Learn to speak business and communicate clearly and transparently. Communication is essential. Let everyone know what’s going on. By keeping constant contact with them, you make sure that both camps are working on the same goals. By working together, they learn to trust you, even though they don’t fully understand how you do what you do. Once everyone works together to achieve the same objectives, eventually, it reaches a point where people make decisions together. And maybe someday, someone will have the realization that developers should sit at the table from the beginning, and take part in the discussions and decisions, and not be seen just as a support function that delivers systems to “the business”.

It is about organization-wide involvement from both business and technical people, and this kind of change must begin somewhere. And it might just as well be IT. You have to open the way, communicate, interact, and try to become a business partner; otherwise, the situation will not improve. And if you make efforts to understand the business people, you speak their own language (you speak “business”), and if you show them that you just want to help, the situation will improve. Maybe you will still have a short-staffed team and too many projects to deal with, perhaps some issues will still remain - such as “Shadow IT” - but when people are informed, they will better understand the situation, will know what to expect, and will ask IT for advice on how to proceed and what they should or should not do, which leads to collaboration and partnership.
