Of course, business people and management must be open-minded about your interaction with them. You can’t just barge into people’s meetings; they have to understand what you are doing in their office instead of being in yours, working. They need to understand that this is also part of your job, to understand better the needs of the employees of the clients or of the organization as a whole. Normally all departments have to communicate, coordinate, and unify their efforts; I speak here only from the side of the IT department.

Trust

So far, what I’ve mentioned about the Business-IT divide was a matter of different perspectives. To bridge the gap, you need more interaction between the departments; more collaboration. But for people to truly collaborate, they need to trust each other.

Trust is one of those things that play an essential role in people’s lives. We deal with trust every day, whether we are conscious of it or not. When we start our car when the traffic light turns green, we trust that those coming from left and right, who have a red light, will stop. When you deposit your money in the bank, you trust the bank not to steal it from you (at least not based on the most known definition of the verb “to steal”). When you eat at a restaurant, you trust that the food is correctly prepared and that no spoiled ingredients were used. When you install an application on your smartphone, you trust that the permissions the application uses are actually necessary for the application to work, not to allow it to steal private information from your device. So inevitably, you have to deal with trust when it comes to the workplace as well.

Trust is not something you can easily observe or measure, but if you distance yourself a bit from the things that everyone else is doing, and look closely, you will see something else, something that is easier to notice, namely “the lack of trust”. Some of these things you can observe even without being employed in the company. For example, are you at the job interview and the HR person insists on asking more and more details about a career break in your CV, even though you have already given them a comprehensive answer? Or also during the hiring process, were you asked to provide five references from people you worked with, phone numbers from your last three supervisors, and contact details of your teacher from second grade? Then after you are hired, you notice that the work environment or the work you have to perform does not match with what you discussed in the interview, and that’s not even all the information the company has withheld from you? You can’t work from home, you say? Why not? Is it because you work for a bank or some business operating in a very regulated environment, or is it because your boss thinks you’ll be lazy and drag your feet if nobody is there to watch you and nag you? You eventually ask for a raise for your accomplishments, but you are told “no” because of the tough economic times and because the company barely makes ends meet, only to later discover that the company actually made its biggest profit ever during the recession? Does your company say they have the client in mind in everything they do, but for someone to get in touch with customer relations, they have to solve a Sudoku puzzle on their call center’s IVR? The company gets involved in social responsibility programs because they actually care or because it’s a cheaper public-relations tool? Do you work on crappy virtual machines with no access to the Internet because the client is afraid you might steal their code? Or have you ever worked on a project where you are behind schedule, but resources are pulled from another project that is ahead of schedule, which just happens it’s on another client’s budget? What do you think will happen if that client finds out they are essentially financing someone else’s project with their own money?

We say about our colleagues that we have a working relationship. But human relationships of any kind cannot work unless there is trust. Think about it. Can you really work efficiently with someone else if you can’t trust that person?

Without trust, we don’t truly collaborate; we merely coordinate or, at best, cooperate - Stephen M. R. Covey[99]

When we don’t have trust in certain persons or in certain situations, we naturally move away from them, we are more cautious, or we have certain reservations. If in traffic we suspect that cars coming from the right will not stop at the red light, we will slow down as we pass through the intersection. If we don’t trust banks, we keep money under our mattress, and we take the risk for thieves breaking into our house to leave not only with the TV but also with all of our life savings. When we don’t trust the food at the restaurant, we have to spend more time at home every day to prepare our meals and then also wash the dishes. If you suspect that an application makes use of more permissions than it should for it to function correctly, you probably won’t install the application anymore.

You need trust. You need it in your everyday life, and you need it to work in a company. Trust is essential for an organization to function properly, and yet, there are a lot of things happening inside companies that put in doubt our willingness to trust. You can’t remove yourself from these situations most of the time (without resigning), so you are faced with working with people you don’t really trust.

And where trust is lacking, all sorts of destructive behaviors start showing their ugly head. Mistakes are covered up, and people begin to play the blame game or make excuses instead of taking responsibility. People withhold information or keep good ideas to themselves to avoid rocking the boat or be judged by others. There is gossip, and people talk behind each other’s backs. Everyone is out for themselves, with secret agendas to get ahead or avoid being fired; you don’t know what to expect from others because you don’t know their plans (sometimes they seem to do the right thing, sometimes not, it depends whether or not it’s in their plan). Some might even withhold information, manipulate or twist facts. People feel unproductive and begin to behave accordingly. All of these things have an impact on the company, since people, in their daily work, are no longer as productive; similar to the examples above, they start to act more cautiously or to have certain restraints in how they act. The authors of “The Speed of Trust” book[100] have a very good name for these; they call them “trust taxes”. These are hidden taxes, just like inflation is a hidden tax, for example. They might not show up in the company’s financial statements, but they are there. It’s stuff like deep management hierarchies to ensure control over the employees. It’s bureaucracy, bad office politics, disengagement, and turnover of employees (and it’s the good people that leave, not the bad ones). It’s losing old clients or even employees engaging in fraudulent activities. And of course, lack of trust can be an issue between IT people and business people. A lack of trust can deepen the Business-IT divide or prevent it from being bridged. Simply put, business and IT don’t actually trust each other.

Time and time again, shit happens in lots of software development projects, for many reasons that collaborate in complex ways. There isn’t a single culprit for which projects fail, so - similar to Agatha Christie’s novel, “Murder on the Orient Express”[101] - everyone becomes a suspect. Clients didn’t know what they wanted or how to ask for it. The business analysts did a poor job of gathering requirements. Developers got the estimates wrong, or management imposed unrealistic deadlines. There were not enough developers on the team. The client repeatedly asked for changes. The application wasn’t properly tested. Or maybe it’s the fault of the sales manager who said anything the client wanted to hear, so they sign the contract and get their fat bonus. “Yes, it’s their fault we are in this mess. They sold a dream wrapped in a promise. What do they care, since in the end, it’s not them doing the job, but those poor developers who somehow have to make it happen? You should never trust salespeople. Never, I say!”

So software projects get a notoriously bad reputation for over-promising and under-delivering. It’s a situation where it’s difficult to build trust because trust is something that’s earned over time and depends a lot on your results. With so many software projects that go down the tubes and don’t produce the desired results, how can people trust IT? As developers, we say that we will do this and that, that we’ll handle things, that everything will be alright, and then what happens? Things turn out differently than what we said, and the results contradict us again and again. And people learn from past experiences. If someone hasn’t kept their word once, they will do it a second time. So bosses start to put pressure on developers and say that everything is important, to force them to deliver. To say that the sky will fall if the application is not in production by X date. But then date X arrives, and nothing bad happens. But developers learn from this experience also. Next time when the boss comes and says that “if we don’t do such and such by Y date, something very bad will happen”, do you think developers will be inclined to believe them again? Then, it doesn’t even matter if some ridiculous deadline was imposed by bosses or resulted from the estimates. As developers, you agreed to do it, so that means a promise that you will do it. And then, of course, people expect you to do it. Expectations are set, then expectations are broken. And then business people no longer trust you. You said you’d do it and you didn’t. You get blamed. But it’s not your fault, or better said, not just “your” fault. So you blame the business for not giving you the information you needed, when you needed it, that they don’t understand certain issues are more difficult and take more time, that it wasn’t developers who cut estimates in half… so trust flies out the window. Everyone starts to think like “Fool me once, shame on you. Fool me twice, shame on me”, and then start to put their guard up or consider contingency plans to deal with everyone else, because they no longer trust them. And everyone starts to pay “trust taxes”. And the reason is simple: when your trust gets broken, it’s “so long and goodbye”. The next time we interact with the person who has broken our trust, we are not so trusting anymore because all sorts of unpleasant outcomes just became possible. And people put in place some control or defense mechanisms to protect against the bad outcomes, measures that are financially costly and time-consuming, and things are no longer as efficient as they could be if everyone truly trusted each other. For example, have you worked in a company where you had to track your work so often that the overhead of doing so was impacting the actual work you were doing? Or in a company where you get into an argument with your boss about the progress you are making, they are not satisfied, and they ask to see all the tasks you’ve been working on so far? “Show me all the tasks in the issue tracking system. Everything you do must be written in there. Then I want you to send me daily reports so I can see your progress”. Or did you work in a company where there were several bosses to one person performing the actual job, a company with a very deep hierarchy in which one layer controls what the lower layer does, which controls what the lower layer does until eventually, you reach the few unfortunate souls who actually do the work?

Trust also means that you can give up control. If managers or bosses don’t trust developers, managing projects becomes taking charge and controlling the work being done. If they look at developers and instead of seeing trustworthy people, they see some geeks dressed up in sci-fi and fantasy T-Shirts with ketchup stains on them, they will think it’s a mistake to relinquish a lot of control to them and will instead take back control up to the smallest details. Did they “surrender” the project in the hands of capable people or not? When something happens, do developers behave in a way that meets expectations or not? If managers or bosses get surprised by something on the project, and they don’t believe they can trust you, then that lack of trust will lead to a heavy environment of “command and control”[102].

Remember I talked about autonomy, mastery, and purpose? You can say goodbye to all of that in the presence of “command and control” because project management from the ’50s tends not to work in most software development projects. Command and control works in the military, but not with knowledge workers. In the military, soldiers must follow orders no matter what. If they get the order to attack the enemy, that’s what they must do. You can’t have soldiers start a discussion about different ways of attacking, pros and cons of each, or have them start a meeting about it while everyone takes turns at the whiteboard to present and support their opinion. In the military, everyone is trained to follow orders. Without that, everything breaks apart. But in a software company, “follow orders”, or as I said above, “I say, you do”, only increases the Business-IT divide. The behavior you need at work is completely different than the one you need on the battlefield. You need people to think, collaborate, and look for the best solutions, not follow orders (especially from those who are not close to the battle, or in developers’ case, the work).

Furthermore, developers hate command and control. They hate when people tell them what to do and how to do it, especially if they have no clue what they are talking about. Command and control works in the army also for another reason: except for the top-level (occupied by politicians), they are all military down the chain of command. A General who gives orders, for example, understands what soldiers do. They were a soldier themselves. You do not join the army as a General; you have to advance in rank. A general knows what a Captain and a Major do, etc… because they were a Captain or a Major. But a boss or a manager doesn’t know what programmers or developers actually do if they haven’t been a developer themselves fairly recently. A boss or manager can be hired in that position without having a clue of how the technical work is actually done. And developers don’t like being told what to do by such a person. Most developer teams are short-staffed, by choice, or because it seems there aren’t enough developers to hire. Somehow though, there is always a plentiful supply of managers to go around, managers that - in the absence of trust - only make the work of developers harder.

Note that I’m not against a hierarchy or against managers. A hierarchy helps with order and organization. There must be someone in charge, with control over schedules, teams, or projects - people who have a higher vision on things. I’m just saying that there has to be a balanced organizational structure that inspires trust. Too many layers of command and control management don’t inspire trust; they instead create “trust taxes”.

For example, the speed of communication is reduced because it takes longer for the information to travel the entire hierarchy. Sometimes communication falls apart if lower levels of the hierarchy receive multiple contradictory decisions from different levels above. The information doesn’t usually flow like a cascade, completely unaltered. It can get diluted, transformed, or completely lost as it goes from one layer to the next (sometimes intentionally). Something that is “nice to have” at one stage might become “mandatory” at the next, just because one of the managers wants to fall into the graces of their hierarchical manager. You saw a perfect example of this in the joke from the introductory chapter of the book, where the developers’ message of “we cannot do this project” travels up the hierarchy until it reaches the client as “this is the type of project in which our company specializes in”. That’s funny and sad all at the same time. Within a deep company hierarchy, high-level decisions are made based on the communication coming up from the layers below. If you were told from the intermediate layers underneath that everything is fine and dandy, you would end up making bad decisions at the top. The CEO may think that everything is OK, but somewhere lower in the company hierarchy, the situation might be rather horrible. And when the problems are finally discovered, the solution found by the CEO to ensure they get real information into what’s happening from now on is to institute more “command and control”.

Another problem with a deep hierarchy is that it may start to look like a ladder of success, one that people will want to climb. Everyone wants to become a manager, basically. Maybe not developers though… developers don’t want that. But managers at one level will surely want to move from their desk in the open space to one in a corner office. The team, the project, the company will have to take the back seat as people pursue their own interests. A deep hierarchy encourages individualism and competition, as opposed to collaboration, because there are not enough management positions for everyone as the hierarchy starts to narrow as it goes up. Then, once they get to the top, people start to watch their backs, so others don’t make a move for their position. They will no longer want conflicts and will avoid all risks, even if they are for the benefit of the organization. They don’t want to make waves or rock the boat. This will affect decision making. It’s not bad enough that decisions are made too far away from where the rubber meets the road (how can you make the best decisions when you get progressively clueless about what’s actually happening inside projects?), but those decisions are made strictly based on reports, status meetings, or PowerPoint presentations. This ends up creating a very slow process. Since they don’t want to rock the boat, they will want to take risk-free decisions (or as risk-free as possible), so they will ask for a ton of reports. Several extra layers of management will now show up, whose only reason for existing is to gather reports from those who do the actual work. And time wasted on reports is time taken away from developing the software - another tax to pay.

Because of a deep hierarchy, things start to be supported and working based on reports (and then with all sorts of processes and rules imposed as consequences of the reports), instead of relying on trust. Moreover, these things clearly show people that they are not trusted; otherwise, why would you have to justify every small thing with reports, and why would work need to be performed by strictly following some procedures? You end up with everyone doing their job and nothing more. Deep hierarchies stifle creativity, lower people’s energy, and internal drive, and reduce empowerment and people’s willingness to act. When something happens that is not covered by procedures or contained in reports, people choose to do nothing about it, so they don’t risk making a mistake. You start to hear things like, “I just did what the procedure said”, or “I just followed the guidelines”, or “it’s not my responsibility/job to do such and such”. Then more rules are added, or the procedures are updated to include an ever-growing number of situations and exceptions. More taxes, basically. In the end, everything becomes a circular matter where managers do not trust developers, and developers do not trust managers. And everything takes more time. Something that used to take 5 minutes now takes 15 because you have to fill in all sorts of reports and tasks in your issue tracking system or whatever. And your boss notices the increase in duration, but somehow doesn’t trace it back to difficult processes and policies that are in place, so now you need to attend all kinds of meetings to explain why you don’t seem to be doing any meaningful work anymore. And you are pressured to do more work, and you feel like throwing yourself out the window or resign. Jumping from the window is probably easier because to write your resignation, you need a pen, and in order to get a pen, you must fill in a form that your boss must approve together with at least two people from finance after you previously filled in a report explaining why you need that pen for.

But trust isn’t an issue just between developers and managers. Lack of trust can cause issues inside teams also. Heck, if people don’t trust each other, you don’t even have a team. If you are familiar with Tuckman’s stages of group development[103], for a team to work together efficiently and deliver results, it needs to pass through the following stages: forming, storming, norming, and performing. Forming is when the team members get together and start to know each other. Storming is when roles within the team get defined, personalities clash, disagreement and conflict arise, but eventually, team members figure out how to resolve conflict, figure out each other’s work styles, and trust starts to develop. In the norming stage, everyone shares a goal and starts to work as a team; people now know each other and get along well. Performing is the last stage and needs no explanation; the team is working at its best.

If you don’t have trust, then your team will get stuck in the storming stage. That means they won’t find a way to work well together. You have no team basically, just a group of people trying to coordinate their work to reach some imposed goal instead of truly collaborating, resulting in more conflict and drama than actual teamwork. In his book, “The Five Dysfunctions of a Team”[104], author Patrick Lencioni states that the lack of trust is the dysfunction that underlies all other dysfunctions of a team. From there on, you have a failure to have honest discussions because of fear of conflict, which then leads to people not actually going deep into issues in order to make informed decisions, which then causes a lack of commitment and an avoidance of responsibilities for whatever decisions were taken. Everything culminates with the team losing focus and delivering unsatisfactory results.

Everything starts with trust in a team. It’s like oil in an engine that runs smoothly. If there is trust, people communicate honestly and openly, are more engaged, have constructive discussions, and team members are not punished for disagreeing. People take faster and better decisions together, and then everyone supports those decisions. They know each other’s strengths and weaknesses, they collaborate and help each other when needed to meet the team goals. People offer ideas, encourage experimentation, and ownership of the code goes to the entire team. When a conflict arises, it’s easier to manage and resolve in a constructive way because people respect each other, there is no tension in the air, the team is more adaptable to new challenges and more effective, everyone trusts the Team Lead, and there is less need of supervision. I talked about “psychological safety” in a previous chapter, the factor that Google discovered makes their teams most effective. Do you think you can build psychological safety without people trusting each other?

Without trust inside the team, people will try to hide their weaknesses, be more concerned with how everyone perceives them, and try to build a false image, instead of actually improving those weaknesses. Without trust, people don’t ask for or offer any help, and interactions are kept to the necessary minimum, with everyone just minding their own business, focusing more on their activity and not on results, or people start working in silos. When there’s a conflict, people begin to blame each other, hide or alter information to satisfy their own agendas, everyone is pulling in different directions, running away from responsibility, and saying things like “I thought you were supposed to take care of that”. Communication gets worse, meetings get more and more lengthy or get repeated because people don’t want to make decisions, while the Team Lead starts doing micromanagement, policing the team and barking orders at everyone. These cost the company time, money, and sometimes even reputation.

When trust is high, you get the opposite. Things work differently when you trust your people’s judgment and their skills, when you trust that they are not hiding any information, that they communicate clearly and transparently, that they ask for help when they are in a situation that they can’t handle by themselves, when everyone understands what is expected of them, everyone is clear on what to do, everyone knows the roles and responsibilities of the others, while the Team Lead does their job of a Team Lead by guiding people and helping them grow.

Build trust

So, is there something that can be done to improve trust? Yes, it is. Trust is one of those things on which people expect others to make the first move. As I said about bridging the gap between business and IT, that the developers must be the ones to take the first step, to learn well the business domain and interact more with business people, developers must also be the ones who have to start trusting the business side. But you have to be realistic. You can’t just start fully trusting people all of a sudden and ignore all the problems that might come from that. People in the company won’t become trustworthy overnight because that’s what you want and because you are willing to place your trust in them. If you work in a poor environment, with 300 people of whom 290 don’t even know you, people won’t change their ways because you think trust will improve the working environment or everyone’s day to day work. You can’t come to work and expect people to say, “let’s all start trusting each other” or declare Fridays as “Trust Fridays” - doesn’t work that way. But you have to start somewhere.

So start trusting people “to some degree” and then incorporate feedback from their behavior to tune that degree of trustworthiness. For example, you have to trust your CEO to have a vision and a strategy and not be asleep at the wheel, you have to trust your line manager or Team Lead, you have to trust HR to help bring in good people everywhere in the company, you have to trust other business units that they are working towards the same goals as you, you have to trust your teammates, trust that other people work to the best of their abilities. But be real. You need to find out whom you can trust, and who not. See how they act, then tune your trust level in them up or down. Too much trust in people can get you into trouble, but too little can be paralyzing to action. Remember that human relationships of any kind cannot work without trust, working relationships included. Trust is built through actions. Let their actions determine the level of trust.

I must admit this isn’t much of a solution. It’s hoping for the best. To hope that you can trust and not end up disappointed. And if you do end up disappointed, to re-evaluate the level of trust you have placed in them. It’s not a solution because you have no control over putting trust in others. But you can have an influence on others with something that you do control: “how you behave”. In your engagement with others, you must behave in such a way as to increase their confidence in you. You need to earn their trust.

They need to see that you are a serious, honest, and reliable person, that you act professionally, you are competent and skilled and constantly try to improve, you take responsibility, and own up to your mistakes, you understand the business, you are proactive and don’t wait to be told what to do, you have good intentions and your decisions are motivated by what’s right for the business, you put in all your effort, and you are capable of delivering results, you come up with solutions, or you engage management to find solutions to situations where you can’t decide on your own, etc. If they see all of these things and understand that you are there to help them, they will begin to trust you. Essentially, you have to behave in such a way that no surprises are coming from you. They want to see that they can count on you and that you are a dependable person. And if something does happen, they expect you to be on top of it.

The icing on the cake would be to honor your commitments; or put another way: to deliver on your promises. But shit happens in any software project, so promises are hard to keep no matter how reliable, honest, or capable you are. If you say you’ll do something and then you don’t keep your promise, you can very easily fall back to the issues mentioned above about setting expectations. So when you make a promise to deliver something, you need to do everything you can to keep that promise. And if, despite your best efforts, your plans go astray and the results don’t turn out as expected because of the many variables of the problem we call software development, what’s left to do is to communicate honestly and transparently. Communicate often and let everyone know what’s happening and what’s preventing you from delivering on your promises. If your results cannot be used to determine whether you are trustworthy or not, people will use the next best thing, the way you usually behave. Then, if you already established yourself as honest, competent, and trustworthy, they will work with you for finding solutions. In doing so, they might eventually reciprocate with trust.

So at the end of the day, all that’s left is for you to become trustworthy, then others, by interacting with you, to eventually show that they can also be people in whom you can place your trust. And when finally people trust each other, a lot of issues just go away. Things become more efficient, and instead of “trust taxes” you get “trust dividends”[100] that pay off in the long run - things like high performance and growth, fast and sustainable innovation, increased collaboration in an environment where people can grow and learn and are not afraid of making mistakes, better execution of the organization’s strategy, increased transparency and communication, less politics and more action, the people’s morale improves, there is a high degree of autonomy and accountability, employees and clients stay longer with the company, and much more.

Meetings and reports

Let’s get right to the chase: the workplace is full of meetings and reports, and developers hate them both. There are planning meetings, status update meetings, information-sharing meetings, design meetings, training sessions, appraisals, and the list can go on. You also have status or progress reports, audit reports, financial statements, performance appraisals reports, incident reports, compliance reports, or any kind of report your manager thinks they need. When developers talk about meetings, they use words like boring, inefficient, unproductive, unfocused, long, frustrating, unnecessary, off-topic, repetitive, “kill me now”. About reports, developers may say they are time-consuming, incorrect, incomplete, useless, “you also want fries with that?”

Interruptions

Meetings and reports are not programming and building stuff, which is what developers usually like to do. Developers build applications. Their code, their configurations, their work is what makes the application run. Managers running useless meetings and asking for a truckload of reports isn’t something that ends up as part of the physical application (if you can even refer to software as something physical). For a developer, writing code is fun, doing reports and attending meetings is not. It feels like when they were children and had to do their school homework, they didn’t really want to do it, but their parents made them. So from the developer’s point of view, participating in meetings and building reports are “interruptions” that are keeping them from doing more meaningful work, like writing code.

Developers need long periods of uninterrupted time to get things done. To be productive, developers need to be “in the zone” or be in “a state of flow”[105]. They need intense focus because programming is a mental juggling act. You have to keep a lot of stuff in your head, from the definition of the problem you are solving, to its solution and parts of the solution, to how the part you are working on relates to the other parts. You need to understand where you are in the source code and how that section of code interacts with other modules of the application. You also need to hold in your head details about the code you are actually writing, to remember variable and function names, to remember what the code written by someone else does ten lines above or below the place you are adding or changing the code, what’s in the scope of the code you are writing, where you are in the call stack, etc. It’s like a Jenga game that you are playing in your head. You need silence and intense concentration to make all the pieces fit together and standing. When the developer gets interrupted, all the pieces come crashing down. It then takes a while to get back to work and into the zone. You don’t just pick up where you left off. You have to start again and rebuild your mental layers one by one and only then continue from where you left of. Every time you are in the zone and get interrupted, you have to rebuild the layers. You have to put all that information back into your short term memory. And that affects productivity because to get into a state of flow again, people need, on average, around 20 minutes. So each interruption can potentially cost a developer 20 minutes if it makes them drop all the pieces on the floor. When you change the subject of your attention from your work, and you now focus it on the meeting you are supposed to have or on the answer to some question someone decided to bother you with, your head will fill with those details as you change the object of your attention. So that can be 20 minutes out the window just to catch up. If your manager calls a one-hour meeting with, say, five developers, and all are in the zone when that happens, then 100 minutes are potentially lost. If the meeting ends up being a complete waste of time, then you also waste five extra hours of development with the meeting itself (a one-hour meeting with five people is not actually a one-hour meeting, it’s a five-hour meeting). When the developers are done with the meeting, they might not even be able to go back into the zone, so you lose even more productivity time. If the meeting was before lunch, developers might take a mental break until after lunch because they know it’s pointless to try to come back into a state of flow only to be interrupted again by their stomach making growling noises. This is also one of the reasons why many developers with side projects work late into the night and come to work the next day at noon having bleary eyes: because at night they can work uninterrupted on their side projects while the rest of the family members are already asleep.

Studies show that a person who is interrupted takes 50 percent longer to accomplish a task. Not only that, he or she makes up to 50 percent more errors - John Medina, “Brain rules”, p.87[75]

Developers work on what Paul Graham calls “the maker’s schedule”[106], which means that in order to be able to do any meaningful work, they need to use their time in units of half a day at least. Then there’s “the manager’s schedule” where time is managed nicely in an appointment book in one-hour intervals (even 30 minutes or 15 minutes intervals make sense here). When your manager calls you into a meeting, the two schedules meet, and then the developer’s time gets split into two or more pieces that might no longer be large enough to get any considerable work done.

For someone on the maker’s schedule, having a meeting is like throwing an exception. It doesn’t merely cause you to switch from one task to another; it changes the mode in which you work - Paul Graham[107]

So whether it’s a scheduled meeting or the manager who wants to have a quick chat for five minutes, developers don’t like it, because, for them, these are interruptions that affect their work. Managers can sit through meetings and spend time building reports, ‘cause it’s their freaking job, but developers are bothered because they get disturbed (except if it’s a colleague asking to join them for a smoke, in which case they have no problem… but maybe I don’t quite understand how that works since I’m not a smoker).

Apart from being interruptions, developers hate reports and meetings also because they have learned, through experience, that many of them are useless. If you haven’t spent a lot of time building a report for your manager, then for your manager to ignore it, or if you haven’t attended any meeting where you stare at the walls and wonder why you were ever invited, don’t worry, you will. The problem with useless meetings and reports is that you don’t know why they are requested. Business people organize some meetings or ask for some reports that (they think) gives them a picture of what is happening in the project. And developers hate wasting time on what they know is useless. If the developers set up an architecture meeting to design something on a whiteboard, or spend some time to put together a network traffic report, or the number of transactions per second, they don’t have a problem with that; those are constructive and useful activities. But they have a problem with meetings and reports requested by managers because many of them don’t produce anything. They are just stuff coming out from the manager’s calendar who lives their life navigating from meeting to meeting, from report to report, everything beautifully organized in small little boxes. For developers, the product is important; for a manager, it seems that meetings and reports are more important. And if you spend weeks preparing for one hour quarterly meetings or something, where each department presents its achievements and plans and where everything has to come out perfectly, and then nobody looks over your reports or hears you out because the allocated time for the meeting expired, then you’ll end up hating them too.

And not only are a lot of them useless, but they are also repetitive. Both meetings and reports. While not much may be done regarding meetings, you could automate reports. But do we want to? Nooooo. “How much time will it take to automate that? Hmmm… too much. No. We don’t have the time”. Somehow though, we have the time to ask for the same daily or weekly reports that have the same structure, charts, and data in it and have them done manually by the manager who constantly has to bother developers to ask for stuff to put in the report. That time is not measured or the impact that it has on work to dig through and analyze lots of data, building the reports manually and wasting time on PowerPoint slide transition effects, finding the perfect project status icons, or other such nonsense.

And sometimes, developers hate meetings and reports because they mean trouble. Every time they text or email their boss with a question or ask for a decision, they reply with, “let’s have a meeting about it”. Sometimes they ask for “a meeting” just to discuss with everyone when is the best time to schedule “the meeting” (I’m not even kidding). There are so many meetings that morale starts to suffer. Unless you’re a manager, being in meetings all day long can really drain your energy. And being in lots of meetings, as a developer, it also means you’re getting no work done anymore. Then, to add insult to injury, upper management decides that:

We will continue to have meetings until we find out why no work is getting done - Unknown

So many meetings and reports are a waste - a waste of time, a waste of money, and a waste of productivity. But that’s not a problem with meetings and reports per se; the problem is with “bad” meetings and “bad” reports. Care to guess what makes them bad? People do.

Let’s start with meetings and see some examples of why they turn bad and end up sucking.

Bad meetings

One big problem with meetings is that there is too much talk. Like in the next joke:

Car accident. The victim: a sheep. Witness: a novel writer.
– Policeman: Please tell us what happened.
– Witness: You see mister policeman… when the moonlight gently embraced the wheat spikelets that were dancing under the touch of the evening breeze, and the clover was sending its sweet, sweet smell into the air, a sheep…
– Policeman: Please sir… relate briefly!
– Witness: Fine. Before the car passed, the sheep was coming out of the grass. After the car passed, the grass was coming out of the sheep.

A meeting turns bad when people stop “communicating” and start “talking” instead. When people start talking too much and saying little, the meeting now begins to take too long, people digress from the topics, some take over the conversation and have at least one opinion on every subject, some bring up other issues that have absolutely no relation with what’s currently being discussed and are irrelevant, some argue with everyone, some people get bored and start checking their phones, the situation becomes tiresome, and the entire thing gets off track then spirals out of control until the allocated time expires and everyone has to leave because someone else reserved your room for another meeting.

This happens because people usually go into meetings unprepared. Lots of meetings are set up without a clear objective or agenda, or if they have one, it’s not clearly defined. Then the meeting might not have the right people in it (too many people present or someone who’s essential for the meeting is missing). Or people did not concern themselves with the organizational aspects of the meeting (the meeting room is too big or too small, the allotted time is too long or too short, the start time of the meeting is at 08:00 or at 18:00, some information needs to be shown to everyone but there is no projector in the room and nobody bothered to print anything, and the list can go on). The meeting organizer might not control the attendees’ behaviors, so people start taking the discussion on different paths. After half an hour, at most, everyone loses interest, has trouble staying focused and start glancing at the clock. Repeat that a few times, and then it’s easy for everyone to no longer take meetings seriously. They will no longer pay attention in meetings, they will arrive late, leave early, or keep themselves busy with their phones or laptops responding to emails of no importance or even paying their home utility bills. Everyone is physically present in the meeting, but their minds are elsewhere. So essentially, they show up in the meeting just because it’s on their calendar.

Another form of being unprepared for a meeting is to reserve the meeting itself for deep thinking. I’m not saying it’s bad to think in a meeting. That would be ridiculous. Thinking is good. But if you organize a meeting to solve one problem or another, you also have to think about the problem and some possible solutions before the meeting. The meeting is then to discuss solutions, exchange ideas, and make decisions. You can’t start from the basis that “we’ll figure it out somehow during the meeting” ‘cause you won’t. You can’t just go like, “and now everyone must think of a solution. You have ten minutes starting… now”. During a meeting, you can’t always think deeply about problems and solutions. You are not just constrained by the meeting’s time limit, but it’s also because everyone is talking, expressing their opinion, and throwing ideas around. You can’t think deeply about one issue because you are engaged in the conversation. You might need to comment on what someone said, argue with someone else, or focus on someone’s idea and end up not fully exploring your own viewpoint. If you don’t think deeply about the problem from the beginning, you might have to organize yet another meeting. Chances are actually to have to organize “part 2” of the meeting you are holding. And even if you don’t organize a second meeting, what can happen is that the discussion can drag on forever, and when the meeting is nearing its, people just say, “Let’s make a decision already, we only have 3 minutes left”. Do you think you can make the best decision when you’re eyes are on the clock, and you’re thinking that the meeting is over? To give an example, when I was in high school, I had good enough grades throughout the school year, but I almost always managed to screw them up right before the year ended. Why? I was already miles away. I knew school would soon be over, the holidays were coming, and didn’t pay close attention to what I was doing. But the last bell didn’t ring yet, so I would find myself in some (unexpected) late exam that I would flunk. This can happen in meetings: the meeting is not over yet, but many people are already thinking about something else. And so, you end up making the wrong decisions. You need to think about problems and solutions before and avoid acting like “ups, there is a problem; quickly, let’s have a meeting to think about it”. “Ups, I have a paper cut; quickly, let’s have a meeting about it”. And then you see hordes of people haunting the company corridors in search of a meeting room because they urgently have to think about something. Don’t do that. You have to give people the time to think deeply about something before the meeting, not during the meeting. When it comes to thinking deeply about something, you should look at meetings like exams in school: you must study before the exam; you cannot study during the exam. And when you deeply think about a problem and spend some time to analyze it in more depth, not doing so on the run, you often discover that you don’t even have to organize a meeting anymore.

Another problem with bad meetings is not just that they are “all talk”, but that they are also “no action”. Once the meeting ends, taken decisions or actions agreed upon are then forgotten. Sometimes this situation occurs when you have meetings with virtual teams, and one person is talking over the speakers, and everyone else says “yes, yes” from time to time, and at the end, you think you’ve decided and agreed on things when in fact you haven’t. Or when you put too many things on the agenda, and you don’t have enough time to address all the topics, so you go through them as quickly as you can. Too much to decide, too fast, not enough time to focus on each, everyone writing stuff down to review the information later, then they forget and never read their notes. The problem being unsolved then shows up again and generates another meeting to figure out what happened. “Didn’t we talk about this once”? And if the second meeting is carried out in the same way, you’ll need to organize another meeting and another. At one point, everyone gets tired and bored of the same talk, again and again, without reaching any conclusion. If there are no actionable results at the end, on which you actually take action, then meetings are pointless. You might just as well meet and talk about the weather.

Then, when the meeting is over, nobody even bats an eyelid about it, unless it’s to complain about how horrible it all was. But beyond that, nobody wonders about things like, “Did I achieve what I was looking for? Did I invite the right people? Were they needed for the whole meeting? Were people engaged, or were they staring at the walls? Why? What went well? What went bad? What improvements can be made? Could we have skipped this meeting? Could I have sent an email instead of calling for a meeting? Can I replace the meeting with a report next time?” :) People don’t ask such questions. They are glad the meeting is over and they can return to their desks to try to get some work done. Organizations are always trying to improve the way they work. They’re thinking about improving all sorts of things, from employee retention to team performance, to customer satisfaction or company profits. But no one seems to pay attention to how meetings could be improved. Somehow, everyone concluded that meetings are awful, and that’s just a reality of life, one with which each employee in a corporation has to live with. Consequently, meetings never get better, and people keep making the same mistakes over and over again.

Bad reports

Let’s move to reports now. What are some of the issues with reports?

One of the issues is that managers and bosses will often ask for lots and lots of reports. If your manager has micromanagement tendencies, they will most likely also have the annoying habit of frequently demanding unnecessary and overly detailed reports. This is called “reportomania”[108]. The problem with software development is that you can’t entirely observe what’s going on unless you are one of the developers. So managers have this problem of having to monitor the work, report progress, and manage something that they don’t really have visibility into. Consequently, managers want to know lots and lots of things and have metrics on everything and everyone, just because they think it will give them a clear and complete picture over what is happening, without actually knowing what is happening. It’s their way of fooling themselves that they understand what is happening and have control over things, when in fact, they do not.

And they will ask for all sorts of shit. Since developers write code, inevitably, you will encounter some manager who will have the brilliant idea of counting lines of source code or the number of commits per day as a measure for developer productivity. I’ve seen reports that showed how many tasks stories usually had. What the heck do you even use that for? What’s the relevance? And then which value is better? Have three tasks per story, or 5? I even know of cases where the team’s budget was divided by the number of story points per sprint. Why? Or they create dashboards on top of dashboards of useless information like feature stories created versus bug created, or the oldest five bugs, and all sorts of other nonsense. They don’t know exactly what they should measure, so they add as much on the dashboards as they can, then try to make some sense out of everything. They try to collect so much information that they might just as well go to the server room and look at all the blinking lights on the network cards and try to make some sense of what’s happening from that. For them, having lots of reports seems like the right thing to do, and somehow better than asking developers or a Team Lead to explain what’s happening. It might be a professional defect, or a lack of trust of which I’ve talked in the previous chapter, or the manager afraid of looking silly, who knows?

The thing is that many such reports don’t help anyone manage anything, possibly only fooling managers into thinking that they do. And when you focus on irrelevant minutiae, you can end up ignoring some more important things that can’t be measured just as easily, like for example, if people are disengaged, or if team members don’t stand each other, or if they can’t work well together. It’s hard to put that into a brightly colored pie chart graph. So it’s easy to fall prey to trying to measure absolutely any kind of parameters just because they can be measured, and ignore other important issues because they are not so easily measurable.

And it won’t be just reports to understand how a certain thing works, but also to gain some insight into what to do next, what decisions to take, how the decisions could be supported by more data, or if a decision was taken what its impact was, how the result compares against the objective. It makes sense. That’s what business reports are for, after all. However, “reportomania” strikes again, and people go overboard with collecting data points and asking for reports. “Man, if we had such and such reports, we could then align the data with the great pyramids of Giza, Easter Island’s stone figures, Stonehenge, and Orion’s Belt and draw some amazing conclusions. That report you gave me today was really cool. Could you give it to me every single day from now on? Ahh… and the boss would like to receive it too, but they want some extra parameters. Can you add them? And Sharon from financial would also like this report, but I know from her that the way you correlated the data isn’t working for her department. Can you give her the raw data as well? And can you expose it in a CSV format? You know how accountants are… Ahh… and can you add a few more data columns in the file so that Sharon can match your reports rows with the data in their system? Thanks, buddy! I knew I could count on you…”

To add insult to injury, sometimes, a lot of reports end up not being used at all. Managers or bosses ask for all kinds of reports to try to understand things or get some insight into whatever situation; over time, however, they begin to realize which reports are useful and which reports are useless. Or the reports might have been used at some point, but with time, somehow, their utility was lost, and now nobody reads them anymore, gives you any feedback, or bothers to tell you to stop sending them. Oftentimes, I suspected that some reports were unread, so I stopped sending them just to see if anyone would complain about not receiving them. Sometimes people do complain, but most of the time, nobody says anything; sounds of crickets chirping. So, if no one complains, then stop creating and sending the report. What’s even crazier is when you know for sure that a report is not used or even read, but you still have to waste time doing it and sending it because your boss said so. For example, when you have an external client for whom you are building software, you have to bombard them with all kinds of reports, even if they explicitly stated that they are not interested in receiving some of them. But you have to send them anyways, to present an image of professionalism, or because it’s part of judicious project management procedures or some shit. And the sad part is that such reports are often built manually or if by some luck they are automatic, someone still sends them manually just so there is someone who looks over the report before being sent to the client, “‘cause we wouldn’t want to find out about our problems from the client, would we?” And not only do you know that they are useless and that the client does nothing with the information, but the reports must be in a specific format. You don’t just provide the information. Nooooooo. The report must be awesome looking, must use only one of the dozen standard templates accepted by the company, with the right font, of the right size, and of the right color, to present an image of competence and professionalism, with all sorts of data points combined in colorful pie, bar or bubble charts that eventually everything starts to look more and more like a screenshot from an Anime for ten-year-olds.

Then a big problem with reports becomes the fact that they generate effort, cost, and lost time. Things that no one usually measures! If you need to fill a time-sheet or something, you might be able to clock in on some administrative or project management tasks, but those will usually be in bulk; you won’t know how much of all the overhead of keeping things running is some particular report that nobody ever reads or reads just once every full moon. To give you an example of the kind of reports I’m talking about, at some point, I worked in a company that would keep track of bugs, what feature introduced them, in which release, and by which developer. For every bug you fixed, you had to find out who caused it. This time did not show up on the time-sheet as “looking for the guilty” but was placed on the time for solving the bug. Then bugs were attributed to the developers. It was a waste of time, and the report was only used once per year for salary increase negotiations. In short, it was stupid. There were people on the team working on complicated tasks, having the balls to tackle the most difficult parts of the application, but they had more bugs (duh!) than those working on simpler things that were reluctant to take on more heavy work. And that whole report measures how many bugs you had, compared to the time to complete tasks. The report showed, for example, that I was a little slower than my colleagues on developing features, but I had fewer bugs. Other colleagues were faster than me but had more bugs. Care to guess what the discussion was at the yearly evaluation? I was criticized for being too slow, and my colleagues for having too many bugs. The product wasn’t getting any better, nothing was done to make sure everyone works as efficiently as possible, and no measure was taken to reduce the number of bugs. Nothing. Absolutely nothing. It was just a way to piss everyone off and waste the Project Manager’s time who had to track these things instead of managing the project. The company used this data as leverage in the salary negotiations, but any potential savings with salary were never compared to the amount of time it took to look for all kinds of information about the features and the bugs, searching for the guilty, fill in the reports, everything for a half an hour discussion once per year. This wasn’t even a report related to the project at hand, it was an employee performance report, but the time and cost to build it was coming out of the project budget.

The result of spending too much time generating reports is that developers start being busy instead of being productive. They work more but with less results. And then micromanagers, to top it all off, start setting up recurrent meetings or ask for additional reports to figure out why the existing reports show a picture of poor progress on the product. It seems that not much work is getting done and that productivity has fallen to low levels. What’s happening? And when you sit with them and explain the cause, you notice on their expression that they realize where the problem lies, but they stick to their choice so they don’t end up looking foolish. They prefer to waste people’s time with useless activities than to admit that they were wrong when they asked for useless reports. Sometimes, what’s even sadder is that the reports don’t do anything besides showing that some manager is working, so they won’t give up on them, no matter what. Have you seen busy managers running around the office asking for reports, updates, and statuses, but never seem to produce anything useful? If you haven’t seen them, you will. Especially in a company with a deep hierarchy like I mentioned earlier, where some managers might ask a couple of dozen reports from their subordinates even though they just use five of them to make decisions. Reports show that they are working or that they are a competent manager.

Another problem with reports is that they may be misleading. People think reports are facts that reflect the existing situation, and only if some report looks strange, do they ask themselves, “Is this correct?” Well, sometimes the reports may not be accurate, or they might contain someone’s optimism or assumptions, or someone’s reasoning about how things should be, or a gross simplification of a complex system. For example, a project percentage complete in a report, something like 33% in a large bold font might actually be the result of some manager that goes around the office and asks whoever is still in the office and not yet out to lunch how much they think they are into the project. Or some report might present a computed average but omit to say what the dispersion of the data is, which might be even more important than the average itself. Or maybe you did some performance tests on an application, and some tests came out really bad, but only report on the tests that went well and discard the unfavorable data until you figure out where the measurements were wrong because it must surely have been a measurement error since the application couldn’t possibly work so bad, could it? It is then also possible that when building the report, either the developers or the manager, wanting to make the report look cool, without realizing it, end up build something that is misleading[109] (it’s usually a developer using a flashy 3D chart library because it’s “so freaking amazing”).

These kinds of things end up unintentionally influencing the viewer of the report. Many times, however, the data or graphs in the report are embellished, “tweaked” or presented in a better light, so that it shows a better image than it actually is, to try to influence the viewer or “help them” draw certain conclusions and not others, on purpose. So basically, it’s lying. Certain components of the report could be highlighted by using specific colors to emphasize good results and de-emphasize bad ones. Or an arrow can be placed at the end of a chart with an upward trend to “suggest” that the trend will continue to go up. Or generate a report on a one year period because the graph has an upward trend, instead of on two years, where you would see a massive decrease in the first year followed by a growth in the second year, that is actually a recovery that did not even reach the initial value before the decrease (I have seen this often on some financial institutions’ websites that show the trend of some shares or investment funds, to trick you into believing that the shares or the fund performed well all of the time). This is a lie by omission, but still a lie. So, people try to anticipate what others are going to think or say, and through the report, attempt to control these matters. The reasons for doing so intentionally are mainly two.

The first reason is one of self-interest. They try to alter people’s perceptions by presenting a more favorable view of things, a view that helps their personal goals, like getting a promotion or some bonus. Maybe the appraisals are coming soon, and they want to look more competent, to highlight their achievements, they don’t want their performance evaluation to suffer, so they embellish things, or postpone presenting bad news after the evaluation, etc. And this gets us to the second reason: they make the reports look better so that “they don’t look bad”.

A bad report is also bad news. And nobody likes bad news. We know this since we were kids in school, and we didn’t want to show our report card to our parents when we received bad grades. Bad news is also a surprise, especially if all the previous reports were good. And your boss doesn’t like surprises, remember? And just like getting an estimate they don’t agree with, when they get bad news, bosses react in a similar matter: like a raging volcano. Bosses seem to be allergic to bad news. They go into anaphylactic shock or something, their pulse increases, their head gets swollen, their face turns red. If you’ve ever had a boss with anger management issues, you already know how they can react when presented with a report they don’t like. So people try to soften the blow. Besides embellishing the report, or present things in a more optimistic light, they can use positive wording and avoid using words that sound like a problem. “We don’t have a problem; we have a situation”, or “We’re not in trouble; we’re facing some challenges”. Or when they present bad news, people could pack them between two good news to minimize the gravity of the situation; it’s better when bad news comes with a side dish of good news instead of being served alone. People try to change the nature of the problems or use words that conceal reality so they don’t have to deal with the boss’ reaction, or with the consequences of that. And the consequences might not be just the boss getting involved in the project in great detail, and to request more frequent reports, to do micromanagement, or become controlling, but it can also mean other consequences for the employee.

They don’t want to show a report that reflects the cold hard truth because they know that when presenting bad news, “the messenger gets shot”. Bosses are “shoot first, ask questions later”, or basically, “blame first, find out the whole story later” (if at all). You quickly learn this. And because instead of calmly analyzing a situation, bosses prefer to scream, yell, and threaten, people end up sugarcoating the negative news they have to communicate. They try to build a cheerful image (not to say illusion) around the report, to avoid threatening situations. It’s not much different from how parents are lying to their children about the existence of Santa Claus, so they don’t ruin the magic of Christmas and avoid disappointing the children, making them upset, cry, or throw tantrums. Then heaven forbid if they get something else than the presents they really wanted.

And it’s not just that they don’t want their boss to get upset, or have some seizure in the office, “because look at how that vein is bulging in their forehead and they started foaming at the mouth”, but also because employees fear career consequences if the report looks bad. Losing a promotion, being fired, being transferred to the North Pole company subsidiary… those kinds of consequences. So they massage the bad news a little bit to soften the blows. If the report looks bad, their boss might blame them for that (sometimes being blamed for something that they didn’t do or had no control over), or it might seem like a failure of some sort, that things aren’t going according to plan or some shit. A bad report makes you look bad, or the team, or the department or whatever. And just like nobody wants to hear bad news, nobody wants to look bad. So in order to avoid adverse consequences, or to diminish their effects, people try to dupe their boss. And this happens to a greater extent in a company where trust is lacking. If people refuse to understand that bad things can always happen, that you cannot only have good reports, and they don’t appreciate when correct information is communicated honestly and in a transparent manner, but instead choose to make threats and behave domineering, then people will make efforts to hide things or show them in a better light, to keep only good appearances.

But all this creates a false image of reality, a “perverted” representation of what is actually happening. And all of the time, people believed things are going well when, in fact, they might be slowly falling apart. And when the true situation comes to light (which always happens eventually), as I mentioned in a previous chapter about communication, it may be too late to take reasonable decisions, and bosses might desperately try to do damage control (react in the moment, make poor choices because of anger, fear, or lack of time and options). Bad decisions can also be taken before the true status of things surfaces because, think about it: a misleading report is a way of choosing what your boss or client sees, which means that any decisions they make, they make based on distorted information and may result in flawed outcomes.

And even if they are not misleading or embellished, another problem that may develop is for the report to become more important than the activity it reports on, sometimes with a negative impact on the activity itself, similar to a student who focuses more on getting a good grade and less on what they actually learn and retain from the study material. The knowledge they get and the skills they might build with help from what they learn become less important than the exam grade itself. Sometimes the student may even completely neglect the learning if they hope they can cheat during the exam. Something similar can happen inside a company too, in many places throughout the organization. For example, does each department of your company have imposed metrics to measure their work? Have you wondered what the main consideration of each department is? Is it to look good in those metrics, or is it to meet the company’s objectives as a whole? Did you notice in your client support reports that a specific complaint occurs in large proportions each month? Do you actually fix the cause of the complaint, or do you start recording that complaint under a different topic, so the reports don’t look so bad? “The [others/miscellaneous] section looks underrepresented; let’s stick some of those complains in there”. Or does your help desk department actually solve issues for your employees, or are your tickets closed in your face just because their SLA reports last month looked bad and they need to improve this month… or else? The service sucks, but the reports might look good. At least for a month, because then another metric will catch everyone’s attention, the number of reopened tickets. Does your call center call customers to offer them deals? Is the volume of outbound calls measured? How many calls does each client officer make? Good. Let’s increase those numbers. But the company has only a limited number of customers, how can the call center increase the number of outbound calls? They call each client several times, right? You improve the metric value, but you annoy your clients who might go to your competition for the sole reason that the competition does not call them two times a day and during the weekends. Do you have reports with the number of lines of code per function? Did you read somewhere that functions should be small and that 100 lines of code should be the maximum allowed? Do you also notice that many functions are larger than that, so you ask developers to refactor the code and clean things up? How will they solve the situation? You might be surprised to find out (and I’ve seen this happen) that any function X larger than 100 lines of code, the developer will break in the middle, without any isolation of responsibilities whatsoever, in functions X_1 and X_2, and then X will have only two lines of code, first invoking X_1 and then X_2. Simple. Problem solved. In all these situations, the entire purpose becomes improving the report and not the activity that the report reflects. Things look good on paper, but in reality, they are not. And if things seem to get better and look so great, some begin to think, “what else could be improved? Let’s ask for even more reports to find out what other situations need our attention. Let’s have some meetings to decide what exactly we need”. And everything starts all over again.

So how do you improve meetings and reports?

Better reports

With reports, you start by looking to see if you actually need them for something. Think well. It may seem at first glance that you need the report, but that might not be the case. For instance, if you care about quality, you might want to fix bugs before writing new features. It’s a good strategy to have, so you might want a report to show you how long bugs remain opened. But is this really relevant? You might have a few bugs reported, but your team can’t work on all of them right now, so some will have to wait. You are working on your bugs and are concerned with quality, but some old bugs might show up in a report repeatedly, and it seems no one is doing anything about them. If it’s a minor bug and you have other priorities, time will just accumulate for that bug while you work on critical defects or maybe even some new features that have a higher priority. If, after two months, someone suddenly shouts, “Seriously? Doesn’t anyone care about fixing that bug?”, how will you react? You will agree with that statement, or will you say that the report doesn’t reflect the whole situation and offers no visibility whatsoever in the current priorities? If you do a proper prioritization, it doesn’t even matter for how long that bug remains open. It will be solved when it’s important to be solved. On the other hand, you may want to have a report that tells you how many “critical” bugs you have or have had so far. Bugs are inevitable, but a lot of critical defects might be a sign that the developers are sloppy or maybe that the requirements were lacking. Building software isn’t black or white, or ones and zeros. So think well what information you want to know, what questions you want answered, and then see what reports can help you with that. Many reports are sometimes demanded because of a knee jerk reaction (“we always did it like that on all the projects, that’s how I learned in management school, the project is growing so we need a dashboard full of graphs and gadgets to have an overview of the work”, etc.). So ask yourself why you need a report and what will happen if you don’t have it.

Eliminate any unnecessary reports and keep only those that help you to make decisions or see their implications, to improve the business or the product, or the value that the software brings, to monitor important things or something that helps you achieve your goals. Reports that keep people informed without organizing a meeting with ten participants periodically are also useful. Don’t measure something just because it can be measured. Measure only what matters. And if you do keep a report, it would really be nice if you could have that report generated automatically for you by your issue tracking system or some other tools you use at work. It’s not always possible to automate things, but if you can automate the generation and submission of a report, then you no longer have to waste time building it by hand. If instead you have no choice and have to manually build reports, do keep in mind that it will consume time from the actual work. So try to find the most efficient way to generate reports to minimize wasted time and interruptions for other team members.

Then, keep in mind who the target audience for the report is. Is it for developers to monitor stuff, for you as a manager to track status and plan things, for your boss to make decisions? How you build the report varies depending on who the intended recipients are. How brief or verbose the report is again dependent on who is looking at the information. For example, a manager might want an extensive report on all feature statuses, with blockages, dependencies, etc., but their boss may want an overview with the main ideas and consolidated data to make quick decisions. The manager might go through the list of features and make sense of each since they know what is behind each status, but the manager might choose to show their boss something simplified, an overall status. Maybe instead of an icon with a shining sun (i.e., all good, no issues), they will show them a sun with a cloud (i.e., there are certain issues) - detailed report for some, simplified for others. The higher you go up the company hierarchy, the more the details narrow. Bosses don’t have time to rummage through small pieces of information; you have to do that for them. And here, we come back to what I said above about misleading reports. What if, by reducing the details, the information becomes biased or too diluted? A report should be clear, to the point, and informative, but it’s also a synthesis of more extensive items. What if it synthesizes too much? As an example of what I mean, consider characterizing someone as “intelligent”. What about the rest of their traits? Are they qualities? Defects? If you want to describe them fully, how many other words would you use besides “intelligent”? 10? 100? 1000? How many words are too few, and how many are too much? It’s the same with reports. When do you know how concise the report must be to capture the essence of the entire picture without losing anything, and how many details are too many and already redundant?

There is no easy way to answer this. It depends primarily on communication. You can start with more details, with more explanations, the report to be a little more verbose, to include in it all the information you have analyzed, and alongside those details to also include the summary of this information. Then see how brief you can be when presenting the report and how much you can give up when communicating things, so the message remains unaltered. Or see how far you need to go into details to support the core idea you want to convey.

So it’s a process of trial and error. There will be questions, concerns, discussions until you find the ideal proportion of details and summaries. Consider the feedback you receive from others to improve the report, but be pragmatic. The point is to try to remove from the details, not add to them. As someone once said:

Perfection is achieved, not when there is nothing more to add, but when there is nothing left to take away - Antoine de Saint-Exupéry[116]

The best reports are those that offer a brief summary or overview, followed by some important ideas and details, and a recommendation with the best course of action. Your boss may follow your advice or take another decision, but regardless, the discussion that emerges from this if things are not clear enough will show you if the report gives your boss enough information or if something is missing. With time you learn what’s needed and what’s not, and your report improves.

Then, the last and best thing to do to improve reports is to stick to the facts. Don’t lie, don’t withhold information, don’t exaggerate or mislead. Don’t put lipstick on the pig or give only positive news without also mentioning the negative ones. Just tell it as it is. Do you really think that everything is always going to go without a hitch and that nothing bad will ever happen? There is no such thing. Things can go south. And when they do, they will have to be communicated promptly, transparently, and correctly, so that bosses or clients can make the right decisions with accurate information. I mentioned above about the messenger of bad news getting shot. That’s the reality. You deal with people, so you have to deal with what comes from that too. But telling the truth, even when it is difficult, is the best approach because it builds trust. If they catch you with a lie, people will start questioning your motives, and now, instead of building trust, you instead lose trust and get all the consequences that come bundled with that.

Now, you can have a gazillion (useful, of course) reports. But in a company, reports are just one form of communication. As already mentioned, according to Harvard Business Review[21], “Face-to-face communication contact is the broadest bandwidth communication you can have in professional life”. And this means meetings. We’ve seen some of the issues with meetings, so what can be done to improve them?

Better meetings

Improving meetings is a bit more difficult than improving reports because it involves people interacting with each other directly. And in any meeting where important things get discussed, and a resolution must be reached, a meeting where people participate actively and get involved, there will, of course, be conflicting discussions and disagreements. This is normal. There won’t always be complete agreement when it comes to deciding on things and making decisions. Disagreements and conflicts make meetings harder to improve, but at the same time, disagreements and conflicts can be very constructive. Some problems can only be solved by having some tough conversations. You want people to challenge each other’s ideas, to look at things differently, everyone to express their opinions and viewpoints, to discuss different action paths, to consider alternatives, to find pros and cons for various solutions.
