That’s how the best solution emerges, a solution that, in most cases, is a combination of all the ideas everyone had. This is what you want in a meeting, to get people involved, for them to be engaged, and to debate issues until the best solution is found.

None of us is as smart as all of us - Kenneth H. Blanchard[117]

But in order to have meetings like this, you first need trust. That’s because the disagreements from a meeting can go into the weeds and turn into unconstructive conflicts. In contradictory discussions, things can sneak in that are not related to the facts that are being discussed: human stuff like irrationality, self-identity, emotions, insecurities, personality clashes, different values, and biases. It’s easy to end up focusing on how a message is transmitted, for example, instead of on the actual message. Or people might take things personally, or strongly express their opinions (because people want to be right, which by definition makes the others’ opinions wrong). Mix disagreement with all of these things, and you can easily end up with a bad conflict on your hands, where people perceive the situation as threatening, then get defensive and/or aggressive. But even though uncomfortable for everyone, conflict might not be an issue if your team knows how to handle it. If they trust and respect each other, they can deal with conflict, be it in a meeting or otherwise. People need to have the courage to have tough, honest conversations. They need to know they can take risks or be vulnerable.

I’ve already talked about trust, team “storming”, “psychological safety”, and how to resolve conflicts in a previous chapter. As I mentioned, if people don’t trust and respect each other, everyone becomes worried that they might be judged or criticized if they speak their mind, they will be reserved in expressing their opinions and ideas, so you might lose essential aspects of the issue you are trying to solve. People avoid or postpone making tough decisions, avoid taking risks, and withhold information instead of sharing it with others. Everyone becomes less active; you are making less and less progress and more and more meetings because people don’t feel secure enough to say what they really think, to generate the tough, honest, constructive conversations everyone needs to be having. You’ve probably been in meetings like these with bosses you dislike. There is tension in the air, you try to guess what your boss might say, or think about the consequences if you open your mouth and say something wrong, people might be afraid to tell the truth if the truth is unpopular, etc. Do you think these kinds of meetings are constructive? Do you want all of your meetings to be like that?

Trust is a catalyst for having good meetings. Much of what makes a meeting good is about how the participants interact with each other. Without trust, you have no collaboration during the meeting or after. For example, even if you make some decisions during the meeting, some might resent those decisions and then not support or even go against the actions needed to make those decisions happen. Refer to the previous chapter and do your best to build trust with the people you work with.

Then, if people gather in a meeting, you’d better have a reason for it. Meetings are needed for people to coordinate, so they all work towards the same goals. You could even say meetings are “unavoidable”. But that doesn’t mean you walk through the company, minding your own business, and all of a sudden you find yourself in a meeting. Meetings must have a purpose. Before organizing a meeting, ask yourself, “is it really necessary”? Can’t you have it otherwise? What do you want to achieve and can’t do it without a meeting? What’s the goal or the expected outcome? Just like reports, meetings have a hidden cost. People have to stop what they’re doing and go to the meeting. The more people in the meeting, the more time consumed. For developers, you’ve also seen this means interrupting their “flow”, so the meeting will cost them an indeterminate amount of time that goes beyond the meeting itself while they try to get back “in the zone”. If the meeting was needed, then that’s the price to pay. But if it could have been avoided, then that’s just waste. That’s why many people think meetings are a waste of time, because without clearly thinking about the need for the meeting and the reason for it, they actually waste everyone’s time. Many things can be solved without having to organize a meeting: you can talk to someone when you go out to lunch, you can talk to someone when they take a break, you can send an email, ask on chat, or instead of dragging the whole team in a meeting see if maybe the Team Lead can help, etc.

Have you ever wondered how much time you spend on useless meetings? I have. Whether or not I had to fill in a time-sheet at the companies I worked for, I always tracked my work in a spreadsheet file. What I did, how much each activity took, and if it was productive or not. That helped me later to remember things, see how much time various things took, or where I could improve things. And I also had an answer at the end of those weeks when I felt I didn’t accomplish much, and I couldn’t help myself but ask, “where the heck did all of this week go?” If you have too many meetings, then you might have a problem. And most of the time, the problem is not that you have too many meetings, but instead, there will be an underlying problem for which you need to have so many meetings: like people’s fear of taking decisions (so they postpone them for a later meeting, and a later one), you might have a disorganized team, unclear goals, or micromanaging bosses who always ask for status meetings, just to give a few examples.

If you do have a good reason to organize a meeting, make sure you also have an agenda. It reminds you why you have the meeting while the meeting is unfolding and tells all the participants what the focus of the discussions should be. I have often received meeting requests that only contained a time, a place, and a confusing subject. So who knows what’s going on! The meeting might be important, some decisions might be taken there that might later affect you, your input might be needed. So you might not be able to decline or ignore it. Instead, you have to ask the organizer for more details, or if it’s your boss sending you the invite, you might not even ask but just show up at the meeting unprepared and with no idea what everything is all about. People accept these things because they happen often and they already got used to the situation. But that doesn’t also mean it’s normal. Each meeting invite should be sent with an agenda. What are the meeting objectives? What topics will be discussed? Who will participate, and why? Who will be leading the discussion for each of the topics of the meeting? Is there some material to prepare for the meeting? If you enter the meeting without an agenda, you risk going around in circles, having superficial discussions or debating unimportant things while everyone figures out what the meeting is about. Knowing the agenda of the meeting sets clear expectations and gives everyone time to prepare. People can compose questions or note important things to ask about; they can think things through more deeply and not without careful consideration during the meeting because they didn’t know or did not expect to discuss one topic or another.

Then, during the meeting, as a meeting organizer, you have to be on top of things. Things can quickly degenerate and go into the weeds instead of being focused on what’s important. So you have to bring things back on track. Follow the meeting’s agenda. And make it about the purpose of the meeting, not about the meeting duration. By that, I mean, it is not crucial that the meeting ends at the right time; it is essential to solve what needs solving. People keep their eyes on the clock during the meeting, quickly go over all the topics to make sure all are addressed in the remaining time, or the organizer gives all participants equal time slots to express their opinion. You can’t tell participants things like “You have two minutes to present your opinion to everyone… in 3, 2, 1… Go!”. It’s ridiculous. A meeting is not like in school, where everyone is waiting for their turn to show their homework or be brought in front of the class for an oral assessment. One thing I used to do for meetings where hard decisions had to be made, and I suspected the discussion might drag on, was to book the meeting room for, say, 1h 30min but to send the meeting invite for 1h. That way, I knew that if we exceeded the allocated time, we still had some buffer before someone arrived to let us know that they have booked the room and kick us out. So be careful not to be too rigid with certain aspects of the organization of the meeting and neglect why everyone is meeting in the first place. Things will have a natural way of settling during the meeting; you just have to make sure people discuss and stay focused on what’s important. You cannot drop a topic and move on to the next point because you risk running out of time. Start with the most important items first in case you still can’t make the time. If people get up and leave because the time expired without discussing everything you had on the agenda, then just organize another meeting. It’s not a waste if everyone was focused and things were kept as efficient as possible; it just means you needed more time than expected.

Then, a major problem with meetings is that once they end, they are forgotten. There is also the risk that five people leaving the meeting will develop five different opinions about what was discussed and agreed upon. To avoid this happening, it’s good to have a meeting minute. But let’s be honest, nobody reads the meeting minutes. It’s just a summary of the meeting, decisions, and actions taken. People have already been at the meeting, so they pay no further attention to the minute. Until something unexpected happens, of course, then they read the minute and say, “that’s not what I recall”, or “you misunderstood”. And that’s precisely why you need a meeting minute. To make sure that everyone understood the same thing and that everyone is aware of the next actions to be taken by each and every one. Because you can’t force people to read the minute after the meeting ended and make sure that everyone is on the same page, you will have to do the minute while the meeting is still underway. Put it on the projector while you are writing it. Mention who attended the meeting, what was discussed, what was decided, what actions to follow, and to whom they were assigned. Everyone looks at what you write, and they can’t say afterward that they didn’t know or that they misunderstood, because what you write there are everyone’s conclusions and decisions, and everyone can comment or point out things. It’s not hard to write, especially if you had a meeting agenda. Simply add the conclusions to each topic. If important topics show up during the discussion but are not for the purpose of this meeting, you can add action items for what you will do with them (organize a meeting later, Jake will take care of it, and so on) without wasting time discussing them. On top of that, the meeting minute is a way to transform “attendees” into “participants”. Have you noticed that in Outlook or other personal organizer software, when you set up a meeting, you have to add the “attendees”? Why not the “participants”? Participants do more than attend a meeting; they actually get involved in the meeting and spend less time checking their phone or looking at the clock.

The last thing to do to improve meetings is to incorporate a feedback loop; try to learn from each meeting, and use the information to improve the next ones. You don’t need to send people feedback forms to fill after the meeting or anything like that; just think about how the meeting went. Ask yourself what went well and what went poorly and what you can do to improve things. Did you have problems with the projector at the beginning of the meeting? Maybe next time you can arrive 5 minutes earlier to set everything up. Some of the participants had passion while the rest had mobile phones? Maybe don’t allow phones to be kept on the table during the meeting. Short meetings tend to take longer than necessary because people talk too much? Maybe have the meeting standing up. Were all the people present necessary for the meeting or not? You didn’t manage to go through all the items on the agenda? Were there too many items, or was the time allocated for the meeting too short? Maybe people diverged from the main topics, and some irrelevant discussions wasted some of the time? As the meeting organizer, did you control the discussion or let it go into the weeds? Did all participants arrive on time? If you always start on time and don’t wait for latecomers, do they arrive on time next time or not? Did all participants had equal opportunities to participate, or did someone hijack the discussion? Were some people disrespectful in some way? Did you deal with them? How will you deal with them next time? Did you book a room but you are waiting on someone else to finish with their own meeting while they are on the phone with a client and they implore you to give them a few extra minutes, and meanwhile you and the other participants in your meeting waste your time waiting on the company’s hallways? Could you have some of the meetings in the team’s office next time? And most importantly, when the meeting is over, ask yourself if it was worth it or not. Could you have carried on with your work with or without that meeting? Did it change some outcomes? Was something decided? Was something clarified? Do you have a new direction or a new target to follow? Did you solve what needed to be solved, or did the time run out? Did the meeting have a conclusion (other than deciding you need to hold another meeting)?

Similar to other things in the workplace (like conducting a job interview, carrying out performance reviews, managing others, building reports, etc.), people don’t receive training on how to hold meetings, and there are no clearly defined rules on how meetings should unfold. You are just expected to know how it’s done. So you will get some of them right and mess up some others. So you need to see what you can improve so that the following meetings are useful, not an ordeal from which everyone runs away when the time runs out like cockroaches at midnight when you turn on the light in the kitchen.

Necessary

Many say that meetings and reports are toxic and should be banned. False! The way they happen is toxic, and that should be improved. You can’t run a company or project without meetings and reports. It’s just not possible.

Reports are there so you can make data-driven decisions. A report should answer a question, solve a problem, or address an issue within the business. They are like symbols and indicators on a car’s dashboard (e.g., seat belt indicator, oil pressure warning, fuel indicator, engine temperature warning light), to see what is happening at any moment and to be able to take decisions. Is it safe to drive and continue with your trip? Do you need to stop at a gas station? Do you need to find a car service? Reports show you what is happening. To give one other analogy, they are also like medical tests (e.g., blood tests, x-rays, biopsies). They provide a picture of your state of health. Maybe you are feeling good, but in fact, some test shows that you will become ill soon or develop some other condition. In case something bad happened, the tests also tell you if you are on the path to recovery and how much longer until you are well again. Maybe you’re not a mechanic or a doctor, but when the dashboard lights or medical tests show you some abnormal measures, you can decide how to respond or what to do next. Reports are for communicating information that can be acted upon. They are underlying arguments for decision making. Lack of information can lead to irrecoverable losses or risky situations that are difficult to control. Without reports, it’s like flying blind.

And once you have the reports, you can have a meeting. In meetings, people share information, debate issues, look for the best ideas, decide on targets and desired outcomes, make decisions, build plans, set priorities. If you have a group of people working on something, you can’t really give up on meetings. A face-to-face, 10-minute long meeting might replace a long email or a long report. If you are doing performance reviews, you can’t just fill in a report and call it a day; you need to sit down with your people and have honest conversations, and that’s also a meeting.

When done properly, meetings and reports are very useful; people focus on what’s important and collaborate to get the benefits from both. Let me say it again: meetings and reports are useful. It’s people that are the problem. Any interaction between people is complex, no matter if it takes place face-to-face where emotions and insecurities can crop up, or if it’s by employing a report where you can easily lose the information you want to communicate or the message can get distorted. The path to better reports and meetings will be messy, but it’s important to get better at them.

Bad bosses

When talking about their boss, people usually think of their immediate supervisor. Because they have some control and authority over people’s work, everyone calls them “the boss”. The boss can also have a boss who has a boss, and so on. But this is not the definition of boss I’m using throughout this book. The bosses I’m referring to are not just the people higher in the company hierarchy, like a team lead, or a manager, or a “director of” something, “vice president” of something else, “head of” whatever, or other top-level executives with a fancy job title that sounds impressive and grants them authority over the people in the hierarchical tree underneath them. By boss, I’m referring to “whoever calls the shots” on the software project you are working on, or the software product you are building. This person might or might not be someone fitting the hierarchical structure directly above you. For example, the head of IT has certain authority and responsibility for all the developers in their department, keeping the lights on and whatnot, and even for making some decision in regards to the projects underway inside the department, but they can’t always call the shots on the projects themselves in regards with the goals of the project, the features that are needed, the budget, etc. So they do not have full autonomy and authority over a project. The boss I’m referring to is a business person, maybe a program manager, product lead, client representative, or in a smaller company, the CEO, or even the company’s owner. It’s the person that “owns the project”. You might think of your Project Manager or Team Lead as your boss, but they are not “the boss”, because although they might be in charge of the team or the project, they don’t actually own it or call the shots on it.

Of course, the kind of boss I’ll be referring to in this chapter can have many things in common with other types of bosses people had to deal with. Any company can have bad bosses; it’s not something specific to the software development industry. The deeper the hierarchy in a company and the higher the number of managers, the more chances to find more self-important bosses with fancy job titles, who treat everyone like their own pawns (often in an arrogant or domineering manner) and are either representatives of the Peter Principle[118] (successful employees are promoted until their skills are no longer enough to get them the next promotion; so they rise to “their level of incompetence” and stop there) or of the Dunning-Kruger effect[12] (incompetent people tend to overestimate their level of knowledge or skills). You might also find control freaks or bigots that try to impose their views on everyone who disagrees with them. Bosses that will try to manage things through intimidation or by spreading fear (thinking that all problems can be solved if they just yell loud enough at everyone). Or impulsive, arrogant bastards that have no remorse, lie how they breathe, blame others, and don’t take responsibility for their actions but take the credit if things turn out great. Bosses who don’t care about the greater good or doing the right thing, but only about making themselves look good. Or those who request an emergency meeting on Sunday night just because they can, or bullies that get away with almost anything because they are the CEO’s nephew, their childhood friend, or whatever. Your boss might even be a psychopath. It seems that the chance of encountering a psychopath in a managerial position is four times greater than finding one in the general population[119]. Isn’t that nice?

Stumbling on a bad boss like this is just one of the realities of working in a company - any company. This is why I won’t talk much about some of these traits unless they apply in the context of developing software. So I’ll focus mostly on those aspects that make developers’ lives difficult and are likely to cause damage in a software project.

Technical (in)competency

The number one issue with a bad boss, the thing that will annoy developers the most, is that they might be completely clueless when it comes to software development.

Technology is dominated by two types of people: those who understand what they do not manage and those who manage what they do not understand - Putt’s Law[120]

Now, don’t get me wrong, I’m not saying that all bosses are clueless. An executive is usually far away from where the action is, and the further you are from things, the fewer details you can observe, you can’t watch the daily progress of things, you have many other things on your mind and many other responsibilities, and it’s normal not to know everything that happens in a project (or in more than one). But that doesn’t make one clueless, just less informed. That’s why you need transparent communication. That’s why there are meetings and reports so that your boss has enough information to understand the situation from a distance and make good decisions. Such bosses know about the things I mentioned in the previous chapters: why code is hard to write, why IT projects are difficult to get right and sometimes fail, they know about the Business-IT divide and its causes and effects, they have a good understanding about what it means to be a developer and how software is built, and so on. But there are certain bosses, and you will inevitably encounter one of this sort at some point in time, that is plain and utterly clueless about how software is built. Maybe the boss has other talents or other management skills that are valuable to the company, but, unfortunately, those skills don’t match what they need to be the owner of a software project or product. I’m not saying the boss has to be a developer or something like that, a boss needs to manage things, not do the work (and as I said before, they are a business person, so wouldn’t have any way of actually doing that) but if the boss calls the shots, then they need to understand how software gets built.

And it wouldn’t necessarily be a problem that they are ignorant about software development if you could get along with them, reason with them, explain them stuff, and convince them of things. But unfortunately, being technically clueless often comes bundled with another problem this type of boss has: that they consider themselves smarter than everyone else in their subordination and that they are extremely convinced that they know what they are doing. Combine these two things together and when problems occur (and inevitably they do) or important decisions must be made, it’s very easy for the boss to deny reality, dismiss the gravity of the situation and make bad decisions against the advice of others. They are clueless and don’t understand things, but have firm opinions of their own and are usually very stubborn in their decisions. They think the only correct opinions are their own. Because of that, you can’t reason with them. Whatever information you offer them, whatever explanations and arguments you come up with, nothing goes ​through into their thick skulls. The boss made a decision; any further discussion is superfluous. Your knowledge, your experience, nothing matters. They know best. They’ve spoken, you must do it. If, by any chance, this boss had some contact with programming in school or someplace before, many eons ago, you also get the speech of “I still know a thing or two. At some point, I was also a programmer. Back in my days, this is how we did things, and it worked better than what you’re suggesting”. Unfortunately, the expression “back in my days” indicates that time is gone, it is no more, things are different now. But they don’t realize that.

These persons are inflexible and will stubbornly refuse to change their minds. Only what they say matters, not your opinions. In fact, when this kind of boss wants your opinion, they will give it to you. As a developer, it’s very frustrating to deal with such a person because they don’t deal with facts and don’t listen to arguments; you can’t argue your point of view before them, nothing. This is either because they don’t understand what you’re saying, or because they think they are smarter than you and (implicitly) always know better. Whatever they decide, you have to do because they are the ones with authority over the project, and maybe not just the project but over your pay raises and promotions or even your employment within the company. They have power over you, but you certainly do not have over them. So you have to do what they say and go to them for decisions. When you have such a boss, all you can do is hope that there won’t be too many occasions when you have to deal with them to make decisions, or that they like the way you do things and have nothing else to add. Basically, hoping for as few interactions as possible with them.

But if you have to often interact with them or have them decide on many things, then you are in trouble. And unfortunately, they like to interact (unidirectionally, however) and come up with all sorts of ideas and requests. A “looooooot” of ideas and requests. You see, because they don’t understand stuff, anything they don’t understand in their mind “must be easy to do” and without bad consequences or any ill effects on the work. So they ask for stuff. And ask. And ask. And ask. And it’s not necessarily a problem that they ask, if only they would ask for things that add value, are important, or at least make some sense. But most demands are unfortunately caused by the “shiny object syndrome”[121]. This is when people get distracted by too many ideas or the latest trends or fads and go off in many directions, spreading their efforts too thin (in this case, the efforts of their team), and eventually end up completing nothing. Instead of focusing on the goals and what is important, people get distracted by shiny things. You constantly start working on new things, and there is enough “work in progress” for everyone, but nothing usually gets finished. Even if you do finish something, your boss doesn’t like it and wants you to do it all over again or make some major changes… fast. And every time they have a new idea, they want it implemented immediately. The end result is like that proverb: “grasp all, lose all”.

This behavior doesn’t just show a lack of vision and direction from your boss, but also generates a lot of waste, rework, and chaos, with imposed (approaching) deadlines. Then people work hard to hit the unrealistic target, a target that immediately gets moved, and now everyone must run after something else… “I want this; I want it now… ah… and I also want what I asked for before, with no delays. Except I don’t want them as I said originally, I want them with some changes. It’s easy to do, right?” And all of this doesn’t just cause problems for the software but has a negative impact on the team as well. There is confusion because people don’t understand why so many changes and direction veer offs, or why the boss is doing all of this (and no, it’s not because the boss has more information about the project, the business, or the organization). The team loses its sense of purpose and direction, with people in the team getting frustrated. The team morale suffers, and so does their productivity. Any employee would expect their boss to be helpful for the company and for the employees, not to cause chaos every single day. People start getting angry. “I worked on this feature for five days, and now that I’m done with it, the boss says they want something else”. And they start questioning “the why” of all of this, and they can only conclude that the boss is incompetent and doesn’t have the slightest clue of what they are doing.

But of course, the boss’s explanation is different. They are just “opportunity-driven”. Normally, that means there is an unexploited business opportunity in the market that must immediately be taken advantage of, before the competition does, or before the window of opportunity passes. It’s a time-sensitive situation for which no effort should be spared in order to take advantage of it and collect the potential gains. All the shifting priorities, the unclear direction, waste, and chaos caused by running after all the nonsense, is in your boss’ vocabulary cataloged as “flexibility”. And in order to be flexible, to be able to pursue opportunities, you have to be nimble, to move fast. But you’re not really nimble. Everything is just a fire drill. Fixing that bug is urgent, that demo for the client is urgent, all the features that the competition has added in their latest release are urgent to add on your product also, such and such must be ready by X date, otherwise the sky falls over. If your boss explains all the chaos by “we are opportunity-driven”, run. Seriously, run! It means “I have no idea where we are at, I vaguely remember where we have been, I have no plans whatsoever for where we are going, I simply jump on everything we bump into like a pack of hungry wolves on a dizzy squirrel fallen from a tree that in my delusional imagination I see like a fat and juicy deer”. That’s because many times, these “opportunities” are not identified by a business intelligence analysis or big data (‘cause your boss doesn’t understand those either) but are simply your boss’ gut feeling or them sticking their finger in their mouth then lifting it in the air. Everything done in the name of short term profits, which often sacrifices the long term sustainable result, and also ruins the team in the process.

And with all of these nasty things they do, without thinking about the consequences or having other objectives beyond the daily or the weekly whim, it’s still the boss that’s dissatisfied. “I’m disappointed that the application wasn’t written in Scala. Our marketing department could have then made our product sound more valuable. Why can’t you build that feature just like how our competitors have it on their website? I told you this morning to make a change in the user interface, and it’s still not done; I can’t for the life of me understand why it takes you so much time to do it. Work harder! Nobody goes home until the things I requested this morning are done”. This is another problem with clueless bosses. Because they don’t understand jack shit, they don’t understand why something takes a few minutes while something else takes five days. For them, developing software is like going to a restaurant. Any food they order from the menu will be served at the table in a few minutes. So why isn’t it the same with tasks and features in software? The only conclusion they reach is that the developers are lazy, want to play with technologies, or whatever, instead of working on their tasks. “That five days thing would probably take a developer a few minutes to do, or an hour tops, if only they were actually working”. And so they start putting pressure on people. They start micromanaging and give people ridiculous deadlines. “I gave you five bugs this morning. Before I leave home at 17:00, I want you to show me all the fixes you did”. The organizational aspects of the team are also not an impediment for them. Is there a Team Lead or Project Manager in charge? Doesn’t matter. The boss goes directly to developers and testers and asks them to do X or Y even if everyone was working on something else. If you have planning meetings for everyone to organize their work, you can kiss them goodbye. You will see every day on what you will work, depending on the mood of the boss. And bosses like that also put more and more work on someone but expect the results to be of good quality and on time. If you explain to them that if you have a donkey and you load it with a bunch of sacks, the donkey reaches a point where it can no longer carry those sacks and gets crushed under their weight, then the boss understands. But if you load a person with too much work, they no longer see that there is a point where things fail. The concept of sacks is simple to understand, but how software gets built, not so much. Now it’s the damn donkey that is a sloth. So let’s threaten it and whip it, and then you’ll see how well the donkey carries the load. It’s gonna take flight. They don’t realize that developers perform worse when pressured, when they’re burnt out, have to do context switching constantly, and their priorities keep changing. The boss also thinks that if people stay in the office 12 hours a day, seven days a week, they get more things done than if they stay 8 hours a day, five days a week. They don’t understand that a knowledge worker is different from a factory worker (which, just to make clear, also starts to make more mistakes and is more prone to accidents the longer they work). So they put even more pressure on people to do more work, faster because they are not happy with how things are going. “Things can certainly be done quicker. For sure. Guaranteed!”

And this is how crap gets deployed to production, and the code becomes a total mess because when you pressure people, they start to take many shortcuts in their work (assuming they don’t leave first) since they have no other choice. The constant changes in direction and priorities, and rewriting the application seven times over, take a mental toll on developers. People get tired, they lose their passion for doing good work, they slow down, become more careless, and insert more bugs in the code. They also accumulate technical debt for no (business) reason, and things slow down even more. Technical debt that the developers are accountable for (not their boss, the boss doesn’t even understand the concept) and will have to pay back at some time in the future. Developers stop thinking about writing a useful application of great quality and start trying to figure out how to minimize the effort of doing and undoing all of their work. So feature implementations become simple prototypes that the developers want to show to the boss as quickly as possible and get some feedback to see what they keep, what they rewrite, and what they throw away. But there is a pitfall in this approach, of which I’ll talk more in a later chapter, namely that the boss does not know that it’s a prototype and asks for it to be deployed in production. ASAP. You can easily end up having to deploy even more crap into production just because you did a poor job at communicating that it’s a prototype. What’s even worse is that sometimes you can’t even use words like “prototype”, or “proof of concept”, or whatever you want to call it, because your boss hates that word. They are opportunity-driven, remember? And to take advantage of all those opportunities, you need to be flexible and nimble. So why do you waste extra time with prototypes? Just build the application already. And if you have doubts or questions about what needs to be built, your boss will say, “Just ask me. I will tell you everything you need to know”. Yeah, right… You can recognize this type of boss in a very simple way: everyone is happy when the boss leaves on holiday and really annoyed when they come back to work.

And it’s pointless to try to explain to the boss that things have to be done in a certain order or a certain way, that building features as quickly as possible creates problems down the line, that the application code becomes fragile and increasingly difficult to modify, that quality decreases and defects increase, that the team can’t go on like this, that they got tired of so many changes of direction and don’t understand the need for all this chaos. It will be futile. Moreover, for any occurring problem, the boss will exclude themselves from the equation. It’s not the chaos at fault, or the continuous changes of direction, or the constant whims or going back on decisions, nooooo… to add insult to injury, it’s, of course, the developers’ fault who did not write the code properly, or wrote it of inferior quality, or they are not good at their job, and that they are lazy. Things should go faster and be developed more quickly. But they are not. “You developers are lazy, for sure”. Your boss thinks the team is incompetent and hard to manage. Otherwise, why would they keep complaining and say that what the boss wants can’t be done or it takes longer when the boss is convinced that it is possible and very easy to do? Your boss wants people that can be told what to do, and then they do it (remember the “I say, you do” I was mentioning in a previous chapter?). That’s all they want. Ah… and the developers also need to be cheap.

Cogs in the machine

Cheap employees that do what they are told, whenever they are told to do so. That’s the ideal developer in the mind of a clueless boss. Because they are ignorant in all aspects of software development, the boss thinks they can do development with anyone (except with the current developers who are probably lazy… obviously). The boss doesn’t understand how software is built, and they don’t understand what people actually do. They simply count people. The team of four is behind schedule? Add one more, and things should go faster than when you only had four. “It takes a woman nine months to make a baby, but nine women can’t make a baby in one month”[122]. The whole IT industry knows this, but somehow the boss didn’t get the memo. They count people and ignore the additional communication channels that get created when you add more people. And they don’t consider people’s skills either. Junior, senior, it doesn’t really matter. You downloaded and installed an e-commerce site for your aunt, so she can sell her hand-knitted scarves online? You will do fine as an architect or tech lead on our project. “But don’t forget to remove those lorem ipsums from the ‘about’ page before deploying the application in production”. Jake will be the Project Manager. “When he was little, together with his dad, they built a treehouse in their backyard, so he has extensive experience with project management”. Are you a designer? “So you know HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, right? There is no point in hiring a more expensive front-end developer”. Testers? “Who needs testers? We have a Product Manager who must verify the application does the right thing anyway. Let them do the tests, not a quality assurance team” (they actually have quality control in mind, not quality assurance, but the boss doesn’t know this difference either). They don’t understand that developers need quiet conditions to work, so to save money, they put them together in the office with the sales team that are always talking on the phone. They then lament that the developers complain about the noise and the working conditions and they always see them wear earphones and listen to music instead of focusing on their work (without realizing why everyone wears the earphones in the first place), “Ungrateful bastards… Instead of being grateful they have a job”. They will give you all kinds of people, inexperienced and poorly trained, interns, or part-time on seven different projects, it doesn’t matter, anything to reduce costs, but they expect you to do a good job just like if you had experienced people completely dedicated to the project (and who, of course, would not be inconvenienced by having an incompetent boss to begin with).

Even if at some point they learn that things are not how they imagine them to be, they will still find something to surprise you with. I remember going to a job interview once. It was for a full-time position, but when I got to the interview, I was told it was actually a part-time job. In fact, it wasn’t even part-time; it was contracting on an hourly basis… from time to time… when they needed it. They didn’t specify this in their job announcement because they didn’t want to scare people away with their slightly more “special” situation. I would have called it their “fucked up beyond all recognition situation”, but the CEO insisted on the word “special”. So what was so special about it, you ask? Well… the company had built a software product some years earlier that turned out to be quite successful and was sold to a bunch of companies. But after it was launched, to keep maintenance costs low, the company fired all of their senior developers and only kept a few juniors to perform maintenance. But, as things always happen, the clients started demanding more features. The company noticed that the juniors they kept were not experienced enough to build those features properly. As a result, they got themselves and the company into some messes from which they could not come out by themselves. So, a few years had passed, and the company had no senior developers (because as people gained experience, they also demanded higher salaries, up to a point when they were simply fired and replaced with less expensive juniors). So the boss’ salvaging solution, and cheap at the same time, was for a senior “to visit” the juniors from time to time, give them work, help them, check what they are doing, and build skeleton implementations that the juniors will then fill up with less crucial code. Only when needed. A few hours per week or per month. Tops! Surely that’s all it was going to take. I could get a job elsewhere, for example, but I had to be at their disposal when they needed me, preferably on weekends, so the juniors can then start working on the provided implementation first thing on Monday morning. I was looking around the office for hidden cameras and expecting at any time someone to jump out of a closet and yell, “You’ve been pranked!”. But, sadly, it wasn’t a prank. It was all real.

Bad bosses believe that all employees are interchangeable and can be easily replaced. A developer is a developer. A tester is a tester. Nothing special. Like 1.5V AAA batteries you can use to power your flashlight, the remote control, the thermostat, or the clock on the wall. If you have a full stack developer who knows very well C#, Java, JavaScript, Python, HTML, and CSS, your boss believes that all programmers have these skills and you can replace them anytime, with anyone. Even if you don’t find someone like them, you can always hire any developer, and in no time at all, they will be as productive as the old developer, right? They don’t realize that even an experienced developer needs time to get to know the project, how work is organized, the business domain, etc. The more complex and bigger the project, the more time someone needs to become productive to work on it. But the boss thinks developers know those things spontaneously, with no effort, with no time investment, without support from others, and that they can start work like a Formula One car starts from poll-position. This is how they think the productivity of any new developer will look like:

But that’s not how it works. Anyone who thinks that’s how it works is either delusional or works in the fast-food industry and just hired someone who flips burgers. No one can be productive from day one on any software product. Not gonna happen! The real output is initially negative because a new person takes time and productivity from others. The other team members help them become productive at the cost of their productivity because instead of working on their own tasks, they now help bring the newcomer up to date. If you plot the real productivity, it looks something like this:

But clueless bosses stick to their opinion even if you explain to them that’s wrong. They have no clue how much it costs to replace and integrate a new person into a project. “The guy is experienced; he’ll manage on his own”. Sure… he’ll be productive just by being exposed to the project; he’ll learn by photosynthesis or something.

Bad bosses see people as replaceable cogs in a machine. They think people can work non-stop on tasks, that they don’t need to learn things, understand things, coordinate, or have discussions with each other, just robots that process tasks like some machine produces doodads inside a factory. And they need to be pressured to do so, otherwise they are lazy. If the boss comes to your office and you aren’t typing, then it means you ain’t working.

A losing battle

But everyone is working hard - very hard - to compensate for all of the boss’ nonsense. And now something paradoxical happens. Because developers do all the hard work, they still manage to make progress, even with all the problems the boss is causing. Consequently, their work ends up hiding the boss’ incompetence. Again, the developers work hard. That’s why an incompetent boss is harder to spot than an incompetent developer and remains longer with the company. The boss isn’t the one that delivers stuff; they just give orders and stuff, and if things don’t fall apart because the boss has a competent team working under them, then nobody above notices that the boss is incompetent. So the boss stays for ages with the company, continuing to receive a salary and frustrating the heck out of those who know they are an idiot but still need to do their work. If things look normal from outside, or nothing bad happens, then your boss’s superior has no reason to question their competence. From all they know, it may be the boss’ credit that things are going well. After all, that’s their job, right?

Sometimes, people figure things out, and they fire the bad boss. But most of the time, the problem is not just with your boss, but with the company itself. Otherwise, why would such bosses continue to remain in the company? If the boss is newly promoted, or a new employee, someone might notice that they are not doing the right thing, or something may happen and they will start a conflict with more senior (and more trustworthy) employees from the team, and at that point, they might get the boot. But if the boss is in that position for months or years, they are clueless and incompetent, and yet nothing happens to them, then you might have bigger problems, problems that go beyond trying to fix the “boss situation”. Can you fix the entire company? Probably not. The bad news when you have such a boss is that many times (if you don’t start looking for another job), you have to put up with them and maintain a balance between doing the right thing at all times and dealing with your boss’ bullshit.

Realistically speaking, that’s unfortunately pretty much all you can do when you have an incompetent boss. In an ideal world, you could go to their superior or even to HR, explain the situation, and the boss will be dealt with. But we don’t live in an ideal world. Unless your boss is running the project into the ground, most of the time, no action will be taken. Think about it? Who does their superior know best, and who do they get along with better from the whole project team? With you or with your boss? Does your boss’ boss even know what your name is? Do you know what kind of relationship they have? You can’t always know who you’re dealing with and why your boss is in the position they are in. Maybe they are a friend, even a relative, or have some other ties with their superior. Perhaps their superior is incompetent as well, and if they expose your boss’ incompetence, they also expose themselves at the same time. Maybe they are the ones that recommended your boss. They surely are the ones who hired them. And if they took that decision, they probably think your boss is good for the job. What do you think you’ll accomplish if you complain to the person responsible for bringing your boss into the company? A person like that won’t want to rock the boat and disturb the status quo. Did you even interact with their supervisor so far, or will you go and say, “Hello! You don’t know me, but I work for so and so, and they are incompetent. Please take some action in that regard. Thanks!” A boss doesn’t like surprises, remember? And this is a very unpleasant surprise you are presenting them with. Do you think they will treat the subject will kid gloves, or open a discreet investigation to see if what you said gets confirmed or not? They will call you and your boss to their office and let you jump down each other’s throats. If you go head to head with your boss, you’ll most likely lose. And then … maybe it’s easier for the company to get rid of you instead of your boss. I mean… you started this mess in the first place. Everything was fine before you decided to rat on your boss instead of doing your job. Your boss’ supervisor may not know who you are, but they know who your boss is: the person with whom they interact daily at work and maybe even on weekends, on the golf course, or on the tennis court. And even if you don’t get fired, you will surely receive a poor performance evaluation at the end of the year because you messed with your boss. Your boss is your boss, after all. They have power and authority over the project you work for, maybe even over you, but you don’t over them. Your job is not to undermine their position but to do as you are told even when you don’t agree with the decisions or the consequences that result from that.

So until someone from upper management figures out that your boss is incompetent and maybe decides to do something about the situation, things in the project and within the team will get progressively worse. And because that can’t go on forever, sooner or later, the mess caused by the cluelessness and lack of vision of the boss, by the constant direction changes, constant writing and rewriting, and all the bugs and technical debt accumulated, everything… must be cleaned up. And it’s the developers who have to do this. And of course, they also get the blame for ending up in such a situation. And not only will you have to clean up your boss’ mess, and still continue working with them in the same manner, but you now have to redo everything, most likely with the same deadlines. So even more pressure on the developers.

Everything becomes more and more stressful, and the situation more frustrating, so much so that people can no longer bear it and leave the company. And the first to leave are the good developers because they are less likely to put up with the stupidity and the incompetence, and are the ones that can easily find another job someplace else. They are also less likely to participate in a “death march”[83] imposed by the boss, to clean the mess they caused, with the boss (of course) not taking part in the cleanup effort, but making the situation harder by continuing what they did to get everyone into the mess in the first place. Left behind are usually the less prepared people who have lower demands on management and more difficulties finding a job elsewhere or people who have no problem spending their time complaining about the situation than actually working, thinking that if their incompetent boss hasn’t been fired yet, they don’t risk much either. What you end up with is what Bruce F. Webster calls “the dead sea effect”[123]. Ah… and of course, someone else that remains in the company is the boss who, following the conflicts with the ones who left, remains proud that they won and had the last word. For them, the fact that the developers are leaving is not a problem. They were lazy and were complaining all the time anyway, and they can always be replaced with someone else. As a matter of fact, the boss can immediately find others just like them… and at half the price too.

Not bad

So what makes a good boss, and can you fix a bad one such as the one I described so far?

Before seeing what might be done, let’s first see what kind of boss we would want to have. Just like before, I’m going to mention those qualities that I think apply most to software development, not general attributes like being a people person, empowering others and involving them in decisions, being fair, honest, trustworthy, and open-minded, having a clear vision for the project and knowing how to set expectations, communicating clearly, understanding the difference between blame and responsibility… what else? Ah right! Not a psychopath!

It makes sense that a good boss will be the opposite of what I mentioned makes a bad boss, right? First of all, they must not be clueless about software development. A good boss understands how software is built and what developers do, they understand that writing software can be complex, they know why IT projects sometimes fail and what can be done to try to avoid that. They are aware of the pitfalls of the Business-IT divide, and they also have good project management skills. When some matters are too technical and go beyond their understanding, the boss gives the developers’ opinion a lot of weight because they know that when it comes to technical aspects, developers know better. That means the boss is open-minded, listens to presented arguments, and trusts the developers’ opinions instead of enforcing rigid decisions on their own. A good boss provides the team members with clear goals and trusts them to find the best way to make those goals happen.

Good bosses know where they are and where they are heading; they see the big picture and understand where and how technology plays a role in it. A good boss normally has the long term benefits in mind, instead of the short term gains. And when they ask for a sudden change of direction, or something is communicated as being urgent, it’s really for a serious reason; it’s not caused by something that’s “shiny”, and it’s a reason the boss can clearly explain and support with arguments. It’s not because they have a gut feeling; it’s because it’s a good business decision to make. They also understand that such decisions have consequences, like maybe the team needing to incur some technical debt, so they collaborate with the team to decide if it’s indeed worth it or what the cost of it is. And such sudden changes of direction are rare because the boss understands the business very well and has a development strategy; they anticipate things, they don’t react to any situation that comes along.

A good boss’ actions don’t negatively impact the team’s morale and performance. A good boss respects people and doesn’t treat developers as their personal servants. They admit when they’re wrong, they don’t pretend they are always right and everyone else is wrong, they listen to arguments, you can reason with them, they don’t micromanage people, and consider the development team as partners that are working towards the same goals. They understand skills matter, the need to hire good developers, and the cost of replacing people, so they try to help create a productive environment where the developers can apply their abilities to the fullest. People feel motivated when their boss is actually helpful and doesn’t negatively interfere with their work. And more importantly, they don’t feel like throwing a party when the boss leaves on vacation, and they don’t get all gloomy when the boss gets back. If they could also write code, they would be the ideal boss :)

For most developers, a good boss is not just someone who understands and masters the business and the domain very well, and someone with good management skills, but is also someone technical, that knows how good quality software gets built, that understands and even encourages good programming techniques and best practices, quality assurance, or discovery through use of prototypes. Basically, a “good boss” is a “developer boss”. But remember the definition I used at the beginning of the chapter for “boss”: they are a business person. Developers would like another developer as the boss, but that’s not going to happen. The Team Lead is a developer, the Project Manager may have been a developer, you might find people in the corporate hierarchy who were developers at one time, but the boss, the one who runs the show and calls the shots, very unlikely to ever be from among the developers.

Not as bad

OK, so these are some traits of a good boss. If you have such a boss, congratulations, you have less stress to deal with. But if you have a bad boss, you might be asking yourself if something can be done to fix the situation. Is there a way to turn a bad boss into a good one? The short answer is “usually no”. From all the bad things I mentioned above about bad bosses, two big ideas take shape. Bad bosses for a software development project are, (one) “completely clueless about building software” and (two), they are “know it all” assholes that wreak havoc on the project.

The thing is, you can’t cure “cluelessness”. The boss simply does not understand. And they are not gonna “get it” no matter how hard you try to explain developer stuff to a non-developer. It just won’t happen. They are either interested in this side of things and make an effort to understand how software is built on a more detailed level, or they are not. And you can surely not fix an asshole. You can’t. An asshole is an asshole, and that’s that. End of story. These are the main reasons you can’t change a bad boss into a good one, and that’s why I said the answer is “usually no”. However, “usually no” doesn’t mean “always no”, which then means “sometimes yes”.

The situations when it means “yes” are few and constitute that probability when the boss is not actually an asshole but is only perceived as such because of the way they behave and how they act. And they can behave and act like that for a reason other than being a “know it all asshole”. For lack of a better term, I’ll refer to this motive as “expectations anxiety”. Expectations from others and expectations from themselves. High expectations. Someone placed the project in their hands and made them responsible for its success. It doesn’t even matter if whoever did this knew they were clueless or not; they are the boss now. And the boss can’t let anyone down. They need to rise to the occasion and make it happen. It all depends on them, right? So they come to believe that their role is bigger than it actually is, so they create this self-imposed pressure to please people (their supervisor, the client, the owner of the company, whatever), to show what they know and what they can do, to give it 110 percent. And so they go overboard with things. When their own boss asks for something, they tend to think it’s urgent and important and needs to be done ASAP. But that’s not enough. They need to exceed expectations, to do even more. So all that “opportunity-driven” crap, or “shiny object syndrome” or whatever you want to call it, is, in this case, insecurity combined with wanting to dazzle everyone and make a good impression. “This is important, that, the other. If I only had this, or that, if I had both. I can’t miss that opportunity. There’s definitely something here. There are so many interesting things I want to do. But the developers are slow. I requested something from them last week, and they still haven’t done it yet, they keep asking questions and complaining that I’m asking too much… what’s up with that?” So the boss gets frustrated when developers don’t do everything they ask for and start to think that they might be lazy, maybe not even working; otherwise, why aren’t they doing what they’re told? So the boss starts micromanaging or putting pressure on people, for them to work harder, to move faster, to show them the changes they demanded immediately. If developers don’t listen, the boss doesn’t want to be responsible. No thought crosses their mind that maybe they are themselves to blame because they don’t know how to run a software project, don’t understand developers, or how they write the software. “But how hard can it be? It can’t be that ‘hard’; it’s ‘soft’, right?” The boss is trying their best, but because of the lack of knowledge in this regard, the approach they end up using is completely messed up. Trying to do more with less and in less time, because that’s how they think they can please their own boss or the client, isn’t helping either. They are clearly overwhelmed by the situation, but they don’t want to admit it and try to do what they think should be done all by themselves, without asking anyone else for help.

If your bad boss is in this category, then you might make a change by helping the boss acknowledge the fact that they can’t manage a software project with just what they know (or better said, what they don’t know), all by themselves, then teaching them that they can trust the development team to help handle the project. You can improve things if you gain your boss’s trust and make them understand that you are their partner in trying to do what’s right for the project, i.e., the things I mentioned about improving the Business-IT divide. The boss is responsible for the project, and they have the anxiety of doing a good job, but without knowing a lot about software development, they don’t yet trust developers, so that they can rely more on them instead of being controlling and telling them what to do. Want you really want is for developers to handle their own work while bosses their own, and to work together as partners. But you can’t be partner with an asshole. So first of all, you need to find out with what kind of person you are dealing with. I’ve said it before in the book: people change only if they want to change; you can’t change them just because you want to. So if you want your boss to change, from someone messing up the project (while trying to manage something they don’t understand), into a person that can instead place their trust in the project team, then the boss themselves must want to change otherwise all your efforts to better things will not be worthwhile.

Find out if your boss is salvageable or a dud by paying attention to your interactions with them. If your boss shows signs of being eager to learn, wants you to explain things, wants to find out more about how you work, when you have a divergence of opinions on things they listen when you present arguments in favor of your point of view, is open to hearing your ideas and they have no problem agreeing to things in writing, then those are good signs. In a nutshell, when you try to go contrary to something they want to do, if they seem like a person you might be able to reason with (maybe not always, but still…), then that’s a sign the situation can be salvaged.

If instead, they’re arrogant and mistreat people, want to control people and put lots of pressure on them for no apparent reasons, when you contradict them or object to their opinions they become recalcitrant, or they don’t listen to you, they are not interested in your opinions, and any argument you may have falls on deaf years, they think they are always right and the smartest person in any room, always want to have the last word and when they fail to find counter-arguments they resort to saying “I’m the boss, you will do what I say”, then they are most likely a dud. Another sign that you can’t save the situation is if your boss throws other people under the bus when something bad happens. And not only do they do that when something bad happens, but they also make preparations to be easier to throw someone under the bus when desired, like, for example, not agreeing on things in writing so that there are no traces of their decisions. They can subsequently point the finger at you and say, “I didn’t decide that; you’re the one who misunderstood and mishandled things”. Or you send them an email to ask for a simple decision, and they decide to hold a meeting instead. A two-minute response in writing is replaced by a half an hour meeting, which leaves no trace; then, if things go well, your boss gets the credit; if things turn bad, you get the blame. That’s one reason, for example, why they might not want you to write meeting minutes either. In the previous chapter, I talked about meeting minutes and why it’s a good idea to write them during the meeting to keep everyone attentive, engaged, minimize misunderstandings, and for all to agree with the decisions and actions taken. I had bosses who were uncomfortable with me doing this because the minute left no room for interpretation. Instead, they were saying, “Focus on the discussion. You can write whatever you want after the meeting. Don’t waste my time with this now”. If this is the kind of boss you have to deal with, one who’s preoccupied more with their image than doing the right things, to create appearances different than reality, someone that spends time sucking up and kicking down and a veteran at throwing people under the bus, then these are clear signs you can’t fix the situation. You can’t trust this person to change because the main problem is who they are as a person, not just that they are clueless about developing software.

There is also a third type of boss, and it’s harder to figure them out: the owner of the company. In a small organization, the company owner can be the boss. They are a person who exhibits bad boss behaviors but not necessarily for the same reasons I stated so far. An owner knows not a different reality than that of giving orders, deciding things, and being in the highest position of authority. Their decisions don’t get discussed; they get done. If they haven’t worked much in other companies before starting their own, maybe they’ve never been on the other side of the discussions, maybe they didn’t have an incompetent boss who had to be convinced of things, maybe others didn’t make bad decisions for them, decisions with which they disagreed with but still had to precisely implement however ridiculous they may have been. As an owner, everyone reports to them, and they make all the decisions. If they are also surrounded by “yes-man” individuals that are not willing to question their judgment, offer alternatives to what they’re proposing, or tell them when they’re wrong, because they are too busy kissing their ass until they give them a rash, then they’ll act much like a bad boss. Their reality becomes “I’m always right” because nobody tells them that they’re on occasions mistaken. If the owner of the company is accessible and you interact with them often, at some point, you can gain their confidence and make them understand things. That’s because, unlike a bad boss who can bury themselves deep in the company hierarchy, a bad owner has no place to hide. If the company hasn’t gone bust, it means that the owner is a capable person, so chances are they can understand things from a broader perspective.

If you’ve determined the kind of boss you’re dealing with, and something can be done to change the situation, then this change must come from the development team, the Team Lead, or the Project Manager. As I said in the Business-IT divide chapter, the change will not come from your boss, who is a business person, because your boss doesn’t understand things in their entirety to even realize that a change is needed. Just like you have to interact more with the business side to bridge the Business-IT divide, similarly, to improve the situation with your boss, you have to interact more with them. It’s easier for you to understand your boss’ work than the other way around. So get involved in what your boss is doing. Communicate often with them (in their business language), ask them about any news, events, or information that you should know about. Don’t expect them to come up with ideas or requests. Try instead to understand their needs, and go to them with suggestions and advice. Make them realize that they are not alone in all of this and that they can count on the development team for help. The mechanism is the same as the one I described in the chapter on the Business-IT divide. Communication and trust are essential. You can’t work effectively with your boss if you don’t trust them, and your boss must also know they can trust the development team. When there is trust, developers are good professionals and show they are working towards the right goals, a partnership relation starts to develop, and the boss learns to take into account the developers’ arguments, opinions, and input, before making decisions.

If the environment is dysfunctional and your boss’ persistence in their idiocy is irredeemable, and you have no chance of success to bring out a more rational set of behaviors in them, you are only left with two options. The first and most obvious is to leave the company. It’s not worth risking your mental health, so exit, stage left. This is the option most recommended by everyone who has had a bad boss at some point in their career. Staying in the job, with the bad boss, is stressful. But so is looking for another job and starting anew somewhere else. It’s not a step you can take easily. You have to weigh in the decision really well. Maybe you like your other colleagues and the domain of activity of the company. Maybe you can’t afford to change jobs right now or have some benefits you don’t want to lose. Maybe you can’t afford to start fresh in another company. And even if you leave the company, there’s no guarantee that you won’t run into a worse boss in the new job. You hope you’ll be better of somewhere else and have a boss that knows what they’re doing, can understand your work, and collaborate well with you, but you don’t know that. So maybe you can’t leave. What do you do then? What’s the second option?

You accept the situation and do the job to the best of your abilities.

So, your boss is an incompetent asshole. They make your job harder, and it’s a struggle to keep one step ahead of them, to counteract or minimize the effects of bad decisions. And you can’t even stand the sight of them. That’s how it is. You’ve determined that you cannot change your boss, and you cannot leave the company either? Then accept these facts. No job is perfect. You were hired to do a job, and following your boss’s instructions is also part of that job. When someone is hired, their work isn’t conditioned by the work of others. I have never signed a labor contract saying that if my boss is completely clueless, I have the right to stop working, but still continue to receive a salary. You still need to do your job. It’s harder to do it while dealing with a bad boss; you won’t be as productive as you might be, you might not be able to give it your best while feeling you are fighting an uphill battle, but you still have to do your job. Try to focus more on your work and the success of the project instead of on your boss.

But while you do that, make sure you don’t get blamed for the whole mess if the shit might happen to hit the fan someday. You do that by documenting things in writing. Keep emails and written conversations with your boss. If you discuss things and make decisions in a meeting, just send a follow-up email with conclusions. Try avoiding meetings and keep things in writing over email. If you do have meetings, write the meeting minutes. It doesn’t matter what your boss says about them; it’s a good habit to get into, to make sure communication (with everyone, not just with your boss) doesn’t break down. Communication is very important. The more you have, the better. If you communicate in a correct, transparent way and give constant status updates on the overall situation of the project, someone at some point will see the big picture and pick up on the chaos, especially if you can send status reports to your boss’s supervisor in C.C. If you can attend meetings with your boss’s supervisor, do so. Make yourself known at higher company levels if you can.

No matter who says what, who decides what, what is built, changed, or rewritten, at some point, the software will still reach the customer in one form or another. Developers do the most important work, so developers always pick up the pieces no matter what happens. But they should not be blamed for the mess if it’s not their doing. If your boss develops a sudden case of amnesia about decisions they’ve made and starts pointing the finger at you for not understanding, getting it wrong, remembering it wrong, or whatever, you should have written documentation that says otherwise. One thing you need to understand is that, except when the boss pretends to have forgotten the decisions they made, in lots of cases, they have indeed forgotten. They have a short memory not only when it suits them for throwing you under the bus, but also because many of the decisions they made were made on the spot. They were not part of a plan; they were not carefully thought out decisions. There were things decided then and there, shallow decisions similar to thinking about what to have for lunch. Do you remember what you had for lunch last Friday? No? Neither does your boss. But not what they had for lunch, but that important decision they took, which they now can’t recall because it was made without thinking things trough or understanding their consequences. Remember that in most organizations, if something isn’t written down, it doesn’t exist. And that accounts not just for things like project goals, processes, actions decided in meetings, or employee performance evaluations, but also for your bad boss’ decisions. Documenting your boss’ fuckups is something that will take extra time from your work and will affect it just as your boss affects it by all the issues they cause. It’s extra “trust taxes”[100] that you need to pay on top of the other mess. And with paying taxes, the idea is to keep them low. This is for “blame avoidance”, not “blame placing”. So you need to keep the effort down to the level of good project management practices, not build a 500-page record file like for a trial in a court of justice. And if you find out that you prefer doing very good work more than documenting average work, then maybe reconsider the idea of looking for another job, and move on.

Bad managers

In any software project with more than a couple of people, you will have a manager in charge of things. Similar to the definition I used in the previous chapter for “boss”, when I say “manager”, I don’t mean any manager in the company structure, like a department manager, for example. I mean someone like a “Project Manager” or someone doing project management work as per the definition of the Project Management Institute[124], who defines project management as: “the application of knowledge, skills, tools, and techniques to project activities to meet the project requirements” [125].

We are all familiar with how projects unfold. They are first initiated, then planned, and then people go to work. Then, a lot of focus is on the execution phase of the project where the Project Manager monitors the progress and compares it to the original plan, making any necessary corrections to make sure the project is completed (ideally) on time, (ideally) on budget, and (ideally) with all of its requirements met. Sounds simple, right? It isn’t.

A Project Manager needs to handle the relationship with clients and project stakeholders, they need to oversee requirements gathering, define the scope of the project and refine the business objectives, build a work breakdown structure of the activities that need to be performed, assist with effort estimations, plan the project with the development team, build schedules, define milestones and deliverables, organize, monitor and control the work, hold meetings, build reports and keep everyone informed, deal with scope changes, handle dependencies and integrations with other projects, manage assumptions and risk, lead the team, coaching or mentoring the workers, trying to motivate them, handling conflicts, keeping the project cost and timeline under control, ensure communication, collaboration and knowledge sharing between all persons involved, manage quality assurance and quality control, maybe even handle some operational activities at the same time. And most of these activities are not sequential steps. They need to be balanced all at once as the company, market, or project conditions change. And many have competing constraints or depend on one another (remember, for example, the “project management triangle”[76] I spoke about earlier).

In the middle

If you think programming is hard, you should try managing a software development project for a while. You have to constantly adapt to new information and all kinds of changes and problems that occur as the project unfolds. And you need to do this while someone else is setting the goals (i.e., boss, client, stakeholders) and someone else is doing the actual work (i.e., developers, architects, testers). That’s businesspeople having to work with technical people. When I talked about the Business-IT divide, you found out that this arrangement doesn’t always go well. It makes sense then that the role of a manager must become one of “mediator”, a very important role, considering that not only don’t both sides see eye to eye, but often, the parties have unreasonable expectations from each other. The Project Manager must sit in the middle and make sure that bosses have a good business strategy that provides the necessary goals and expectations for the development team, while the developers’ work is aligned with business objectives. At the same time, the manager should shield the team from outside noise (mostly bad bosses) and be allowed to do their job efficiently in order to reach those goals and meet those expectations. So a good manager needs to manage both up and down.

And to do that, the Project Manager needs to understand two worlds: the business world and the technical world. The Project Management definition given above is nice and all, but there is a small problem with it. It’s generic. It applies to any kind of project. Digging a well is a project, building a shack is a project, organizing a party is a project, mounting a large screen TV on the wall above the fireplace is a project, building software is a project. The project management skills, tools, and techniques (cost management, schedule management, resource management, risk management, planning, monitoring and controlling, etc.) might have the same name and mean the same thing in every project, but you can’t apply them the same across “any kind” of project. The way you keep schedule under control for a software development project might prove to be completely disastrous on a construction project, for example. So not only is project management knowledge important, but the domain in which the project management skills, tools, and techniques are applied is just as important. So, the Project Manager needs to know the business very well.
