And since the project is a software project, it’s also important how developers build the software that solves the business problems and/or requirements. Like a boss, a Project Manager doesn’t do the actual work but has influence and control over the work. Putt’s Law might apply for a boss, but it’s awful if it applies to the Project Manager. So, a Project Manager needs to understand what they are managing and what their people do. Most importantly, they need to understand what the team “can” and “cannot” do.

It often happens for the client or boss to try to impose unrealistic schedules or have impossible expectations from the development team. At the same time, the developers might lose sight of what’s important and focus too much on technologies or “the latest fads”, things that bring no real value to the business. The Project Manager must recognize when the issues and concerns of both sides are valid, when to place more pressure on the developers (e.g., because they act like spoiled brats with toys), or when to push back on imposed targets from upper management or the client (e.g., because they behave like unreasonable people). The Project Manager needs to be the voice of reason, to support both sides in getting a better understanding of each other’s way of thinking, to ultimately make good decisions that benefit the project. Only if there is a dialog between the two parties, if there is collaboration, the recommendations of the development team are taken into account, and the team is involved in the decision-making process, only in this way can decisions be made on the entirety of the project context and realistic solutions and fixes to any problems that may occur can be found.

Communication

And a crucial role in all of this is played by communication. To bring both parties together, the manager must be a good communicator. Being a technical person and having a good understanding of the business is not enough if they don’t also know how to communicate. The role of “mediator” depends a lot on communication skills. Just to give an example, a long time ago, when I was a young programmer (and pretty much nothing else, professionally speaking), I was fixing some issues with one of our client’s application that somebody else built for them a few years earlier, and we later inherited. The issue proved to go much deeper and be worse than everyone anticipated, and it was taking me some time. I initially estimated the number of days everything would take, but, as it happened, I was wrong. And then I was late on my estimate. My boss “summoned” my manager and me into her office and asked me to explain what was happening and why it was taking me so much. As a young programmer, I didn’t know much about interacting with top management, and my boss was not what you might call a technical person, so we were speaking two different languages. The discussion was getting nowhere. She started to get angry, and I started to become frustrated that I couldn’t make her understand what the issue was. My manager intervened and, imagine this, started “translating” what we were saying to one another. I get the chuckles when I think about it now, but that was what was happening at the time (and it wasn’t as fun then). What my boss said, my manager was repeating in words I would understand. And what I said, my manager was repeating in words my boss could understand. She eventually understood what the issue was and why it took longer, and I understood what was worrying her. My manager helped us both to see things from one another’s perspective. That was good technical skills, business skills, and communication skills from the part of my manager.

Formal or informal, written or spoken, using charts and pictures, face-to-face or using technology, conscious (paying attention to how you say what you want to say) or unconscious (by gestures, posture, or facial expressions), within or outside the organization, no matter how it happens, there is communication. You can’t escape it. Software, like many things, is built by people. And people don’t all know the same things, and even if they did, they might act differently on the same information. There also isn’t one person who knows everything. So in order for people with different knowledge and skills to make some common goals happen, they need to collaborate and make decisions together. People need to communicate in order to convey their thoughts, ideas, or intentions and send and receive information among themselves. Communication is very important on a project of any size and any type, and in software development, that’s no exception. Heck, even ants need to communicate with each other to bring some dead beetle back to the nest. I mentioned since the beginning of the book that poor communication is one of the reasons for software project failures, so everyone needs to communicate effectively. Without communication, things just fall apart. And this is all the more true for a manager.

Without communication, you are basically on your own. You are doing work in isolation. How much do you think you can accomplish without communicating with anyone? Not much. At least not for a long time. Developers need long stretches of uninterrupted time to be able to get in the zone and do their best work, but after they finish their task, feature, or fix, they need to synchronize with everyone else to know how to proceed with the next thing. Long stretches of uninterrupted work time don’t mean “the whole project’s duration”. You can’t work alone when you are part of a team. If everyone does that, everyone loses the big picture. It’s hard to work when you don’t know what the others are doing. So you are not even a team. Worse even, people start making assumptions about what others are doing, what else is going on, what needs to happen next, or what is important. Having information from all parts of the project is mandatory. Decisions are taken based on information. And the Project Manager must make sure that the correct information is available at the appropriate time and is distributed to the right persons. This is an activity that takes a lot of the Project Manager’s time because the more people involved in a project, the more the number of communication channels increases and, implicitly, the more attention must be given to communication. The formula for the number of communication channels is N*(N-1)/2, with N being the number of people in the team.

And this is just for a team of members that work closely together. Add stakeholders talking to your Project Manager, and your communication channels might look like this:

In their role as a mediator, the Project Manager stands between these two groups: the team and the stakeholders. The manager needs to pay great attention to this aspect. Because stakeholders don’t do the work and are usually positioned further away from the project, they have no fresh, up-to-date information about it. They must ask for the information, or it must be given to them. Key stakeholders might need to make decisions and can’t do so without information. And they must be given this information in a format and by using concepts that they understand (i.e., of a non-technical nature). Also, regarding decision-making, they need to be told about the consequences of those decisions on the plan, schedule, budget, or quality of the software. They often don’t see the impact on the actual work carried out on the project, and it’s the manager’s job to provide these details as well. Then, it often happens that different stakeholders look at things differently, so misunderstandings can happen. It’s, again, the manager’s job to gain agreement among stakeholders when this occurs, so that the team gets a clear message about what needs to be done and thus minimize unnecessary changes or rework. The manager must keep the stakeholders engaged and informed on a continual basis. They need to manage stakeholder expectations with ongoing and effective communication; otherwise, it happens with them what I said earlier about what happens when working in isolation: stakeholders begin to make assumptions about the project, the work, the results, etc. And you don’t want them to wonder what’s going on. If you use Agile and deliver every couple of weeks or so, they can see progress because you deliver something every sprint, but if the feedback loop is larger, they might start wondering what’s going on. It’s like when you order some gadget from an e-commerce site, and it doesn’t get delivered in the amount of time you’d expect. What do you do then? You look online and track the AWB, or make a call to the call center to ask what’s happening to the package, why didn’t it arrive yet. It’s the same with the project. Stakeholders need to know what’s happening; otherwise, they get nervous, impatient, and they come looking for you, wasting your time and always interrupting with questions of “are we there yet?”. You need to always keep them informed. The saying “No news is good news” doesn’t really apply when it comes to stakeholders, clients, or bosses. If they start asking for information instead of it being offered to them, they might also develop the tendency to micromanage things making your job of managing the project more difficult.

So, project Managers inevitably end up spending a lot of their time communicating. But of course, it’s not just the manager doing the communication. In reality, when it comes to communication on a project, you don’t get a nice isolation like in the previous image. As the dynamic of the communication changes, the circles multiply and get bigger and bigger. Communication increases or spreads outwards to stakeholders, perhaps to other teams, departments, customers, vendors, etc. The manager needs to enable communication and make sure the information keeps moving on every channel, not just between stakeholders and the team. Let me say that again: on every channel. So from this regard, the manager must behave like a “communication custodian” (for lack of a better term). Communication itself can happen or cannot. Or can happen poorly (like in the example above, of my former boss and a younger version of myself). The Project Manager must make sure that it does happen, and that it’d done clearly, in a transparent manner, and it’s efficient and effective. If communication stops, so does the project.

Failed communication

And now we’re obviously getting to one of the first problems with bad managers: they are not very effective when it comes to communication.

Some managers don’t act like “mediators”, they don’t act like “communication custodians”, they don’t make sure communication is effective, they don’t try to identify communication gaps and address them. For them, communication is something that occurs to the degree it just happens to occur. When problems arise because of communication deficiencies, the manager reacts to them instead of having tried to anticipate them. I’m talking about an “observation” of communication problems instead of a “prevention”. To offer an example, consider the goals of a project. You cannot send an email to everyone at the beginning of the project, saying that “This is what we are trying to achieve with this project. These are the important points” and then call it a day. People will immerse themselves in work, and the goals will become fuzzier while everyone focuses on details instead of the big picture. The manager must remind everyone what the objectives of the project are, what is important for the business, why the project was started in the first place, etc., and not to notice at the end of the project, or on every milestone, that people didn’t really understand towards what they are working on. Even when you assign people individual tasks to work on, you must explain what they have to do, the importance of those tasks, their priority, etc. If work just lands on people’s desks with no proper communication on what it’s all about, don’t be surprised if the result won’t be the one you expect.

Another problem with communication is that some managers don’t always know how to choose the best form of communication. They send an email or write a document when they should be holding a meeting. Or they write messages on chat when they should be having a face-to-face conversation. Most of the time, though, they set up meetings when they should find some other form of communication. “We need to establish such and such. Let’s discuss it for a few minutes. It’s more efficient like that than writing an email”. More efficient for whom? For the manager, of course. I mentioned in a previous chapter about the maker’s schedule versus the manager’s schedule[106]. A spontaneous meeting at the wrong moment can cancel the productivity of developers for the entire day. It’s effective to have a face-to-face conversation with someone, but be careful not to interrupt them when they are “in the zone”. If the developers have headphones on, it’s probably a sign that they don’t want to be disturbed, not because they love music so much. You can also cause the same problem with reports. Because, as a manager, you are not the one doing the work, you do not have exact facts and figures about the work in progress. You need to ask for details from those who do the work in order to build a snapshot of the project. By trying to gather as many details as possible, you may end up asking for too many reports or for too much data from those actually doing the work, interrupting them again. I talked in the chapter of meetings and reports about these things, and in what quicksands you can get yourself into, so I don’t want to repeat it here.

Sometimes, these communication problems are caused by the fact that the manager is a (recent) former developer that got promoted to be in charge of the project. Communication is not their strong point simply because they still think and behave like a developer, and they haven’t yet shaken that mindset. This kind of manager blows it mainly for two reasons. The first is that they don’t adapt their communication style according to their interlocutor. They don’t take into account who their audience is; they communicate with everyone in the same manner: using the same language as when they were a developer. That works with team members, system administrators, other Project Managers with a similar background, or technical people, but it will not work with clients, upper management, vendors, HR, or salespeople. It’s about different communication styles, I can even say different languages, but still, the manager can only package the message in one way. And the communication is often dry and direct, especially when delivering bad news; they don’t expect and prepare for the wave of questions that follow the announcement of bad news, and they don’t think about solutions or possible corrective scenarios. They just announce the bad news, causing a surprise for bosses who, as we know, don’t like surprises. If you get promoted to a management position, you must learn to communicate at different levels and in different ways, to match the new responsibilities you now have. And so we come to the second thing that a (recently) former developer turned manager screws up when it comes to communication: they forget that they no longer communicate with a computer, but with people.

The single biggest problem in communication is the illusion that it has taken place - George Bernard Shaw[126]

When you talk with a computer, you actually send it instructions to execute. The machine can’t talk back. But communication does not mean that you just talk. You are not just the emitter of information. It takes at least two people to communicate, and since you can’t both talk at the same time, you obviously also need to know how to listen. Many managers have the habit of talking too much or repeatedly interrupting others when they are talking. They listen enough to see where the conversation is heading, not really paying attention, then interrupt to offer their point of view, as if trying “to debug” the conversation or something. They talk or announce something, and somehow, it’s then the other person’s problem what they understood from that. When it comes to communication with people, however, things don’t work like that. Communicating with another person can sometimes mean to just keep your mouth shut and listen. Only in this way, you can make sure you understand what the other person said, and you make sure you are, in turn, understood. An example would be the one of doing performance reviews. As a Project Manager, you might be in charge of evaluating the people who work on the project you are managing. You need to have face-to-face discussions with each member of the team, to know how to listen and to make an effort in understanding what’s being communicated, to be able to read between the lines, paying attention to the other person’s body language, giving constructive feedback, and in turn, accepting feedback, to be able to clearly communicate your conclusions and decisions to the other person, to agree on goals and make sure the person understands what they need to do. You can’t assume that the other person understands your message and agrees with it just because you opened your mouth and words came out of it.

You can improve communication by using technology or having a process in place or some procedure of what, when, and who needs to communicate, but at the end of the day, it all boils down to interactions with people. And I think I made it pretty clear from the previous chapters of how fun it is to work with people. Many things can interfere with communication: emotions, language, culture, a lack of trust, people taking things personally, conflicts, etc. Communication is not something simple, it’s not something you can learn from a book or from a course, it’s not a formula that you can apply or a framework that you can use. You have to practice, and you have to practice daily. Because they have to be a communication custodian, something that requires effort every single day, many give up on management and return to development - too much hassle.

Another problem that arises when it comes to communication is that some managers communicate incorrectly on purpose. That is, they withhold details, or they distort the information they transmit. This happens most often when the manager communicates with their boss (or with higher executives). When they have something to tell their boss, they try to sugar coat things, present matters in a better light than they actually are, or present only the good news, delaying or sometimes not even giving the bad news at all. This may be because the manager wants to look good in front of the boss, look more capable, or have more chances to raises, but most of the time, the situation is caused by the boss themselves. The boss can’t react calmly to receiving bad news and starts yelling, threatening, and throwing tantrums. And managers learn this behavior, and they try to avoid it. Although managers know that communication should be done honestly and in a transparent way, they choose not to do this because they are worried about how their boss might react… and worried about the consequences, like not being offered another promotion or a high profile project to work on, being fired, etc. For instance, incorrect communication might involve presenting estimates. If the team makes an estimate and the result is higher than the manager thinks the boss will like to hear, they might choose only to communicate the estimate for the best-case scenario, that is, the most favorable case from some estimates that are most likely already overly optimistic. Thus, the manager communicates an estimate without any margin of error and, in doing so, commits their team to an unrealistic schedule. Another example of incorrect communication relates to assumptions and risks. The manager may choose not to communicate assumptions and risks or to minimize their severity or likelihood of occurring. Or, when a change is requested that is clearly detrimental to the project and affects either the scope or the project schedule, the manager can choose to keep their mouth shut instead of trying to explain to everyone what impact the changes will have and recommended against them being implemented. The manager may also postpone escalating certain things that they cannot solve or doesn’t fall within their abilities, or they could postpone notifying stakeholders of project delays; then certain (optimal) corrective measures may become unavailable because they waited too much to present the bad news or escalate problems. And the list of examples could go on.

Communication with bosses may be difficult because bosses have more power than the manager, and there can always be unpleasant consequences, but this is one of the realities that you have to accept when you are a Project Manager. It’s part of the job description. You need to communicate in good and in bad. It won’t do any good to postpone or to embellish bad news. Anyways, things come to light eventually. You can’t try tricking people forever and hope for the best. People always find out the truth, and when they do, it’s a surprise, an unpleasant surprise. And the first thing that gets affected is the bosses’ and the stakeholders’ trust in the manager. And where there is no trust, communication suffers because people no longer think only about the information that is being communicated but also think if there are no other elements hidden behind it, other things that they are not aware of. In other words, they place in doubt the accuracy of the information being transmitted. The result, then, is that work on the project becomes less efficient because of all the things I mentioned in a previous chapter regarding trust. So if you have bad news to communicate, be a brave manager, and announce it. Truthfully. Don’t sugar coat things, don’t wait too long (but don’t rush in immediately either), take time to understand the problem, so you properly present the facts and the impact, be prepared to answer your boss/stakeholder’s questions and address their concerns. Be ready with solutions and recommendations or how you intend to deal with the situation, and be prepared for when bosses will ask who’s to blame or why you didn’t see this earlier. It will suck to be you. It won’t be easy. But that’s what it is. As I said, it’s part of the job description.

Tools of the trade

Much of the manager’s time goes to communication. But “communication” is just one of the skills a good Project Manager must have. Remember the definition I’m using? A Project Manager is the person that applies knowledge, skills, tools, and techniques to project activities in order to meet the project requirements. What kind of knowledge, skills, tools, and techniques? The project management kind, of course.

Many Project Managers in the software industry were developers as well, and they got into this new role either because they wanted a new challenge, either because someone needed to fill that role and top management decided that it should be the most senior of the team members because they already know the project, there won’t be a need for much training, and it will be cheaper than spending money on a recruitment process. Others slowly slide towards tasks of this kind because project management skills are needed, and no one else can or wants to do them. By not having specialized training, they accumulate experience on the job, often by trial and error. So they make mistakes. I was a similar case. I slowly started doing management tasks because there was no one to do them, but they had to be done. I’ve been a Project Manager in various occasions, the last occupation code in my work card is actually that of a “Project Manager”, but I don’t have what you might call formal project management education or training.

I said it, and I’ll say it again: it’s harder to be a Project Manager than to be a developer. There are many things to keep in balance while working as a Project Manager, and, to have better chances of success doing that, you need a rich toolset in terms of project management knowledge. And trial and error is not the best approach to build that toolset. With learning technologies or programming, I mentioned in a previous chapter about doing “honest mistakes” on a personal project or prototypes, and then learning from those mistakes. When it comes to practicing project management skills, you may not have a personal project available, one with a setup similar to the one at work, with stakeholders and other developers doing the work, so you will be forced to make mistakes directly on the company’s project. So, you need to minimize making mistakes; otherwise, you risk spending a lot of time in your boss’ office, explaining yourself. You might get the hang of things eventually, but why suffer when there are books like the Project Management Body of Knowledge Guide (a.k.a. the PMBOK)[127], just to name one resource, where you can learn essential things before you encounter them. If you have become a Project Manager, you must know what this job is all about. But even so, books like the PMBOK are just guides. They don’t give you answers or solutions to everything; they don’t give you a winning course to follow. They only give you a toolbox. You need to know which tool to pick up from that toolbox, depending on the situation. There are many things that a Project Manager does or participates in, and there is no one-size-fits-all approach. You need to know how to adapt your knowledge, skills, tools, and project management techniques to the conditions and fit them to the project and the organization. So you have to make an effort and learn the job of Project Manager just like you put in the effort and learned technologies and programming: from books, blogs, feeds, podcasts, taking part in online communities, various meetups in your local area, project management talks or conferences, etc., to have more information at your disposal, make the best decisions possible and avoid as many quicksands as possible.

I’ve already talked in a previous chapter about many things that can steer you into quicksands from this area of project management if you don’t know what you are doing. I don’t want to reiterate what I already said; I just want to briefly remind you of some of them, as guidelines for the directions in which you should invest in acquiring new project management knowledge. First of all, managers must be involved in hiring new people. They have to make sure that the right persons get hired, that the right people hold the interviews with the candidates, to help write job requirements, and to participate in evaluating candidates. Once someone is hired, the manager must make sure the probationary period is used properly and that the new employee is given all the help needed to have a smooth integration into the team. The person’s progress in this period must be documented. Then there are performance reviews that need to be conducted, improvement plans must be agreed with non-performers, goals discusses, and progress towards the goals monitored. People need to be offered support to perform to their best abilities, and it falls within the manager’s responsibilities to remove obstacles from the employees’ path, to see what in the working environment badly affects the employee’s work, and to eliminate it, fix it, or escalate it. The manager needs to contribute to a safe working environment where people can make honest mistakes and are helped to learn from them. Toxic employees must be fired. Salaries must be aligned with the work being done and in relation to the other team members doing the same job. The manager must ensure that their team receives the necessary training and that everyone is motivated. And these are just some things they need to do in regard to the people working on the project. Then there are the “technical” things a Project Manager does. For example, oversee requirements gathering, do a proper prioritization of features, build a realistic schedule and defend it from people that have problems understanding words like “optimism”, “forecast”, “target”, or “commitment”, be on top of identified assumptions and risks, plan, re-plan, adapt the plan, re-plan some more, monitor and control the execution of the project, make sure that the people who have to talk actually talk to each other, handle change and keep scope creep under control, deal with the project (inevitably) being late by “acting” instead of “reacting”, and constantly hold up a sign with what “success” means for the project.

I also mentioned many of the things from the previous paragraph when I talked about being a Team Lead. Quite often, I saw Project Managers with similar responsibilities. Like a Team Lead, the Project Manager can become the voice and image of the project and, by extension, of the team working on the project. You have to be a bullshit umbrella, assign and delegate work (while you still remain responsible and accountable for the results), deal with people constantly, deal with conflicts, seeing people as more than resources in a Gantt diagram, being fair, knowing when to impose an approach or making a trade-off, understanding when to incur technical debt and when not to, bridging the gap between Business and IT, look for solutions to any kind of problems with the team, etc. As a manager, you will be responsible for the efficiency of your team. To be fair, a Project Manager is more focused on the project and its form of organization, while a Team Lead is focused more on the team and on the technical aspects, but as the two (team and project) cannot be separated, inevitably the roles of Project Manager and Team Lead often overlap.

But there is always a difference: if you are a developer turned Team Lead, you can still do programming, “to sit with your ass in two boats”, as I called it. If instead, you became a Project Manager, you can kiss writing code goodbye.

Project Manager first

The manager role is different from that of a Team Lead or a developer. Even if you can do something better, because you are, or were, the best developer in the team, it doesn’t mean you can still do it. Your job as a Project Manager is not to do the work but to make it so that your people can do the work, then also make sure the work actually gets done. If nobody else but you knew how to do something or if you were entirely in charge of a certain aspect of the project, teach someone else to do it and perform a handover. You can no longer keep development tasks for yourself; you can’t mix the “the manager’s schedule” with “the maker’s schedule”[106], even if you try to put your coding sessions as meetings of 4 hours or more each. So you need to focus on management knowledge and build a new toolset when you become a Project Manager. Don’t wing it. Make an effort to limit the trials and errors. Try hard to truly understand the profession and educate yourself as a Project Manager. Take your new role seriously, because if you don’t, what happens is that you will tend to do project management activities just to get rid of them because you dislike them, or rather, because you like other things better and you want to do those instead. You will try to stay close to the technical aspects of the project. You will still behave like a developer but now with more decision-making power, because of the new position you have in relation to the team. If you’re this kind of a manager, decide what you want to do, management or development, because you can’t do both. Compared to a Team Lead where you can still be hands-on on development work, as a Project Manager, you don’t do that anymore. Excel and Outlook are your new IDEs now. Get used to that.

And not only will you not be able to do development anymore, but if you insist on it, all sorts of other things might happen. For example, you might become a bottleneck and cause the team’s performance to suffer since you can’t write code while you manage, or vice versa. You also risk and focus strictly on technical benefits and neglect the business benefits of the project. If developers have a whim for using a particular technology, framework or language, to refactor or rewrite something that is not necessarily needed to be changed, you could fall into the trap of indulging them in doing so, when maybe you shouldn’t. Or you might not want to incur technical debt, although, given the situation, that might be the best thing to do for the project and the business. Technical debt makes sense only from a business perspective, not from a technical one. If you still think like a developer and still continue to write code, what you are doing is focusing on minutiae and risk losing sight of other important things. You might miss the big picture, or you can forget to look ahead and scan for signs of dark clouds gathering on the horizon, and then you find yourself under heavy rain with no umbrella. And then you start responding to problems instead of trying to anticipate them.

A good manager should try to anticipate problems before they happen. All that “monitoring and controlling” activity means to constantly look where you are, where you want to go, and decide what actions to take to get there. Looking ahead is important for that. There will be problems along the way, and instead of just responding, you want to anticipate and prevent them. But some bad managers just respond. Something happens, and they respond. Some other thing happens, and they respond. And so on. Of course, you can’t anticipate anything, and sometimes shit happens, and you just have to respond to that, but other things can be seen coming from a mile away. But only if you pay attention. The things you respond to can be of various types. For example, they might be failures to “monitor and control”. The manager is just assuming everyone is working on what they need to be working on and that everyone’s work will be delivered on time. Then all of a sudden, the project is one month behind schedule. Only then does the manager get involved. “Why did this happens? Why didn’t you tell me?” Well… why didn’t you ask? Instead of keeping an eye on the ball to see what is happening and what could be done to prevent delays or at least minimize them, they get involved only when the damage is done and broken things now need fixing. And of course, the first thing they reach for, and sometimes the only one, is imposing overtime. Another example I can think of would be some event that’s known in advance, but the manager never bothers to tell developers until it’s too late. “Hey guys, the contract with such and such provider expires at the end of the year. We need to integrate a new provider before the new year starts… next week”. I’ve even seen situations when a single developer was working on some project, with the manager asking from time to time, “How is it going, Jack? Fine! How is it going, Jack? Fine!”. Then six months later, Jack resigns and leaves. And surprise… Jack didn’t do Jack shit. A similar thing might happen with project dependencies. Your project can’t move forward unless some other team does their part first, but instead of watching the dependency and monitor its progress, or keeping communication channels open, they just agree on a delivery date. Then that date comes and goes, and the manager sees an unmet dependency… so time to respond to the situation.

Those are just a few examples of problems first being allowed to happen and then solved, instead of being prevented. The manager waits for something to occur before they start managing. Obstacles are removed when they become blockers, not before the team encounters them. The manager is not proactive, and when they wait for things to happen, they inevitably become a chief firefighter. “Drop everything you’re doing right now and work on this problem”. That’s basically the style. And this style causes some problems of its own. First of all, urgent things take the place of important things. You focus on the problem just to make it go away, and you can neglect some consequences or the long-term impact of the fix. Because you react to problems, you might go for the first solution that goes through your head, without thinking in depth about what might be the best solution. To find the best solution, you need to take some time to gather the facts, spend some time to sketch out some pros and cons, take time to then go through the solutions and select the one that seems the most appropriate. But when you are up to your years in the problem, you will not take the time to think deeply about it but instead jump straight to trying fixes, because doing something seems better than doing nothing. But you will have no guarantee that you’re performing the right actions since you are basically doing damage control. Instead of doing fire prevention, with more solutions available to you, now that things are on fire, you have only one choice: the “water hose” (often accompanied by imposing overtime and putting lots of pressure on the team). What you are doing is apply a bandage, like a doctor who, instead of preventing disease, now has to treat the symptoms. Don’t let problems occur; try to prevent them. And whatever you do, don’t ignore problems. If you ignore them, they rarely go away; they just get bigger and bigger.

Responding to things when they occur is just like texting while driving. You don’t pay enough attention to what’s gonna happen on the road, and you might identify critical situations too late. A good Project Manager pays attention to the road and practices defensive driving. They allow for unseen hazards, account for road conditions, anticipate what mistakes other participants in traffic will make, look further ahead, keeps an appropriate following distance from the vehicle ahead so that they have enough space and time to maneuver around bad situations. They look ahead, not just in front of the car, because they want to avoid pedestrians, instead of reacting desperately and turning the wheel violently to avoid them ending up on the car’s bonnet. Unlike someone who just took a driving exam, an individual practicing defensive driving knows more strategies and has more skills to safely drive a vehicle and prevent accidents before they happen. As a manager, to be able to recognize problems, prevent them, or be better equipped to handle them when they occur, you need knowledge and a rich toolset of project management skills. So you must invest in your training as a Project Manager.

Overdoing it

But there is also the reverse of the medal. You can come across a Project Manager who actually has a proper project management formal education… too much project management formal education. They have all the certifications that a Project Manager might wish for, and they are not afraid to use them. I’m not saying there is a problem with having knowledge, skills, and know project management techniques. It’s not. But some managers become obsessed with these things. And here comes the problem. Just as a developer sometimes becomes obsessed with applying all the design patterns from the “Gang of Four” book[128] because they think that will give them a good design of the application and a good quality of the software, in the same way, a Project Manager like the one I refer to here thinks that if they apply to a tee everything they have learned from books and project management certifications, in the same way, the result is guaranteed and the project will be a success. If they apply everything “by the book”, things can only turn out for the best, right?

Instead of being pragmatic, this type of manager exaggerates by placing all sorts of systems, processes, and procedures in place. Everything must be documented in great detail and uploaded on a shared drive with a well-defined folder structure, meeting minutes in one place, project requirements in another, with documents classified by type and purpose, where later you can’t find the information you are looking for because of the sheer number of files and end up being prosecuted like a common criminal if you forget to upload the files at the right time, or you copy them in the wrong location or omit to notify all persons in the distribution list of that document list that’s clearly defined on page 147 of the working procedure described in the document “coreproj_t021_work_proc_v6.32_20191102_new(final).docx” which you clearly never read you bastard, otherwise you would have known who all the recipients are, and you would have sent the notification on Wednesday, not on Thursday as you did.

And every feature must be planned in excruciating detail and split into one-hour tasks. Each task must be assigned to a developer, a tester, or a code reviewer and must always reflect the true status of the work being performed. Every day, before leaving for home, people need to update each of the tasks with their new status. And of course, work must be tracked using time-consuming tools from which the manager can extract beautiful reports with a single click of a button, on which developers are forced to waste a lot of their time using it instead of an Excel file with ten lines that would have probably done the same thing, but much more efficiently. And everything needs to be formal; nothing has to happen if person A or B has not explicitly given their consent. “Want to change a label? Did you perform an impact analysis? Do you have approval for the change? Who signed the approval?” Everything is rigid, constrained, and artificial. Whether it is important or not, for everything, there is a procedure, some steps to follow, some well-defined actions that must be done exactly as described in the documentation. Everything becomes excessive: excessive planning, excessive documentation, excessive formalization, excessive need for approval, etc. Flexibility and creativity go out the window, and everything is transformed into a ritual that must be followed to the letter. It’s just another form of command and control… in bureaucratic form. Nobody can make any decision on their own unless it falls in between the rules put in place by the procedure (i.e., developers can’t be trusted with decisions, so the procedure makes decisions for them). I’ve seen situations in which a change took five minutes to code but a few hours to document who requested it, why, who did the change, who tested it, why a certain solution was chosen and not another, who performed the code review, who approved the deploy, and who deployed it. Heaven forbid if the feature then caused some bug. You would fix it in a few minutes but then never see the end of it… And every time something happened that was not covered by the procedures or incorporated by the process, things had to be added to the procedures and process to improve them. It was like unit testing for Project Managers: just like when you add a unit test for each new bug you discover, in the same way, you enhance the procedure for each new situation that the procedure doesn’t cover (yet!) so that the next time you know what to do. And if you are lucky, the procedure is adapted to match the work, although I’ve seen countless cases in which the work was forced to match the procedure just as smoothly as trying to get a square peg through a round hole.

In an earlier chapter, I gave a cruise ship business example and mentioned that at some point, a company might need a new ship built. A ship gets built on a shipyard. Have you ever seen a naval shipyard? There is a lot of scaffolding around the ship, cranes everywhere, train tracks, all sorts of welding equipment, power transformers, materials, and so on. Everything needed to support the building of the ship. The kind of Project Manager I’m talking about here is the one that ends up putting more work and effort into the shipyard than into the ship itself. The shipyard becomes more important than the ship. It’s all about having the well oiled naval shipyard, and then the ship comes out perfectly at the end. Likewise, in software projects: the processes must be done right, the procedures must be followed precisely, reports, meetings, approvals, documentation, all must be perfectly executed, and the software comes out as it should, right? Wrong!

The disadvantage with an approach in which you are focusing on having or using the perfect process isn’t just that you have no guarantee that the product will come out properly in the end, but also that all things will take forever to be built. I mentioned previously that, from my experience, the project management overhead amounts to about 20% of the execution time of building a product and that you have to account for this time when estimating things and building schedules. Well, if you have a heavy process in place, this time overhead will be more than 20% because if you are obsessed with having the perfect process before you work on the product or do anything else that is not yet covered by your procedures, you will first need to update the procedures. In other words, the scaffolding around the ship gets bigger and bigger until it will start to get in your way, big time. A heavy process is inappropriate for building software, and it becomes rigid because there are many unknowns in developing software, and at any time, any kind of situations can occur that were not initially requested, planned, or estimated, and that won’t fit nicely inside the scaffolding that you have put in place.

Many fall into this trap because that’s how many project management books are written. You see well-defined processes, with instructions on what to do at every step, what are the procedures you need to have in place, what needs to happen, this document needs to be used, these are the inputs for this process, these are the outputs, these are the tools used, etc., well-defined boxes that you need to fill with the right thing at the right time. When poor project management is the reason why a software project fails, many think it’s because what is written in the books was not respected, when in fact, sometimes, it’s precisely because there has been too much emphasis on what is written in the books. With all those well-defined processes in there, you might form the (wrong) idea that things are predictable and that they unfold in a well-defined order. But it’s not like that. The reality is more chaotic, more disorganized, more random. Software projects are not well-behaved beasts. A winning solution is something specific to a project. Use the project management best practices and tools to look for answers when something occurs because you can’t simply lay out everything from the start and expect things to fall into place as the project unfolds. On most projects, that will never happen.

On the other hand, you can’t go without any processes or procedures. That’s not good either. You need some kind of structure in place. But you have to know how to put just enough of it in place so that it doesn’t become too rigid. Processes and procedures can’t always model reality, especially when it comes to software development. So when reality doesn’t play well with the processes and procedures you’ve put in place (just as when you make plans and reality contradicts them), don’t try to hold on to them too much. What’s important is to produce quality software that brings value. The processes and procedures you use are secondary to the product, not the other way around. Heavyweight processes and procedures don’t guarantee the success of the project; they only guarantee that the developers will be pissed off because they always have to do something else than code. Good developers - people who understand what’s important - are proactive and don’t wait to be told what to do, are better to have than a good process. Sometimes Project Managers need to back off, let their people work, and keep just enough tools in place to make sure they work on the right thing. The shipyard must not become so big that you can no longer see the ship being built inside of it.

Just another boss

Then, another problem I’ve often seen with bad managers is that they don’t consider themselves part of the team. What do managers do, after all? They manage things and people. So some of them think they are above the development team. They don’t work “within” the team; the team works for them. So they think of themselves as more important than the people who do the actual work. The primary failure of such managers is when they manage people. They see the team only as an execution unit. The manager might have to deal with details of that execution unit (i.e., deal with individual people from the team), but they don’t regard them as more than that: execution units, tasks of equivalent resources as bars in a Gantt diagram, beautifully aligned, with one bar starting where a previous bar ended. This type of managers are the ones for which jokes like the following get invented:

A young Programmer and his Project Manager board a train headed through the mountains on its way to Wichita. They can find no place to sit except for two seats right across the aisle from a young woman and her grandmother. After a while, it is obvious that the young woman and the young programmer are interested in each other because they give each other looks. Soon the train passes into a tunnel, and it is pitch black. There is a sound of a kiss followed by the sound of a slap.

When the train emerges from the tunnel, the four sit there without saying a word. The grandmother is thinking to herself, “It was very brash for that young man to kiss my granddaughter, but I’m glad she slapped him”.

The Project Manager is sitting there thinking, “I didn’t know the young tech was brave enough to kiss the girl, but I sure wish she hadn’t missed him when she slapped me!”

The young woman was sitting and thinking, “I’m glad the guy kissed me, but I wish my grandmother had not slapped him!”

The young programmer sat there with a satisfied smile on his face. He thought to himself, “Life is good. How often does a guy have the chance to kiss a beautiful girl and slap his Project Manager all at the same time!”

People from the team notice that the manager does not see them as partners. So they don’t consider the manager to be their partner either. They see the manager as part of the “other side”, the business side. There will eventually be frictions between the manager and the team because the manager focuses on managing the project and ignores or makes too little effort to manage the team. According to a Gallup study [129], only one in ten people have the talent to manage others. So you can imagine that many Project Managers will perform poorly when it comes to elements of “human nature”, and not necessarily because of project management knowledge or skills. All projects have a human component. Some managers are better able to manage that component, others less so.

A manager like that, who considers themselves “outside the team”, won’t back the team when needed. If it happens for the manager to have a bad boss as described in the previous chapter, the situation becomes even worse. The manager is the image of the project, the voice of the project; they are responsible for the project and made accountable for everything that happens on the project. And I mentioned already, when a problem occurs or there is bad news to communicate, the Project Manager ends up having stressful discussions with the bad boss, who can get angry, start screaming, and threatening to fire people. If you contradict a boss like that in support of your opinions or those of the development team, the boss will first think that there is something wrong with you, before wondering (if at all) if they are the one in the wrong. And the boss also wants to have the last word most of the time. People have to come to them with arguments supported by evidence; the boss can just pound the table with their fist while saying something. And when you go against your boss, most of the time you’ll lose. This is the reality, and it’s a lesson that any Project Manager learns quickly. As I said, it’s part of the job description when you are a Project Manager. But that doesn’t mean you have to enjoy it. Nobody wants to end up in situations like this, and it’s normal for anyone to try to avoid them. The problem with a manager who doesn’t consider themselves part of the team is that they will put less effort into doing the right thing for the project and for the team when getting caught in such a situation with their boss. To give a few examples, instead of explaining that estimates are just estimates (optimistic, and often wrong), to explain that the team can’t work under pressure indefinitely, that it doesn’t always help to add more people to a project to finish it in less time, clearly state that developers are not lazy or stupid and often have better information about a situation, so it’s best to hear them out before dismissing their opinions, or their suggestions, to name just a few, the Project Manager instead sides with the boss. Because it’s simpler, safer, and with less harmful consequences. The manager and the team members are not “in it together”, so to speak, so the manager is no longer a mediator, is no longer the voice of reason, but turns into a proxy for their boss. A proxy who takes orders from above and just passes them on. In other words, they no longer do their job as a Project Manager (you know… the knowledge, the skills, the tools, the techniques) but become another boss. There are still some chances of them being “shot” as the messenger of bad news, but now the team is made to bear most of the blame if something happens.

When you have a manager who acts like a boss, and not as a Project Manager, things spin out of control on the project. Developers were dragged through meetings and discussions, they were asked for estimates, they had to sit down for planning, schedules were built, milestones defined, all those things that define what to do and how to do it, and as soon as people start working, it’s all discarded and thrown out the window. Work is erratic, priorities keep changing, what was a priority yesterday is no longer today, or vice versa. New development keeps being added, the scope of the project is constantly increasing, and everything is urgent, and all is needed “yesterday”. And developers soon realize what’s causing all of this: the combination of a bad boss and a manager who doesn’t know how to say “no” to the boss and does anything the higher powers want, no matter the consequences (for the team and the project of course, not for the Project Manager).

But knowing when to say “No” is a critical project management skill. Without it, a lot of problems occur, especially relating to project scope. It becomes more important what the boss wants “noooooow” than what is best for the project in the long run. Long-term objectives get sacrificed for short-term gains (assuming they even are gains). But the long-term objective will also have to be reached; that’s what the project is all about after all. So near the end of the project, everybody will be forced to start working overtime to catch up on all the time the team wasted with the changes demanded by the boss or because the Project Manager allowed them to change direction as many times as they wanted, because they had a fixed idea about something, or because they’ve read something in a leaflet when they were waiting in line at the toilet of an airport and thought that “we absolutely need this”.

Inevitably, changes will occur after you’ve planned a project, as I mentioned in a previous chapter. Some of these changes are important and will need to be done, but some are often whims or gold plating requests coming from the boss. In such cases, when the boss wants something, the manager must see if the requirements are anchored in reality, and if not, they should intervene and bring some common sense into the whole thing, reasoning with key stakeholders not to push for things into the project that are not important, to be a mediator between what the boss wants and what the development team can do effectively. Basically, they need to tell the boss that “Look, these are all the things that must be done, and this is what the team can do; choose the ones you want, because we can’t deliver all of them”. Project Managers should keep the boss at bay and let the team work on what is really important. But many managers prefer to side with the boss and unconditionally accept any new requests. Then, they put pressure on developers to make the new changes, but at the same time, to abide by the initially agreed schedules. Instead of trying to reject the unnecessary extra work, they add it on top of what already needs to be done while keeping the same deadlines. If the developers want to add something to the project (framework, language, etc.), something that was not initially discussed and agreed upon, this change is immediately rejected by the manager, or developers have to perform an analysis, come up with arguments, evaluate the impact. But any change the boss wants is immediately accepted, and it’s a fucking priority. It becomes evident to developers that the manager is not on their side and that they are just cattle hitched up to a plow, and they have to pull at it whenever the boss cracks their whip. And the Project Manager is “the whip”, who then starts to obsessively ask if it’s finished and how much longer does it take.

Then, if the boss can do whatever they want and the manager doesn’t even try to reason with them, then the boss will start to get the idea that all of their ideas are good and that the Project Manager is there to follow orders, not someone with whom they should consult with, in all aspects related to the organization of the project. When you don’t say “No” to the boss, not only does the scope of the project change uncontrollably but from that moment on, “anything goes”. The boss can go directly to developers and ask for things, bypassing any form of organization you, as the Project Manager, have put in place. You can also easily end up with a death march on your hands because the boss was utterly clueless and made a promise to someone to deliver the project on a delusional deadline before consulting with their Project Manager or their team first.

Sometimes the Project Manager not only doesn’t say “no” to the boss, but they also make matters worse by trying to anticipate what the boss will do or how they will react. They know the boss doesn’t like surprises; they don’t want them to start yelling and losing their temper, so the Project Manager starts to anticipate the things they think their boss will do. “Guys, I can’t possibly go to the boss with this estimate. It’s too large. You added padding, isn’t it? Admit it”. Or “I know you said the end of September at the earliest, but I told the boss beginning of September, so they don’t freak out. We’ll figure it out somehow” (now it’s “we” all of a sudden, but they really mean “you”). “Those changes you wanted to make to improve the performance of the application by 30%, I had to tell them we will double the performance, otherwise they would not have considered it’s worth the effort” (and now you have to double the performance since a 30% improvement will look like a failure). Or “I know you guys want to build a proof of concept first for that new application architecture that you’re unfamiliar with, but I can’t tell the boss we will be spending two full weeks just testing an idea. We need to show progress. Can you guarantee that the result will be a positive one?”. And the examples list could go on.

If the manager doesn’t know to say “No” to the boss, they not only lose their negotiation power but at the same time, they lose the team’s trust in them. Developers see that the manager is just the boss’ minion and figure out that their manager can, at any time, throw them under the bus to avoid looking bad in front of the boss. So they begin defending themselves against some of the manager’s behavior. “The manager thinks we added padding and cuts the estimations? Very well, next time we will add padding; we do the estimate, add 50%, then multiply everything by 2. Did a task take less than what we initially estimated? No problem! We’ll do nothing until the estimated time expires so that the manager doesn’t get any ideas of cutting estimates even more next time. We want to add some technologies that can potentially impact the cost or schedule of the project? We simply add them without telling anyone. We are playing a game of unrealistic schedules and expectations anyway, so why wouldn’t we, the developers, make some of the rules?” And these are just a few other examples that contribute to everyone paying the “trust taxes”[100].

A Project Manager should help the team, not make their lives harder, but because they behave more like a boss than a Project Manager, they end up doing the same crap that a boss does, with the same consequences that result from that. For example, they start ordering people around, “command and control” style. The Project Manager’s boss does command and control with them, why wouldn’t they do the same with the team? They’re not going to take one for the team, so the team better do what they say so that nothing uncontrolled occurs. The Project Manager starts to have the same problem as the boss when it comes to “expectations anxiety”. They get evaluated based on how the project unfolds, so they become stressed out trying to please their boss. For this reason, they want to be in control of things, so they don’t get evaluated on something that the team does, and that’s not to their liking. Unfortunately, though, they start to monopolize the decision-making (unless you count the decisions imposed by their boss), impose solutions, deadlines, and make commitments in the team’s name without consulting with them first. And things don’t turn out well. There is no way they can. Remember that developers are closer to what is happening because they are the ones developing the application. The higher you are in the hierarchy, the further you go from the work, the knowledge and understanding begin to dilute. If the Project Manager does not consider themselves as being part of the team and is on the boss’s side, what they are doing is to distance themselves further from the actual work. You end up with two bosses on one project. The Project Manager is still in charge of the monitoring and controlling of the project, but the project will inevitably suffer as the manager tries to make a good impression, and by doing that, they redefine what the success of the project means; i.e., “whatever the boss wants”. But that’s not the Project Manager’s job.

Yes, the boss wants things, and yes, it’s the Project Manager’s job (together with the team) to find solutions to make it happen. But it’s also the Project Manager’s job to be the voice of reason when certain requirements are detrimental to the project. I’ve met managers who recognized certain requirements to be bad for the product but decided to keep their mouths shut. “If they want shit, we give them shit. The customer is always right. Right?” As a manager, if you start saying or thinking that way, it means that you actually recognize that what is being asked of you is shit. But maybe the boss doesn’t realize it’s crap. Go ahead and explain it to them, and if they insist and they are idiots, and you don’t have a choice, then do your job. Keep the email exchange in which you complained and advised against it (so you don’t take the blame), then go ahead and do what you are told. They are your boss, after all. But don’t immediately say that if they want shit, you will provide them with shit; that’s not what it means to be a Project Manager. It’s your job to challenge the higher powers when needed so that a good product gets built. Many focus on schedules to be done on time, on costs to be kept in check, on the application being packed with features (often, with the manager also looking good during all of it), and so, they neglect quality. They forget that the project must come out well, not just “come out”.

Sure, there are companies whose business is selling shit in a fancy box, or very well tested shit as long as they don’t have to do any maintenance afterward. If that’s the case, it’s not the Project Manager’s job to decide to change the content of the box or its packaging. If the company wants to make money regardless of the consequences of how they do it, the Project Manager is there to support the business. But few companies are like that (because they don’t survive for long). A lot of software applications come out bad not because it was desired, but because it happened. And one of the major reasons why this can happen is for people to no longer ask the important question of “Why are we doing this?” It’s up to the Project Manager to ask this question, but because they become a proxy for their boss, it doesn’t happen anymore, and things slip into chaos because “why this is important” just transforms into “anything goes”.

Remember when I mentioned about autonomy, mastery, and purpose[60] as factors that lead to better performance? If the manager does command and control, they take away autonomy. If they don’t ask “why”, then the “purpose” factor is also affected. It’s hard to find a purpose when people don’t know why they are doing the things they are doing. Why is this important? Why is that needed? Why is it needed now? What happens if we don’t do it now? What happens if we don’t do it at all? The team needs to know why priorities get changed. As a manager, do you really want your development team, the one building the software that will make more money for the company, or offer some competitive advantage, or make operations more efficient, or whatever, to be left wondering about “why” they are doing certain things? Do you want them to figure out what’s going on and what’s really important based only on the different decisions you impose? Sometimes, because they are a proxy for the boss, not even the Project Manager knows why some things have to be done, which is even worse.

Without knowing why something is requested, needed, or important, people will just think it’s because the boss wants it, or the manager wants to avoid upsetting the boss, or to cover their own back. I’ve even encountered a situation when a feature was insisted upon because someone was obsessed with having it. Why were they obsessed? Because they insisted on it on a previous job, on a similar project, in another company, and it wasn’t built. So now they were trying again to get it from their new team. It was unfinished (personal) business, basically. I’ve also seen cases where orders come from the top to improve “this or that” and people didn’t know why. Someone looked over some reports and drew some sort of conclusion that certain aspects needed improvement, so they issued the instruction, and everyone had to make it happen, on the principle of “I say, you do”, to discover later that the report was the issue, there was absolutely nothing wrong with the activity itself.

When the manager is just a proxy doing command and control, chaos occurs, with the same consequences that I mentioned when talking about a boss that creates chaos. And eventually, the developers will start asking themselves their own version of “why?”, like “why should I continue working here?” Or, “why shouldn’t I look for another job?”

The Project Manager must not pass along what the boss asks of them without asking “why”, or worse, let their team wonder “why”. People need information to do a good job. But the manager isn’t giving their team information, just orders. They don’t involve the team in decision-making; they don’t even ask for the team’s opinion. The manager expects the developers to keep them informed of everything, but doesn’t reciprocate with the same, and inevitably ends up doing “mushroom management”[130] and keep the developers in the dark without them knowing what’s actually going on. And to add insult to injury, the developers will probably also be the ones the manager will blame if things turn out bad (‘cause apparently they can’t follow orders). “Mushroom management” is just as getting into a taxi and telling the driver to start the engine then go left, then right, then right again, straight ahead, left, straight, right, left. And then, to top it all off, to also complain that you have arrived at the wrong destination, or that some streets you wanted to take were one-way streets, or that the bridge that you had to cross was closed. Just tell the driver where you want to go, and he’ll use the best route to get there. Depending on what you tell him you want, he might take you on the fastest route, on the shortest path, or maybe you want to visit the city and agree with him to drive by the most important tourist landmarks. On the same train of thinking, just tell developers what you need and why you need it and let them figure it out how to do it, don’t command them at every step.

But a proxy manager, since it’s their neck on the line, does not want to leave things in the hands of the developers. Nor can they acknowledge the nature of the relationship they have with their boss (as if the others don’t already see it). So they fool themselves into believing that “they have this”, that they can make decisions no matter the situation, that they know best; they are the Project Manager, after all, right? And when things don’t turn out the way they want, it’s the developers’ fault, of course - who had no way of knowing (since the manager has kept the information hidden from them), but it should have been obvious to them that that was not how things were supposed to be done. And it’s enough for the team to do something wrong once or twice, and all of a sudden, the manager starts doing micromanagement to make sure they have more visibility into what developers are doing, so they don’t end up again in a similar situation.

And here I must mention another category of bad managers: the “micro”managers. I’ve already mentioned a few things about micromanaging bosses. Bosses micromanage too, but this is more of the managers’ delight. The boss pounds the table with their fist and yells more, or throws tantrums, etc.; however, the manager’s choice is to micromanage. This and the annoying habits of “reportomania”[108] and demanding lots and lots of meetings. I spoke about these too. Many managers micromanage because they think that in this manner, they have control over things. They don’t. Micromanagement is just an illusion of control. All it does is piss off developers because the manager tries to observe and control everything in the smallest details, but they might not understand the work, since they are a manager and not a developer. Even more, when things don’t go the way they want, the manager tends to do even more micromanagement to tighten the control. A good manager should keep everything under a close watch, all the time, to weigh things down, to try to anticipate issues, etc., but not so much that they fall in the trap of micromanagement. All micromanagement does is to trigger employee disengagement and affecting the trust relationship. It’s a sign that the manager doesn’t trust the developers. The developers, of course, notice this and, in turn, start to reciprocate the lack of trust. And again, all this attention to tiny details - for the manager to have the (false) confidence that everything turns out the way they think it should - is detrimental to the attention to bigger things (the “why” I was talking about earlier; micromanaging means focusing on the “how” and trivia instead of on goals and what’s important).

Another problem with micromanagement is that with time, people might get used to it. When that happens, developers have already learned that there is no point in making decisions on their own. If you micromanage and make the decisions, they will just ask you what to do every time, regardless of the situation. But usually, good developers will leave because they are less likely to put up with the situation, and what remains behind are the least skilled people and with fewer demands on management. And as a manager, you can micromanage and order a bad developer around all you like; it ain’t gonna produce the results you expect. And this gets me to the last point I want to make about bad managers. From what I’ve said so far, it probably won’t be hard for you to figure out what it is: the team - the people that actually do the work - is secondary to the bad Project Manager. The manager doesn’t pay too much attention to the people, or they use the wrong management style with them.

Management style

And it’s often easy for the manager to pay little attention to the people. The Project Manager focuses on Gantt charts, plans, schedules, milestones, reports, meetings, and status updates. They focus on tasks and features, on how the work must be done, and on the things that need to support that work, like processes and procedures. A Project Manager manages the project, after all. By the Project Management Institute’s definition, a project is the “temporary endeavor undertaken to create a unique product, service, or result”[125]. An endeavor means trying to do or achieve something, and some managers forget that you can’t do or achieve anything without an actual team of people. They end up not caring about the people, or they don’t see themselves as part of the team, or they side with the boss. The thing is, they neglect the team and end up managing people like robots or spinning wheels inside processes and procedures. They try to avoid dealing with “the human side” of the project equation. If conflicts arise or discussions are needed for appraisals, giving feedback to people or trying to motivate them, for example, they try to avoid these things, or minimize them, or do them quickly in a hurry, or using trivial techniques like “carrots and sticks” that don’t work but are simple to implement. Or they prefer to leave things like that to the Team Lead while the manager doesn’t partake, but just wants to be informed. I’ve seen this often. There is a Team Lead and also a manager, and the Project Manager feels responsible only for the project, not for the team. The team is the Team Lead’s problem. But they forget that without that team, they don’t have a project to manage. And if there is indeed a Team Lead that handles the team, the manager is now already two levels higher than the people doing the work, so it becomes easier for them to make some of the same mistakes a bad boss would make, like thinking developers are interchangeable or easily replaceable, and that cheaper ones can be hired at any time.

So managers need to pay close attention to who actually does the work and be mindful of the management style that they use with them. Based on my experience, many managers have an approach, assumptions, or attitudes that are faulty when it comes to managing software developers. Many managers fail at their job because they apply the “Theory X” type of management. “Theory X” and “Theory Y”[137] was developed in the sixties by professor Douglas McGregor to describe two contrasting aspects of managing employees. In “Theory X”, the manager assumes that people are lazy and avoid responsibility, that they lack ambition and have little motivation, that they need to be told what to do and then need close supervision (sometimes of the micromanaging kind). Other characteristics of “Theory X” are that the manager takes all the decisions, people are seen just as resources, mistakes get punished, and that “carrots and sticks” is a good motivation technique to use. In “Theory Y”, on the other hand, the manager trusts their people and empowers them. The manager believes they are responsible people who don’t need close supervision as they take the initiative and ownership over the work they do and responsibility for its results. The manager has a good relation with team members and involves them in decision making. People have internal motivation, and the manager must bring that to the surface by creating a healthy environment that supports their development, growth, and, ultimately, their productivity.

“Theory X” is an authoritarian style of management, which often leads to an “us versus them” attitude (i.e., management versus employees), while “Theory Y” is a participative style, based on trust and collaboration. The “Theory X” style of management works mostly with assembly-line workers or manual laborers (i.e., cogs in a machine) while “Theory Y” is better suited for knowledge workers, like software developers. Developers often work on new, unique things, which have not been built before, therefore, they need more freedom of movement, and their input is very important when it comes to the work being performed. They are not assembling gizmos on a production line and can’t be managed in that way.

Note, though, that “Theory Y” doesn’t mean to let the developers run the whole show. It doesn’t mean “the freedom to do whatever they want”. That would be chaos. It means that the manager works side by side with developers, and everyone does the job they are best at: developers write code while the manager makes sure that people are moving in the right direction and don’t deviate from the project’s goals. Sometimes, the manager is forced to apply elements from both theories, sometimes they have to lead, sometimes they have to control, with different team members or with the same team members but at different moments in time, or in different contexts, as the situation demands. But the problem I’ve seen in many Project Managers is that they tend to apply “Theory X” most of the time and with almost everyone. And when I say “apply”, I’m not saying that managers know both theories and consciously decide to use one approach or another; I’m saying that’s the way things happen because the focus is only on the project while the team is just an execution unit within the project. It’s the difference between “using the people to do the work” versus “collaborating with them on the work”.

Your attitude as a manager affects the team. When you ignore people or treat them badly, and you don’t create the working conditions for everyone to perform, the team will become demotivated, and morale will drop. And if morale drops, so does productivity. But people’s morale is not on the radar for many Project Managers. It’s up to Team Lead to do that, assuming there is a Team Lead. After all, people are at work to work, not have fun, build relationships, or whatever. To work! This kind of manager doesn’t focus on the team’s morale or the working environment, but then they act surprised when people start leaving. And the first to leave are the good developers, while the project is left with the weak employees, who are not very interested in what’s happening, or they are happy that they still have a job and nobody is firing them. Then, a bad manager will put even more focus on processes and procedures and will resort to more command and control with those people who remain, as if you can save something from a weak team with processes, procedures, and direct instructions. And if you are to remember just one thing from this chapter, remember this: you need a good development team. If you don’t have a good team of developers, you already have a problem that can’t be solved by any amount of project management knowledge, skills, tools, or techniques.
