At the end of the day, it’s people that make projects succeed.

Lost cause

Before ending this chapter, there is one question that needs to be answered: “can you fix a bad Project Manager?”

This has a simple answer. No!

It’s not a “usually no” like I said about fixing bad bosses, it’s a “no”, plain and simple. Unlike a clueless boss who doesn’t know any better, a Project Manager should know better. Anyone can be a boss, but not anyone can be a Project Manager. If the Project Manager tries to be a “know it all” asshole, to a certain extent, you can handle them like a bad boss: you can document everything, so you don’t get the blame for your manager’s mistakes. You can leave the company and move to greener pastures elsewhere. Or, you can accept the situation and do your job to the best of your abilities; if the manager is authorized to take decisions on the project (by themselves or together or as a proxy for their boss), then it’s your job to support those decisions (i.e., you have a job to do no matter if your Project Manager is a good one or a bad one). But you cannot change the Project Manager because that change depends solely on the Project Manager.

A boss may not understand software development or how to manage a software project as they are a business person, but the Project Manager is not someone from the business. They are a person with technical skills who should already know how software gets built since few IT companies hire managers from fields other than software development. A manager is supposed to be a skilled person. Just as a developer must make efforts to learn all kinds of things, so should the manager learn all kinds of techniques and keep themselves current with project management techniques and practices. If they don’t, how can developers change that? Buy them books? Force them to read “Peopleware”[138] at least once per year? Send them to conferences? There is no way. Just like not everyone is cut out to be a programmer/developer, not everyone is cut out to be a Project Manager.

There are a few things though that you could do to improve matters. The first could be to have a face-to-face discussion with your manager, to address your concerns, the things that are not working, or the things that are bothering the team. Talk things out and try to reach an arrangement of some sort. Remember that you have to work side by side with the Project Manager every day. You don’t have less frequent interactions with them as you would with a boss, for example. So it’s worth having a discussion calmly and professionally to try to improve the situation. It most likely won’t be a pleasant discussion, but it’s worth a chance to improve things. Then, what you can do is to go to your Project Manager’s boss, assuming they’re not the kind of boss I described in the previous chapter and that your manager is nothing more than a subordinate to your boss. If there is no nepotism involved or no other relationship exists between the Project Manager and the boss, then for the boss, both the developers and the Project Manager are in the same bucket. If there is a conflict or a problem between the developers and the Project Manager, it’s the Project Manager’s job to deal with the situation; after all, that’s one of the things in the Project Manager’s job description: to handle whatever is going on with the project, be it the development team or something else. If the manager can’t keep their team in check, then the boss sees that as a failure from the part of the Project Manager to do their job. If they get bothered, the boss can fire the manager just as they can fire developers. The last thing you might try to do is get HR involved to have the Project Manager transferred or fired. You might succeed in building a case against the Project Manager by documenting everything. Get your colleagues involved and have them document all the issues also. They are also affected by the same manager and most likely share your same opinions about them. The Project Manager might be a manager by title, but most likely, they’re not part of the higher executives or upper management ranks; therefore, in the grand scheme of things, they are just another employee for HR, instead of a powerful boss. And like the rest of the employees, they also have appraisals or can be fired if there are performance issues regarding them.

Unlike with your boss, if you do go against your Project Manager, there might be some chances of success. But remember that there can always be undesired consequences. Try to find other solutions (like cooperation or finding some other way to make it work) before you decide to get rid of your Project Manager. The boss can fire a developer or the Project Manager just as easily, but the willingness to do so might not be the same in both cases. In a conflict between developers and managers, the company might take the manager’s side. A manager might be seen as more valuable than a person doing the grunt work. Like the rook, the knight, or the bishop on a chessboard, for example, as opposed to pawns. So people might think twice before kicking the Project Manager out. If they produce results, why should they fire them, right? And the irony could be - similar to a bad boss who goes unnoticed - that the team members themselves are productive enough even with a bad manager that it hides the fact that the manager is not good at their job. So if the manager doesn’t make themselves look bad in front of their superiors, then from a broader perspective, for upper management, there seem to be no problems. Even if there are some telltale signs that they might not be the best of managers, chances are bosses don’t understand the long term effects this can have on the team. So ask yourself if it’s worth getting into conflict with the bad Project Manager. Not only are you at risk of looking bad, but there is also a chance you will not get rid of them in the end, and you’ll be stuck with the manager, in which case you must reconsider things since it might become harder to work with them now than it was before you tried to improve things.

There is, of course, the case when the manager is still inexperienced and still learning things, but you can tell if they have potential or not from the way they act. The main telltale signs that they might grow into a good manager can be observed in the way they see and treat people. If they try to assist their team, if they try to clear obstacles, if they try to improve the working environment, if they try to work things out together with everyone involved, if they protect and support the team members in bad decisions taken above, working on making the team more productive, then those are good signs that they can become good Project Managers.

The manager’s function is not to make people work, but to make it possible for people to work - Tom DeMarco and Tim Lister, Peopleware, p.34[138]

Of course, opposites of the bad things I mentioned so far are also a good indicator. If they’re a good communicator, if they are concerned with the “why” and “what” of what needs to be built instead of focusing only on the “how”, if they get involved instead of complaining that you are not doing things properly or not doing them fast enough, if they are eager to deepen their knowledge of project management (not just for what they needed at work, but similar to how a developer who during their free time learns other technologies and languages than the ones they use at work), if they don’t get obsessed with deadlines and costs and are willing to sacrifice anything to get them, if the value that the project brings is important to them, or if they can think further than this week, sprint or milestone. If they have the right approach, everything else can then be learned through training or gathered experience.

Bad developers

You didn’t think I was only going to talk about bad bosses and bad managers, did you? Bad developers can lead you into quicksands just as fast as bad bosses and managers can, if not faster. I insisted since the beginning of this book on the importance of hiring good developers. Since they do the heavy lifting in any software development project, they can make or break it. And with this, I’ll go straight into the first issue about bad developers: developers can be incompetent.

Lack of skills

Developers can lack intelligence, and they can lack skills. You need intelligence to solve problems (developers are first and foremost problem solvers), and you need skills as tools to implement the solutions you came up with. When asked in an interview what the most often-overlooked risk in software engineering is, David Lorge Parnas[139] said it’s “incompetent programmers”[140]. He went on to say that it’s estimated that we need a large number of programmers, but that the estimate is actually misleading:

It is not a quantity problem; we have a quality problem. One bad programmer can easily create two new jobs a year. Hiring more bad programmers will just increase our perceived need for them. If we had more good programmers, and could easily identify them, we would need fewer, not more - David Lorge Parnas

The interview is from 1999, but these statements hold true just as well today. More even, the entry bar in the IT industry is now lower. As an example, when I started in this profession, one needed specialized studies and a graduation diploma in Computer Science to even be considered for the job. These days, with all the newly available, stupid friendly technologies that make it so much easier for clueless people to enter the software development industry, any fool who can spell “computer” is considered a candidate.

When it comes to skills, bad developers are the ones that affect the quality, security, and maintenance of an application. A lack of quality can affect an application in different ways. The application could crash often, it could respond slowly to user commands, it might lose data, or it might not solve the problem it was intended to solve. And these are just the things that can be observed from outside. Usually, quality problems start from within the code. The quality of the code affects the final quality of the product. And the problems can vary from small in size, like badly named variables, methods, and class names, functions with side effects, or abuse of global variables, to other bad coding practices like writing highly coupled code with no separation of concerns, no modularity, to violations of KISS, YAGNI, DRY, SRP, and SOLID principles, or ignoring error handling, having zero tests in place, or having everything hardcoded instead of configurable. Some developers don’t even pay attention to formatting, or think that version control means archived files with a timestamp after the file name. A bad developer is not concerned about such things. Good developers, on the other hand, pay attention to quality from the beginning because they know that quality cannot be stapled onto the application later on. Something similar happens with the security aspects too. You must be aware of them from the beginning, so you avoid nonsense actions like writing passwords into log files or storing them as plain text in the database, so you don’t display error messages that show too many implementation details to the user, to prevent SQL injection and cross-site scripting, to not blindly trust user input, expose administration URLs, or end up with an insecure authentication and authorization mechanism (in regards to this last point, I’ve seen confidential data available to any user all of the time, just not displayed on the screen… by using HTML comments to hide it).

Another thing good developers know and bad ones ignore is the fact that, after the project is delivered or installed into production, there will be changes needed. It’s called maintenance. Maintenance doesn’t just mean bug fixing, increasing reliability, or improving performance; often, maintenance also means upgrading existing functionality to match new business contexts or even adding new features that users realize they need to do their jobs better. But a bad developer does not think about these matters; they think no farther than writing code and deploying it. If the application is running and people are using it, it means it’s over and done, right? It’s not actually like that. I’ve rarely seen software abandoned immediately after it was written. The business environment will change, and the application will have to change with it. If the code is unreadable, if it takes a long time to understand what the code does, if you fix or change something and something else breaks, or it is increasingly difficult to add the necessary features, these may be signs of a bad job being done when building the application. Good developers know that code will be read more times than it will be written, so they make an effort to make it readable, and also to structure, organize, and decouple things properly. Bad developers just want to write the code and call it a day.

The more you work in the industry, the more people you work with, the more projects you work on, the more the chances of stumbling on someone’s disastrous idea of how code should have been written. And sometimes, that bad code you are looking at right now might be your own code from twelve months ago.

That’s another reason why many code bases are bad: because inexperienced people worked on them. One of the software industry’s problems is that many programmers are put in situations way over their heads, they find themselves in positions for which they are not at all prepared, and inevitably they are forced to learn on the jobs. And most of the time, they don’t learn from good, quality code, but from existing code, in whatever form or shape it may happen to be. There are companies where a junior can deploy whatever code they want to the production environment, whenever they want, without a more experienced developer doing a code review or making sure the right thing is being deployed. Then things fail, then things need to be fixed, patched, hacked, or whatever. Imagine, for example, if a doctor would learn how to do surgeries by actually doing surgeries, without receiving proper training and without supervision. That’s unacceptable, right? People’s lives would be put at risk until the doctor finally figures it all out (if at all) and begins to understand the difference between how a bad and a good surgery looks like. But in software development we do that, it’s acceptable, even if in some cases someone’s safety really depends on that software. But a junior is not necessarily a bad developer. They are just not a good developer “yet”. When you lack experience, you inevitably make mistakes and a mess on projects because you just don’t know any better. But that doesn’t mean you’re incompetent; it just means that the industry has a problem as a whole, with many companies not putting enough effort into limiting potential problems that may be caused while an inexperienced person gains the necessary experience.

I won’t talk about inexperienced people in this section or people that were inadvertently thrown too far from their comfort zone that then have to make the best out of the situation by whatever means available to them at the time. We all go through such situations, no matter what we do or in what field of business we happen to work. We pick up bad habits, sometimes we are too pragmatic in solving a situation, and we choose a shortcut, or a hack, or something… anything. But at some point, we become proficient in what we do. We learn new things, we gain proper understanding, we accumulate experience, we discover the correct or efficient ways to do something. In this chapter, I will talk about those categories of programmers that do not become better with time. To keep to the doctor analogy, it’s the doctors who aren’t getting any better even though they continue to perform surgeries. Why is this happening? Mainly for three reasons: they don’t care, they can’t, or there is something wrong with them.

Let’s start with the first category. Some are simply not interested in software development. It’s just a job for them, one like any other. They don’t really care about what they are doing; they just want results, so they don’t get fired - any kind of results. The kind of result you don’t take any pride in is just fine. These kinds of programmers are not really interested in technology or software development; they just want a paycheck. Maybe they became programmers because some of their friends were developers, and they saw them doing well financially. Perhaps they wanted to be able to work from home or keep flexible hours or because they figured it’s a profession in high demand, and it offers some sense of job security. Any other well-paid job with these characteristics would have done; it just happens it’s a job as a programmer.

There is nothing wrong with taking a job just because it pays well or if it has other benefits. But the problem in software development is that you must continuously learn in order to be good at what you do. And this requires time and dedication to the activity. If you are not really interested in what you do, and this is just a job like any other, you will only do what is strictly necessary to keep that job, and nothing more. In other words, your skills are mediocre most of the time.

You can find these programmers everywhere. Look on online programming forums and Q&A websites, for example. It’s those programmers that ask all of those questions that get closed or that can be answered by simply searching for a couple of minutes online then reading the first pages in the search results. But they don’t do that. Why? Because they have a job to do, they don’t know how to do it, and they are not willing to put in the effort of understanding how it’s done properly. Since they are not passionate or genuinely interested in their job, they are not interested in reflecting on the problem to try and acquire the skills to solve it. They only want the solution. They post a question and expect others to solve the problem for them. They are the kind of people that when they get back a response of “It depends. What you are trying to do?” they abandon the question and open another one asking for the same thing but on a more insistent tone.

These are the programmers (‘cause they sure are not developers) who expect to be provided with what they demand without them needing to even try for themselves. They have a job, they have Internet access on a high-speed connection, they even have a salary, but can’t be bothered to search for information to create a solution on their own. They expect other people to do the work for them. This kind of programmers, when they find on a forum some answer that solves 99% of their problem, they post a malicious comment like “I had to look somewhere else for the complete solution”, so they down-voted or clicked the “dislike” button. “Maybe next time, post a complete answer”. If I am to use an analogy, in the saying “give a man a fish, and you feed him for a day; teach a man to fish, and you feed him for a lifetime”, this kind of programmers are the ones who want a fish every day. They are not interested in learning how to fish. They just want the fish. And not just any kind of fish. The finest choice of fish. Wild salmon fished on the line. These people will never be good developers because - to keep with the analogy - they don’t want to pick up the fishing rod. Somehow they manage to get fish every day so that they don’t starve or attract attention to the fact that they can’t really fish.

The second category of bad developers, when it comes to skills, are those developers who, even if they are interested and passionate about what they do, they aren’t good at it. They get excited as soon as they see some new technology or framework, or attend a conference and are dazzled by what they found out while there. Everything is cool and exciting for them; they want to become “hackers” (whatever that means for them)… but they just can’t do it. They practice, they work hard, but the skills don’t seem to stick to them. Stuff doesn’t “click”. As in any other profession, there are those who are good at what they do and those who are not. And this begs the question: are good developers born or made? And again, just as with any other occupation, the answer is always “both”. Your brain has to be wired in a certain way for what you are doing; otherwise, things don’t “click”. Of course, as a programmer or developer, it’s not enough to just be talented. If you have a talent but don’t practice it or invest the proper amount of time into the activity, to acquire knowledge and tune your skills, then you will most likely suck. But if you are not talented or don’t have a gift for an activity, practice alone might not get you in the same league as someone who is also talented at it. Let’s take painting as an example. I, for instance, can paint if I set my mind to it, but I can’t paint something people will want to spend money on or hang at home on the wall. I’m just not good enough for that. Technical drawings I can do. Sketches, diagrams, plans, I can do that. But art? I don’t have what it takes for that, and no amount of practice or investment of time in that activity is going to make a significant difference. With my abilities, I might be an architect, but by no means an artist painter. Something is missing, something innate. Some are born with this “something” in large quantities, others in smaller amounts, but it must be there; it can’t be absent. And here comes the catch. How do you know if you have that talent or not? And in what quantity? The answer is that you have to do the activity and keep an eye on your progress. If you think good programmers are born, you will not try to write any code, and you will never know if you would have been good at it or not. The idea is to try and see. But the reverse is also true. If you think good programmers are made, you will put a lot of effort into this activity, and you will ignore the signs that show that being a developer isn’t for you. You might be a hard worker, but if what you are doing doesn’t get easier with time… something is not right. And with this category of programmers that I’m mentioning here, things tend not to improve over time, or progress is very slow. This category of developers is like football fans that can’t play any football. They love the sport, have a favorite team, know all the stats and scores, they take part in the community, but when they play the actual sport, their game is mediocre at best. They can be the first to show up on the field and the last to leave the locker rooms, they can practice dribbling, shooting, tackling, study other players’ game, etc., but nothing does the job. They fail to become professionals.

A common trait I’ve often seen with this type of developer is that they usually don’t ask for help. Deep down, I think they know they are not made for this job, but they try to prove to themselves that they can make it by stamina and hard work alone. And instead of asking someone more experienced for help, they then try even harder to learn things without knowing on what to focus more, so they fill their heads with all kinds of information that manages to confuse them even more.

And finally, the third category: the “disturbed” individuals. I’ve tried to find another word to express what I want to say, but unfortunately, I can’t find a kinder word to describe these programmers. To be completely honest, “disturbed” is a bit of an understatement. In this profession, you will inevitably encounter all kinds of examples of “how not to develop software”, ranging from code that you can joke about, bad code, very bad, extremely bad, and up to horribly bad or abysmal code. But there is another category beyond all these when it comes to badly written code, a special category that bears the name of the individual who wrote it. That’s how uniquely bad the code is. These individuals have a special ability: they can write obfuscated code. Obfuscated code is produced by tools, but on rare occasions, you can find someone that can write obfuscated code without even trying. There are such people. I’ve met a few.

I remember one person in particular that stands out from the rest. What did this man do, you ask? Let’s say he liked spaghetti. No, not the Italian pasta. Spaghetti code. That’s how he wrote the core module of a web application me and some other miserable souls later working on. This was the module on top of which the rest of the application was raised, and for some time, he was the only one in charge of that module. Enhancements, bug fixing, whatever it was, he was the one doing the changes. It was an overall bad idea to have just one person handling a very crucial part of the application, but the team was small, so inevitably, everyone become masters over some modules and not others. In time, the development moved towards higher modules of the application, so the core developer - with fewer and fewer things to do - moved to greener pastures… as one normally does. No handover, no documentation. “Just read the code; it’s self-explanatory”. And indeed, it was self-explanatory, but not in the way anyone expected.

There were classes with thousands upon thousands of lines of code, all of it contained in just one method. Well, there was one exception; a class contained two methods. But as we found out later, it was only because the first method exceeded 64 kilobytes in byte code when you tried to add more code to it, and the compiler would throw a “code too large” error. If I think about it, all classes having just one method was the only thing that was consistent throughout the entire module - that, and the fact the code was horrific everywhere you looked. Magic numbers everywhere, variable names with no obvious meaning whatsoever, sometimes even misleading names, parameters of type Object with “instanceof” tests that sometimes were cast directly, in full confidence, to one class type or another, code duplication everywhere but with subtle differences that didn’t allow you to refactor the code into something more reasonable, code filled with global variables from which you could never determine in which state the application was, code with twisted logic, most of the methods were public static final (this was a Java application but there was no use of OOP principles anywhere, everything was procedural). There was code that seemed to do nothing, but when you removed it, the application would crash in mysterious ways. This was a “fun way” to discover new ways the module worked. We would add code that threw exceptions when the seemingly unused sections got executed and when you saw the exception, everyone would gather around you to ask what steps you took to trigger the execution of that piece of code. But that didn’t always work as many exceptions were caught and swallowed. Then, the nastiest thing was that all of the code was a long series of nested “if”s that tested if some string code is contained in some string parameter, and you could never figure out at what position in the string that code was or how long the code itself was. It was mostly three characters long, but occasionally some four-character code showed up from some obscure XML file or some code that was using reflection. You see, somehow this individual figured out that the best way to exchange information with the front-end was by either passing around long numbers that were actually two or three numbers stored into a single long variable, at different bit positions, then using bit masking to get them back, or by moving around strings of concatenated values with no delimiters whatsoever. If for the numbers we had the bitmasks and could figure out which is which, for strings, you had to somehow know the positions, which, as I said, were not fixed. Various sections of the code looked for the same substrings at different positions. If you messed with those strings in the wrong way, the “if”s got all messed up, and various pieces of code ended up being executed at random. The same would have occurred if some of those two or three numbers stored as a long happened to overflow their allocation, which by some miracle, never happened.

It was a complete nightmare to debug or make changes to that code. Nobody got it right the first time. Or the second… You usually had to roll back your changes and try your luck one more time. Having an encounter with the code was like having an encounter with a bear in the forest. You peacefully go about your business, singing hiking songs, and you suddenly see a bear in front of you. You stop, freeze for a few seconds, then very slowly and without making any loud noises or sudden movements, you’d back up the way you came from. Everyone was hesitant to touch that code, and everyone thought that the company would have gotten the better end of the deal if they paid this individual to stay at home and do nothing, far, far away from any of the company’s computers. In the end, all that horrible code managed to be isolated in one section of the application. The code was practically confined there like a monster imprisoned inside a cave, then sealed with a powerful magic spell and a warning sign placed at the entrance to the cave for anyone foolish enough to dare enter.

Poor attitude

Then comes another kind of developers. They have excellent skills, innate talent, and passion for programming; they are continually updating their knowledge and constantly try to become better. But… they have a problem - an attitude problem. They have a huge ego, they are arrogant, stubborn, think the world revolves around them, and they don’t play well with others. Just like there is a greater chance to encounter a psychopath in a managerial position than finding one in the general population, when it comes to software developers, there is a higher probability than in other circumstances to stumble onto a “prima donna”. Wikipedia does a good job at describing what a “prima donna” is:

From its original usage in opera, the term has spread in contemporary usage to refer to anyone behaving in a demanding or temperamental fashion or having an inflated view of oneself and a narcissistic attitude[141]

I will continue to use the term developer when referring to the prima donna, although it would be more honest to use the term programmer. That’s because the prima donna just wants to program, and nothing else interests them. Prima donnas are very skillful programmers. They are very good at what they do, also because - in lack of a better way of saying it - they don’t get distracted by anything else.

Prima donnas are very passionate programmers, but they often lack social skills and emotional control. They affect the morale of teams because they are always confrontational to anyone who doesn’t share the same passion, view, or opinion as they do, which usually is everyone else. Prima donnas know they are very skillful programmers, and they make sure everyone else knows it too. But it doesn’t stop here. The prima donna goes on to explain to everyone how incompetent they are in comparison. Everyone disagreeing with the prima donna’s opinions is immediately dismissed as incompetent. All prima donna’s decisions are right, all other decisions are clearly wrong, but everyone is too blind to see it. They don’t shy away from making rude comments about other developers’ work or rewriting their code without telling anyone, just because they know how to do it better. When someone gets something wrong, the prima donna will happily explain to them the mistake… or better said… rub it in their face. The prima donna thinks he’s passionate, while everyone else thinks he’s angry and treats people poorly. And I’m using the “he” pronoun because most prima donnas you will encounter will be men. The best way to describe a prima donna is as a “passionate asshole”. The relationship between the prima donna and the others is affected, and they start to resent him. And that’s easy to do against someone who isn’t a team player, thinks he is always right, and everyone is wrong, wants to have the last word in any conversation, easily insults people, lacks patience, and tends to immediately overreact when someone makes a mistake, no matter how small. A talented programmer with a diva attitude can wreak havoc in teams and projects, especially if he’s a senior put in charge of many aspects of the application.

Another thing is that the prima donna does pretty much whatever he wants, whenever he wants. He’s picky on what he works on, doesn’t work on bugs unless he has no other choice, allows no one to touch his code (his code is perfect, everyone else’s code is garbage, so he doesn’t want others ruining it), work schedules don’t apply to him, meetings are for other people (unless it’s about some technology and he’s the one presenting, in which case everyone must attend), will learn non-job-related technologies on company time (the project will have to wait, I guess), and can easily waste even more time on some forum or website, contradicting someone who wrote a blog about the comparison between framework A and framework B and he doesn’t like it. And he’s usually allowed to behave like this. As I said, prima donnas are very skilled and talented people. They might be essential for the project and very hard to replace. Any average programmer behaving like this wouldn’t be tolerated, but for the prima donna, management often decides to look the other way.

Handling a prima donna situation is hard on management. That’s because you have to look at the entire situation, not just at what the prima donna is doing. The skills of the prima donna are important, might even be essential, but at the end of the day, when you put them into balance with all the problems the prima donna causes and all the contributions the rest of the team is making, can you say it’s always a positive outcome? What’s more useful, a team of good developers with various skills that complement each other, or a very skillful person in just one or a few specific areas? Does the prima donna reduce or increase collective performance? Will the diva’s behavior drive away all the other developers in the team? What level of turnover are you willing to accept before you do something about it?

Sometimes, prima donnas are not intentional assholes; they are simply not aware of what they are doing. Sometimes you can sit with the prima donna and have a discussion of the sort of “you do realize what you are doing, and how you are behaving, right?” and be surprised to discover that he doesn’t. And often, it’s not just exclusively his fault; it’s also everybody else’s fault by accepting the prima donna’s behavior and not saying anything. They sit there and stew in their own juices, feeling bitter about his behavior instead of saying something to the prima donna. It’s like having a neighbor who continues to listen to loud music without realizing they are bothering everyone else until someone knocks on their door and tells them to turn the music down. Such a discussion sometimes helps, but many managers don’t even try because they are afraid of upsetting the diva who can then decide to leave. But by failing to address the issue, what they manage to do in the process, is to sacrifice other members of the team.

You also have to be aware that you might slowly lose not just your team in this way, but also your prima donna. You might not be willing to fire your prima donna, but he might leave on his own. That can happen for various reasons. Sometimes because he can’t stand working with these mere mortals that don’t give him the needed attention when he’s (constantly) whining. Or some other company might give him more authority or cooler things to play with. Or maybe so many people from your team have already left that now the diva needs to do their mundane work too, which of course he will not like or will not be able to do, depending on the skills that are necessary. The prima donna is an excellent programmer because he’s a specialist, but he doesn’t know everything well, like things other team members might be responsible for.

A situation like this always feels like driving a super sports car at high speed; you might get faster from point A to point B, but you also risk losing control of the car and, on the way there, crash it into a ditch. Sometimes that might be OK. You take the prima donna and unleash him on some prototype or proof of concept that you need to be done fast. You know the prima donna will do it with great chances of success, especially since he’s working alone. But sometimes this is not OK. On most projects, you need people with the right skill sets that can work well together, not a super talented individual that’s hard to work with. Keep these things in mind when you decide what to do with your prima donna.

And unfortunately, you encounter attitude problems in many other developers, not just in prima donnas (although, in prima donnas, those are exaggerated). Most developers want to be cool, become hackers, ninjas, gurus, developer advocates, software evangelists, or anything else with a “chill factor” in the title. And it doesn’t stop there. Developers compare themselves with others and evaluate themselves relative to peers. It’s one reason why online community forums have reputation points or some reward system that shows who the best contributors are. People try to gain points in the eyes of others, be it online or in their group of friends or colleagues. They try to be cool and impress others by how much they know or by what they can do. They use vim for everything, compile their own web server, build their own frameworks, write inline assembly in C, program robots or drones in Lisp, or whatever. And they also try to avoid uncool stuff. It’s uncool not to use TDD for everything. It’s uncool not to use the same frameworks the coolest startups are using. It’s uncool not to attend the most awaited meetup of the year. It’s uncool not to know all the shortcut keys from your IDE… oh, sorry… vim. It’s uncool not to know the most obscure thing about your programming language of choice.

Developers like technologies. And they also like to start “holy wars”[142]. Windows or Linux? Java or C#? Chrome or Firefox? OOP or FP? Batman or Superman? Star Trek or Star Wars? Tabs or spaces? A lot of programmers think that their favorite ”{insert language/framework/tool/paradigm/etc., here}” is the best. And when developers find themselves in a debate about such things, they react as if you insulted their mother or something. It’s no longer just a difference of opinions; it’s personal. It’s human nature to be subjective, and I understand if someone defends a language they like, or because they invested a lot of time, energy, and effort learning it, if they earn their paycheck in that language and it pays for their children’s university, or if they discovered that language after struggling with some soul-crushing language before that, and the new language seems like a gift from heaven or something. I understand these things. But I have witnessed situations when completely clueless developers, who didn’t even write one line of code in a language or knew next to nothing about it, were arguing against it with great conviction. Seriously? Is it so important for you to take one side or another that you ain’t bothered to seem like a complete idiot who repeats like a parrot a bunch of things they heard from someone else or read online about a topic they are actually clueless about?

All technologies have pros and cons; in lots of aspects, many are even similar. So trying to make one idea win and another lose is entirely useless. Different languages offer different ways to solve a problem, different kinds of abstraction, they are different tools in your toolbox. They broaden your horizon and offer you new ways of thinking about things. It’s better to be aware of multiple languages and techniques than to develop tunnel vision when reaching your hand out to pick up a tool for that new problem you encounter that is unlike anything you’ve seen before. Stop investing too much energy into conflicts over topic X or Y and focus more on developing yourself. Adopt an open attitude, not a dogmatic one where nothing can be subjected to criticism, and nothing admits any objections. Of course, in your spare time, you can do whatever you like. You can try to be cool, and you can split hairs on whatever comic superhero you want. But bad developers do so while at work. They cannot let go of personal preferences and think about what is needed in the development team, on the project, or in a particular situation. They try to force their own preferences on others instead of taking the time to objectively examine things and see what applies best given the context (even if it’s something they don’t like). All work on the project stops, and they proceed in attacking anyone that has something bad to say about their preferences. In a sense, they behave not very different than football fans who love a particular club and dislike others for no apparent reasons. “What did you say about my football team? Take that back!”

Over-Engineering

And because we like technologies and have strong preferences for one or another, what happens is that many projects end up containing technologies, not necessarily because they were the best choice for the job, but because someone had the loudest mouth and pushed to have them. We want to play with this technology, we want to play with that technology, you want to show everyone else what awesome things you can do with that technology that only you know. But then we take that awesomeness too far, and we do many things that we think are awesome, but are not. We don’t know when to stop. We go into the weeds. We start behaving like people that when they were little, their mother refused to buy them a chemistry set, and now they want to turn everything into an experiment. And then the project becomes our small laboratory for trying out cool new technologies. We throw technology at problems, as many and as cool as possible. Whatever is new and others are already using attracts us too, and we want to try it. We are interested in what’s new and cool instead of what’s useful and effective for the problem that needs solving.

If we don’t have a problem to use it with, we invent one, or we generalize another. We like technologies, but we also like challenges. Not enough challenges in your work? No problem. Create them. Anything will do. Compile your own Linux kernel for maximum performance, then ask yourself why you are the only one for whom a specific application feature doesn’t work but instead fails with weird permission errors? Or refactor the application to use all 23 patterns[143] from the “Gang of Four” book [128] to make it super flexible and what not? Or let’s use only bleeding-edge technologies with the newest, fanciest features to build cool solutions for problems we don’t have yet. Functional programming is making a comeback? Let’s rewrite the application in Erlang or Scala or F#. Need a front-end framework? No problem! Use the one that popped up in your RSS feed this morning while you were drinking your coffee and catching up on things. And of course, you will use it, but obviously, you then start to discover its limitations and desperately open issues on GitHub and complain that no one is answering you. And when you can’t figure it out on your own, you drop the thing and start looking for something else to add to the project and which you think will solve your problems… only to start doing the same thing all over again, but with something else.

Instead of having conceptual integrity, many software solutions become an amalgam of languages, frameworks, and libraries resembling a french bouillabaisse with as many kinds of fish and shellfish you could get your hands on at the local fish market. We tend to ignore the fundamentals, tried and proven practices, sometimes even common sense, and we jump straight to new technologies. We obsess about trying out cool things and playing with technologies, and our focus becomes narrow. We forget about other important things around us, like having a job to do within a set of constraints or that we have clients that need the thing we are building when it still provides value, not when developers are done playing with it. This kind of bad developers end up writing crappy, over-engineered software using the latest fads. Sure, technologies expand your horizons, they can also improve productivity, but they can also limit your solutions to those the technology supports, force you to do it their way, then really make it a pain to maintain an application where every feature is like a jigsaw puzzle of technologies. And what do you do when you become constrained by some technology? Add one more, of course… And the code is not necessarily bad or of poor quality, but it’s unnecessary code that complicates the application and introduces undesirable complexity.

Developers often go into the weeds because they go with their first impulse, jumping headfirst. They begin to sketch a solution before they’ve established what the problem is, identifying its causes, or spending enough time to think deeper about it. “Why are we wasting so much time discussing and analyzing the problem? Let’s write some code. We’ll figure it out eventually”. Bad developers think that if they are not writing code, they are wasting time, so they start writing code before thinking. Don’t forget that you must first solve the problem. Writing code is then how you implement the solution. You may find a better solution while writing the code because you discover and learn more things as you implement the current solution, but that does not mean to jump straight into things without having any solution at all. If you do, chances are higher that you will end up with a faulty solution that treats only the happy path and omits cases that you didn’t even think could happen for the simple reason that you haven’t spent a proper amount of time to think about what might happen.

And the examples when we don’t think deeply about things but throw ourselves headfirst into solutions, proposals, or opinions could go on. For example, it often happens (and I find myself guilty of having done this too) that when a new developer joins the team, they start saying things like “Ah… but everything is wrong here. Why was this done this way and not that way?” They immediately offer their opinion and want to change things before even trying to understand why things are the way they are or how they ended up like that. I’ve seen such behavior with other professions also, like plumbers and dentists. They start talking about the work before they’ve even entered the bathroom completely or before you’ve fully opened your mouth. “Oh my… what’s this? Who did this job? I would not have chosen to do it like that. We must change it… we can’t leave it like that”. And developers behave the same. “We must change it… we can’t leave it like that”, and start changing code that’s already been tested and running in production without thinking about the consequences. And not only do they mess with stuff that doesn’t concern them, but they are also nitpickers. The architecture of the application is blown to bits, but instead of looking for solutions to fix it, the developers argue that a class has more than 1000 lines of code and waste their time breaking it into two classes of 500 lines each and call that an improvement. But then 500 lines seems a lot as well. So they keep splitting hairs and readjust a section of code without bringing any real benefit to the application, possibly even introducing some new bugs during their wonderful “improvement” process.

I also talked about estimates in a previous chapter, mentioning how they are often optimistic. Well, sometimes, they are very optimistic. Some believe they are so cool that they think nothing can stand in their way. “What? A complex application that nobody had built before? Pha… If I put my mind to it, I’m sure I can write it over the weekend”. Obviously, half a year later, the thing is far from being done. And then you hear things like “Oh… I realized where I made the mistake. If I just use language XYZ, I’ll finish it immediately. If I put my mind to it, I’m sure I can rewrite everything in language XYZ over the weekend”. They dive headfirst into things without thinking more deeply about what they are doing or what undesirable consequences they might produce.

Not code? Not interested!

Then, another problem is that some programmers don’t want to get involved in what it means to run a project except from a technical perspective and writing code. They don’t want to be developers; they want to remain programmers. They immerse themselves in the code and are not interested too much in the context of the project, the company, the business, or the management aspects. They just want to write code and play with technologies. Things that aren’t technical in nature or not related to programming get neglected. Not designing the application? Not coding? Not installing servers? “Not interested!” They hate meetings, they hate reports, they don’t want to take part in planning, be involved in defining features or writing documentation (but they will complain when they have no documentation for something they need… just saying), don’t want to deal with clients, and don’t actively communicate but wait for the information to be extracted from them then complain that the manager interrupts, asks for status updates, or demand they fill in their work in the issue tracking software. When exposed to things they don’t like, instead of trying to understand them or find out why they are needed, they prefer to complain, again and again, that they are kept away from programming. So they try to postpone any non-technical activity as much as possible, to the point where they can no longer avoid them and have to attend a meeting or something while dragging their feet and mumbling like a small child being forced by their mother to clean their room when they’re still watching TV. Some programmers don’t even think it’s necessary to read their freaking emails. And then the manager has a meeting with them, and they can’t find them in the office because they are already out to lunch since they didn’t bother to check their schedule for the day. They put horse blinders on their eyes and intentionally narrow their focus. Coding and all things technology are fun; everything else is not.

And these things become dangerous because programmers transform into boys with toys who, like young children, just want “to play” and refuse to do other stuff, like taking a bath, putting on their pajamas, brush their teeth, or go to bed because the next day is a school day. So how does a programmer play when ignoring everything else? With technologies, of course. “Let’s use Cassandra ‘cause MySql is so the ’90s. Let’s put something in the cloud with Hadoop, distributed and such. Let’s refactor this legacy piece of code that we don’t need to change - but really bothers us ‘cause it looks ugly - by using only lambda functions. Let’s learn Python and automate this chore that takes us only one minute per week to do. Wow… how come we didn’t discover this technology earlier. We should have used it from the beginning of the project. Let’s rewrite everything we’ve done in this new thing. Wow… how cool is this other thing, let’s explore it” - everything at the expense of the tasks that had to be done and which were more important. Screw the risks. Screw the tasks. Screw the deadlines.

Another issue that comes bundled with this “allergy” to all that is not technical in nature it that a professional defect begins to develop, in that programmers try to solve everything with technology, no matter the problem. The sound quality is bad during the conf-call when talking from the laptop’s microphone? “Let’s install some sound processing software or something that can filter the background noise from the conversation”. Or how about using a pair of headphones with a microphone instead? Did it take the first 5 minutes of the meeting to set up the presentation on the projector? “Maybe we should have a PC permanently connected to the projector, running some sort of server to which I can upload the presentation, and then the server just displays it”. Or maybe next time, arrive 5 minutes earlier to have the time to properly set up your presentation before the rest of the participants arrive? We are so obsessed and focused on technology that it becomes the first thing we reach out for when a situation comes up. We play with our toys and work only on what we think is cool that we end up ignoring everything else.

Programmers that don’t make an effort to also understand other aspects of software development - besides technology and writing code - will often get into conflicts with their Project Manager. They try to do what they want on the project, without much regard for the consequences. And when the Project Manager comes in and asks them why a feature is taking so long or when it will be ready, the programmers get upset. They accuse the manager of not doing what is right but caring only when something is done, caring only about the schedule and about the deadlines, being interested in seeing things taking place faster, and not necessarily better. “Even if it’s not appropriate to change the database now, it’s better this way. Even if it’s not the best time to rewrite a piece of the application, it’s better this way”. The manager doesn’t understand that and doesn’t agree with that. And the developers don’t agree with the manager’s opinions. So they each start pulling in different directions: developers to write code as they want, to use whatever technologies they desire, to continue their little experiment on the project, while the manager - who can’t do the actual job - having no choice but to start interrupting people, asking for status updates and holding meetings, to ensure that the proper features are delivered on time. I’m not talking here about the kind of manager described in the previous chapter. I’m talking about managers that see the work going into the weeds and try to bring it back on track using management techniques, which unfortunately don’t work. When programmers say, “we need to use such and such technology”, it’s pretty hard for a Project Manager to contradict them if they don’t themselves have a technical background.

For programmers that don’t try very hard to understand what their manager does, the manager is just the person that constantly interrupts them and wastes their time organizing all kinds of meetings, asking for status reports, building all sorts of useless spreadsheets, obsessing about deadlines, and pretty much nothing else. And then developers wonder what else the manager does all day long long. And it’s then simple to come up with the explanation that “not much” when they don’t understand the manager’s role. If your manager behaves like this, before assuming they are useless, keep themselves busy all the time, and do nothing but interrupt you, think first if maybe you might be the problem.

I have met good developers who could be trusted to carry out a project from beginning to end, but when it comes to many developers, not all of them are reliable. A lot of them think they could manage better without Project Managers constantly interrupting and telling them what to do, but of course, they won’t. Even if you could do without a Project “Manager”, you can’t run a project without project “management”. The role might become distributed between more members of the team, but it will still be there. Like it or not, you need to handle other things besides writing code. And it takes experienced and mature developers to do that. Not programmers, but developers. Programmers who only want to code and want to be excused from other activities on the project are not mature enough to self manage and run a project to a good completion. For this reason, you can’t leave the whole project in the hands of such developers. Remember autonomy, mastery, and purpose? Those are good things to have for your people. But you need the right people, not someone who wears horse blinders on their eyes and only see what they like. Developers have a high understanding of what is going on with the product, but what’s going on with the product is more than technologies. There are also organizational aspects. Can you imagine programmers that don’t care about these speaking directly to executives or clients? Or managing the budget? Let’s be serious. They will all buy themselves some Mac computers, board games, nerf guns, bean bags, and hire masseuses or “programming cheerleaders”[144].

The Team Lead or the manager is essential when dealing with such developers because they have to make sure they do the work that’s needed with a sense of responsibility, and not do the work they like to do. Programmers, just like bosses, can suffer from the “shiny object syndrome”. The only difference now is that it’s about technologies instead of features. Not only are they in love with technologies and create over-engineered solutions by packing the application with all sorts of cool (but unnecessary) languages and libraries, but programmers also have a short attention span. They get excited and then change their minds very often when it comes to what language, framework, or library to use. Then the following week, they discover something new. They get super excited about it also, then lose their focus once something else shows up. Then repeat and repeat. If those technologies end up in the code, the project will never be done but just be stuck in a constant state of… “renewal”, I guess?! So, if developers go into the weeds, someone has to bring them back on the right track. Developers who chase the latest technology are always working on the most exciting things first and then on the important ones. Project priorities are optional for them. So they have to be kept in check. You want them to fix the bugs they added to the code, not to spend hours discussing the advantages of functional programming or the differences between two software paradigms. And you want them fixed properly, not sloppy, hacky, patchy, or whatever gets the job done so they can then move to something nicer to do, and less boring. When they add a new technology, someone needs to make sure it benefits the project, and it’s not just another ingredient in their chemistry experiment, which could cause an exothermic reaction, then explode.

Failed communication

Another thing developers are not good at is communication. I mentioned throughout the book how important communication is, and I find myself in the situation of having to talk about it again. And a lot of programmers suck at this. I’ve sucked at this too. But who am I kidding… I still do.

There are a lot of mistakes we developers make when we communicate. Let’s start with the most obvious: we can’t simplify our language and avoid technical jargon when speaking to non-technical people.

When we talk to someone else about our work on the project, everything that comes out of our mouths sounds perfectly clear to us. It makes sense. We use technical jargon, we go into a lot of technicalities, we assume the other person has just as much information as we do, we sometimes use bad analogies that confuse things even more, our interlocutors become frustrated that they don’t understand what we are saying, while we get angry that they don’t get it, and so on. And then we also tend to make a great display of emotion when trying to make a point or trying to impose our opinions on others: “This is mandatory to do! We should absolutely fix that! This is a terrible idea! That’s not how we do things!” We forget that those we talk to don’t understand why things are the way you say it and often, because of our display of emotions, nor do they realize if we are just passionate about a topic and complete geeks, or if the situation is genuinely dire and if something is not done “right now”, there will be trouble.

You have to be mindful of who you’re talking to. Try to be brief and to the point. And most importantly, make sure your message has been understood, not just listened to; otherwise, communication problems will arise. And when they do, we tend to complain that others are dumb. Sometimes they are, but most of the time, they are not. You have to remember that for most non-technical people, the work you do as a developer is some sort of black magic. What makes sense to a developer doesn’t necessarily make sense to anybody else. That’s just how it is. It’s frustrating for a developer to deal with people who are not even able to fill in a bug report with more information other than “the application doesn’t work”, and then having to start an investigation to find out what’s going on, but that’s the situation. So when it comes to communicating with others, you must make sure others understand you, because most of the time you will bear the consequences of a failed communication, or you will be the one who has to fix things. Just like you need to understand a problem to build the right solution, to work well with other people, there must be understanding. As a developer, you can’t throw jargon around or go deep into technical details and then place the blame on others for being dumb and not understanding you. It’s your responsibility to get the message clearly across, so you don’t need to rely on your manager to intervene as a translator for you (like it happened to me when I was less experienced). It’s easier for the developer to make themselves understood than for others to understand the developer. You have to dot the i’s and cross the t’s for them. And remember that what is important to you may not be to them, and vice-versa. For you, as a developer, the quality of the code or the elegance of the design may be important. For others, it may be on-time delivery of the application, cheaply, and feature-packed. It’s no use trying to explain something that’s important to you, to someone who may have other values than yours. Be aware of that.

Another problem when it comes to communication is that, often, it’s not developers who initiate a conversation, but others. As developers, we find ourselves just writing code with people coming to us to ask us things, if the task is ready, or how much longer it takes. Because we don’t say anything. And we also complain when others come bugging us in search of this information. And we don’t really pay attention to communication when it happens either. We try to get rid of it so we can get back to writing code. “Just a couple of hours left”. “I’m almost done”. “It’s about 99% finished”. Each day, several days in a row. Or when we get stuck on some coding problem, or some bug with the tooling, or some other blocking issue, we don’t tell anyone, we don’t even take a break to clear our head. We continue banging our head on the issue, like a floor cleaning robot that hits a wall, backs off, then hits it again and again. You push yourself to finish it, without asking for help from anyone, without telling a soul about it, then Friday evening, when you are asked about it, you say, “I’m almost done”. You should update the status of the tasks you are working on, without the need for the Project Manager to go looking for you at the end of the working day. And say you don’t know how much it’s going to take when you don’t know that. Having people come to you and drag every word out of your mouth might work once or twice, but then you teach everyone that you are untrustworthy when it comes to communicating things, and you force them to always come to you and ask, “are we there yet?” Only developers know what’s under the hood; others don’t know when something is ready unless you let them know. So communicate your progress, ask for help, and escalate problems before it’s too late.

And be careful when you tell people something is done, that everyone shares the same definition “done”. Avoid misunderstandings. “Done” with hard-coded stuff inside the code, which should actually be configurable, is not done. If you’ve completed development, but the task is not yet tested, it’s not done. If a feature is developed and tested but cannot be deployed, it’s not done. “Done” means you can forget about it and work on something else. It doesn’t mean “it’s done, but…” there are a few loose ends that I need to tie on later, or “it’s done, but…” I need to clean up an entire pile of smelly bullshit code before the release. I’ve seen this happening often, and it’s easy to spot a project where this has occurred because development slows down as you get closer and closer to a milestone or a release. It’s a sign of an improper job in communicating that the product is ready, combined with an inadequate statement of the definition of “Done”. What did you forget, or omit, or what mess remains uncleaned, that needs to take extra work before putting the application in production?

The first 90 percent of the code accounts for the first 90 percent of the development time. The remaining 10 percent of the code accounts for the other 90 percent of the development time - Tom Cargill[145]

You need to communicate correct progress to your manager since only developers understand the code and know when it’s done. A car with hamsters on a wheel under the hood instead of an engine is not a car; it’s just a fancy hamster house. And this gets us to my next point.

You might build a prototype to test some ideas out, figure out how something works. Or you might not know precisely how to solve a problem in the actual application, so you throw things at the wall until something sticks. You’ll refactor later once you get it working properly. And then, the prototype ends up in production, as it is (something commonly referred to as a “protoduction”[146]). Why? Because you did a lousy job explaining to your boss or client that what you built is something held together with bubble gum and spit, something cobbled together to give you insight into how to “actually” make it work, something missing its quality and having no robustness. And now that you have that insight, you need to “actually” build the “real” thing. This is also a communication problem about what “done” means. A much more serious communication problem. Remember that your boss or client doesn’t understand what you do. When it comes to software, they can only judge things by their cover, usually a working user interface. If they see a functional, decent looking user interface, it must be working, right? They don’t see the code, they don’t see the missing error handling, they don’t see the hardcoded username and password, they don’t see the repetition and duplication and all the hacks, they don’t know everything is a mush of technologies that only work together on a happy path with carefully selected inputs. It’s your job to get it through their thick skulls that what you built is crap, and it’s just supposed to be used for learning and avoiding introducing crap on the real application.

I’ve seen this happen a few times, and it eventually ends up sucking for everyone involved… except for the guy who wrote the application. That’s how it usually happens. There is a developer in the company that management thinks is a rock star, so they unleash them on all the new projects. They quickly put something together and show it to the boss. Boss likes it. And they like it especially because it was put together in record time. They don’t understand why it was done in record time, and the developer doesn’t explain. “So ship it!” The rock star then needs to move on and work on the next new thing. So whatever they built and deployed to production is now placed in the hands of a team who gets a quick handover from the rock star developer (if at all). If you’ve been in this situation, I think you know what happens next. The entire thing falls apart. You get crashes and incidents, people struggle to keep the thing running, they have trouble understanding all the technologies the thing is built in, they start to add all the missing pieces to the existing functionality, while the rock star developer isn’t around to answer questions since they’re busy applying their talents on to the next big thing. The biggest problem is that, as with any application, new features will be requested, which need to be added on top of the mess, increasing the garbage pile until it fails under its own weight and needs to be scrapped and rewritten from scratch, under the shocked looks of bosses and customers who can’t understand how the team managed to destroy the application. Yes, they think the team is responsible for the failure. The poor souls that had to endure the whole mess now also get the blame. The application gets abandoned or rewritten, and everything takes longer than if it were properly done, once, from the beginning.

This type of developer is still a bad developer. The problem is not that they are incompetent or lack skills. The problem with this type of developer is that they don’t know how to say “no” to upper management. “Build me that thing in three days!” That’s not something possible to do, but instead of saying so, they just start working on it. Put together with duct tape, chewing gum, spit, whatever it takes to please the boss and make it happen in three days. And then the boss says, “put it in production”. Other poor souls have to then deal with the consequences while the rock star moves to do other projects and other projects (in the same manner, of course…) because they are the only one that can (the rest of the developers are, of course, some idiots that the boss doesn’t know why they are still keeping around). But the other developers have a fault of their own though: they accept the situation and say nothing. They accept the bullshit and end up cleaning it up daily. It takes years for management to figure out the problem is this single developer, who, ironically, has upper management as their accomplice in all of this. Until that happens, though, the rock star receives raises, compliments, gets offered the chance of working on the most important projects, and… raises the bar to an impossible standard for the rest of the developers. This developer is “a hero” in the eyes of upper management who, until they figure out they’re not, they keep perpetuating an awful situation and causing even more problems.

Then, including the communication between developers is messed up. They have technical discussions with each other but forget that one is a junior or another a front-end developer, while everyone else goes deep into details about the back-end architecture. Many technical talks can end in conflict or hurt feelings because everyone is trying to express their opinion before even spending some time listening to what the problem is. Or they reject someone else’s solution because it doesn’t fit their preferences or it doesn’t make use of their favorite technology. Sometimes we need help figuring out how to deal with some problem, but do we ask for help, or bounce ideas out of some fellow developer? We don’t. Or you arrive to work one day and try to deploy the application, and it doesn’t work. There are all kinds of weird errors you haven’t seen before, to discover later that one of your colleagues stayed up late last night and changed the build without telling anyone. You also notice they’ve updated the database version, and now you have to wait for them to show up at work because you don’t know how the build works anymore, and you don’t even know if the build and the database are the only things they’ve changed. Or you pull an update from version control, and everything is in conflict because you worked on a piece of code that another colleague decided to refactor, although their work wasn’t related to anything they’ve changed. All of these are communication problems, where, instead of letting fellow developers know about certain things or keeping them updated, they are let to discover them by themselves when confronted with the accomplished fact. You can see that also in the reluctance of many developers to add comments inside the code. They write the code only for themselves, not for others. They don’t care if what they wrote is as clear as possible to everyone else, like, for example, the reasons why something was done a certain way. You also notice the same reluctance when you ask them to document stuff. “You can look in the code to see what’s going on. The code is sacred”, they say. I don’t even want to remember how often I had to go to another developer and ask them about decisions taken in their code, only to be looked at like I was from another planet or something. And this was assuming the developer still worked in the company because sometimes I got the answer that “Albert decided it that way. But he quit some time ago. And we don’t remember why”.

Lost cause

So, I’ve mentioned a few things that make a bad developer. The question is now, “can you fix a bad developer”? If you paid attention to the previous chapter, where I asked if you can fix a bad manager and mentioned the reasons for not being able to do so, then you already know the answer. It’s a “no”. You can’t fix a bad developer. Remember also what I meant by a bad developer. I haven’t talked about inexperienced developers who inevitably made and still make mistakes because they just don’t know any better yet. I meant developers who are not getting any better with time and/or who have attitude problems.

You can help an inexperienced developer become better. I’ve talked about several ways you can do this throughout the book. You can offer them support, guidance, and be available to answer their questions. Mentoring is another option. They can do pair programming together with a more experienced developer or participate in code reviews. You can also have a face-to-face discussion with them to address the mistakes they’re doing, the things that are not working, the things that need more attention, or whatever, but it then depends on the developer if they make a change for the better or not. You can’t download stuff into their brain by force. It all depends on their willingness to learn, to try things out, to make mistakes and learn from those mistakes, to take responsibility for their work and for the process of improving themselves. “No one was born a scholar”, goes a saying in my country. You had to learn everything you know, whether we are talking about hard skills or soft skills. You must be curious to learn and be willing to put in the effort to grow. If they do that, then inexperienced developers have a great chance to turn into good developers, not bad ones. Then, if they have an attitude problem and you point that out, do they become more mindful of the way they behave, or do they then make some efforts to keep their emotions under control? That’s how you recognize the difference between inexperienced and bad. Are they trying to become better? Better at seeing the big picture? Better skilled? Better at interacting with others? If they keep having attitude problems and/or there is a lack of progress or interest, then you have a bad developer on your hands. Remember my example with the “disturbed” developer above? Well, that guy wasn’t hired the day before; he was in that job for years. But in those years, he didn’t make any progress, and his attitude stayed the same: not giving a fuck.

Good developers do give a fuck. I could offer code reviews as an example in this regard. Bad developers don’t really like code reviews. Sometimes they are even against the idea. They don’t like others criticizing their work, or don’t understand the need for code reviews. The code works, right? What the heck do you want more? Why should the code also be readable? Why should it also be maintainable? Why? Why? Why? They behave like bad construction workers that hide their crappy work under some plaster and a few layers of paint. If you can’t see what’s underneath, then there is no problem, right? Same with the code. The application works and shows no visible defects, while code is hidden under some plaster and many layers of paint. Code reviews help with having quality software, not only because there are more eyes looking at problems and on how their solutions were implemented, or catching more bugs if more people involved, but there is also the fact that developers are more careful when writing their code knowing that other developers will review their work. They will also learn better from their mistakes because they don’t want to have a fault pointed out more than once in code reviews. They want to write something good that others can appreciate. But you do so only if you care about your work. Do you think a bad developer wants others to appreciate what they do? Nope. They don’t want others to look at their code because they don’t see the point or don’t want others to see the crap they’ve made. And for sure, they don’t want to work extra to clean it up or change it or have any discussions around the code. Or they think they are too cool to receive criticism or advice on how to improve. They wrote the code, and that’s it! What else do you want from them? Good developers, on the other hand, will want to learn from code review. They’ll ask about comments or notes they receive; they will want to know why it is better that way. Or will try to convince you, with arguments, that their solution is better. They’re interested, inquisitive, curious, and willing to have a conversation about improving the code because they understand it’s about growth and becoming a better developer. One who is not interested will just complain, kick up a stink, starts acting defensively, and eventually say, “OK, whatever… I’ll do as you say”… and then holds a grudge because they always get bad reviews. Why? Because they don’t improve as a developer, and their code is just as bad now as it was 50 reviews ago.

Once again, it depends on the developer if they want to learn or if they revise their attitude. You can show them the issues they have or the problems they are creating, but it depends on the developer if they care to do something about it or not. And by caring, I mean caring about all the essential things. For example, a prima donna cares about his code but is still a bad developer because he cares too much about the code and not enough about everything else, like the overall outcome of the project, the company, or his teammates. You can point to the fact that he’s behaving like a diva, but it is not enough. He must catch himself acting this way and reconsider the behavior. Similarly, when during code reviews people point out to someone that their code is lacking, they must be willing to do something to improve it. Developers also need to control their impulses and think of solutions to the problem before writing any code. They must understand on their own that there is no “best technology, language, or whatever”, and that contradictory discussion started strictly on one’s preferences have no purpose. They must realize that technologies must first show their value before adding them to the project, not use them simply because they are cool or happen to be bleeding edge.
