Cool and new is often not the right tool for any job. They should also notice that there are other things besides writing code, not be reminded of it or others having to point out that fact. They need to understand they have to play well with others, and that work in isolation within a company is not always possible or desired. They need to develop the right habits and keep in mind why they are at work. The project is not one’s personal experiment. The company did not hire developers to give them cool things to play with. They hired them to solve problems, and it would be nice of them to solve the problem by not creating more problems in the process, or worse, by creating new jobs for other developers.

Good developers strive for quality code and best practices using the proper technologies. They don’t get fixated with the latest or newest fads, or with personal preferences and wishes, and they don’t participate in heated arguments without substance. They understand that work is not about what “they” want; it’s about getting things done. And getting things done involves making trade-offs: knowing when it’s useful and convenient to do (or not do) something, knowing when to compromise, when to follow the rules and when to break them, to know when to deliver fast and bear the consequences, or know when to take a stand and get their way. And to do this, developers have to be committed to their growth as professional software developers. Nobody else can put this into them.

Outsourcing

Let’s start with an obvious fact: for many companies, making software is a cost. It’s a necessary evil in a world where almost everything is run by software. I touched on this subject in the chapter regarding the Business-IT divide, where I mentioned that IT is not a strategic partner, and software isn’t seen as an investment. IT is seen as a support function or as an execution unit. And often, it happens for this “support” function to be an expensive one. Maybe some servers need to be purchased, or a lot of software licenses. You also need to pay people’s salaries in the department, salaries that, except those of management, are most likely among the highest in the company compared to the rest of the employees. Since IT is not seen as being part of “the business”, that is, a first-hand contributor to the business activity that brings in the money, it’s easy to include the cost of the IT department and of software development together with other costs that the company has to operate. And now, the higher-ups in the company default to doing what they do with every other cost: they try to control it, or better said, “reduce it”.

But before going on and mentioning some of the specific quicksands, I just want to clarify what I mean by “outsourcing”. I’ll start with a definition from TechTarget’s SearchCIO website that captures the meaning in a good and concise format:

Outsourcing is a business practice in which a company hires another company or an individual to perform tasks, handle operations or provide services that are either usually executed or had previously been done by the company’s own employees[147]

You can outsource locally, within your town or country, or to another country or even continent. I’ll be talking about the later options, building the software in another country, within another culture, either if it’s part of the company (“offshoring” [148]) or some other company (“offshore outsourcing”[149]). I include “offshoring” (still part of your own company abroad) in the same outsourcing bucket since you can run into some of the same quicksands if you don’t manage things properly.

You can step into some quicksand even when outsourcing locally, within your town, or maybe in a smaller city in your country where the cost of living is cheaper, but the chances of messing it all up are lower because those people speak the same language as you, the cultural differences will be minimal or non-existent, and you can always pay them a visit to see what they’re doing, or even relocate some of your won employees to work closely with those of the other company.

The main point to take is that it’s developing software within “another culture” and having less face-to-face contact with the people there. What you used to produce or were handling internally is now being handled by another company - a service provider - for you.

Sometimes, companies start directly with an outsourcing solution for software development, without having their in-house developers before that. That’s because - I’ll say it again - IT is seen as something separated from the business. So much so that you can have someone else do this part for you. It works with the clothing industry, right? Why wouldn’t it work with software development? Others are doing it, so why shouldn’t we? Often though, it’s a transition from an in-house IT department to outsourcing, to reduce cost, and (often also) combined with the fact that people are unhappy with their own development shop (for reasons mentioned in the Business-IT Divide chapter, which are sometimes not even the developers’ fault). Upper management often keeps the IT department under-staffed to reduce cost, and they also start putting more pressure on them to work harder and faster (which translates to unpaid overtime, of course; otherwise, you can’t get “more bang for the same buck”). Getting more done with less, and in the same time, is a way to reduce cost, or at least be more efficient with the cost. But there is a limit to how much pressure you can put on people, so at some point, you reach a performance plateau (if you are lucky, otherwise you get a decrease) or developers get fed up with the situation and resign. So now, inevitably, management has to realize that they need more developers to replace the ones that left. So the company opens up some positions, but they refuse to pay market wages - which may happen to be greater than of the developers who left - because they want to keep costs under control. “Surely, you can find someone at the same salary, or preferably cheaper, right?” But the developers you find are inexperienced and not very good because only they agree to work on the salary offered by the company; the good developers want more money, of course. And those who remain on the development team refuse to hire inexperienced or bad developers just because they are cheaper. So management gets upset with the capped performance and the fact that they need to pay a lot of money for experienced developers, so they think that they can move all this arrangement in a country where labor is cheaper. They think they can get the same skilled professionals from somewhere else, but less expensive.

Another reason to move everything to another country might be because you can no longer find enough talent locally. If you have a shortage of skilled developers locally, outsourcing gives you the opportunity to hire the best experts you can find elsewhere. If on the local job market the demand for developers is higher than the supply, you don’t really have a choice, and you must look elsewhere. This might happen too. It’s a possibility. Sometimes though, what happens is that companies trick themselves into thinking that they can’t find enough developers locally. That’s because they don’t find developers that charge the amount of money they would want them to be charging. So this often also boils down to less money to pay developers. And sometimes, companies think that they will also have their software faster since cheaper developers mean you can afford more people to work on the same thing.

Then, some companies fall into the trap of believing in what many outsourcing proponents suggest, that outsourcing frees up time and resources for companies to focus on essential activities, on the core business, and innovation. Things like payroll, bookkeeping, help-desk, call centers are more or less common to all companies, so you might outsource these parts if you get the same quality of service, and it’s cheaper. It makes sense. But care should be taken when outsourcing software development. If the business relies on custom software to function, or the needed software is the business itself, companies should think very carefully when outsourcing that development. It might seem you are focusing on the goals and direction, and the offshore teams focus on implementation, and everyone does what they’re best at, it still seems to make sense. But things like payroll or help-desk are not the bread and butter of most businesses (unless you are the service provider that offers payroll or help-desk services). These are things that you can afford to forget about, and outsourcing indeed works well for such categories of functions. But the development of software that runs your business is, most of the time, not included in this category. It’s not like in the clothing industry where fashion designers study fashion trends, sketch the clothing design, create master patterns, select the materials, and then send everything somewhere else to be sewn together. Software development isn’t clear cut like that. You can’t make decisions in your company, define everything that the software needs to do, and off you go, send it somewhere else to be put together; that doesn’t work very well in software development. You can’t leave all the aspects related to implementation to a third party; otherwise, you do nothing but increase the Business-IT divide and increase all the problems that result from it. The reasons that cause projects to fail that I mentioned so far in the book or the reasons that lead you into quicksand don’t go away when you outsource software development. Worse still, some are aggravated by having virtual teams[156] far away in another country, another time zone, and definitely because of another culture. Then there are specific outsourcing issues that arise and add to the things I already talked about.

Still your people

When outsourcing, you first and foremost need to know what people you will have at the service provider. There are those that think that a project will be done better, faster, and cheaper if they outsource it, but they ignore how the service provider might actually make that happen. They practically put all of their trust in the provider for having the right/best people for the job. But do they? Or not? Are you willing to go on faith? You need to make sure - when selecting a provider - that they can deliver on their promises. People are important, so it would be good to have some interviews with them, to get to know them, to know if they are capable or not. I’ve seen cases when the service provider doesn’t have people available at that time, but, so as not to lose the project, to quickly put a team together. Any kind of team. Do you want any kind of team, or do you want one with experienced people? Then how do you know that they are experienced people and not fresh out of college? Do you take their word for it? Just like your company has outsourced something to reduce the costs, likewise, the service provider also tries to keep their prices low, to be more competitive on the market, and to attract more customers. And since much of the cost that a company like this has is with its employees, just as your company may have tried too before deciding to outsource, they, in turn, might try to reduce costs by hiring cheaper people. And many outsourcing providers prefer to hire young people. Being young means they have fewer family obligations, no mortgage yet, have more enthusiasm and are more energetic, thus more likely to work longer hours. They are also more easily replaceable and in larger supply than experienced developers, so they can hire more developers for less pay. But of course, what happens is that - as your own company discovered before outsourcing - cheap people are also inexperienced, with experienced people demanding more (this rule applies regardless of the country and the cost of living there). The service provider though, might not shy away from hiring inexperienced people, especially if you don’t ask yourself any questions about what kind of people you are getting.

When it comes to software development, strength lies in experience, not in numbers. But many are happy when they get two offshore developers at the price of a local one, and then forget to ask themselves if skills-wise, they are what’s needed. By the way, this is related to what I mention in the chapter about bad bosses, that some are just counting employees and don’t take into account their experience. You should keep your reasoning about local talent and apply it to offshore developers, and make sure you find good people, and, yes, at a cheaper cost due to different standard of living. But somehow, the part about “good, talented” gets lost, and people are just happy that they are cheaper.

Many problems stem from the fact that people wear horse blinders on their eyes and only focus on things “being cheaper”. Often, an outsourcing contract is negotiated at the top levels, between business and salespeople, who don’t know the technical aspects and the difficulties to develop software with a difference in culture, language, timezone, or knowledge thrown into the mix. The only important thing for them is to reduce costs. But the software has some criteria for success. I talked in a previous chapter about why it’s important to define success before you start a project. It’s even more important to be mindful of the definition of success when you outsource it. To say that, “It doesn’t matter who is building the software as long as it’s cheaper” does not work in software development. Was the project a success just because it was cheaper? I doubt it. I even lived situations when, during the middle of the project, the higher-ups started asking, “Are these people any good?”. Well… don’t you think you should have asked that question before starting the project with them?

Success doesn’t just mean it’s cheaper. And success depends on the people working on the project. To make sure you’re not wasting your money, you need to have discussions with the developers from the service provider, similar to the job interviews you would hold when hiring for your own company. You need to be able to trust them and the work they will be doing. Many neglect these aspects. “They are not our people; they are theirs. It’s their job to give me the right people. That’s why we are paying them”. Well… things aren’t quite like that. All the personnel administration headache is on their heads, and you have the convenience that you can get rid of a resource very quickly, without complicating yourself with the dismissal process, documenting all the mess, etc. You simply tell the provider to replace them or remove them from the project, and that’s that. They are still employed at the provider, but they no longer work for you. So indeed, it’s their employees, their problems. The outsourcing provider handles the human resources aspects, and you don’t care to a certain extent. But the work they do is actually your problem. So you have to make sure they do it well because you will be using the results in the end. So be careful not to wash your hands of the responsibility completely. You have to make sure those people do the right thing for you. The product is yours. The responsibility is yours. Don’t take your hands off it. These people need to be an extension of your company, or you will have problems. Treat them like your people, even if they are on someone else’s payroll.

And once the project is underway, you need to know what’s going on there. Once your virtual team starts working, you need to make sure people don’t cut any corners. If you are overseas, on a different timezone, the remote team works long periods of time without supervision. There is supervision from the provider’s managers, but they might put pressure on the developers to finish things within the agreed time frame even though that means sacrificing quality or doing a poor job. You also need to make sure that the team is not working crazy hours that will take a long toll on performance (12-14 hours a day, six days a week, might be some manager’s idea to make up for lost time and keep within signed contracts, and might even work for a week or so, but not if it’s all the time; I even heard of managers that were very proud that their people worked like that… WTF?!). Or that no people are added to the project without you knowing about it, in an attempt for them to recover time (thus increasing communication channels, the time needed for training, etc., and making the problem more serious). Worse still is if your people are assigned to work on several projects at once, in which case you have to incur context switching costs that you had no idea existed. So basically, you need to make sure that their managers run the project the way you would like it to be run. What you don’t know can actually hurt you, as opposed to how the saying typically goes.

To be successful with outsourcing, you need people with a sense of ownership and who can deal with a high degree of autonomy. I want to remind a bit about the difference between a programmer and a developer that I made earlier in the book. What you need to make sure of is that you have developers, not programmers. And that they are committed to your objectives. Don’t just interact with a Team Lead or manager without knowing if there are 5 or 10 people behind them, or a variable number depending on how many other projects the service provider has to deal with that week. Maybe you think it suits you to have more people with no extra cost assigned to work on your project, but this has the disadvantage of increasing the number of communication channels, so overall, the work suffers. Get to know the people, train them, evaluate their performance, so that you know who you keep and who you don’t on your team. Treat them like your own employees and expect the same accountability from them. You can’t leave these things just to the provider to deal with.

If you don’t take care of these people, it’s very easy then to adopt a mentality of “I say, you do” and start treating them as remote resources instead of collaborators. I have already mentioned why this mentality is problematic; I will not repeat it here. What I want to say in addition, is that given that these are not your people and that they are actually employed at another company, if you keep this mentality up for an extended period of time, there is a risk for it to transform on the other side into “You say, I do”, or even worse “I do, I don’t think”. If they are just doers, and you don’t take their opinions into account (which inevitably happens with “I say, you do”), and you take all the decisions, no matter how small, etc., it’s normal then for people to get used to it and end up not caring for the big picture or for the business, for people to have very little initiative, and for them to focus on doing technical stuff based on the specs they receive and nothing further. They can then begin to develop an even more dangerous attitude of “It’s not mine, I don’t really care”. And this is a big concern for your project because you’ll not be perfect in giving them directions, you will make mistakes, mistakes that they will discover during the implementation. When that happens, at best they will say, “We found such and such problem. What do you want us to do next?”, and at worst, they will ignore it and move on because you taught them that their opinion doesn’t matter anyway, that thinking is done someplace else. Then twelve months later, all the ignored problems will surface, maybe long after your project is over. You will then “happily” remember all those moments when you told them to shut up and do what you say… and faster.

So be mindful of your attitude. You want people to actually “participate” in the development of the software. When people just focus on doing their job, things can go south pretty quickly. Programmers will only write code; testers will only test. “It’s not my job; it’s their job”. If they are blocked by something or need more detailed specifications, they will let you know, then wait. They don’t come back to ask for a status, nor do they try to work on something else; they just wait for you to do the thinking. When you then ask them why they are sitting around, they calmly respond that they have already told you that they are blocked.

You need good, proactive developers to build software. Developers that don’t need to be told what to do. And not just developers, everybody. And this doesn’t change if you outsourced the development to someone else. So have good developers to whom you can explain what’s needed, instead of feeding them instructions with a spoon, otherwise they will not understand which of the things you ask are important and which are not, and which have priority and which have not, and more importantly, they know “why” they are doing certain things. Share the vision. The “why” is essential. They must also understand what the destination is, not be forced to discover it mile by mile. And since developers are closer to the application, they may have good opinions, or they may notice things you have not thought of. Being from another culture, they might see things in a different way, and that may sometimes prove an advantage to your organization. But only if you (at least) listen to their ideas and their feedback. So really engage them in the development of the solution, don’t just give them orders. The people you have there need to think, not just follow instructions. You can’t make software without thinking. It’s brains and muscles. You can’t keep the brains and outsource the muscles.

It will then be necessary to invest in these developers’ training, even if they are not your employees. Training is an aspect that cannot be neglected. The provider’s employees receive some specs and have to produce the software within time and budget (in fact, it would be fairer to say that the team should provide business value, not just cost reduction). To understand the specs, they need to understand your business. You can’t have them just write software. All programmers can write software, but it doesn’t mean it will be “the right software”. The virtual team might have the necessary technical skills, but don’t think that your company no longer has to do staff training. You need to have a knowledge transfer. Continuously. Not just at the beginning of the project. The virtual team members need to understand your services and business model; they need to know your goals and expectations. You outsourced the writing of the code, but don’t forget that these developers need to know your business as well. I have often seen situations when the domain is unknown to people at first, and they don’t understand certain concepts that have become second nature to you. It will take time for them to learn. So involve them in the process, don’t just throw them work over the fence.

Hidden costs

So you need to invest in people who are not your employees. And not only are they not your employees, but in outsourcing, the risk of these people leaving is higher than if they were your employees. Turnover is high in outsourcing. Many stay with a company just to gain more experience, then move on to another job, for a larger pay that matches the newly acquired experience. The offers are numerous, so job-hopping is quite large. That’s why many times you can’t even have a stable team, because every six months or so, some developers leave and you have to bring in new people on the project, which must be integrated, trained, etc. Heck, if that provider goes bankrupt or something, you lose all their know-how in one go, and you have to start over somewhere else. Can you then just consider only how much you pay per developer? That alone doesn’t give you the entire picture of outsourcing.

So maybe you will have higher costs than you expected with people’s training and problems caused by turnover. It may not be a cost of money - depending on what contract you’ve signed with the provider - but it will certainly be a cost of time (and maybe quality). Depending on the situation and how often you have to travel, you may also have some costs with plane tickets, hotel accommodations, time lost with actual moving from one place to the other, or with the timezone difference. The project management overhead will also be higher. There might be network delays (maybe not everyone has fiber optics as you have in your office). These are things that can be measured at some point, but there will also be some that might not be easy to measure. Anyway, these are extra reasons to have good developers over there, people who can handle a high degree of autonomy. You can’t think of everything, you can’t describe everything you need in a specification, and you can’t define a faultless process to manage the development, so it’s best to have people at the service provider that can think on their feet.

Then consider that these people also did outsourcing for others before they did for you. Maybe they worked in another domain, or perhaps for clients from other cultures than your own. Can you imagine how many styles of work they need to know? If they have been taught one style for one client, and the next company has a different style, habits may have formed. Maybe for a client they had to follow strict procedures while you need a more loose approach and more flexibility. Suddenly, you have to take that into account, because the re-learning will be done on your time and your dime. These are hidden drawbacks and costs that occur along the way. It costs you to make sure things go well.

The highest hidden costs, though, you will pay because you lose control. Or better said, because you “give control away”. By “control”, I don’t mean the kind from “command and control”; I mean control as in being in the driving seat and having full visibility on what’s going on and where things are headed. I mean giving up on some of the details. And that won’t necessarily be something you do consciously. It may happen on the principle of “out of sight, out of mind”. You can end up neglecting things if you are not “hands-on”. Nobody likes surprises on a software project. When it’s a project somewhere else, without your involved active participation, surprises can be even more unpleasant. Have you tried troubleshooting a computer problem over the phone? Imagine how fun that is when you’ll have a complex and remote business problem to deal with. Many think that they only provide requirements and the service provider deals with coding, testing, project management activities, with everything, while you only ask for status updates once a week, or pay them a visit once per semester or so. That would be the theory, but in practice, it is not like that. You need to make sure that testing is done according to your standards, that they use management practices that you consider appropriate, that the code is of the quality you desire, that the code is maintainable, extensible, secure, and does the right thing in the right way, and that the product is not riddled with technical debt because the team was forced to cut corners to meet deadlines (I use the notion of “technical debt” here so that you know to what kind of issues I’m referring to and what problems result from that, but most likely it will not be “technical debt” but a “mess”; incurring technical debt it’s a decision to do something technically disadvantageous in order to get a business advantage, it doesn’t mean to cut corners just to deliver when you said you would deliver). It’s your job, then, to make sure they do the right thing, the right way. Perhaps you consider such aspects to be implicitly understood, but maybe they don’t consider the same. If you take your hands off the project and leave everything strictly to them, a lot of things will happen without your knowledge, or you’ll be made aware of them too late when you’ve already lost some decent solutions to try to make things right.

When you outsource, you give up a certain degree of control, but even so, you still have to keep your paw on the project to avoid surprises. The best way to do this is to have someone in your company who, at all times, knows what’s going on with the project and how people are doing their work. You need a manager of some sort, but mandatory, a developer or a capable technical person who can look under the hood. If you can have someone you trust with them there, then even better. Either way, you need visibility into what’s going on. You can’t outsource everything. You have to have your own people who know what needs to be done. Someone who can do things ranging from code reviews to making sure the application architecture is solid and ensure that all business concepts have been properly understood and can be found adequately implemented in the code, and make sure that the team is actually working towards your company’s goals. You need someone full time. Depending on the size of the project, that might even mean a handful of people, not just one or two - people on your own company payroll.

If you don’t have your own informed people, you carry high risk with the project. If that service provider goes bankrupt or something, or you are not satisfied with the results, you risk having to throw what they did in the trash and start all over again because no one knows what’s in there. Some new provider comes along, they say they don’t understand the code or that the code is an unsalvageable mess, and they will want to rewrite everything from scratch. Will you then be able to say otherwise? Can you disprove their claim? But if you already have someone that knows what’s in there, at least you can save something, maybe even train another team somewhere else to continue work on the project.

If you have no visibility and no people inside, and you leave them to their own devices, you end up relying strictly on the image they will present you with. In other words, you have to trust them. And then the following question comes up: do you trust that the image they present to you is real? Or are there any chances to be pure fantasy? A serious company doesn’t mislead or deceive you, but not all of them are serious companies. In addition, regardless of the company, you can start the outsourcing journey with your left foot because they don’t build the project ‘cause they’re nice, but because this is their business, from which they make their money. They are selling you an outsourcing service. If you are a new customer, many may try to impress you, to put up a good performance at the beginning with building some proof of concept. “Read requirement documents for two weeks to fully understand what needs to be done? Noooo… Let’s jump right in so we have something to show the client and for them to see progress. We’ll figure it out later after we sign the contract”. Even if they do a proper job, if it’s the beginning of the relation, they certainly make a greater effort than they would for normal work. Again, to impress. First impressions matter. But then, they will inevitably slow down. They can’t constantly work like that. But to not lose you as a client, they make that effort. How do you know then, if you won’t have someone inside, what will be the real work they will do? How will you know if they will build what’s needed or if it’s something that just keeps up with appearances? How do you know the result is complete? How do you know if it’s of the right quality? It costs you to know these things.

Then, once they have you as a client and you have invested in the project, it’s harder for you to give it up. It’s called the sunk-cost fallacy[157]. And outsourcing companies have figured this out too. It would be awful to stumble onto a company that does everything to keep the project going and not lose you as a client. In case you didn’t understand what I just said, let me put it more bluntly: they would do anything so that you keep giving them money. Your project becomes secondary. What comes first is you paying them every month. So be mindful of this. The service provider may not have your company’s best interest in mind but their own. All companies want to make money, and a service provider is no exception. And that’s true even when their money-making strategy doesn’t align with your company’s business goals. So once that occurs, guess to know what happens next? They start lying to you.

The team is dysfunctional? They will never tell you that. The team is just fine. “We didn’t quite understand some things you asked us to do, but we are not going to tell you yet. We’ll work on things that catch the eye first, and we’ll figure out later what you really need. We don’t want you to form the idea we don’t understand what we are actually doing”. That expert in the NoSQL technology that’s essential for your project to succeed… well… isn’t quite an expert. “The application shows weird errors then all of a sudden is fine? That wasn’t a bug, and we didn’t fix anything. It must have been a browser caching thing. Try clearing your cache. You did that already? Try again later”. Of course there are daily backups of all the databases. That deadline they agreed upon for the first milestone? That was a little too ambitious from what the developers were concerned, but their management decided to force it either way, so you don’t consider another provider and walk away with all that cash you could be spending in their shop. They’ll make it happen somehow, since deadlines are important. I already mentioned in a previous chapter that people become obsessed with the deadline, even at the risk of producing an inappropriate product. This manifests even more when you build software somewhere else. Meeting the deadlines is the best way for the provider to show that things are fine and dandy. But how will they hit the deadline? I mentioned insane working hours. That’s one way. The second is to deliver broken software (although they know it’s broken). You might not have seen this old movie called Gung Ho[158], with a Japanese corporation taking over an American car plant. There is a scene when the American workers deliver incomplete cars in hopes of fooling the Japanese executives that they could hit their imposed target of producing 15000 cars in one month. But the ruse fails when the main character of the movie tries to drive one of the cars away, and the car falls apart. The same can happens with software too. It looks good on the outside, but under the hood, everything is torn to shreds. Security of the code, code quality, good design, performance, etc., sacrificed because… deadline.

That’s why some horrible projects go on: because some want to make money while others can’t bear to pull the plug, they can’t, or still have some hope, even if the true situation becomes visible with the naked eye, with each passing day. I know cases of projects made in another country that got canceled, and then the companies started to fix the software locally. They had cheap people at the service provider and no one to verify their work. And everything was going extremely well until… it wasn’t. At all. Was it cheaper? Overall, it was not. It ended up costing more - a hidden cost that became visible only at the end. When you rewrite the software locally, you basically swallow the cost of outsourcing. That might be possible if you have a big company with high profits, so the company doesn’t go bust, but regardless, the time lost is nonetheless a terrible waste. So don’t make the mistake of outsourcing projects, then taking your paw off the software. You need to know what’s going on so that you can pull the plug on the whole thing if necessary. It’s better, after you put in a month in it to realize that these people aren’t right for you, that they don’t understand, or their work isn’t of the proper quality, and try with some other service provider, than to have this realization at the end of the project when it’s too late to save anything, maybe not even your company. If you go bankrupt or your company closes, the service provider can work for other companies anyway; they are not fully affected by your bankruptcy. And remember the project management triangle [76]. It’s all a balance of cost, schedule, and scope. If you are happy that the outsourcing provider is doing it cheap and fast, beware that somewhere else, things might fall apart to compensate for it. If it looks too good to be true, it probably isn’t. Check!

Different cultures

Let’s switch gears for a moment now. In the definition of outsourcing I used at the beginning of the chapter, I said that it’s about developing software within “another culture”. This is where the fun really begins: with the culture.

It’s hard to define what culture is[159], but one definition I liked was this one:

Culture is the collective programming of the mind, which distinguishes the members of one group or category of people from another - Geert Hofstede[160]

People in different cultures have different values, beliefs, behaviors, norms, and habits. They make different assumptions about things, their communication style might be different, their perception of things or their thinking can be different. And the list could go on. You can think of culture as a form of human conditioning that derives from one’s social environment. Culture affects thinking and behavior, and it’s something that can unconsciously trigger the way we respond to situations. Our conditioning dictates our default behaviors. To cut it short, if people are from a different country, it’s safe to assume that they are different from you and might also do things differently. How do you see burping and slurping at the table, for example? Tipping at the restaurant? Blowing your nose in public? How about a lack of eye contact? Is that dishonesty? Respect?

It’s hard to tell if something someone did was automatic because of their cultural background or if they had a different reason for doing it. Sometimes, you can’t even evaluate an action as right or wrong, because of different interpretations of the same thing. You can see this on user interfaces, for example. A Chinese user interface might look complicated or even badly designed to a Westerner or a European person, but it doesn’t actually mean that it is. It’s just how you perceive it, being from another culture, and becoming accustomed to UIs looking in a certain way. Let me give you another example. Some time ago, my wife bought a one-week intensive skincare program, or what I like to call “separating women from their money program”. Either way, it came in a box with seven vials of different creams. One vial was for oxygenation of the skin, one for exfoliation, that kind of stuff. You had to use one of the vials per day, in a specific order. This is how the box looked like:

My wife thought that’s weird, and so did I. The order should have been from left to right… obviously. But is it wrong they were the other way around? Of course not. We both just interpreted it as such because of our conditioning. Recent research[161] shows that language shapes the way we think. Since our native language is written left to right, that’s how we tend to organize space and time without even realizing it. Therefore, what seems obvious to you might not be so for someone else. What is considered true in one culture may not be so in another. And any situation can be good or bad depending on who is looking at it.

A mentality such as “I say, you do”, for example, can also manifest itself due to cultural differences. There is this thing called “the power distance index”[162], a measure of how someone from a culture generally reacts to a person in power. People in cultures with a high power distance index are less likely to question authority (which in this case is the client or the client’s employees). They are thought to respect authority and will not question things even if they seem wrong. They might not argue with you; it might even be rude in their culture to say “no” to you directly. Many are also afraid to ask questions out of fear of looking foolish or unintelligent. I mentioned that you have to treat the people at the service provider as if they were your employees, invest in them, and take into account their opinions, but if you, as a client with authority, tell people how to do something, they may consider that they have no right to an opinion of their own. That’s just how it is for them. So even when you want people to really “participate” in building your product, you may encounter some “holding back”. So before outsourcing something or during the collaboration, both sides must make an effort to understand each other and find out what makes them tick.

But let’s be serious now, you will not begin to study the culture of others, and neither will they study yours. That’s not going to happen. You can learn stuff about each other, but you will most likely not be able to understand each other fully. The problem with cultural differences is that everyone had a lifetime to practice in their own culture and too little or no time to practice in the culture of others. No training material, books, or cultural exchange workshops can bridge this gap and expose those things that are mostly unconscious to all of us. It simply cannot be done.

Nevertheless, you need some cultural awareness, so you don’t enter on your default mode when assessing a situation and then immediately jump to your own conditioned conclusions. You need to set some rules and expectations, on both sides, to understand each other’s work styles. To be understood from the beginning that you see and think differently and that it’s normal for misunderstandings, different assumptions, and conflicts to arise at some point. Then established a way to approach these situations (different cultures have different ways of resolving conflict also; if there is a conflict between parties, you will try to resolve with what you know about your culture, not about theirs, which can actually cause even more harm). Take some time to understand where both parties are coming from. This helps both sides be more understanding and less judgmental (i.e., how do we see things and why we react differently).

Besides “the power distance index”, another notion to be mindful of is that of “the four stages of cultural awareness”. I’ve encountered this in an article[163] by Stephanie Quappe and Giovanna Cantatore. They define the four stages of cultural awareness as being: the parochial stage (“my way is the only way”), followed by the ethnocentric stage (“I know their way, but my way is better”), the synergistic stage (“my way and their way; you chose the best way depending on the situation”), and finally, participatory stage (“our way; people come together to create a culture of shared meanings”). From my personal experience with outsourcing, cultural awareness stops at the second stage and maybe spills a bit into the third also. But that’s about it. People don’t put in the effort. And that’s normal when you think about it: it’s all about conducting business, not being adopted into a different culture.

But the most important thing, no matter what, is to pay attention to communication. Communication is the first victim of cultural and language differences. A lot of frustrations arise from this. The same statement can mean different things to different people because it passes through cultural filters built from all the experiences of growing up in a different environment. You think you are talking to people in plain English, but what they actually hear is subject to interpretation as the message being transmitted traverses their personal filters.

Then there is the fact that they might not understand or speak English well enough. I mentioned the importance of being able to communicate in English in a previous chapter; I won’t repeat it here. The accent might be the hardest thing to deal with. It’s very tiring to have a conf-call with someone and not understand a thing because of the accent. I’ve also been in many meetings with people having a strong accent or somehow seemed to leave their words unfinished when talking, and the only thing I could say in reply was, “Can you say that again, please?”. There is a limit to how many times you can ask someone to repeat before the conversation completely stalls. When that happens, you start to fill in the gaps with something you think the other person said or meant. So, not only is everything people say subject to interpretation because of cultural conditioning and because we think or do things in a certain way, unconsciously, but now, you also have to fill in the dots, which means making assumptions. And, to top it all of, it’s not just you who will make the assumptions. Because of bad English, or because they don’t master the language well, people can be hesitant to communicate or to ask questions, even when they know they didn’t understand something. It might be difficult for them to get their message across without feeling awkward, so they don’t even try. They have gaps in their understanding, but they don’t address them. Enter assumptions again. And asking, “Do you have any questions?” doesn’t help either. They respond with “No”. Actually, they do have questions, but they don’t know how to ask since they don’t have a good grasp of the English language.

So don’t assume stuff. Check that things are clear by always looking at what they are doing and using the suggestions from the previous chapter about meetings and reports to build good visibility into the project. Make minutes of the meetings, write down what was agreed and what the next steps to follow are. And try to keep only one communication channel with everyone, for all to see the same thing, for everyone to know the steps to follow and the actions to take. Without clear indications, people may accidentally ignore something important. This way, you avoid later saying to them that “We agreed to do that. Why didn’t you do it?” Which brings me to the next point.

“Yes” doesn’t necessarily mean “yes”. “Yes” might mean that they understood your words, not that they necessarily agree to do what you asked. Or “yes” might mean “we are determined, and we’ll do our best”, but that doesn’t necessarily mean it will happen. And the problem isn’t just with “Yes”. They might also have problems saying “No”. In some cultures, saying “No” to your face might be considered disrespectful, or saying “No” to someone in a position of authority might result in consequences for the person (see the “the power distance index” I mentioned above). So they might postpone a response, beat it around the bush, or they will try to provide details so you figure out on your own that they are actually trying to say “No”. It becomes very frustrating that it’s difficult to be on the same wavelength even on basic communication matters like “Yes” or “No”. And these problems also manifest themselves when it comes to communicating bad news or point out your mistakes, even when they know you are wrong.

Saying “No” to you, directly, might be seen as rude, but be aware that they might also be reluctant to do so because they are afraid you will take your business elsewhere. It’s like the following joke:

A young woman starts a new job at a general store. On her first day, her employer says to her: “Remember! We never say ‘No’ to customers, even if we don’t have the product on stock. We lie, promise things, whatever is needed to stall them until we receive the item. Otherwise, they will go elsewhere to spend their money, and we don’t want that”.
All said and done. A month goes by; she gets the idea. Some man then enters the store:
– Do you have gloves?
– Of course. What kind do you want? Made from leather? Knitted? With two fingers? With five?
– Leather gloves. With five fingers.
– With what will you wear them? A coat? A jacket?
– A coat. Winter is coming.
– What color is the coat? Blue? Black? Brown? Gray?
– Kind of… black, I guess.
– I suggest you bring the coat with you tomorrow, to see what gloves would match best.
Happy that the young woman paid so much attention to him and wants to help him make the best purchase, the man leaves. But when he’s about to go out the door, an angry individual enters the store with a toilet lid in one hand and a bathroom tile in the other, and starts yelling:
– Lady! Look! This is the toilet lid. This is the color of my bathroom tile. I showed you my ass yesterday. WILL YOU SELL ME THAT DAMN TOILET PAPER NOW?

So pay attention when they avoid saying “No” or postpone sending you bad news. “Everything’s fine” or “we are close to delivering” might just mean that the shit is waiting for the fan to be turned on. That’s why I mentioned that you have to have your own people who are involved and know what’s under the hood: to minimize misunderstandings (because they will say one thing, but the code will say another) and prevent people from straying too far when a misunderstanding occurs. And speaking of misunderstandings, misunderstandings will develop - a lot.

Misunderstandings arise when I use my meanings to make sense of your reality - Stephanie Quappe, Giovanna Cantatore[163]

There is simply no escaping this. You and your outsourced team don’t share the same world view. You evaluate things and assess situations about the other by using your own culture as a point of reference. Misunderstandings will, inevitably, occur. But if something occurs, besides fixing the problem, try to understand what happened, so you recognize the situation in the future before it occurs again. And pay close attention to what caused the issues, so that indifference or ill will don’t end up being attributed to these misunderstandings. Did they intentionally do something other than what you said? “It’s a misunderstanding”. Did they intentionally work on something they knew was a low priority? “It’s a misunderstanding”. They knew they would miss the delivery date but didn’t tell a soul about it? “It’s a misunderstanding”. They lied straight to your face? “It’s a misunderstanding”. It becomes very easy then to hide behind this expression and then, in turn, behind the different language or the different culture. Again, a person who knows what’s going on in detail can prevent such situations from happening and identify if something is really a misunderstanding or not.

And you’ll waste a lot of time repairing these misunderstandings: conf-calls, meetings, training, investing more time to enhance the documentation, setting up new processes and procedures, etc. Furthermore, the solution itself often has to wait too if you are in another time zone, with many hours apart. In this case, you may need to leave directions in writing or by email. Then, your virtual team members come to work, and they don’t understand the message, so now they may wait for you to come back also, to ask for more details or to clarify things further. And so on. Everything starts to slow down, work synchronization becomes a pain, management overhead increases. This is another hidden cost you pay with outsourcing: lots of things slow down. Communication is the first victim, but it’s not the only one. Responding to change, for example, is another. I talked about changes to software in previous chapters: there will always be change. If you have a team halfway across the world, changes will be more difficult because they will be “with delay”. And here is where what I said above becomes even more important. It matters what kind of people work for you at the service provider. If you have proactive people who understand the domain and that you trained well, they’ll be able to anticipate things, and they can make decisions even when for you it’s midnight and everyone is asleep. So you have to invest in them, to work at smoothing out the cultural differences, and involving them more in the project, even if they may not be very willing to do so. If instead, you consider them only an execution unit and you just send them tasks to perform, they’ll wait for you for everything. If it’s something new, they start asking many questions. They ask a question, then wait for an answer. They want to do something; they’ll wait for approval. They are doing something; they wait for feedback. They discover some parts of the application impacted by a change; they wait for an analysis and a decision from you. Everything takes a thousand years to be completed.

Final responsibility

I’ve mentioned a few quicksands you can get yourself into when outsourcing and a few ways to avoid them, but in closing, I just want to reemphasize the fact that outsourcing comes not only with a reduction of costs but also with some responsibilities on the part of those that outsource their development. Everyone understands the difference between “cheaper” and “more expensive”, but not everyone understands how software development is done. Even fewer companies understand how building the software somewhere else will impact development. So, attention needs to be paid to both of these aspects: building software and building it somewhere else, by someone else. When you outsource, you need to be “hands-on”, especially if you outsource software that’s part of your core business. It’s vital to have someone you trust, who knows what’s going on and who understands all aspects of product development, someone who can track things and take corrective measures if they see something happening that veers work away from the goals of the project so that you don’t discover a mess six months later when nothing else can be done to fix it. In other words, you can’t really outsource all of the development; you have to have your own people, who even if they don’t actually contribute code to the project, they keep their eyes on the ball at all times. A developer is close to what is happening, so you need a trusted developer (or more) on your side (or, most preferably, your own people at the outsourcing provider).

The best indicator, in my opinion, to know if your little outsourced project will turn out well is if the people at the service provider prove to be reliable. Do they understand the business and know what needs to be built? Are they proactive people who can work by themselves, or do you always need to feed them with a spoon? If you are not always keeping a watch on them, do they make a mess of things? Are they good people or just cheaper resources? Who’s building the software matters a lot, so make sure you get good developers, then treat them as an extension of your company. This means investing in them to ensure they work the way you want them to work, even with all the communication challenges, differences in culture, and misunderstandings.

Remember also that at the end of the day, you get what you pay for. So be aware of what you’re buying. Outsourcing doesn’t all come down to software being cheaper to build, possibly using the least expensive service provider that you could find that’s willing to give it a try. Would you buy the cheapest food? How about the most inexpensive house? The cheapest car? The cheapest clothes? No? Why not? Because of the quality, of course. That’s something everyone understands. The cheaper something is, the lower the quality. If software is a cost for you, and you want it cheap, don’t imagine things are any different than the examples I just mentioned. If that software is running (or is) your business, don’t just look at the price tag, be hands-on, put in the effort, and get properly involved. You give up some control when you outsource, but don’t make the mistake of giving up all the control. You need to make sure they build the right software. This is your responsibility, not only theirs.

Scrum

There are various software development methodologies. There are the so-called traditional methods like Waterfall, Rational Unified Process, or the Spiral Model. And then there are the Agile methods of building software (always “Agile”, with a capital “A”) like Scrum, eXtreme Programming, or Kanban. Companies might also be doing some hybrid of these, or maybe following in-house methodologies, or just hacking things together by following no particular method of work.

These methodologies have their pros and cons, their limitations, and types of projects for which they are better suited. There isn’t a “one way” to build software, although, for a lot of projects, the Agile methodologies tend to fit better the nature of software development where you often encounter unclear requirements, uncertain estimations, constant scope changes, etc. So many companies nowadays are doing (or at least advertising that they are doing) Agile, most likely, the Scrum variant on which I’ll focus in this chapter since probably that’s what you will be exposed to when you start on your first development job in a software company. If you don’t know what Scrum is, you can start by reading the Scrum Guide[164]. Go read it! I’ll wait…

The idea behind using Scrum or other Agile practices is that, in today’s environment, things move very fast. Everything becomes about how fast you can adapt to an ever-changing business environment. Using a traditional approach for building software might no longer be the best option, because, by the time you finish with all your requirements gathering and planning, the environment might be completely different, throwing all that effort out the window and forcing you to start all over again, not to mention if you spend months or even years working on an application before having a first releasable version. Today, companies need to move with agility to quickly adapt to market changes, be competitive or keep their customers competitive, quickly chase new opportunities in a cost-effective way, deliver value, keep in front of the competition, etc. Companies that realize this, thus want to move with more agility, to be better equipped in responding to this dynamic environment. They notice their old ways aren’t working anymore, they got tired of software projects going over budget, take forever to be built, or end up lacking some important features. They want what’s called an Agile Transformation, and then they choose Scrum to bring about this transformation. And when they do, they see it as a lifeline; they think they’ve discovered the holy grail of developing software.

You do it!

Most companies are doing Scrum because it’s simple to understand (ignore that part from the guide where it says “Difficult to master”, that’s not important right now…), it looks like (and is often sold as) a process, seems simple to implement (it basically tells you what to do), and it’s non-technical. Although people really want the benefits of Scrum, they don’t always understand what it’s actually about, so they approach it in the only way they know how: as a process. They think that by following the process, doing the ceremonies, implementing the steps, or however you want to call it, somehow things will fall in place, and an Agile transformation will occur. They want to be Agile but have approached it incorrectly by trying to fake it till they make it… no brain involved. The effort might eventually bring satisfaction once people start to think about what they are doing and finally “get it”, but until they do, things will be a struggle, and a lot of errors will be made.

In addition to those who adopt Scrum in an attempt to become more Agile, there is another category of companies that don’t really want an Agile transformation. All they want is to move with the times (i.e., if everyone - especially the competition - is doing software development in a certain way, so should we). They don’t really care much about Agile or Scrum; they just want to advertise themselves as an Agile company. They just want the Agile and Scrum buzzwords. They want to do Scrum because everyone else is doing it. These are the kinds of companies that will cram the newest programming languages into a legacy project built with deprecated technologies just because it sells better and gives clients the impression that they are buying modern software. Along the same lines, they think that Scrum is new (if you can consider something that’s been around for 25+ years as new), Waterfall is old; when you want software built, you don’t go to some people doing Waterfall, you go to some that do Agile, right? So it’s all about placing an Agile “sticker” on the company to boast that they can do more.

Fasting is a practice in several religions of the world. It’s a means of purifying the body and the soul, and it involves total or partial abstinence from certain foods. In case of partial abstinence, you might restrain yourself from consuming meat, eggs, dairy, or any other foods that contain animal products. During periods of fasting, what happens is that many products start to be marked as being fasting products. Shops set up a special aisle with such products, or the manufacturers themselves draw customer attention by placing a sticker on the products that says: “Fasting product”. The product is the same as it is on any other day of the year, but now, all of a sudden, it’s a fasting product. Nothing changed in the taste of the product, in its quality, in the ingredients, the way it was produced, not even the wrapping is different. Nothing! Well, not quite nothing; the product might be more expensive, for the shops to try to make a bigger profit during the periods of fasting. But apart from that, and the sticker, nothing is different. When the time is right, companies will do that no matter the situation. Other examples I’ve seen of stickers placed on already existing products are “Lactose-free”, “Gluten-free”, or “Vegan-Friendly”. At least in these cases, they could have changed the wrapping or the packaging since they don’t need a certain period of the year to advertise their products as such.

Sadly, that’s the form of Scrum some companies actually do. Some organizations are trying to figure things out, while others don’t even care and just want a sticker. Some companies use Scrum properly, but I won’t be talking about that; that’s not what this book is about. This book is about the quicksands. In the types of companies I am talking about, people struggle with Scrum usually because these organizations consider Agile to be something that only the development teams have to do. Upper management thinks that if the development teams do Scrum, they will somehow get an actual Agile transformation, or otherwise enough change to justify the presence of the Agile sticker. In these companies, Scrum is selected by management as a development methodology and imposed on project teams. The CEO decides that the company needs to become Agile - for whatever of the two reasons mentioned above - so one day, they announce to everyone that “Starting today, we are Agile!”. Or, developers are called into some executive’s office, and a discussion like the following takes place (and I’m not even joking):

“Executive”: That project you all work on… You need to do Scrum from now on.
“Developers”: ?!?! … Don’t we need a Scrum Master and a Product Owner to do Scrum?
“Executive”: You can fill those roles among yourselves.
“Developers”: ?!?! (looking at each other)
“Executive”: Questions?
“Developers”: ?!?! (still looking at each other)
“Executive”: Good. Now go back to work and place a recurring meeting in my calendar. I want to attend your demos.

Of course, that’s complete rubbish. If a company is to be Agile, “the entire company” needs to be Agile. It’s not something you just decide to do, or actually… decide on the development team to do. It’s a change in mindset. For example, you can’t keep things like traditional “Command and Control”[102] attitudes in the company’s top layers, while placing all the responsibility for making Scrum succeed somewhere lower in the food chain. The developers should now follow the Scrum rules and commit to 100% delivery every sprint or else… while in the rest of the company, it’s “business as usual” doesn’t really work. Bosses and managers need to understand the new mindset. Clients also. You can’t have a client who isn’t involved, who tells you what they want, then go missing, only to get back to you six months later and demand you deliver what you promised. And they want you to deliver everything they asked for, before the date they imposed, and it’s your own damn business how you make that happen, by using Scrum or whatever else you want, it doesn’t really matter to them. An agile transformation needs to start from the top and flow downward; the other way around doesn’t really work. It’s useless if the team uses Scrum to perfection, but at the top, people don’t have the right values. But I’m getting ahead of myself… Let’s first talk about a few things that occur in Scrum teams and later have a look at the big picture, which includes the whole company.

The Scrum Master

Because it was decided that Scrum is something that only the development team will do, management is unwilling to invest too much money in this (like I said, in some instances, it’s all about the “Agile” sticker), so one of the developers is placed as a Scrum Master. Being a Scrum Master is a full-time job (at least when you begin working with Scrum), so a developer having to do this part-time cannot be successful. And now a thing starts to occur. If you noticed, so far, I said “doing” Scrum. But Scrum is a framework. You “use” a framework; you don’t “do” a framework. Because the developers “do” Scrum instead of “using” Scrum, they have this desire to do it right, and at the same time, this fear to not do it wrong (you can find something similar with people doing REST[165]; they are afraid they are doing it wrong and always ask the question: “Is this a RESTful web service?”). The result is religiously following what the developers think is a process or methodology for building software. And that is a fail however you put it. Because Scrum is a framework, it is a general thing; it is something incomplete. What matters then is what you build on top of it, i.e., your own techniques and practices.

If, however, management at least tries to make a minimum of effort to make things work, they will hire a Scrum Master. A junior Scrum Master. Someone without experience. That is, the next cheapest solution than to get a developer from the team to fill this role part-time. Because they lack experience, what this junior Scrum Master will do, is start with the same thing a developer would: religiously following the process. Sprints? Check. Stand-ups? Check. Backlog? Check. Planning? Refinement? Review? Retrospective? Check. Check. Check. “Hmmm… seems we are doing Scrum by the book” (which, by the way, is a guide, not a book). And this Scrum Master might be well-intentioned and might be passionate, but because they’re a novice, they don’t actually understand how to use Scrum, it’s just rigid adherence to everything they read. And there’s a lot of knowledge out there, and the Scrum Master is trying to absorb all kinds of good information, but they immediately apply it to the team, without fully understanding it and without anticipating the consequences of what they are doing. They basically experiment on the team in the process of learning, without understanding why, and without being able to fully explain it to the team, who are forced to follow, with frustration, some steps that they don’t understand. The Scrum Master is super excited about everything they discover and put into practice; however, they notice that the rest of the team members aren’t as excited as they are. So they somehow conclude that things need to be more fun in order to be more engaging. So they work on that (you learn better when you have fun, right?) starting from subjecting the team to inspirational Agile videos, forcing the format of retrospectives to mini team buildings, or role-playing games, or “bring your mother to work Fridays”. They are well-intentioned, but they do a lot of damage because “Monkey see, monkey do”[166] isn’t the approach a new Scrum team needs. And if someone points it out, they get defensive and start yelling at the team that it’s the “Shu” from “Shu Ha Ri”[167], you baboon. Give it some time…

Another option is for a Project Manager to be put in place as a Scrum Master, and then (because of professional deformation as a Project Manager), you continue to do traditional project management, but in iterations. This Scrum Master plans things out and assigns people work, they challenge team estimations, each sprint end becomes a deadline, the Daily Stand-Up turns into a daily status, or retrospectives turn into criticism that people did not respect their commitments. Basically, you end up with “Command and Control” Scrum. If they force people to work overtime each sprint, to get 100% delivery, then things easily transform into a fight between the developers and the Project Manager… oh, excuse me… the Scrum Master, everyone pulling in different directions. And the fight continues until one day some developer discovers that “commitment” has been changed to “forecast” way, way, waaaaay back in the 2011 version of the Scrum Guide[168], while the Project Manager turned Scrum Master is all about “commitment this” and “commitment that”. So the developers print the guide, highlight with a marker all the occurrences of the word “forecast”, give it to the Scrum Master, and… kindly suggest what they should do with their precious “commitment”.

Scrum defines a team as consisting of a Product Owner, Developers, and a Scrum Master. When it comes to Scrum Masters (and not just this role), the major mistake many companies make is that they try to fill in a position. That’s all; to check one of Scrum’s components with an X. Because they are not very serious about the Agile adoption, they neglect to realize that this person should be at the helm of the Scrum implementation, and therefore not everyone can be a Scrum Master. You can’t simply “recycle” someone from the existing team, or hire a junior that’s as new to Scrum as everyone else. You need an experienced Scrum Master when starting on the Scrum journey. They will act as the training wheels on a bicycle when you first learn to ride it. An experienced Scrum Master knows the success stories, but also the failures. They understand your circumstances and know how to help the team build on top of the Scrum framework. They keep an eye on everything and make sure that the values and principles of Agile materialize in your practices. And because your practices will evolve over time, they also monitor how your new approaches of doing things align with the Agile values and principles.

An experienced Scrum Master can notice when the team uses practices that move them away from the Scrum guidelines. They notice when the product backlog turns into detailed upfront requirements instead of a list of features, when stand-ups turn into status meetings, when sprints become mini-projects with a deadline at the end, when the Product Owner is not involved, when the team doesn’t work at a sustainable pace, that people are silent at retrospective meetings, or that agreed action items in the retrospective get forgotten, and problems always reappear, and many other things that others might miss if they only focus on checking some boxes of steps when they do those steps.

When you stray from the Agile practices, the Scrum Master’s job is to provide guidance and help you get back on track. And I want to emphasize the word “guidance”. The Scrum Master doesn’t impose Scrum on anyone. There is nothing worse for a team than having a Scrum Master obsessed with Scrum and with forcing it down everyone’s throats. An experienced Scrum Master has passed the stage of “let’s worship at the Scrum altar”, or “I’m a certified Scrum Master, so I know what I’m doing”, and they have learned what works and what doesn’t, and how to guide their team without becoming a bully or look like an idiot who daily comes down from Agile mountain with the tablets of Scrum commandments. A Scrum Master is about leading and coaching, and a good Scrum Master spends time with the team, interacts with them, understands them, knows that software is made by people and that people are just as important as following the Scrum Guide. And to be able to do these things properly, a Scrum Master must have certain skills on three major fronts.

First of all, they need to be very familiar with Scrum and Agile practices to teach others. You can’t assign someone as the Scrum Master if they don’t know Scrum. Maybe the person has the right attitude, they are smart, and curious, and like to learn, etc., and it makes sense they can also learn Scrum, but they won’t be what is needed because they can’t help you with your Scrum practice. They can’t help the team to improve or grow, and they can’t help you make a change if they don’t even know what Scrum is all about or what being Agile means. As I said, you are not just filling a position within the team. Many hire junior Scrum Masters to keep the cost low, but they just end up paying a salary to someone who can’t really help them. You can’t just pick someone off the street and make them a Scrum Master. It doesn’t work that way. That’s why it also doesn’t work to have a developer from the team act as a part-time Scrum Master. It’s about recognizing problems and situations and coming up with suggestions for improvement; it’s about instilling new values and behaviors; it’s about a completely different mindset. Some people think that a Scrum Master is some kind of a personal assistant that facilitates meetings and Scrum ceremonies, takes meeting minutes and notes, makes sure information radiators are up to date or reminds team members that it’s time for the Daily Stand-Up. Yes, they do these things, but that’s not the point. You don’t become Agile like that. So, your Scrum Master needs to know their stuff. And this doesn’t stop just at knowing Agile practices and principles, which gets me to the next point.

The second important thing a Scrum Master needs to have is people skills. Their job is not just coaching the team on how to use the Scrum framework, but also helping the team get better, motivating the people, keeping them focused on the goals, challenging them when needed, help with conflict resolution when necessary, etc. It’s in people’s nature to resist change, and in addition, a lot of things can occur that can potentially hinder the adoption of a new way of working, so the Scrum Master needs to have the skills to sell everyone on the benefits of doing Scrum. You can’t do any of that if you don’t know how to deal with people. Then come new situations, blockages, or conflicts, you have to know how to interact with all sorts of people, when to impose your point of view and when to just let something go. The Scrum Guide doesn’t mention all of these things. You need someone who has already encountered such situations and knows how to handle them. You need someone with good soft skills. As mentioned previously in the book, it’s things like being a good communicator, having leadership skills, dealing with difficult people, being emphatic, innovative, creative, being a team player, etc. Although the Scrum Master’s responsibility is to promote and support Scrum, and not act as a Team Lead, they still need to have similar skills as a Team Lead and understand how teams work (and by that, I mean real teamwork, not just people coordinating their work), what dysfunctions can affect them, and why a safe working environment is essential for people to perform at their best.

The third thing a Scrum Master needs to know is how software gets built. Scrum works regardless of the domain, and the Scrum Guide doesn’t say that the Scrum Master should be a technical person, but let’s not forget that we’re developing software, not something else. In any field, the way you do the work is affected by the nature of the work itself. I believe that a Scrum Master cannot help developers become Agile unless they understand their work and what they do. For example, when the team debates the advantages and disadvantages of certain technologies, libraries, or techniques, it’s hard to help them identify areas of improvement or, on the contrary, possible risks or problems, or foster communication for that matter, if the Scrum Master doesn’t even understand what the discussion is about. So the Scrum Master must understand the developers’ language and their technical practices. They can’t improve things if, from all the discussions they have with developers, they don’t understand certain parts and only try to focus on the Scrum aspects. A Scrum Master must continuously assess the situation and ensure that corrections and adjustments are made. It’s the whole “inspect and adapt” mentioned in the Scrum Guide. Many of the situations that come up may be of a technical nature. How can they help the team inspect and adapt on everything if they don’t even understand what some things are about? Good Scrum Masters are former developers or have a computer science background. As developers improve their practices and techniques, the Scrum Master may need to learn together with them. Obviously, not at the same knowledge depth, but at least at the same pace. So they need some technical fundamentals. They must know how software gets built. Be careful, though, if the Scrum Master has a technical background, or is a former developer, don’t think you can put them to work to supplement the team and write some code when they are not facilitating Scrum events. They might do that to help the team or remove blockers, but that’s not their job. They need to be a full-time Scrum Master; otherwise, you risk wandering off the Scrum path and into quicksands.

I’ll say this again, to be successful with Scrum when you start with this new method of work, you need an experienced Scrum Master to guide you, a Scrum Master with skills from the three categories I just mentioned. But even if they want to hire an experienced Scrum Master, considering these are companies that are just starting with Scrum, many do not know how to hire them. How do they know if they are any good or not? They don’t have experience with this. Well, they tend to hire the ones who have more certifications. Scrum (and Agile in general) is better at building software than other more traditional methods, so it became very widespread. As it happens when things go mainstream, inevitably there will be some that will want to take opportunity of the fact. The Agile community is no exception. You will find actors that don’t necessarily have any real experience with Scrum (they are just monetizing on a commercial opportunity) but shine at selling you stuff like consultancy, courses, workshops, Agile tools, and of course, certifications. So, what do you want to be? A Certified Scrum Master? Certified Scrum Product Owner? Certified Scrum Developer? Certified Scrum Professional? For modest amounts of money ranging from $500 to $5,000, you can get any diploma you like, from Agile Achiever to Agile Champion, to Agile Evangelist. You really want to be something like a champion, not just a mere achiever, so pay the big bucks, please! If the Scrum Master is a converted Project Manager with other project management certifications under their belt (showing a broader level of knowledge and expertise, and ability to work in any project environment), then even better.
