But if you hire such a certified Scrum Master, there is no guarantee that you will get someone good (certifications don’t guarantee anything; I mentioned this several times throughout the book). So the chances are that such a Scrum Master will demand to be sent to various courses to get even more certifications, they will probably not help you with much, then leave angrily saying that Scrum can’t work in this company of frustrated and closed-minded individuals that resist the changes they want to impose (i.e., whatever they mechanically learned for their certification exam).

As with many other professions, it takes years to become good at something, and a Scrum Master is no different. So you have to look for people with some years of experience under their belt (5+ years of experience is, in my opinion, enough time for people to understand both the good and the bad, the advantages and the disadvantages of what they do). Look for a developer who made the move to being a Scrum Master or someone who did just that as a career. I would avoid converted Project Managers, especially ones with many years as a manager under their belt, with possible habits that they can’t shake.

The last thing I want to mention about Scrum Master, and the importance of hiring one with experience, is that a Scrum Master is local to the team, but their responsibility doesn’t end there.

The Scrum Master helps those outside the Scrum Team understand which of their interactions with the Scrum Team are helpful and which aren’t. The Scrum Master helps everyone change these interactions to maximize the value created by the Scrum Team - The Scrum Guide[164]

This means that the Scrum Master is a coach not just for the team, but also for others in the organization. Everyone needs to know what’s happening; everyone needs to understand the rules and the values of Scrum. And it’s the Scrum Master’s role to educate everyone, something very hard to do if everyone thinks Scrum is something the development team “does”, while everything else can stay the same.

And they must do this without being in control. You’ll also hear a lot about servant leadership[176]. The Scrum Master is thus a leader and a master, but they are not in control. They don’t order people what to do or force decisions on the team or the organization. Instead, they influence people; they help and offer support for the people to develop and perform to the best of their abilities. They also need to remove impediments to allow this to happen efficiently, so people understand and apply the Scrum framework better. The Scrum Master’s work is all about empowerment and teaching people to be responsible for sorting things out on their own, giving them all the tools needed to do the work. Once that happens, and people finally understand and know how to do things, they can take over the Scrum and manage it on their own.

Going back to the analogy of the Scrum Master being like the training wheels on a bicycle, once you have learned how to ride your bike, you don’t need the training wheels anymore. They only acted as a support, so you don’t fall over. With Scrum, once everyone understands it, the Scrum Master should no longer be needed. If people have the right values and right practices and do the right things, then they don’t need a Scrum Master to tell them when they make mistakes or when some inefficiency needs fixing. The team itself recognizes that. Everyone in the organization recognizes that. So the role of a Scrum Master is one that’s supposed to go away, eventually. Or at least that was the theory. In practice, however, unfortunately, the job of a Scrum Master remains necessary because people can slip back into old habits, the ones they had before adopting Scrum. There will always be problems; there will always be emergencies. It’s not hard then to start taking shortcuts and wander off the right path. So the Scrum Master must be there to bring them back on course and keep them engaged with what’s important. The Scrum Master acts as the immune system of the Scrum implementation. They check that everyone does their job to the best of their abilities, and when there are signs that things are not going well, they intervene. And if they have to intervene frequently… that’s not a good sign; it’s a sign of illness.

More realistically speaking, if the rest of the organization doesn’t really care, are set in their old ways, and still go by their old habits, the Scrum Master needs to throw themselves on any grenade that upper management might toss in the team’s direction. The grenade can take many forms. I’ve already mentioned some of them above. Bosses want 100% sprint delivery, every sprint, or they start screaming and threatening when a story can’t be completed on time. The team should estimate in hours or man-days, not silly story points or T-shirt sizes. The team’s velocity must always grow (if they managed to do 100 story points this sprint, they should do 110 the next one). The sprint is in progress, but bosses insist that the team should take on another important story, in addition to what they already have in progress, and to commit to solving it along with the rest of the issues they planned to do this sprint (with this Scrum thingy you should do more in less time, right?). Clients and bosses turn into a “peanut gallery”[177] during the review meetings, focusing on the negatives and ignoring the positives. The development team organizes and manages its own work until the team does something that’s not to management’s liking, and everything turns back to “command and control”. Or the team has some bad news to communicate (and inevitably, they will give some bad news since few software projects go smoothly), and bosses go straight for the jugular and want to participate at the Daily Stand-Ups or ask for daily status updates until things improve. And the list could go on.

If you don’t have upper management’s support, you will fail with Scrum. Scrum must be understood not only by the development team or the Product Owner, but also by managers, bosses, clients, salespeople, and all the rest of the business units or departments involved in building the product. The Scrum Master will have some convincing to do with everyone. Their job isn’t just about making sure that the development team follows the practices and principles of Scrum, but also to check that others within the organization understand this new way of working and this new mindset. It’s not an easy job to do. If the Scrum Master works in a company that just wants the “Agile” sticker, the chances of success are minimal. One of the jobs of the Scrum Master is to remove impediments to the development team’s progress. Guess what? If people believe that Scrum is just another way of flipping burgers, then bosses, managers, clients, or the rest of the organization, can all become obstacles to the Scrum team. Higher-ups may not listen to a Scrum Master unless they were hired to work at an organizational level, not just at the team level (and then they are more of an Agile Coach instead of a Scrum Master). So, a Scrum Master from within the team going to top management and explaining Scrum is like a developer going to them and trying to explain source code. I’m not saying it’s impossible to change their ways, but it’s difficult because they only think about the schedule, the delivery, the cost, and “managing by exception”. Their ways of working are fine; it’s the developers that should deliver more and faster. That’s why they are doing this Scrum thingy, right? So you’re not going to accomplish much because they are not open to change, and their values don’t align well with those of Scrum. But I’ll get to that later…

The Product Owner

Let’s now switch gears and mention a few things about the Product Owner too. Hopefully, the company pays more attention to selecting a Product Owner than in choosing a Scrum Master. In this case, you can’t hire someone with certifications, or put someone from the development team to fill in “a position”. It takes someone with experience in the domain, the business, the market, and the product, so they can tell developers what exactly needs to be built. And now comes the first problem with regards to Product Owners: that they’re someone who tells developers what to do. Sounds like a Project Manager, right?

When companies place a Project Manager in the role of a Product Owner, the first problem is that the Product Owner isn’t, in fact, an “owner”. They’re a proxy for the client, stakeholders, boss, or whoever makes decisions about the product. It’s someone who receives orders from above then just passes them onto others.

A Product Owner does indeed represent the desires of clients or stakeholders, handles communication between them and the development team, and it’s their job to interact with the layers above to gather information and so forth, but they must have a say in defining the product, to be a part of the vision of the product, and to sit at the decision table. A true Product Owner needs to be in charge; they cannot be just a proxy that does what they’re told. Just like you need a Scrum Master to really be a “master” with Scrum, in the same way, you need a Product Owner that is indeed an “owner” of the product. For the Product Owner to succeed, the entire organization must respect their decisions; says so in the Scrum Guide[164]. If you have a proxy Product Owner instead, they can, of course, come up with proposals and suggestions, but they are not in charge of the product, they have no authority, someone above them decides, and the Product Owner just transposes the requirements into backlog items and makes sure the team delivers them. Basically, their main responsibility is to make sure features are built on time, that deadlines are met, and milestones are hit. With a proxy Product Owner, there is often no room for negotiation about schedules, deadlines, milestones, or what the product must contain.

Things with a proxy Product Owner don’t work out as smoothly as with a real Product Owner in terms of communication and understanding of what needs to be developed. That’s because a proxy Product Owner always has to ask “above” when they’re not sure about something. And this takes time. Any questions that the development team has, or any decision that needs to be taken, no matter how small, turns into “I’ll check/ask and return with an answer”… a few days later, if at all. The development team must now wait for a response, one that a real Product Owner could have given them on the spot, or a decision they could have made right away. But since the team shouldn’t be sitting around doing nothing, because that’s not financially effective, the Product Owner will have to make assumptions, and development will be performed on these assumptions until they receive an answer. Or the team might need to work on something else from the backlog that does not require extra information. And then, at the end of the sprint, during the Review Meeting, you might have the unpleasant surprise to discover that instead of receiving feedback on what should be done next and what can be improved, to get criticism on all the things you did wrong and how you need to fix them. With a proxy Product Owner, you risk building the wrong product, generate waste, or spending time each sprint fixing some of the stuff you made in the previous sprints.

So, if they’re a proxy, at least the Product Owner needs to be a good proxy and proactively handle their role in the team. I say “proactively” because a proxy Product Owner can easily go idle and wait to be told what to do, or interact with the team only when necessary. Scrum has events, and it’s easy for certain activities of the Product Owner to start to revolve around them. Like for example, the refinement of the backlog. “Hey guys, when should we do refinement? Two hours meeting, every Thursday at 14:00. Great! See you then”. Or after sprint Planning, you decide what stories you will take in the sprint, then the Product Owner disappears. “I have meetings all afternoon. We’ll talk tomorrow at the sprint Daily. See ya”.

A Product Owner needs to be involved all the time, not just at the sprint Planning, the Daily, or one Refinement Meeting. They need to set priorities and order the backlog, define and detail the stories before refining them with the team, to be completely immersed in the product, to be there for the team, with the team. The Product Owner must have everything ready before the development team can start implementing things. A good Product Owner is like a good host who sets the table for their guests. You have everything you need at the table, you don’t have to get up to get a fork, salt, or more napkins, they bring the second course at the right time without the guests starting to get hungry after the first course or still chewing on it, and so on. This is how a Product Owner should behave in relation to the Scrum team also. They must be there with the table set, everything prepared, and ready at any time to answer the team’s questions or make decisions. If they’re not the ones making the decisions and constantly have to wait on others for answers, choices, or direction, it will take ages for the development team to receive the information they need, or they end up discovering it while the work is underway.

I don’t mean to have detailed specs in place before the team begins to work on stories in the sprint. You can do things “just in time”, and it’s acceptable to discover things or find out more information as you are working on tasks because, in Agile, things rely on the conversations, the collaboration, and the interaction between people. But to have these things, the Product Owner must be available all the time, not only Thursday at 14:00, at the sprint planning, or at the Daily; otherwise, you end up without well-defined stories and without the conversations you have to have about them too. Then you risk the team saying at the sprint Planning about stories to “just pull them into the sprint, and we’ll figure it out later” and then discover a lot of problems during implementation, problems that could have been avoided if people just collaborated effectively.

Another problem with Product Owners, somewhat related to sporadic involvement and combined with the fact that development is done in iterations of (often) two weeks, is that the Product Owner risks acquiring a short-term vision of the product or focusing on what needs to be done next sprint and end up neglecting the big picture. Do you have two-week sprints, and the product vision spans two weeks also? Not good! You need to think ahead at what the product should contain and do some longer-term planning. Just looking around the next bend is not enough.

Having a properly constructed Product Backlog helps with this. It needs to be continuously refined and ordered to show a clear direction of development. The Backlog is a living thing and needs to be handled as such. What happens in many teams is that the Product Backlog ends up as a pile where features, bugs, changes, and enhancements are thrown one on top of the other, and then, during the Refinement Meeting or sprint Planning, people choose something they find useful to work on for the next couple of weeks. You know what you’ll be working on this sprint and maybe the next, but you forget what the final goal is.

It’s not about building detailed plans (we already know what happens when plans meet reality) or to draw out all the sprints in advance and decide what each one must contain, but it is about looking ahead. Each sprint - and the work you select for the sprint - needs to be the next best thing that’s needed for the product; it’s not just doing some features from the backlog. I’ve seen situations where people didn’t work on what was important because something wasn’t ready, or there was an unsatisfied dependency or an important resource was not available. Something that should have been done later, something less important, was taken in the current sprint because that was the only thing people could work on. Why? Because they didn’t make sure that “the table is properly set, that everyone has plates, cutlery, napkins, etc.”. For example, Scrum teams are supposed to be cross-functional, having all the needed competencies to do the work. If you work on a UI intensive application, you will certainly need wire-frames and designs. So you need a designer on the team. Your application might also have a persistence layer with a large database behind it. You might need to set up backups or data recovery mechanisms, do configurations, optimizations, or database migrations. So maybe you need a DBA in the team. Or you might need an expert on something, but only for a short time. Having underutilized designers, DBAs, or experts present 8 hours a day, five days a week, only on your project might not make sense financially. Companies always want their employees working at full capacity, so sometimes multiple teams might need to share a designer, a DBA, or an expert of some sort. Designs need to be finalized and approved by the time a feature is pulled into a sprint. The database needs to be set up and configured by the time developers need to add the business logic on top of the persistence layer. So you have to think ahead of time about when you will need these people, so you don’t realize at the Sprint Planning meeting that you are blocked or that you can’t work on a story because it’s not your turn to have access to these resources. So, the Product Owner needs to be aware of these situations and together with the developers and the Scrum Master to plan a way to have these things organized so that everything is available when needed.

Also related to this aspect of focusing only on the next two weeks and neglecting the big goals of the product, pay close attention to another thing that can manifest itself when you’re not careful about the long-term objectives: scope creep[86]. Scope creep is mostly a concept found in traditional development methodologies like Waterfall, where you have a fixed and (presumingly) known scope from the start. During the execution phase of such projects, the scope slowly increases in an uncontrolled manner with other project constraints, like budget and schedule, remaining the same. In Scrum, you don’t have a fixed scope (unless you count the scope of each sprint), so this concept doesn’t really make sense. You can think of all the Product Backlog items as the scope, but as I already mentioned, the Product Backlog is a living thing. It constantly changes as you work on the product, you discover new things, the markets change, regulations change, or feedback is received from stakeholders, clients, users, and so on. This is what it’s all about with Agile methods: to respond to changes caused by these situations. “Agile methodologies embrace change” is something that you will often hear. This is the cornerstone of Agile methodologies. But that does not mean that in Agile, “anything goes” when change is concerned. You still need to manage change.

As I mentioned in a previous chapter, when talking about scope creep, change can be good or bad, needed or unnecessary, important or insignificant. This isn’t any different when you start using Scrum. The Product Owner must carefully analyze change requests and decide what to do with them; otherwise, they risk focusing on delivering features and adding stuff on top of the product and risk losing sight of the items that bring true value. Just like in the case of scope creep, you need to resist the impulse of doing things “now”. Instead, the Product Owner needs to think carefully if a change improves the product and really brings value, or if it does not, and when is the best time to introduce such a change. You can add features to the product all of the time and be under the impression that the product is getting better, but without realizing, with each feature, you are increasingly moving away from the important goals you want to reach, and you may end up building the wrong product.

Agile embraces change, but you still have to realize that you have limited resources in the team. The time used to work on one thing is time you can’t use to work on another. So if you want to add new work, some previously planned work will have to be shifted to make room for it. I saw situations when, during a review meeting, the team received some minor feedback, mostly aesthetics, things that were then incorporated into the next sprint, and shown at the next review meeting to please the boss. But those changes could have easily waited for a later time, or (in my opinion) they shouldn’t have been implemented at all. You cannot afford for people to realize that they can ask for trivial changes and always receive them. When a Product Owner receives feedback after each sprint, they must ask themselves whether they should incorporate the feedback or not and what is their business priority over the other backlog items. That’s why they must be a true Product Owner and not just a proxy, so that they don’t just do what they are told and assign “the immediate feedback” more importance than the things that already exist in the backlog. They need to be able to say “no”, or at least, “not now”.

When it comes to change, more care should be taken when that change is requested during a sprint. The team planned the sprint, estimated, started the work, and maybe the Product Owner comes and says, “Hey guys, can we add this extra story in the sprint? I don’t think it will take you more than 30 minutes to do, right?” Or maybe “can we change this little story with a bigger one? We can, right?” The scope is flexible in Scrum, but within the sprint, it’s usually not. There is some flexibility in the work performed during a sprint as new things get discovered and understood, and stuff can be negotiated or rearranged, as long as that doesn’t affect the sprint goal, but that doesn’t mean you can add more work on top of what was already selected for development. If you add work that was not initially planned to be done during the sprint, without removing other things to make room for the extra work, and keeping everything under the same two-week schedule of the sprint, then that is indeed scope creep.

Another thing that can happen to a Product Owner is to end up becoming more focused on milestones, schedules, and deadlines than on obtaining a valuable product. Either because the Product Owner is a former Project Manager with old habits that die hard, or they are a proxy with deadlines imposed from above, there is the risk that the Product Owner will focus on complying with an apriori established schedule. The whole project is planned and then divided into chunks of two weeks each, all of the sprints get stuffed with the features that need to be performed in that sprint, milestones are defined every six sprints or so, or for the company’s end of the year party, or before the CEO’s birthday, or the visit of that important client. Everything is about the schedule. By X date, we must build Y features, with all of the work beautifully sliced into two-week portions.

I already mentioned not to look at the project on a time horizon of only two weeks, for how long a sprint lasts, but you can’t schedule everything from the beginning either, or build execution plans, because it won’t work. It’s not a chance that with Agile methods you develop software in short iterations, because as the timeline increases, so do the unknowns and the risks, estimates become obsolete, all sorts of unforeseen issues show up, and so on. When you focus on the schedule, and less to all of these things that can happen, you will inevitably be forced to add hacks or shortcuts in an attempt to reach the deadline.

There are a few things that start happening when the focus is placed on schedules and deadlines instead of what brings the most value next.

First of all, sprints become mini-projects with a deadline at the end. It’s not just about committing the team to finish all the stories in the sprint, but during the Sprint Planning Meeting, the focus of the discussion becomes about how to stuff as many stories into the sprint as possible so that all the agreed features are ready before the next milestone. The Product Owner becomes controlling and believes that the team must do what they say when they say so. They start doing command and control and manage and assign stories like tasks in a Gantt chart. “We take this out of here, we put it over there, we do these two tasks in parallel”, and so on, to fit as many boxes in the sprint without leaving any gaps. Things lose their value and priority since everything has to be done by the next milestone anyways. Estimations suffer too. The Refinement turns into a big estimation meeting of all the stories in the backlog, ‘cause how else would you know how to fit and combine boxes in each sprint if you didn’t estimate them? Then rarely are these estimates revisited as the project progresses and new things get discovered and learned about the application. When something does not come out as estimated, the solutions are to put pressure on the team, to make people work overtime, to cut corners in code, to test only optimistic cases, and a bunch of other things that harm the quality of the product; just so that plans and deadlines agreed at the beginning of the project are followed.

Then, the team’s Definition of Done flies out the window. If the end of the sprint is approaching and you have, for example, some incomplete story who’s development may not be finished, or maybe its code review was not conducted, or perhaps the testing team didn’t have time to run all their test scenarios, or the story lacks something that prevents it from being deployed, what do you do? Do you still consider it done? You can skip on the code review this time, right? Or just this time you can move the testing in the next sprint… “under the table”? Or deploy it later? Or how about you instead return the unfinished story into the Backlog, and in the next sprint, you re-estimate the remaining work and finish it properly and transparently? I’ve often seen (and been guilty of it myself) for people to neglect the Definition of Done just to complete the sprint in its entirety, because every sprint end is a deadline, and every sprint is a commitment, and you don’t want to show those above the team that some stuff spilled into the next sprint where you were supposed to work on something else, right? If you failed to fit all this sprint’s work into its time box, this would obviously affect the work of the next sprint, and the next, right? So immediately, people can conclude that you are lagging behind, and they will begin to put pressure on the team to catch up in the following sprints.

If you turn a blind eye to respecting the Definition of Done, the Product Owner just ends up accepting a bad product. At the end of each sprint, you should have a product increment that can be delivered to the final customer or which can be installed in production. How will you install something in production when you know that the last increment wasn’t properly tested? Or that it may have some issues that could have been caught by the code review you decided to skip? If the decision is a well thought out one and everyone takes responsibility for it, then no problem. Sometimes the business can accept some risk or can operationally solve some of the problems that may arise. But in this case, the business doesn’t even know. They see the sprint with all the stories done. They don’t know there are problems with the product caused by the great deadline that had to be respected. And here is where what I said at the beginning of this section about the Product Owner comes in: they really need to be an “owner”. They have to be in charge, and their word must have weight, and if there are problems with the product increment, they can say “no”, “skip”, “insufficient”, or whatever. But when the Product Owner is the one that puts pressure on the team, or if they are a proxy working under pressure and focusing on deadlines, chances are that the Product Owner will not say anything about it. Of course, the Scrum Master should notice these things occurring and raise some flags… but more about that later.

Values and principles

Before I go on and mention a few things about the development team also, I have to point out an important thing when it comes to Scrum and Agile in general. Many have failed while trying to implement Agile practices. And when they ask why, the answers they receive from everyone else are in the form of “you are doing things wrong”. Basically, it’s your fault for not knowing what you are doing. These kinds of answers always annoyed me since they don’t explain how you are doing things wrong. I mean… the Scrum Guide is less than twenty pages long, the Manifesto for Agile Software Development[178] with all its principles, even shorter. How the heck can you get that wrong?

I said this before, but I’ll say it again: it’s all about the people. You can fail with Scrum, Agile, or whatever other methodology you want if you don’t have the right people. So who are the right people for Scrum? More than anything else, it’s people that have the Scrum “values”. And you act in accordance with your values because values determine your priorities and drive your behaviors. If you read the Scrum Guide carefully, you will see words like “commitment”, “courage”, “focus”, “openness”, “respect”, “transparency”, and “trust”. These are human values, not characteristics of a process or a methodology, so they tend to be forgotten when the focus is placed on “doing” Scrum the right way or jumping straight to the steps to follow, the team organization, the roles, events, and artifacts. I said Scrum is not a process; it’s a framework. It does not cover any possible situation. You have to build on top of it. And when you do, you must ask yourself, “What values will be guiding me?”. This is why Scrum fails in many companies. This is what people are “doing” wrong. People don’t have the right values. You can’t follow values mechanistically; you need to live them and believe them. With values, you can’t fake it till you make it. You either value those things and take actions and behave in accordance with them (and then your work aligns with your values), or you don’t. Sounds philosophical? It’s not. It’s the reason Scrum is “simple to understand but difficult to master”[164].

When I started with Scrum, I was also about “the process”. Whenever I talked to Agile coaches or experienced Scrum Masters, they were mentioning these values while I was rolling my eyes impatient to “do” Scrum without all that nonsense that, in my mind, was just about making the “process” more complicated and mystical, to charge more for courses, training or whatever. I just wanted to focus on “the process” and what I must “do” to get things done. Only years later did it click for me. Up till then, I was like many others, trying to religiously follow the steps, looking at Scrum as if it were Humpty Dumpty[179], minding my step so that I don’t fall off the wall, crack my head open, and spill my yolk.

Professionals who live by the values of Scrum can figure out how to use it best and apply it in their particular situation, for the needs of the product they are building. To be honest, if the people in the company share these values, you don’t even need Scrum because they will figure out the best way to get things done. They will try things out, keep what works, discard what doesn’t, and improve things that look promising. If, on the other hand, you don’t have the right people, then no methodology works. Scrum doesn’t work either. Although these things are mentioned within the Agile world, few are the ones who emphasize them (maybe because it’s so common sense that it’s obvious), while others are too busy selling you books, courses, certifications, planning poker cards, and themed office supplies, to even care.

A lot of companies adopting Scrum want an “Agile transformation”. But a transformation is a change and one that’s not as simple as just applying Scrum on top of the same old practices and ways of thinking about things. Doing the same thing differently might look like a change, but it’s not the right kind of change to trigger a transformation. This is another way of saying that you do not make Scrum fit within your current beliefs, practices, and habits; instead, you need to change behaviors to fit into what Scrum is all about. That’s the real change. And it’s not something that’s easy to do. Many don’t even know what their values are, let alone having to change them.

So how are these values reflected in the organization? They are reflected in the way you behave, and how you handle the different situations you encounter.

For example, Scrum doesn’t work without “trust”. I talked more about trust in a previous chapter. What I say there is also valid here. You have to trust that people have good intentions and your interest (or the client’s interest) in mind and that they want to bring value. You have to trust their expertise, that they learn from their mistakes, and that they want to better themselves and build a good product. Scrum is no longer command and control. You now tell the development team what you want, and it’s their job to make it happen. Then you have to trust the team to do the right thing, that they are committed and focused on what’s important. For example, the Scrum team must work at a sustainable pace. Only in this way can you maintain a good level of productivity, avoid people getting tired, make mistakes, or be tempted to hack things if they feel pressured. But what does “at a sustainable pace” mean? If the pace is too slow, what’s happening? Is it the team’s real velocity? They totally apply themselves to the tasks, or are they just messing around? Remember, developers don’t commit for the items in the sprint; they do a forecast. So open up your video streaming service or social media applications and start dragging your feet since you didn’t commit shit this sprint, right? If the team failed some stories in the sprint, was it for proper reasons, and then you trust them to learn from this mistake and try to avoid it next time? Or they didn’t finish the stories because they are lazy, unskilled, or they lack focus? Everyone needs to be interested in the product and the work they are doing. You can’t have developers who don’t want to grow or developers who are only concerned with themselves and are not interested in anything else. If someone says, “I need help with something”, others can’t answer with, “it’s not my job”. If they don’t have the skills and can’t, it’s one thing, but not caring is a totally different thing.

Do you trust your people? Because Agile doesn’t work unless you have people you can trust. This is something that the Agile community doesn’t emphasize; it pretty much lets it be “obvious”, because in the end… you can’t achieve anything, in any field, if you don’t have the right people - good, professional, involved people - having the right values and behaviors, that commit themselves to do a good job. As for commitment, this is not something that only the development team has to do. How about managers and bosses? They usually only have demands or requests and become controlling when something they disagree with occurs. How about being committed to helping and supporting the team, letting the team figure things out instead of trying to get them to work on a leash. Or at least try to behave in a responsible fashion that doesn’t get in the way? How about stakeholders trusting and respecting the Product Owner’s decisions? Or how about the Product Owner trusting the team’s judgment when they say something is difficult to do, or shouldn’t be done that way, or can’t be done at all. Or how about when something needs to be refactored, or some technical debt repaid, to give the team time to handle these issues instead of pushing for more stories in the sprint and then carry everyone through meetings to reprimand them for not finishing all the work in time.

Then there is “courage”. Often, an Agile practice will expose existing problems in the organization or with the work culture, things like distrust, lack of transparency, bad management, bad policies, flawed processes, etc. Often, courage means drawing attention to the ugly issues you see, or to the things that others don’t want to hear about, and accept the consequences that can result from there. It means saying and doing the right things. I mentioned in the previous chapters what can happen when you go against your boss or your manager. What are you going to do when you can be fired if your boss doesn’t like the news you are communicating, or don’t like how you manage the project, or if your recommendations don’t suit them? Will you still try to make things better? For example, what will you do when your boss thrashes at the team and demands commitment for all the stories in the sprint, and doesn’t even stand to hear the word “forecast” being mentioned? Or what will you do about people who insist that the burn-down charts look flawless all of the time? If the Scrum Master notices the definition of done being stomped on, that the Daily Stand-Up becomes a status meeting, if people are afraid to speak in the retrospective, or discover something inefficient in the organization, what are they going to do? If the Product Owner notices that some business demands don’t make sense, do they oppose the requirements and refuse to do them, or do they keep their mouth shut and just accept everything the higher-ups push into the product? If you discover managers above the team that choose to distort information, what do you do? What if you come across people who are delighted with the status quo, want things to remain exactly as they are, get upset about the change you are trying to introduce, then start hampering your Scrum adoption?

If people are afraid to tell it like it is, then many things start to suffer. Like “transparency”, for example, a crucial pillar of Scrum. Transparency means that everyone knows at all times what’s going on, that there are no surprises and no differences between expected results and actual results. If people are reserved in unwrapping some of the issues they find, things start to become opaque. Communication also suffers because it takes place in a filtered way, or the information is massaged before being communicated. Certain things that should be known stay hidden or sometimes, even worse, are intentionally swept under the rug. “Inspect and adapt” then starts to take up a new meaning… a negative meaning. Instead of the team reflecting on how to improve things and become more effective, they look at how dysfunctional the environment is and then adapt to survive in it. Quitting on trying to change the system and accepting to go with the existing flow is in itself a form of adaptation. So people take fewer stories in the sprint, or overestimate features, or take shortcuts, or keep their mouths shut, etc., anything to avoid taking the blame or being put in uncomfortable situations that are often not even caused by them.

No matter how well people work within the Scrum team, if their work is negatively impacted by the organization’s existing processes and procedures, that will not compensate for the things that are not within their reach to amend. So their only option is to escalate them and have others at higher levels of the company be willing to get involved to solve them and want to improve things for the future. And because Scrum is all about “inspect and adapt”, the results of the actions taken by upper management must also be made transparent. That’s why Scrum is not something you can only do inside the development team, because all of their efforts can be nullified by the stupid way others in the organization behave; people with power but also obtuse enough to not want to hear about negative or inefficient things, let alone do something to fix them.

Courage and transparency also have a role during retrospective meetings. How do your retrospectives look like? All rainbows and butterflies? Or are the problems put on the table and discussed? Are you trying to improve things? Do you try to understand the repetitive cases when people do not complete their tasks in time, or do you shrug your shoulders and say you’ll try harder next time? Do you take actions that you then actually execute upon? A retrospective is for the team to examine itself and to improve based on feedback you collect from everyone involved in the development. Positive, but also negative feedback. If there are bad things to fix or improve, then you need to talk about them. You can’t improve things if you don’t acknowledge and discuss them. Here is where trust comes in again, as well as the confidence to speak out without the fear of being attacked, criticized, get in trouble, or that management will take actions to punish people that point out bad issues or admit mistakes.

And people will make mistakes. When they do, how do you deal with them? Are they an opportunity to learn and improve, or are they an opportunity for top management to display their authority? You failed to deliver one story from the sprint, and now you are in a meeting with top management to explain yourself? Why? Is success the only allowed option? Is doing the right thing and failing accepted or not? If a company doesn’t tolerate people’s mistakes (honest mistakes, not caused by indifference, inattention, etc.), then your Scrum implementation will suck. Retrospectives will be fake, people will cover things up so that they don’t get punished, they’ll pull fewer stories into sprints to make sure they have a better chance of finishing them all, people will no longer work at full capacity but will put buffers in place, everyone minds their own business because to help others means to take time away from their own tasks, any inefficiencies they observe, they will keep to themselves to avoid being criticized if they speak out, they stop taking active action to improve their work because those actions might fail, etc. And this is where the value of “openness” comes in. Everyone needs to be open about all the work that’s being performed, with good and bad. Scrum exposes problems within the organization, and people need to be open to at least listen, take criticism, have honest discussions about them, acknowledge and accept their existence. No one likes to hear bad news, but some go as far as sticking their heads into the sand, like an ostrich. And if the higher-ups don’t acknowledge the problems or inadequacies Scrum exposes, things remain unchanged. Well, maybe the higher-ups resort to their old practices of raising the pressure, setting up systems to punish or reward employees for their work, asking the team to commit more, etc.; a reaction similar to performance appraisals applied only to employees, while the systems inside the company get ignored. If the problems are with the organization, it’s of little use trying to improve people’s individual performance. That doesn’t compensate for what’s broken somewhere else. It’s similar in Scrum: if the problems are somewhere else, even if the team is an expert in Scrum, they will only be able to change things in their immediate vicinity, inside the Scrum team. But the system is still broken. If the organization is a mess, using Scrum in one layer of it won’t actually fix anything. An Agile transformation won’t occur with Scrum teams working in isolation. Higher management needs to be open to the communication coming from the Scrum team and take action to improve things.

Empowerment

But before talking about people being open to hearing about the issues that a Scrum team can uncover and do something about them to improve things, first, people must be open to making a change in the way the team works. Typically, people doing the work are coordinated and controlled from above. Ownership of the project is with a Project Manager of some sort; the team just works to make things happen according to the manager’s plan. Now, with Scrum, the organization needs to empower teams to self-organize and be in charge of their own work. As I mentioned above, many companies think Scrum is something that only the development teams should do, so they don’t allow them the freedom to do things as they think is best. The decision and control structures remain the same; it’s only somewhere below that the implementation changes… they are doing this thing called Scrum. But only in name, of course, because in true Scrum, the team is no longer told “how” to build the software, they are told instead “what” people want from them, then the team decides which is the best way to transform those requirements in working software. Ownership now moves to the team doing the work. They have a job to do, and they figure out together how best to do it, without managers planning their activities, assigning tasks, or controlling work. In fact, Scrum teams have no Project Manager.

But just because Scrum does not define the role of a Project Manager, it does not mean that Project Managers get removed from the company. If the company decides to move to a Scrum-based development, these managers might be reconverted into Scrum Masters or Product Owners, as I mentioned above. When this happens, there is a high chance that you end up with a hybrid (if you can call it that) of Scrum mixed with traditional project management, and you usually end up with the worst of both worlds. The Project Manager might now have a new official role, but they might stick with the same mentality and ways of approaching things as they did as a Project Manager, with the team being led and controlled by the newly named Scrum Master or Product Owner by following “a process”, similar to how visitors are guided during a museum visit: “And now we enter this room. Then we move to the next room. I request you to stay on the path between the red velvet ropes. And please don’t touch anything”.

Then, having no Project Manager role in Scrum doesn’t mean there are no more functions that pertain to project management. People still need to chart o course for work, to make decisions, to plan things out, to monitor, to supervise, to exercise some form of control on the work being performed, etc., but these things now get distributed between all members of the team. The manager’s role now gets distributed among all team members; that’s why it doesn’t explicitly exist in Scrum. People figure out together the best way to organize these functions between themselves, how things will unfold, in what order, and so on. Basically, many of the Project Manager’s tasks must be delegated, and if the manager doesn’t always have in mind that the team needs to self-organize, this may seem to them like a loss of control. And then what do they do? Well, they want to take control back, of course. And if that happens, it’s no longer Scrum; it’s traditional project management with command and control, and focus on schedules, with the “resources” from the team being disciplined on what they did wrong every couple of weeks at the retrospective meeting, or every day at the Daily “status” meeting. For these reasons, as I mentioned above, it’s not always a good idea to put a senior Project Manager in the Scrum Master position but to have a Scrum Master who understands well the principles and values of Scrum. A true Scrum Master will recognize the things I just mentioned happening as anomalies and can sound the alarm. That’s assuming someone is willing to listen to this alarm signal.

The best way for teams to be empowered and become self-organized is if they have support “from above”. Instead of recycling the Project Manager position into an internal Scrum Master or Product Owner role, I think it would be more useful to give Project Managers a new position above the Scrum team, not inside it. I must again mention that it isn’t enough to require development teams “to do” Scrum, while at higher levels or throughout the rest of the organization things to remain “business as usual”. If a company is to be Agile, the whole company needs to be Agile. A Project Manager can take a buffer position between the Scrum team and the rest of the organization, to deal with things that are external of the Scrum team. Internally, the team members are self-organized and empowered to do the work however they see fit, but being part of a business in which not everyone understands (or even cares about) this Agile thingy, you need some sort of Scrum integration with the rest of the organization, so that the team can function better in this context. And Project Managers can help with this, offering support in three main areas.

The first area is helping with communication and coordination. This is valuable especially if there are multiple Scrum teams working on the same product. A top layer of coordination can help with dependencies, stakeholder management, help to set a consistent set of objectives across all teams, make overall and teams’ progress transparent for everyone, manage risk, manage the budget, help with release planning, and provide assistance with issues or blockages that are outside the perimeter of Scrum teams themselves.

An important point here is the one about helping with dependencies. In any software development effort, you will encounter dependencies in all shapes and sizes. There is no escaping dependencies. You might not have thought about it like this, but for example, we depend on each other to do our jobs. Testers depend on developers to be able to do their job, but developers also rely on testers to catch things that they might have missed when writing the code. Testers and developers could both depend on the Team Lead to offer support or make certain decisions. Everyone depends on the Product Owner to properly define what needs to be done. Each member of the team depends on stakeholders for feedback on the developed product. You can depend on other departments within the company, on vendors, or other Scrum teams working on the same project and on the same source code. The budget for developing a new project may depend on the maintenance work you have to do on an older project, the one the new project is supposed to replace. Meeting the sprint Goal depends on stories being refined, decomposed in independent items, and adequately prioritized, so that team members don’t trip on each other’s feet.

A Scrum team is also supposed to have all the necessary competencies to do their work, without depending on external resources. From what skills are concerned, it would be nice if all of the developers in the team would be full-stack developers, but today that’s not always possible. So, inevitably you will have specialization within the team. You will have UI designers, back-end developers, front-end developers, testers, and everyone else needed to get the job done. At least in theory. In practice, however, some people may be “shared” or “part-time”. I already mentioned designers, database administrators, or other experts (like architects, for example) that you might need on the team. If they are not fully utilized during sprints, to make sure each employee works at full capacity (for financial reasons), upper management might decide to share such employees between teams. Or if the company has a good specialist in some domain on board, they might be tempted to have this person provide their input and support to everyone, so that each team benefits from their expertise. In both situations, though, what happens is that people will start depending on a few persons who aren’t always available. If you have a person spread between seven teams, you risk six of them to have to wait while this resource is handling something within the seventh team.

As I said, you will always have dependencies of different forms. You can’t get rid of them. Moreover, nowadays, due to the complexity of software products, there aren’t many big projects that do not depend on one form or another of external resources, teams, or other projects. But the problem is not that there is a dependency. The problem is not that you depend on others. The problem is when that dependency slows things down to a crawl or becomes a blocker. Regarding specialists, a solution can be to hire more people. Even if you realize that they are not used 100% of their time, as a whole, it might be cheaper like that than to have six teams of 9 people all waiting on the same person that’s always busy. But in the case of several Scrum teams working on the same product, things aren’t always as easy to solve. So teams need all the help they can get to sort things out.

When every team is busy with their self-organization, it becomes easy to only focus on the work performed within the team and not communicate enough or interact sufficiently with other groups. Dependencies become things that others have to do for you, to provide them before you need them, and when they don’t, you wait, you complain, and make threats until you (eventually) get them. The other teams behave the same as you in regard to their dependencies. Everyone goes about their own sprints, and when the time comes to integrate all the work in the larger product… fingers crossed. The problem with having dependencies is that it’s very easy to think that it’s someone else’s responsibility to meet them. Others do the work, so if they don’t deliver on the dependency when you need it, it’s their fault. Wrong! It’s also your fault.

The only way to work efficiently when you have such dependencies is to keep an eye on the big picture at all times. Dependencies need to be identified, dependencies need to be tracked, everyone needs to know what others are doing and how their work, in turn, affects them. A dependency is not something that others do, and when they are done, you continue by doing something else also, to pick up the baton, so to speak. “I do something for you, you do something for me”, doesn’t work either. That’s not how a dependency should be handled. It must be a form of collaboration: doing something together. Of course, some work on the dependency more than others, and some have greater responsibility for the dependency than others, but everyone has to be involved. When it comes to dependencies, you have to watch them like a hawk. You have to define them, know when you need them, who works on them, what their status is, etc.

And here is where the layer above the teams comes along. Someone needs to remind people that there are multiple teams, departments, or whatever, and they all have to collaborate. They can coordinate and track activities, provide support, and ensure that the right people interact when needed so that dependencies are available when required. They can make sure dependencies are transparent, that people get their priorities straight and work towards the same goals, and work is made visible, since sometimes, one team may not see what the others see and vice-versa. It’s about alignment, setting everything up for everyone to work at optimum speed, and not hinder each other.

Everyone should be involved in managing these dependencies, but sometimes communication breaks down, and you end up in dumb situations when, for example, something stops working in the middle of the sprint because someone else changed an API on which you are dependent upon, and now you have to drop everything and upgrade to the new version and find out that “Our Product Owner told your Product Owner. How come you found out about it just now?”

I must once again mention, as I’ve done so many times already throughout the book, that communication is crucial. When talking about managers, I also said that much of a Project Manager’s job involves communication, and stated that they should act as “communication custodians” (for lack of a better term), enabling communication and making sure the information keeps moving in an effective, correct, and transparent manner. And to minimize and solve dependencies, of course, a lot of communication is needed, and someone needs to remind people to communicate not only within the team but also outside of it. Many times, there are communication problems even inside the Scrum team. People should interact and communicate continuously. Someone notices a problem? They should let everyone know. The requirements are not clear enough? People ask for more details. Somebody sees something that can be improved? They make a suggestion. Someone needs help? They ask for assistance. But I’ve often seen team members wait for the Daily Stand-Up to communicate things, or wait for the Refinement Meeting, or some important discussions that take place around major events like releases or milestones. And so, you find out too late that they are blocked by something, that the goals are not clear enough, or that the processes in the company are inefficient. Scrum Master is there to facilitate collaboration and communication and can do something about it within the team, but when it comes to communicating with other groups or departments (especially related to dependencies and blockages), any help is welcome.

This layer of management can help with communication and prioritization across all teams, to avoid misunderstandings when everyone is working on what they think is valuable, but you end up with a situation where, even though this value is positive, it’s not totally positive. What I mean by that is that some bring value to the detriment of others resulting in a positive outcome as a whole, but not a positive one from everyone’s provided value, all combined together.

The second area I want to mention is one of coaching. In the Scrum Guide, there is this section about the Scrum Master’s service to the organization. It states that the Scrum Master leads and coaches the organization in its Scrum adoption. The Scrum Master doesn’t just help a team internally, but they also help others in the organization (outside the Scrum team) to understand, accept, and put into practice this new way of developing software. Sounds good, but it’s not that simple. I’ve already stated why that is, earlier in the chapter, when talking about Scrum Masters. If the rest of the organization doesn’t really care and they’re not open to a new way of working, they’ll remain stuck in their old ways. Without upper management’s support, the Scrum Master role risks to remain contained within the Scrum team, for the team, and unable to provide service to the organization. So Scrum Masters need all the help they can get to bring about a change in the mindset of people. Empowerment and self-organization may seem to some that everything is now in the hands of developers, so they are worried that things will go haywire or that they will spin out of control. They need some reassurance that things won’t become unmanageable. And whom better to provide this reassurance than their Project Managers? Another important role in this part of coaching upper management is that of buying the team time to better learn Scrum themselves. A lot of learning will involve experimentation. Some things will work out well; some won’t. The team will then inspect and adapt, keep what works, and discard what doesn’t. Of course, everyone is happy when things go well, but when things don’t turn out so great, management can very quickly fall back on their old command and control habits and get involved in fixing the situation as if the team is incapable of extracting itself from the situation and need to be told exactly what to do. The team must be given sufficient time to self-organize and figure things out. Upper management must understand that it’s about a proper balance between empowerment and management and that when things are not to their liking, the solution may not be the typical one of tightening up their grip on things, but maybe the opposite, to forgo a certain degree of control and place more confidence in the Scrum team.

But of course, the team members must also be able to organize themselves. Just like saying, “Starting today, you are Agile!” doesn’t work, it also doesn’t work to tell the team, “Starting today, you are empowered! Now go self-organize!”. It’s like giving someone who has never driven a car the keys and saying, “Take it for a few laps around the block”. They’ll drive it into a ditch or a tree because they don’t know how to operate the car, and they don’t know the traffic signs and regulations. Same with a Scrum team. Now, the project management is no longer done by a dedicated person with the role of “Project Manager”, but by all the members of the team. But are they capable of taking over all of these new duties? Can they plan their own work properly? Can they communicate with others? Can they notice how efficient their organization is? Can they find solutions to the inefficiencies? Will they follow through on their solutions? Can they manage conflicts within the team? Can they deal with team members who don’t carry their own weight? Can they compromise when it comes to choosing between something technical and something business-specific? Are they even concerned about “non-technical” issues? Do they understand the extent of their empowerment, or do they believe they can do whatever they want, whenever they want? Do you have any guarantees that they can fend for themselves and can make decisions as a team? Heck, the team might even be in the early phase of Tuckman’s stages of group development[103], and they may not have found yet a way to work together effectively, and now you place them in the situation of having to organize their work by themselves? They won’t be able to self-organize since they didn’t even form completely as a team.

Even if they are professional, proactive, responsible, and disciplined people, who work well together in the team, they still need help. You can’t empower them without making sure that they can manage everything by themselves. The Product Owner is a business person, developers are technical individuals, so only the Scrum Master can coach them in self-organization. And again, Scrum Masters needs all the help they can get. A Project Manager has significant experience with something like this and can guide them and help them build all the necessary skills.

The third and most important role that such a management layer must fulfill, as a continuation of the second area of influence, is to try to create a working environment conducive to Scrum. In previous chapters, I mentioned about “psychological safety”, or about autonomy, mastery, and purpose[60]. I also mentioned the Business-IT divide and talked about organizational culture, which I referred to, in general terms, as “the working environment”. These things are important when using Scrum, and they find themselves outside of the Scrum teams and their practices. You have to be aware of them. Scrum defines a framework for developing software with focus on the Scrum team, but it says too little about what’s going on in the rest of the organization, especially about the values of a company and about their consistency with those of the Scrum team. Through such a buffer layer, consisting of Project Managers (that is, well-trained people), you can work to integrate Scrum into the rest of the organization, to get a working environment that truly supports the Scrum teams, and allows problems exposed by Scrum to be solved. If the environment remains set on a mentality of “us versus them”, Scrum will remain confined internally to the teams, and the chances are high that it will be Scrum in name only. This layer should help with the adoption of Scrum values and practices and their integration into the whole company. This layer gives more power to a Scrum Master and their service to the organization.

But since this is a book about the quicksands, needless to say, this often doesn’t happen. It’s obvious from what I’ve said so far, that for the three areas of this buffer layer to materialize and for this layer to be useful, that managers must themselves be mature enough to realize another style of management is needed (see, for example, the “Theory X and Y”[137] I mentioned earlier in the book), to give up command and control and themselves embrace the Agile values. As trained individuals in terms of management practices, they must be the first to change and start doing things differently, before they can be helping others in the organization, both above and below. And of course, it often happens that Project Managers don’t change (primarily because they are afraid of losing control). Consequently, just another management layer gets created, with the same practices and habits that perpetuate an environment of command and control, a centralized structure of decision making, heavy on status meetings and requests for detailed reports (since now Project Managers are even further from the work that’s actually being done than if they were part of teams), compliant to all of the bosses’ desires, who punish people when something happens that they don’t like, or put their paws all over the projects and run them however they see fit. They don’t care about empowering or self-organization. Scrum teams are just execution units who have to answer to their every whim, as fast as possible, since they are Agile, right? Even if you have experienced Scrum Masters to collaborate with this layer, if it’s a traditional management layer, it will still be in vain.

When the Scrum team is controlled by “traditional” Project Managers, who are breathing down people’s necks all of the time, instead of focusing on encouraging and helping the team to “inspect and adapt”, the team, in turn, starts to focus on “how not to make mistakes”, to avoid upper management from descending on them like an eagle does on a mouse wandering astray in the field. Scrum values end up lost, and people just start following rules. “Stand-ups? Sprints? Backlog? Planning? Refinement? Review? Retrospective? Check, check, check, check, check, check, aaaaaaand… check!”. I said it once, and I’ll say it again. It’s necessary to have and be guided by the Agile values above the Scrum team also, not just within the team. Agile values limited within the team, with a deep command and control hierarchy in the rest of the organization, does not work.

Technical considerations

But even the Scrum values, empowerment, and self-organization don’t mean anything if the development team doesn’t have the proper technical skills, and they fail to use proper technical practices. What is attractive about Scrum is that it seems like a simple management method that doesn’t put special focus on technical considerations. But that doesn’t mean technical practices are not essential. Scrum is a framework, so what matters is what you build on top of it. And that must include technical practices, tools, and techniques. The development team forgets this. They get focused on planning meetings, stand-up meetings, sprints, demos, and so on, and forget that they must also use appropriate technical practices. You can live the Scrum values, but if your technical abilities are lacking, the value you can add to your product will suffer nonetheless. This means that you can’t get all the benefits out of Scrum with an inadequate development team.

I’ve talked in a previous chapter about the importance of having a solid foundation of knowledge as a developer and then also learn about higher-level practices such as how to organize your code, how to properly name things, avoiding code duplication, writing highly cohesive and loosely coupled code, learning about refactoring, code reviews, writing tests, automation, logging, security, design patterns, design principles like SOLID, about conceptual integrity, or about using tools in your daily work, things like version control, collaboration tools, issue tracking systems, and so on. Other important things you need to know and I have already mentioned are knowing the business domain very well and remembering that everything is a trade-off. You need a high dose of pragmatism to be a good developer and avoid going into the weeds, as explained in the chapter about bad developers.

You need professional, pragmatic developers who have not only the necessary skills but also the willingness to want to learn constantly and improve themselves. Many companies, wanting to keep costs low, make the mistake of hiring inexperienced developers then believe that the confinement of the Scrum framework is enough for those developers to still be Agile, do a good job and build a valuable product. But that doesn’t happen, because inexperienced developers simply don’t know much about the best practices and techniques that experienced developers have grown to appreciate, so they don’t use them (maybe not the best analogy but, “you can’t use fire to cook a proper meal if you haven’t yet discovered fire”). Success is not guaranteed by following only the Scrum Guide. You need experienced people with the necessary technical skills that also know how and when to apply them; otherwise, when (in theory) they get empowered, they will still blow it. In Scrum, you must trust your developers, but of course, this trust must be earned somehow.

Besides experience and technical skills, serious doses of maturity and discipline are also needed. When you don’t know certain technologies or techniques, you can’t use them, and that’s not good. But then, when you know a lot of technologies and techniques, you can become overzealous in wanting to use them all; you basically go to the other extreme. We have already presented some things that developers tend to take to extreme in the chapter about bad developers. “Do we do pair programming all of the time, even for trivial things? We do. Do we use TDD for absolutely anything? We use. We won’t deploy anything until we have 100% code coverage for tests? Absolutely! Do we rewrite everything in a new language every sprint? Hell yeah!” See where this is going? A Scrum team must be composed of mature, pragmatic, and disciplined people, that can also understand the business perspective and that of the customer or of the users. They must not forget that, above all, they must bring value. They have to leave personal (technical) preferences aside, look at things objectively, and constantly ask themselves at what moment does a practice like TDD, pair programming, or whatever, no longer brings value? In other words, where do they cross the line and take things too far?

However, there are certain practices that I think you cannot go wrong with when it comes to developing software using Scrum: continuous integration, continuous delivery, and continuous deployment.

Scrum says that, at the end of each sprint, you should have a potentially releasable product increment. That means that whatever you developed in the current sprint can be deployed into production if the Product Owner so decides. Moreover, with Scrum, the idea is that at any point in time, the client can stop the project and say, “We are satisfied with what we have so far. It solves all our problems. We don’t need anything else for now. Deploy it and let’s make some money”. At least, in theory, it should be that way. But what I saw in many teams is that the potentially releasable product increment isn’t all that… releasable. The developers can demonstrate the increment, but the increment isn’t what you might call “releasable material”.

Scrum defines the Review meeting, a meeting in which the development team “demonstrates” the work they have done, ask for feedback, and collaborate with stakeholders to decide what to do next. Basically, everyone comes together to make sure work is and will be done on things that provide value. And I would like to emphasize the word “demonstrates” because I often saw the Review Meeting transforming into a “demo” meeting. And there’s a problem when that happens. A demo is all about showing something and maybe explaining how it works, while a review means to assess something with the intention of possibly making decisions about it or operate changes to it. In simpler terms, a demo mostly resumes to showing stuff. Because it doesn’t include a proper amount of feedback, collaboration, and decision making, you should try not to get stuck on the demo part of the Review Meeting to such an extent that the demo actually becomes the entire Review Meeting. Otherwise, things begin to resemble a theater play, in which the actors (i.e., the development team) give a “performance” in front of the public (i.e., stakeholders, clients, etc.). At the theater, the audience does not provide actors with feedback; they don’t discuss what expectations they have from the play, they don’t decide with the actors what should be changed for the next “performance”. They sit there and watch the play and at the end give applause if they liked it. If that happens to your Review Meeting, then you have a serious problem. So remember: it’s a review, not just a demo.

There are certain signs that show if a Review Meeting is a demo or an actual review, signs that occur during the sprint, but also during the demo itself. For example, do you sometimes find yourself bending the Definition of Done for some stories just so you can present them at the demo? Maybe rush testing for work that the developers managed to (barely) finish on the last day of the sprint? Or perhaps you have a big story in the current sprint, a story that is “la pièce de résistance” for the Sprint Goal, and the team realizes halfway through the sprint that they won’t be able to finish it in time. You won’t have much to show at the demo if the story is not ready, so what do you do? Will you give up on the code review to shave some time off the effort? Give up on tests? Maybe you hard-code stuff or resort to a basic version of some algorithm instead of the complete implementation you agreed upon at the sprint Planning? If there are any problems with a story that isn’t properly implemented, that normally prevents it from being “Done”, do you still force it in “Done” to make the task look good and present it at the demo without disappointing the Product Owner or the stakeholders?

Here is another thing to ponder upon: do you “prepare” for the Review Meeting, or do you “rehearse”? I’ll carry on with the theater analogy I gave above. A play lasts an hour or two, but people prepare well in advance. The actors learn their lines, rehearse, the set is built, and the props are put in place - everything for a performance of 1-2 hours. After the play finishes, the set is disassembled, the props go back into storage, actors go to their homes, and the audience does the same. So how much do you prepare for the demo? Do you repeat the steps you will be performing during the demonstration? If you discover bugs as you rehearse for the demo, will you carefully prepare a happy path of execution so that those bugs don’t show up during the demo? Do you record videos to make sure you have a backup of what to show in case the real thing doesn’t work? Do you actually put all the team in a meeting room and rehearse the demo a couple of times just to make sure all things are covered and everyone knows what to say during the actual demo? If the answer to these questions is “yes”, you should ask yourself if the demo is or is not more important than building a proper product that brings value. And while you’re at it, also ask yourself what the relation of the Scrum team is with its stakeholders, bosses, or clients and why the demo needs to be done “just right”.

Sometimes, people end up focusing too much on the demo because of their stakeholders. Do you have some old school bosses or managers above the team? Are they the kind that demand commitment on 100% story delivery in each sprint? If you fail a story from the sprint or communicate what problems were encountered or what risks exist, will you be reprimanded, scolded, or receive negative remarks? Instead of stakeholders providing valuable input and feedback on the increment, to discuss and agree together on realistic next steps, and make sure everyone is on the right track, do they just stand there and stare into space while someone quickly goes through all the list of features that were developed that sprint? Or even worse, do they nitpick on buttons not being large enough or about not liking their color? Or do they turn into a “peanut gallery”[177], as I mentioned earlier, focusing on the negatives and ignoring the positives? As a result, do you catch yourself highlighting only the team’s achievements, or sugar cote things to try to build a more cheerful picture of progress and create the impression that things are going well?

Earlier in the chapter, I said that sometimes sprints could become mini-projects with a deadline at the end, and there is the risk to force all stories to be finished in order to hit the deadline, and so, you end up sacrificing the quality of the product. When you have a demo at the end of the sprint, where you need to show everything you did - otherwise, your boss will scream at you - it’s even more stressful for people to finish everything they’ve pulled into the sprint. So they hack things, cut corners, ignore other things, create a mess, and lower the quality of the software. All in the name of the mighty demo. You might end up with nice demos, but also with crappy software. And in the process, you are lying to stakeholders because, during the demo, you show them something that’s working and communicated as “Done”, and you show them certain progress, while in fact, things are different; things are not done, and the progress is only one for half-arsed done stories. And maybe everyone will be happy at first, but over time things will start to slow down. Half-done things will start to accumulate, there will be more and more bugs, the consistency of the technical solution will start to get diluted, stuff will have to be rewritten, technical debt will have to be re-payed, things that were “Done” will have to be “Re-Done”, all of this because people wanted to have nice demos instead of properly working software.

And here I come back to the practices of continuous integration, continuous delivery, and continuous deployment. Only when it’s in production, it runs correctly and efficiently, and someone is actually using it, only then is the software truly “Done”.

Release early, release often - Eric Steven Raymond[180]

If you focus on the demo part, you might have a good demo but end up ignoring the other important stuff: the feedback, the discussion, the collaboration, and the decisions taken among the participants, which are essential for building a good quality and useful product, one that can actually start to bring value to the company or the client. This is where an experienced Scrum Master can recognize that the team ended up working not for the product or end users but for the demo, keeping stakeholders happy or avoid being yelled at, while things slowly go down the drain. Then, they can sound the alarm and try to keep everyone focused on what’s important. And I think the best way to maintain this focus is if you deploy the changes in production often, to be forced to build something that’s actually “Done”, not just something that looks “Done”.

When everyone has to integrate their work often and at any time the code can be deployed to production at the Product Owner’s request, or even directly once developed, you can no longer make it with half measures.
