You will be forced to do a good job. Is your boss yelling at you during the demo? You should see how they will yell when something deployed in production isn’t working as well as you showed it at the demo. If you deploy to production only at large milestones, or even at the end of the product, you will be tempted to bend the Definition of Done. But you’ll have time to repair things until the release, right? Wrong! Because what happens is that you carry on improper implementations or bugs from one sprint to the other, until you eventually need to deploy what you built. What happens then? Before the release, you will have a few sprints of only bug fixing, refactoring, and all kinds of work to try to get rid of the luggage you’ve been carrying from sprint to sprint. If something were indeed “Done”, you wouldn’t need extra work to make it complete, repaired, and deployed, would you?

So deploy often in production and have people use the application in their work or activity (even as a closed beta or something), so that you can collect feedback, find out what else is needed, and discover bugs. Otherwise, you will just deliver stories without knowing exactly if it’s really done or if it is what’s truly needed. In addition to that, if you deploy things that people use in their work, you will be forced to work on full features, not on the architectural layers of those features. For example, I’ve often seen (and I admit I am guilty of doing this also) that stories get broken into technical layers: in this sprint we’ll get the database stuff ready, in the next sprint we’ll do the back-end, and then, in the next sprint, the front-end. You might build something in this manner each sprint, but is it useful? What will you show at the demo? The JSON with which the back-end API responds to requests made from outside the application? Do you run SQL queries on the database during the presentation? Will you then collect feedback and have a discussion based on the JSON data or database records? This might show that you’ve worked during that sprint and made some progress, but is it a usable increment? That’s the idea behind Agile: to periodically receive feedback on something that works, so you build something that brings value, not just “build something” every two weeks. In Scrum, you should write and release software as if every sprint was your last. This is the best way to make sure you build the right thing, that’s how you build a full application; otherwise, you will postpone important things for later when perhaps you no longer have a project. The idea is that you can stop the project at any time and use the software you’ve built so far. You cannot tell stakeholders or the client that “You know… the application looks good and does what you want, but right now everything is hard-coded, dependencies are mocked, and you have no way to administer it…” simply because you wanted the demos to look good. So focus on making fully working software, not half-assed software (or crap built as fast as you can) that looks good during the “demo”.

It takes time

Finally, two more important things to remember when it comes to Scrum and Agile.

First of all, you need to realize that Scrum isn’t a silver bullet. Companies that really want the benefits of Scrum think that if they change the working methodology, they automatically get rid of all the problems they had with software development until that moment. They think they can take the developers, pair them with a Scrum Master, get someone as a Product Owner, have the newly formed team follow the Scrum Guide, build artifacts, participate in the meetings, follow the process, show up at the demo, and voilà… software is served. What’s worse is that they expect to see immediate improvements. And then, when people see that their grand expectations don’t materialize immediately, they start saying things like “I don’t believe in this Scrum thing anymore” like it’s some magic spell that wore off.

Scrum will make problems visible, but will not magically fix them. To fix them, everyone must work to improve them. It’s just like losing weight. You have to do a lot of things. You have to change your eating habits, stop being lazy, exercise, make conscious choices rather than default on habits, monitor your progress, see what works and what doesn’t, set reasonable goals, learn from your mistakes, incorporate what you learn into your next actions, and so on. It’s pointless to climb the next day on the scale; you will not see any results. It takes time.

So then, the second thing to remember is that you need patience. Adopting Scrum is not just a change in how work is performed; it’s more about a change in mindset. People start “doing” Scrum before they understand it, and they “do it” mechanistically, as a process. But Scrum is about values, collaboration, communication, transparency, building trust, empowerment, and ownership. Developers must learn to self-organize while people in the rest of the organization must accept and participate in this new way of working. This requires time because the biggest change needs to happen in the organization, not just inside the Scrum team. Continuous improvement is not something you do just once, but continuously (duh!). It takes time to learn and collect feedback, it takes time to understand, it takes time to apply what you’ve learned, it takes time to adapt to the new information, and it takes time for the organization to embrace the new values and behaviors. It will take time for the people and the culture of the organization to change. Change takes time. And there will also be resistance to change. People have emotions, are stubborn, others will defend their position within the company (read “some managers and bosses”). You need to account for this in your Scrum adoption; otherwise, everyone will give up after a few sprints when no major impact can be seen.

Agile practices are cycles of learning and improving. You need to look around you to see where you are, what you can do to improve, take action on that, collect feedback, adapt your practices as a result of the feedback you gathered, then repeat. So when you hear that people succeeded or failed with Scrum, most of the time, it has nothing to do with Scrum itself. What Scrum does, is set up a structure to get continuous feedback on “what” you are building, “how” you are building it, and “why” you are building it. When you start doing that, and you have the support and participation of good people in the company (not just the developers), only then can you say you are Agile.

Picking up the pieces

Let’s face it; the software industry has somewhat of a bad reputation. For companies, this often means a lot of software projects go over budget, are late, deliver only part of the required functionality, are canceled, or fail entirely. For users, it usually means crappy software that is hard to use, has bugs and doesn’t fully solve the problem it was meant to solve. So one might naturally ask, “who is to blame for this?”

Developers do most of the work when building software, so when that software turns out bad, as it might be expected, they get a lot of the blame. For example, you might be a stakeholder with a brilliant idea and money to spend, you might have the best Project Manager in the world, have an army of trained testers, and business analysts to write the best specs, but someone needs to write the damn code; otherwise, there is no software. Who wrote the code for some crappy software? Developers did! So, developers write crappy software, right? It’s easy to follow such logic when you don’t understand what developers do, and you don’t know (or you don’t pay attention to) everything involved in building software. If there is something wrong with the software, few wonder how the software ended up like that, and fingers start being pointed at developers; they are guilty unless proven innocent.

Professionalism

To be honest, though, sometimes, you can’t prove the developers’ innocence. It’s not as if they are innocent angels that can’t mess things up. Part of why the software industry has a bad reputation is indeed because of bad developers. Some are unskilled, unprofessional, and/or undisciplined. I’ve stated several times throughout the book that you need good developers to build quality software. Bad developers can indeed make a complete mess of things. I even dedicated one full chapter to bad developers and what they can do to lead a project into quicksand. You will find incompetent developers; people that act unprofessionally, are immature, lazy, unskilled, undisciplined, or don’t want to take responsibility for what they are building. There are indeed such developers. If they’ve exposed confidential information in the URL or have written it inside log files, or if they saved passwords as plain text in the database, they over-engineer stuff or pile together a crapload of technologies just to have something to play with, write spaghetti code, use copy-paste as a form of code reuse, like only to write new code and not fix bugs, write unmaintainable code, or are unable to communicate properly when problems or delays occur, or any other inanities that blow your mind in a bad way and frustrate other developers who later have to come in and fix things, it’s normal to blame developers (and for a good reason), and it is normal to have “demands” from them to show more professionalism. If they create the mess, then they deserve all the blame. And if they break stuff, they get to keep all pieces, and they are responsible for putting them back together.

So we definitely need good developers - ideally, craftspersons, as advocated by the Software Craftsmanship movement[67]. If you are not familiar with Software Craftsmanship, it suffices to say that the objective of this movement is to raise the bar of professional software development. The idea is that, to build good software, you need craftspersons, people that have a strong desire to constantly learn, and strive for excellence in their work, people for which the quality of the software is important. The movement also tries to bring back what was lost from Agile: the technical practices that people often ignore if they become too focused on what they think is the right “process” to follow (which is, unfortunately, much of how Scrum has been advertised to companies).

Basically, to stop writing crappy code and bring forth a positive change in the industry, we need good developers. We need better developers. With better skills and better technical practices. With a strong code of conduct, in which the crucial aspect is “professionalism”. I know a lot of developers who should get their hands on a Software Craftsmanship book ASAP and start learning some stuff. But turning all of them into craftspersons, or replacing them with craftspersons, doesn’t entirely solve the problem, because the problem is not just that many developers are unskilled, unprofessional, and/or undisciplined. Yes, there are unskilled developers. Yes, they need to get better. Yes, they need to behave responsibly. Yes, they must be professionals. But are really all of the problems caused by developers?

When we put all the focus on developer skills, it’s hard not to perceive messages asking for professionalism as “you are either a craftsperson or a bad developer that makes crappy software”. Guilt-tripping might make developers step up their game, but better skills, better technical practices, and a better attitude toward work from developers solves or repairs only the mess caused by developers.

But there is also a second type of mess, caused by other people in the company, not just developers. It’s easy to ignore other aspects of the software development and blame only those who write the code, but it’s not just developers that are working on a project or software product. Bad software is a result of several things that intersected and interacted in unfortunate ways: unclear or incomplete requirements, poor prioritization, poor communication, bad management, absurd clients, office politics, etc. We can’t ignore these aspects - and all the rest of the people in the company responsible for them - and have expectations only from developers to make things right.

For example, think about imposed or unrealistic deadlines. Estimates provided by developers (often optimistic) get further trimmed or even set aside because bosses know that if they tell a client how long a project will actually last, and how much it will most likely cost, they can get scared and give up on the project, or go elsewhere to have it built. So, the boss will promise more than can be delivered, and they will sugar coat the news of how much it will cost and when it will be ready (in other words, they will lie about it). They know that once the project starts, the client will be reluctant to give up on it. No matter if you call it sunk-cost fallacy [157], loss aversion, or escalation of commitment[181], they know that clients won’t give up easily on a troubled project because, in the end, they need the software, that’s why they started the project in the first place. But clients are no dummies, so they will add contract clauses with penalties and what not, in case there are delays, the software has bugs, or it lacks some of the agreed-upon features. So what does eventually happen? Well, developers must somehow deliver the product within the agreed deadline. And how will that happen? Most of the times, they are forced to cut corners, hack the code, give up on best practices, or whatever else takes time and management doesn’t consider “essential” (which often also includes technical stuff for which only developers should be responsible; “You can’t write code without having a harness of tests? Are you such a bad developer?”). Very often, developers are also pressured to work overtime (unpaid, of course, since paid overtime would add even more to the cost of the project), which leads to burnout and mistakes that add to the issues already caused by an unrealistic timeline.

Then, businesses often respond to problems instead of anticipating or taking precautions for certain risks not to manifest themselves. If developers anticipate certain issues and want to do something to minimize risks, management doesn’t want that. They just accept the risks. And then what happens? There will, of course, be some problems or troubles, which must obviously be mended. Developers are now forced to become chief firefighters. If you wanted to be a firefighter when you were little, but somehow ended up a software developer instead, don’t worry, you can still extinguish fires, only of a different nature. And with fires like these, there will be emotions and frustrations that will cloud your judgment, you will most likely also have the client, boss, or manager breathing down your neck, and you end up doing things that will later reignite other fires (i.e., shortcuts, hacks, giving up on best practices all over again). Developers then try to put in place some measures to avoid such crises happening again, but are they allowed? Nope. Just patch it, restart the server, whatever; pour some water on the fire, then hurry up and get back to work, time’s a-wastin’. And you can add other things on top of these. You don’t have specs, and things come out bad? “You did a poor job learning the domain; some things were obvious”. Things changed seven times over throughout the project, and now you are running behind schedule? “You badly estimated the work”. Was the deadline ridiculous? “You didn’t work hard enough”. Priorities change so quickly you can’t respond to the demands? “You’re not proactive”. You didn’t slave away to respect a commitment your boss made? “You are not a loyal employee”. The software has bugs? “You’re not a good programmer”.

Sometimes these issues are caused on purpose, but often they are also caused because people don’t know any better. For example, I’ve been a lot of things during my career. I’ve been a programmer, a developer, a tester, a Team Lead, a coach, an architect, a business analyst, and a Project Manager. I’ve also worked with lots of people, from other developers to business analysts, Project Managers, Scrum Masters, Product Owners, to human resources specialists, to salespeople, CTOs, CEOs, and clients. I’ve made mistakes in all of my roles, and I saw others make mistakes in all of their roles. It’s not enough (and also not fair) to dump everything on the developers. I agree that in today’s world, where everything is run by software, the developers carry great responsibility and need to be professionals. I stand one hundred percent behind this statement. But this is only part of the problem.

Let’s look, for instance, at another example. I’ve heard more than once words like the following, or something on the same line of thought:

How many times per day do you put your life in the hands of an ‘if’ statement written by some twenty-two year old at three in the morning, while strung out on vodka and redbull? - Robert C. Martin[182]

I don’t entirely agree with this statement, but I can’t disagree with it either. That’s because I’ve witnessed people working weird hours, in overwhelming situations, having to do things while utterly unprepared for the nature of the work or the difficulty of the task. But they were not doing that for fun. Think about the above statement a bit. Why would a twenty-two year old write code at three in the morning for something that can potentially put your life in danger? Why at three in the morning? Because they couldn’t sleep? Because they are so passionate? Is it because of too many energy drinks? Is it because they were drunk and somehow decided it’s a good idea to write code while under the influence? Or maybe, just maybe, because they had to respect an impossible deadline imposed by a boss who wanted to make money or comply with the terms of a poorly negotiated contract? And why a twenty-two year old? Who allowed them to work - assumingly without the necessary skills and knowledge - on a project where someone’s life may depend on a single “if” in the code?

Just as I said in a previous chapter, that you cannot “do” Scrum only inside the development team; likewise, you can’t build quality products if only developers are professionals. Developers bear the brunt and do most of the work, but this doesn’t mean that everyone else’s work can be ignored. You can’t build something of quality if you don’t have the right people at all levels within the company, people with the right values, that work closely with developers, or at least understand what their work consists of and try to support them.

This isn’t purely a developers’ problem; it’s an industry problem. And the industry is made up of other people too, not just developers; people who often have a lot of authority and decision-making power and are guided only by financial benchmarks or gains. Furthermore, most of the time, they are not the ones to bear the consequences of those decisions, but someone else; or somebody else has to work hard to still create a good outcome out of the decision. And so, you end up with senseless decisions that affect the quality of what is being built. For example, I haven’t so far seen good developers wanting to put a prototype in production and then complain that the thing is unstable and lacks features. Or sacrifice long term goals for short term gains. Not one good developer who threatens other developers that if the application is not in production by some randomly chosen date, “I will fire you all”. And I’ve never heard a good developer say to others, “Hey guys… you know what we haven’t done in a long time? Start a death march… I really miss a good, soul-crushing, death march”. I have also not seen developers who want the software to be built fast and cheap and force other developers to work (unpaid) overtime to get it. Or developers that want to outsource an essential piece of software to the other side of the planet, in a country where people don’t even understand basic English let alone understand complex business requirements. I haven’t seen developers add even more work on top of the crapload of work they already have to do but still insist on hitting the same deadline. I haven’t seen developers who cut estimates in half, then call you in their office and ask you to explain why the team is behind schedule. I haven’t seen any good developers to want to work with bad developers just because they are cheaper, or to intentionally keep development teams short on staff to save a buck or two. I haven’t seen good developers who think you can do a good job with unskilled people. I haven’t seen developers think that when everything is going well, that’s how it’s supposed to be, and when something goes wrong, it’s all the developers’ fault. And I haven’t seen developers who, when other developers have accumulated enough experience to be considered true professionals, to fire them and replace them with cheaper twenty-two year olds that have trouble writing “if” statements correctly.

Most developers I’ve met (excluding the kind I mentioned in the chapter about bad developers) actually want to do a good job and build a product to be proud of, but obstacles get thrown in their way by others inside the company who do whatever they want with the power and authority they possess, ignore all arguments presented to them and are only interested in doing “anything” to make a lot of profit from “something” while investing as little money as possible into it.

The main idea with Software Craftsmanship is that programmers need to continuously learn, to build good skills, and have a profession, not just a job. Only in this way can you build high-quality software: if programmers don’t just have a job, but they are craftspersons, like in medieval times. And here, the similarity to medieval craftsmanship, I think, breaks down or at least becomes forced. Why? Because in medieval times, craftsmen didn’t have Project Managers, or bosses, or CEOs, and they were not working with sales and marketing people. The client wouldn’t tell the craftsman how to build their products, what tools or materials to use, or what techniques to apply. If you wanted a good quality product, there was one person making it (maybe together with their apprentices), using the practices they considered the best. And that was pretty much it. As a developer, you will have clients, salespersons, managers, and bosses who decide on things, and you will have to deal with those decisions, even if you know they are bad. This often happens in a company that rests on a command and control structure. The boss says something, you as a developer have to do it because you are seen as nothing more but an execution unit. I have rarely seen bosses listen to common sense coming from the developers who do the work. In a command and control structure, like the army, for example, people should follow orders no matter what. And if the orders or decisions are wrong, then the commanding officer will have to deal with the consequences. In software projects, it’s not those who give the orders that have to deal with the consequences. Yes, maybe at times those who give the orders get fired or something, it happens, but usually, the development team is just thrown under the bus and has to deal with the mess caused by the bad order.

If something ends up wrong with the software, no matter the reasons, it’s still the developers that need to fix it or deal with the consequences of whoever’s mess this was. They need to pick up the pieces because they are the ones doing the most important work. And picking up the pieces doesn’t just mean fixing the code; it goes beyond that. Picking up the pieces also means trying to fix “the system”. As I mentioned in the chapter on the Business-IT divide, there is a disconnect between developers and others inside the organization, caused by people having different perspectives on things. The business is viewed as the mind of the operation, while IT is seen in the execution role, a support department for “the business”. As long as the business does not see developers as partners and collaborators, bad decisions will inevitably be made and whose consequences will be reflected in the work that developers have to do. And developers can’t always solve these problems in a smooth way, and so, you end up with crappy software. Because the work of a developer is some sort of black magic for many business people, you can’t have high expectations from them to understand how their decisions impact things. The business won’t let developers influence and participate in management decisions because they all of a sudden have a revelation that it’s better this way. Someone has to show them that the system is broken. And the burden of educating others about the software development process falls on the shoulders of developers, ‘cause on whom else? Developers must be the ones to gain the business’ trust and show them that they need to be partners. And that they can be reliable partners.

The Software Craftsmanship movement says that if developers want to be treated like professionals, then they must behave like professionals. And I agree. Indeed, the way you behave (honest, reliable, responsible, admitting to your mistakes, acting in a professional manner, taking pride in doing a great job) is one of the prerequisites for gaining the trust of others. Yes, technical practices and skills must always be present so that developers stop writing crap, cause applications to become unmanageable, or make it increasingly difficult to add new features. Yes, developers need to master the business domain to come up with the right solutions. Yes, developers need to get involved in many more important aspects of software development, not just those related to technology. And certainly, communication plays a crucial role, especially when it comes to notifying of setbacks, setting and managing expectations, or engaging management to find better solutions; communicating correctly and transparently is just as important, if not more important, than having the right technical skills. But - and there is a “but” - all these elements that make you a trustworthy professional, a competent person that’s dependable and can be counted on, they are all insufficient.

Just one layer

The Software Craftsmanship movement, for example, insists on developers having a profession, not just jobs. Meanwhile, though, guess who else has jobs? Your boss who imposed that death march because they poorly negotiated a contract. Or your manager that can’t protect their team from bad decisions taken above. Or sales managers that mislead clients. Or how about the clients who have no idea what they want from the software but know exactly when they want it? They all have jobs. But shouldn’t they have a profession too, not just a job?

Building software today doesn’t just depend on craftspersons and their apprentices, all of them disciplined and responsible professionals who use sound technical practices like those of eXtreme Programming. It depends on a lot of other factors. And by other factors, I actually mean “other people”. You need everyone (first and foremost those in upper management) to understand that, in building software, you can’t make important decisions or plan things out without having the input of those who actually do the work. Or once you’ve started a project, you can’t just leave everything in the developers’ hands and miss collaborating or interacting with them on a permanent basis. You’re not acting appropriately if you just visit the developers once in a blue moon to make sure that everything is okay and to whip them if they are behind schedule. Everyone else besides developers needs to understand that they must be professional as well. These people can treat developers as professionals only if they, themselves, are familiar with the definition of “professionalism”.

Focusing only on developers and what they should do differently, it’s like trying to add a healthy ingredient into an unhealthy burger and, by only doing that, to somehow expect that it will influence the other layers of this junk food and, in the end, as a whole, everything to transform into something healthy.

The analogy with software development would be like saying that you bring in good technical practices and a new developer mindset with the premise that it will trigger a mechanism that propagates into the other layers of a dysfunctional company that makes bad software, and thus, create a transformation into a company that will all of a sudden start producing quality software.

But let’s be real. Developers are not in the best position to educate people from the rest of the company or to impose a better way of working on everyone else. They are too low in the food chain. We, developers, can behave professionally, and by doing that, try to spark a change towards professionalism in others, but if others don’t want to change, then we don’t really have many additional options available.

When the rest of these individuals - “that have a job” - make a decision or do something that risks causing factors that lead to crappy software being built, and they can’t be convinced with arguments, developers should say “no”. That’s what it means to be a professional, not just an employee with a job. To keep to a good standard and when that standard can’t be met, to have the courage to place your job on the line to do the right thing. Basically, the developers should impose their views on the company. You can handle a fight like this with people provided you have someone to reason with, but only up to a certain point. Most likely, it’s the company that imposes something on developers than the other way around. I said in the chapter about bad bosses, for example, what can happen when you go against your boss. So even this last stronghold from developers can end in failure. Not just because it’s too simplistic to say that you can throw your job out the window to do the right thing, as if a job was a pair of dirty socks that you can change without too much effort and without consequences for you and your family, but also because for upper management, developers are many times seen as just cogs in the machine. If you do the job you were hired for, people sometimes don’t even know you exist. And before being a professional, you are an employee who has to do what they are told. You were hired to do a job, not say “No” to it, and then suggest other alternatives you’d instead prefer. If you say “No”, they will replace you with someone who says “Yes”, as you do with a defective cog in the machine. And when that happens, you might no longer be able to talk about a profession, since you won’t even have a job.

So if there is nobody you can reason with - if there really isn’t - all this effort from developers to show others that there is a better way can fail. It’s not a 100% winning formula. It can be a losing battle. If you are a professional but people don’t acknowledge you or respect you as such, and they disregard your views, you can choose to stay and try to do what you can, or you can leave to another company, a company that shares your values. But if you take your professionalism and your pride in your work, and you take them somewhere else, this won’t solve the problem of crappy applications produced by the software industry. There will still be companies that make bad decisions (and let others bear the consequences), focus on the wrong activities, or employ bad people (in development or other roles), resulting in crappy software. And so the problem gets perpetuated. Unfortunately, to change people’s mindsets, there is no solution as prescriptive as “use these technical practices, apply these ways of working, etc”.

Developers can change how they behave and how they work, and improve on the nature of their relationship with others, but they can’t change the way other people behave or do their own work, especially if they don’t want to change. Sometimes you can influence them with your behavior, encouraging and helping them, but at the end of the day, it all depends on them. But developers have really no other choice but to struggle with this situation, while under constant pressure to meet deadlines and being busy fire fighting in various events. For software development to improve, someone must bring forth a change. And developers must be indeed the drivers of that change. They must be the ones to say, “Enough!”. Because who else? The sales manager who sold a PowerPoint presentation full of futuristic features? The CEO who promised the client that the software would be ready in six months without even consulting with the development team? The marketing people who don’t want to negotiate which features the development team can realistically deliver and insist on having everything within an impossible timeline? The obsessive boss who’s always complaining, “Why is it taking so long? Just get it done already!”? The Project Manager, who, instead of helping the team, only knows how to put more pressure on developers and impose overtime?

I have already said that this approach is not necessarily meant to succeed, not only because you can’t change people who don’t want to change, but also because it is simple for people to see such actions like Software Craftsmanship in the same way as the Agile movement or the implementation of Scrum: as something that only developers have to do. And you may end up similarly to all the lousy Scrum implementations out there where you change something in the development teams, but at the company level things remain the same as before. You somehow have to work on the whole system, not just on one layer (keeping on the junk food analogy: if you want healthy food, you need to change all the ingredients in the burger, not just one).

Initiatives like the Software Craftsmanship are very welcomed. Software Craftsmanship is trying to establish a standard of how developers should work. And it’s a good standard. The problem is that, in my opinion, this standard is insufficient because it tries to sell “craftsmanship” only to developers. We cannot forget all the other roles inside the company that are involved in building software. Companies that build crappy software might be dysfunctional in their entirety, not just inside the IT department. We can’t overlook this while we are trying to focus on technical practices and a new developer mindset in only one layer of the company. Yes, we need good developers, and the Software Craftsmanship movement is a good starting point, but more than that, we need some sort of “Corporate Craftsmanship” movement to change the values and behaviors of people at all levels within the company. Everyone must behave professionally, to be craftspersons, to understand the importance of having good people, to understand all decisions and bear the consequences of those decisions, everyone to be trustworthy, and everyone to collaborate with others, to take pride in their work without being pressured into doing something “crappy”, and to crave and be committed to producing something of quality. But it might be a while before that happens if you ask me. So, until all of the roles are filled by craftspersons, not just the part of the developer, until everyone gives up on the “us versus them” mentality and really puts an effort in collaboration, it’s still the developers that remain in the position of having to pick up the pieces.

In ending

And here we are in the final chapter of the book. Without going into too much detail, in broad strokes, I would like to recap some of the things I mentioned throughout the book, just to wrap things up.

When it comes to building quality software, it all starts with having good developers. Without developers, there is no software, plain and simple. So you have to pay proper attention to the hiring process in order to bring in good developers. Then you have to follow their progress, and keep only those people who are pulling their weight and are contributing to a healthy team and a good work environment. The hiring bar gets lower and lower as more and more companies need software, so don’t make the mistake of neglecting this hiring process. And don’t neglect the working environment either. You have to be mindful of what happens in the project and in the company as a whole, not just within the team or with each and every individual. Software is built by teams of people, but even the best of teams, with the best people, can have a difficult time doing their best inside an organization that isn’t supporting them.

Good developers must have a solid foundation of knowledge, must want to learn continuously to improve their skills, and to be, first of all, good problem solvers. It’s important to first solve the problem before writing the code. Then, in much of the work that a developer does, trade-offs will be involved, trade-offs that become more and more apparent when the developer ends up having more extensive responsibilities such as leading a team in the role of a Team Lead.

I then talked about software estimations and about all the problems that come up from them when people refuse to understand that an estimate is just an “educated guess” (based on knowledge and experience, yes, but still a guess, not a certainty). Or how the stubbornness to try to meet a deadline (often imposed and having nothing to do with reality) and focusing on recovering what seems like lost time when things don’t turn out as estimated, often causes inadequate software to be produced while, at the same time, negatively affecting the development team.

Another thing that affects software is “change”, which needs to be properly managed. Change is the only constant in software development, so it’s vital from the start to clearly know what you want to achieve, to understand what brings actual value, and define what a successful outcome means for the software you are building, so that you have a clear understanding on what to do with all the changes that you will encounter throughout the project. You constantly need to prioritize and plan, and when confronted with reality, with things not turning out as anticipated and with unforeseen situations occurring, to know how to adjust the path so that you still get to where you need to go. For this, you have to monitor what’s happening on the project regularly, to know where you are, to know if and where you deviated from your strategy, and know what actions are available to choose from, in order to get back on course.

Something else that cannot be neglected is the Business-IT divide and the fracture that exists between the different parties involved in developing software, all based on an “us versus them” attitude, in which there isn’t much room for trust, collaboration, and partnership. Things are then aggravated by having a bad boss calling the shots and the chaos they create when they run a software project when they are technically clueless and don’t understand the work of their subordinates, or by bad managers who choose to behave like bosses instead of acting as the voice of reason, or they set up cumbersome processes and procedures, with many meetings and many reports, or fail at the most important task of a Project Manager, that of maintaining communication at an adequate, correct, and transparent level. Of course, the subject of bad programmers and developers can’t be neglected either, who by lack of skills, poor attitude and big egos, or by being too enamored with technologies to care about anything else (sometimes not even the success of the project they are working on), can also cause problems that lead to bloated software and over-engineered implementations.

Towards the end, I also talked about outsourcing, and how focusing on cost reduction (similar to the fixation of hitting a deadline and recovering lost time) causes all kinds of problems that produce inadequate software or even complete failures as projects become the victim of cultural differences, misunderstandings, and lack of involvement. And I mentioned building software using Scrum and how people end up concentrating on a process they use to deliver half-backed features as fast as possible, losing sight of the crucial things that provide the ingredients of developing quality software, such as the Agile values and principles, the necessary change of mindset with regards to the way the work is carried out, the quality of developers and the technical practices they use. And it’s not just the quality of the developers that matters; everyone involved in software development must be skilled, behave professionally, and contribute to a healthy working environment, otherwise, everything comes out a mess, a mess that, when it happens, has to be (still) cleaned up by developers, ‘cause by whom else?

All these were examples of where and how quicksands can form. I tried to talk about many issues and explain them from several angles, but as I said early on in the book, that doesn’t mean that everything I said will happen or will occur in the same order or in the same way. The solutions I presented are also the result of my personal experiences and failures and are not necessarily the only ones, or the best, and it doesn’t mean they’re timeless. It’s what I found out worked best, given my situation. Your circumstances and your results might be different because they depend on the project, the domain, the company; they depend on you, on your experience, and on the people you work with. Remember, as a developer, you may be mostly dealing with technology, but at the end of the day, any company is made up primarily of people. And where there are people, there are problems. If you want to make things right, it doesn’t mean that others will fully agree with you or at least be interested in the same approach you’ll want to use. And since people can’t be programmed like computers and cannot be made to behave deterministically, you will always discover surprising ways in which software projects can go wrong.

Then you probably noticed in the book that I kept changing the persona when talking about one thing or another. I talked about others, sometimes about you, sometimes about others again. Since the beginning of the book, I mentioned that in terms of your job as a developer, there will be many things that “you” will have to do, but there will also be many other things that won’t be about “you”, but about “others”. Let’s go full circle now and mention that it’s not just about “others”, it’s also about “you”. Maybe “you” are the one I’m talking about in the book, and “you” are the one who’s pointing things towards quicksands and not just the one who has to pay attention to quicksands around them. I have been in this situation on several occasions, and to be honest, I will surely find myself in that position in the future also. Do you think that you or I will no longer be doing some of the things I wrote about in this book? We will. People find themselves many times over in such situations because software development is difficult, applications are increasingly complex, people are not always reasonable or professional, you work with lots of constraints and many unknowns, and so inevitably, somewhere, something’s got to give.

So you might ask, “what now”? According to this book and everything written in it, does it mean you’re doomed? Is everything destined for failure? No! Certainly not. Most books are not like this that you’ve just read. Most books often focus on the positives; they address the ideal cases or standard ways things should work or how things should be. “If everyone were a certain way, if everyone did this or that, if we all followed ten steps, seven principles, or five ideas, then we would all be healthy, rich, and happy, we would only have successes in life, and all the software would be bugs free”. But that’s not how things can turn out in reality. In an ideal company, everyone is a reasonable person, people trust each other, they are professionals and work together to make things happen. In the real world, though, problems and challenges are inevitable, with most of them being related to people. We are all complex creatures; we have emotions, we have problems, we have obligations, some are inexperienced, and in over their heads, etc.; nobody is perfect. Most people don’t want to do bad things on purpose, and almost all are usually well-intentioned. Just like with bugs, you don’t want to do them, but because there are so many things happening, bugs are inevitably showing up. It just happens. You have to keep so many things in balance that you end up dropping some of them on the floor. The ideal developer, manager, boss, Scrum Master, tester, or colleague doesn’t exist. The perfect software project doesn’t exist either. So, when things go into the weeds, most books don’t talk about what you could do to get back on the right path once you deviate from it.

There are many positive things in the IT industry. Software development is challenging, lots of fun, and there is always something new to learn or discover. I didn’t talk much about positive things because this book is different. This book is about the “quicksands of software development”. But having said that, realize that quicksands are here and there, not everywhere. What I tried to do is point out that when you do software development, just like when you go to the beach, you can’t only think about the landscape, or how blue the sky is, how warm the sun, about the golden sand, the seagulls, or the white foamy waves, etc., to be aware that there might also be quicksands in some areas. This book is about making you aware of some of the dangers, to know where to look for them, and to avoid them, so you can continue to enjoy your trip to the beach without your beautiful stroll turning into an ugly memory. If there are quicksands, it doesn’t mean you should no longer go to the beach. It just means you have to be more careful and be more prepared.

So consider this book a point of departure. Keep in mind the quicksand examples I presented, be aware of them, learn more about them, and try to avoid them. You will probably encounter further types also. For example, I focused on things related to software projects or tangent to software development; I haven’t talked much about things you’ll find in all companies and all jobs like heavy bureaucracy or bad office politics. You’ll need to know about such things too at some point. I discovered many of them by stepping in quicksand and struggling to get out; of others, I already knew from what information I managed to accumulate on my own, or being passed down from more experienced developers I’ve worked with. I’m confident that I’ve managed to stir up some curiosity so that you do some extra research on the things that drew your attention. Don’t neglect what’s around you, pay attention to your environment and the things you encounter, and try to figure out why things are the way they are, identify unpleasant situations and understand them better before they get worse. I hope you found this book useful in providing you with some information on how to do that, so you recognize the warning signs and avoid stepping directly into the quicksands and end up feeling entrapped or frustrated. Thanks for reading. And good luck!
